The authors ask how students implement cognitive and metacognitive processes, how those processes differ by performance, and how students describe their own strategies in stimulated recall interviews.

The approach combines fine-grained digital trace data from a Moodle-based environment with semi-structured stimulated recall interviews. Fifty 13-year-old students from two Finnish secondary schools and five seventh-grade classes participated; after screening for low engagement, 42 students were included in the main analyses, and 17 students completed interviews. The learning environment included a planner, timer, search tool, writing tool, and annotation function, and students wrote a 200–300-word essay in 45 minutes on artificial intelligence and the school of the future.

Results showed that writing dominated the task time, but successful students differed from less successful peers in the way they organized SRL processes: they re-read more, made more transitions among processes, and exhibited higher transitivity in their process networks, suggesting more cyclical and coordinated regulation. Interview data indicated that high performers monitored their writing more actively against task requirements and used re-reading and planning in more explicit, strategic ways. The paper concludes that combining trace-based process analysis with qualitative recall provides richer insight into how young students regulate learning in digital writing tasks and suggests implications for designing personalized supports and teacher education.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines writing performance in a computer-based multi-source essay task. High-performing students scored substantially higher on the essay outcome than low-performing students, and their SRL process patterns—especially re-reading and coordinated transitions among reading, writing, and monitoring—were associated with stronger written products.
finding.measure: Essay scores on a rubric-based writing task
finding.study_size: n=42 (main analysis); high/low groups n=14 each
finding.effect_size: d=5.63 for the high-vs-low essay score grouping criterion; d=0.98 for re-reading differences; d=0.97 for number of edges; d=0.93 for transitivity
finding.std_deviation: essay SD not_reported; process SDs reported in paper but not required here

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies self-regulated learning as enacted behavior during the task, including orientation, planning, monitoring, evaluation, and time management within a constrained 45-minute setting. High-performing students showed more adaptive monitoring and more cyclical SRL patterns, indicating stronger self-regulation during task performance.
finding.measure: Digital trace-derived SRL process durations, transitions, and interview-coded self-reported strategies
finding.effect_size: d=0.98 (re-reading), d=0.97 (number of edges), d=0.93 (transitivity), d=0.77 (orientation→writing transition)
finding.std_deviation: reported in paper for some variables; not_reported here

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on metacognition and strategic regulation, especially monitoring, planning, and evaluation while composing from multiple sources. High-performing students showed higher metacognitive strategy knowledge and more explicit monitoring of essay quality against task standards, consistent with stronger metacognitive control and strategic adaptation.
finding.measure: Metacognitive strategy knowledge test; trace-based metacognitive processes; stimulated recall interview codes
finding.study_size: n=42; metacognitive test n=26-28 depending on comparison; interviews n=17
finding.effect_size: d=0.90 for metacognitive strategy knowledge; d=0.93 for transitivity; d=0.95 for write→re-read transition
finding.std_deviation: metacognitive strategy knowledge SDs reported in paper but not required here

finding.finding_summary: Beyond generic literacy, the content of the writing task focused on AI and the school of the future, so the paper also substantively examines students’ domain learning in this topic area. Post-task domain knowledge was higher for high-performing students than low-performing students, suggesting better topic-specific learning alongside stronger SRL.
finding.measure: Domain knowledge test on artificial intelligence and school of the future

paper_profiles.title: Problematising L2 listening pedagogy: The potential of process-based listening strategy instruction in the L2 classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This doctoral thesis examines the long-standing problem of how listening is taught in second-language classrooms, arguing that common ‘listen, answer, check’ routines emphasize product outcomes rather than the processes and strategies learners need to become competent listeners. The study asks whether a process-oriented form of listening strategy instruction (LSI) can serve as a more effective and pedagogically sound alternative in an EFL university context.

The intervention was implemented as a qualitative action-research project over three consecutive semesters (Fall 2010, Spring 2011, Fall 2011) in the Upper Intermediate English course at Ritsumeikan Asia Pacific University in Japan. Six classes and 121 learners participated, with two teachers (the author and a co-teacher) using the same LSI approach and materials. The program integrated 13 listening strategies into a 15-week course through a cycle of introduction/awareness raising, practice, review, and extension, while data were collected through questionnaires, interviews, classroom observations, pre/post tests, and a research journal.

The thesis concludes that learners and teachers generally viewed LSI positively and that the iterative action-research design helped refine the intervention across phases. It reports that the approach increased attention to listening processes, strategy use, and the possibility of transferring strategies to new listening tasks, although some parts of the pedagogy needed further refinement. The study also identifies contextual factors shaping implementation, including the Japanese university EFL setting, class size, teacher experience, the use of both traditional and computer-assisted classrooms, and the importance of aligning strategy instruction with existing course materials and institutional constraints.

finding.finding_summary: The thesis reports consistent positive perceptions of listening strategy instruction (LSI) from both learners and teachers across three action-research phases, and indicates that students reported perceived listening improvement and better strategy awareness. However, the evidence is largely qualitative and based on perceptions, with limited quantitative support from pre/post-semester test scores rather than a clearly reported controlled effect.
finding.measure: Student and teacher perceptions of listening strategy instruction; pre/post-semester listening test scores; reported listening strategy recall and projected strategy use

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the thesis is that process-based LSI promotes listening-related strategy use, metacognitive awareness, and transfer of generalizable listening processes to new listening events. Students reported recalling strategies, projecting future use, and benefiting from teacher modeling and explanations, suggesting development in self-monitoring and metacognitive engagement rather than only immediate listening performance.
finding.measure: Listening strategy recall; projected future strategy use; interview and questionnaire reports on strategy awareness and transfer

finding.finding_summary: The intervention produced practical implementation principles for planning and delivering LSI in university EFL classes, including a repeatable teaching cycle and iterative refinements based on classroom data. The thesis suggests the approach can make listening instruction more purposeful than the prior ‘listen, answer, check’ routine, but it does not provide direct workload or time-efficiency metrics.
finding.measure: Action-research reflections on feasibility, sustainability, and classroom implementation of LSI

paper_profiles.title: A Critical Review of Research on Student Self-Assessment
paper_profiles.population: K-20 students (with emphasis on K-12 and undergraduate/postsecondary contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a critical review of research on student self-assessment, with a focus on studies published largely between 2013 and 2018. The paper asks how self-assessment should be defined and operationalized in educational settings, distinguishing formative self-assessment from summative self-assessment and arguing that self-assessment is most useful when it functions as feedback that can guide revision, strategy change, and deeper learning.

The review synthesizes 76 empirical studies, including two meta-analyses, and organizes the literature around consistency with external judgments, student perceptions, achievement, and self-regulated learning. The reviewed studies span K-20 contexts and multiple subjects, with many classroom-based interventions in writing, science, mathematics, language learning, and vocational education. The author emphasizes that formative, criteria-referenced self-assessment supported by rubrics, scripts, modeling, and feedback is associated with better learning outcomes and stronger self-regulated learning, whereas summative self-assessment is more often inconsistent with external evaluations.

The paper’s main conclusion is that the field should shift away from an overemphasis on whether students can accurately self-rate and toward understanding the cognitive, affective, and pedagogical mechanisms through which self-assessment supports learning. It argues that self-assessment works best when students are given clear criteria, opportunities to revise, and instruction in how to use self-generated feedback to improve performance.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports consistent positive effects of formative self-assessment on writing outcomes. Across 20 non-meta-analytic studies plus a meta-analysis of 10 studies, students who used self-assessment with revision supports produced better writing; the Graham et al. meta-analysis reported an average weighted effect size of 0.62 on writing quality.
finding.measure: Writing quality / written assignment scores

finding.finding_summary: The review includes studies in which self-assessment supported speaking English and related language-learning outcomes, and it characterizes these studies as generally showing better achievement for treatment groups than comparison groups. However, specific pooled effects for speaking/listening outcomes are not reported in the review text.
finding.measure: English speaking / language-learning performance

finding.finding_summary: The review describes several studies in mathematics-related contexts, including math word problems and dart-throwing as a self-regulation task analog, and states that formative self-assessment was associated with stronger performance. Specific math effect sizes are not reported in the review text, but the direction of results is positive overall.
finding.measure: Math word problems / performance on task-based outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review cites science-related self-assessment studies, including sixth-grade science report self-evaluation and studies using genetics tasks, and reports positive achievement-related patterns for formative self-assessment. No study-level effect size for science outcomes is provided in the review text.
finding.measure: Science reports / genetics task performance

finding.finding_summary: Across a wide variety of non-literacy subjects, the review says treatment groups outperformed comparison/control groups on outcomes ranging from dart-throwing and map-making to vocational tasks and exam performance. The achievement literature reviewed was overwhelmingly positive for formative self-assessment, with two meta-analyses also yielding positive average effects.
finding.measure: Mixed academic performance outcomes across disciplines (e.g., map-making, vocational tasks, exams)
finding.study_size: 25 achievement studies in the review; 2 meta-analyses
finding.effect_size: g=0.34 (self-grading on subsequent tests); other studies not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that formative self-assessment is associated with improvements in self-regulated learning, motivation-related beliefs, and student perceptions of usefulness. It reports that students using rubrics/scripts were more self-regulated than controls, with very small to moderate effect sizes (η2=0.06–0.42), and that self-evaluative standards improved self-efficacy, attributions, and self-satisfaction in one study.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning questionnaires, motivational beliefs, student perceptions
finding.study_size: 12 SRL studies; one cited study n=70

finding.finding_summary: This is a central focus of the review, especially metacognition and self-regulated learning. The paper concludes that self-assessment supports goal-setting, self-monitoring, reflection, and task selection, and that rubric-referenced self-assessment was associated with all three SRL phases (forethought, performance, reflection).
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning, metacognition, task selection, think-alouds, self-report questionnaires

paper_profiles.title: Selangkah Lebih Dekat Bersama Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses formative assessment as an approach to improving learning quality, contrasting it with summative assessment that is often used mainly for grading. The authors frame formative assessment as a process-oriented evaluation that helps teachers collect evidence of student learning so they can adjust instruction, provide feedback, and better support student achievement.

The study was conducted in English Education programs at two private higher-education institutions in Ponorogo, Indonesia: Muhammadiyah University of Ponorogo and STKIP PGRI Ponorogo. Using a qualitative design with observation and questionnaires, the authors describe how lecturers implement formative assessment in practice, especially through one-to-one assessment, small-group assessment, and larger-group/end-of-course feedback.

The main conclusion is descriptive rather than comparative: lecturers at both institutions had already used formative assessment, though not always consistently or in ways that fully incorporated the results into instruction. The paper argues that formative assessment helps lecturers understand student comprehension, identify weaknesses, and make instructional adjustments, but it does not report causal evidence or quantified effects on student learning outcomes relative to business-as-usual or summative-only instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes formative assessment as a way for lecturers to understand student comprehension, identify where instruction needs repair, and decide whether to change teaching strategies. In this qualitative study, lecturers reported using one-to-one, small-group, and larger-group assessment to support feedback and instructional adjustment, but no quantitative workload or productivity outcomes were reported.
finding.measure: Lecturer-reported use of formative assessment practices; instructional adjustment and feedback processes

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment helps monitor student understanding and support achievement in English language courses, but it does not provide direct outcome data such as test scores or proficiency gains. The findings are based on qualitative descriptions from lecturers about using formative assessment to check whether students have met learning objectives.
finding.measure: Student understanding/achievement as described by lecturers

paper_profiles.title: Differentiated Instruction in Secondary Education: A Systematic Review of Research Evidence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review examines the empirical evidence on within-class differentiated instruction in secondary education, focusing on whether adapting content, process, product, learning environment, or learning time improves student academic achievement. The authors frame differentiated instruction as planned classroom adaptations based on assessment of students’ readiness, prior knowledge, interests, or learning profiles, and they explicitly exclude between-class tracking/streaming and fully computerized adaptive programs.

Using a best-evidence synthesis of studies published from 2006 to 2016, the review identified 12 unique empirical studies (14 papers) conducted in mainstream secondary settings. The included studies covered a range of differentiation approaches, including generic teacher training in adaptive teaching, ability grouping/tiering, individualized reading conferences, mastery-learning-like remediation, and differentiated problem-based or project-based instruction across subjects such as mathematics, science, reading, and prevention education. Most studies were quasi-experimental; one was a survey study. Sample sizes ranged from small to large, and the studies were conducted in the United States, Europe, Taiwan, and Africa.

Overall, the review concludes that differentiated instruction shows small-to-moderate positive effects on student achievement, with effect sizes across studies ranging roughly from d = +0.509 to +0.741 when an outlier is omitted. However, the evidence base is limited and heterogeneous, and the authors caution that stronger conclusions cannot yet be drawn about which specific forms of differentiation work best, for whom, and under what conditions. The paper also notes that some subgroup patterns appear in prior literature (e.g., low-achieving students may benefit from convergent approaches such as mastery learning), but the secondary-education evidence remains too sparse for firm conclusions.

finding.finding_summary: Across several included studies in secondary mathematics, differentiated instruction generally produced positive achievement effects relative to business-as-usual instruction. Reported effects included a very large researcher-made mathematics test gain in one project-based differentiation study (e.g., combined d = +4.504 for grades 6-7 in Altintas and Özdemir) and smaller but still positive effects in other math studies (e.g., d = +1.085 in Bal; d = +0.539 overall in Bikić et al.; d = +0.376 overall in Bhagat et al., though not statistically significant).
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement tests / algebra tests / trigonometry tests (mostly researcher-made)
finding.study_size: multiple studies; individual studies ranged from n=57 to n=168 and larger nested samples
finding.effect_size: varied across studies; examples include d=+4.504, d=+1.085, d=+0.539, d=+0.376
finding.confidence_interval: varied by study; examples include [3.879 to 5.130], [0.479 to 1.692], [0.228 to 0.851], [−0.064 to 0.815]

finding.finding_summary: The review includes science-focused differentiation studies that generally favored the treatment over business-as-usual instruction. For example, Mastropieri et al. reported positive effects on science achievement for inclusive eighth-grade classes using tiered materials and peer tutoring (combined d = +0.386), with gains on both unit tests and a high-stakes end-of-year test. Another adaptive-teaching study in science also showed a small positive effect (d = +0.133, combined sample) though it was not statistically significant.
finding.measure: Science achievement tests / unit tests / high-stakes end-of-year science test
finding.study_size: multiple studies; e.g., n=213 in Mastropieri et al. and n=623 in the adaptive-teaching study
finding.effect_size: varied across studies; examples include d=+0.386 and d=+0.133
finding.confidence_interval: varied by study; examples include [0.115 to 0.657] and not_reported for the combined adaptive-teaching result in the text excerpt

finding.finding_summary: Differentiated reading instruction showed mostly small positive effects in the included middle-school study. In Little et al. (2014), the individualized reading approach (self-selected books plus individualized conferences) produced near-zero to small positive effects on reading comprehension and fluency across sites, with the largest site-level effect at South MS (combined d = +0.266, p<.05) and other sites near zero or small positive values (e.g., d = +0.030, +0.007, +0.135).
finding.measure: Reading comprehension and reading fluency tests
finding.study_size: n=~3,000 across groups in Little et al. (control and treatment samples varied by test)
finding.effect_size: site-level effects ranged from d=+0.007 to d=+0.266; overall effect small

finding.finding_summary: One included differentiated-instruction study targeted alcohol, tobacco, and other drug (ATOD) prevention rather than a traditional school subject. The flipped, learning-style-informed intervention produced a large positive effect on the researcher-made ATOD survey (d = +1.374), compared with business-as-usual prevention instruction.
finding.measure: Alcohol, tobacco, and other drug (ATOD) survey / prevention knowledge outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review discusses motivation and interest as part of the rationale for differentiation, and several included interventions explicitly used student interest or learning profiles to tailor instruction. However, the review’s extracted quantitative outcomes are academic achievement measures rather than direct social-emotional measures, so evidence for this category is indirect. Where reported, the differentiated approaches were designed to better engage students and align with their interests or learning styles, which the authors suggest may support learning, but no stand-alone social-emotional effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student interest / learning profile alignment (indirect; not a direct outcome measure in the extracted studies)

paper_profiles.title: Classroom assessment and pedagogy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article argues that classroom assessment should be understood as an integral part of pedagogy rather than as a separate technical add-on. Black and Wiliam review theory and prior research to propose a broader model of pedagogy in which formative assessment, dialogue, planning, and summative assessment are linked through teachers’ instructional decision-making and through the inferences drawn from evidence of student work.

The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it synthesizes literature on pedagogy, formative assessment, classroom dialogue, feedback, peer assessment, and teacher-made summative assessment. The authors emphasize that effective instruction depends on eliciting evidence from all students, using that evidence responsively, and keeping learning on track through contingent interaction, comment-focused feedback, and peer/self-assessment.

A central conclusion is that formative and summative purposes should not be treated as sharply separate. The authors argue that well-designed summative assessment can support learning, but that high-stakes external testing can distort instruction by encouraging teaching to the test and narrowing the curriculum. They also argue that teachers should have an active role in summative assessment, provided that reliability, comparability, moderation, and training are addressed.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that assessment systems can either support or undermine instructional aims depending on how accountability is structured. Drawing on prior research and policy examples, the authors conclude that high-stakes external testing can narrow teaching and create negative washback, whereas integrated formative-summative systems and teacher involvement in summative assessment can better align assessment with learning goals.
finding.measure: Policy and system-level analysis of assessment design, accountability, validity, and curriculum effects

finding.finding_summary: The article contends that teacher-led moderation, portfolio use, and assessment embedded in classroom work can improve the usefulness and feasibility of summative assessment within schools, although they may require additional training and support. It reports that moderation and standardisation processes in the KOSAP project were viewed by teachers as valuable for rigour, consistency, and confidence, but no quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, moderation/standardisation processes, and feasibility of internal assessment systems

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes evidence that formative assessment practices support dialogue, metacognition, self-regulation, collaboration, and critical thinking. It does not report a new quantitative effect size in this article, but argues from prior studies that interactive dialogue, peer assessment, and feedback-oriented assessment help students develop these durable skills and improve learning processes.
finding.measure: Dialogue, metacognition, collaboration, peer/self-assessment, and classroom interaction quality

finding.finding_summary: The authors discuss formative assessment as supporting motivation, engagement, and learner agency by emphasizing feedback that moves learning forward rather than grades alone. They argue that comment-based feedback, peer assessment, and responsive classroom dialogue can help students see ability as improvable and maintain engagement, but the paper provides no direct study-level quantitative estimate.
finding.measure: Student motivation, engagement, agency, and response to feedback in classroom settings

paper_profiles.title: Higher education assessment practice in the era of generative AI tools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools such as ChatGPT-4 and Google Bard/Gemini perform on assessment tasks in higher education, with a particular focus on whether these tools can demonstrate the kinds of knowledge and skills that assessments are intended to measure. The authors motivate the study by arguing that GenAI creates both opportunities and risks for assessment practice, including support for teaching and learning as well as threats to academic integrity and authentic assessment.

To investigate this issue, the authors created three master’s-level case-study assessments drawn from data analytics, data science, and construction management. They asked ChatGPT-4 and Bard to solve the tasks and then manually graded the AI-generated outputs using criterion-referenced assessment and a standard letter-grade scale. The evaluation focused on qualities such as subject knowledge, problem solving, analytical reasoning, critical thinking, accuracy, discussion, and presentation.

The paper concludes that both systems can produce strong, coherent responses in disciplines where large amounts of public training material and online resources exist, especially data analytics and data science, but they struggle more with complex, project-based construction management tasks. The authors argue that GenAI can support learning and feedback when used appropriately, but it can also limit learning and employability skills when used unethically. They recommend redesigning assessments for the GenAI era, combining plagiarism detection with AI-content detection and human review, and using more authentic, contextualized, reflective, and presentation-based assessment formats.

finding.finding_summary: Across three master’s-level assessment case studies (two in data analytics/data science and one in construction management), ChatGPT-4 and Bard demonstrated durable skills such as problem-solving, analytical reasoning, and some critical-thinking/presentation ability, but performance varied by discipline. The paper reports no quantitative effect sizes; instead, it qualitatively compares the AI outputs and notes that both tools handled some tasks well while struggling on more complex, project-based criteria, especially in construction management.
finding.measure: Manual rubric-based evaluation of AI-generated assessment solutions for problem-solving, analysis, critical thinking, discussion, and presentation
finding.study_size: n=3 assessment case studies (2 AI tools evaluated across 3 tasks)

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-Learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how formative assessment can be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard Learning System, in a university setting. The authors argue that frequent low-stakes assessments with immediate, detailed feedback can help students learn continuously across the semester rather than only preparing for end-of-term exams.

The intervention described is a series of weekly or fortnightly online tests on Blackboard, using question types such as multiple choice, true/false, matching, fill-in-the-blank, and essay items. The paper reports on students’ perceptions of continuous assessment and the Blackboard test option using a questionnaire administered to university students. Reliability of the survey scales is reported (alpha = 0.67 and 0.81), and the authors analyze differences across Business, Engineering, and IT streams, finding statistically significant differences in views toward continuous assessment and the Blackboard test option.

Overall, the paper concludes that students generally support formative assessment delivered through Blackboard because it provides immediate feedback, breaks learning into smaller topic-based assessments, and helps students monitor strengths and weaknesses. Students in Engineering appeared more enthusiastic than Business and IT students. The paper is largely descriptive and perception-based; it does not report a controlled comparison of learning outcomes or achievement gains, though it argues that formative assessment may improve summative grades and be especially helpful for lower achievers.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that the Blackboard-based formative assessments helped them reflect on mistakes, identify strengths and weaknesses, and keep track of whether they were on course. The paper frames these effects as improved metacognition and self-monitoring, but it reports perceptions rather than direct performance gains.
finding.measure: Student perception survey on feedback usefulness, self-monitoring, and checking progress

finding.finding_summary: Students generally supported frequent internal assessments and valued the immediacy of feedback and the convenience/flexibility of online tests. The paper suggests these features reduce delay in learning and help sustain engagement with the subject across the semester, although some students also reported stress from too many tests.
finding.measure: Student perception survey and open-ended responses about continuous assessment and online testing

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on general academic learning in university subject courses and reports that students believed frequent small-topic assessments with immediate feedback would support learning and ultimately improve summative semester examination performance. No direct achievement outcome was tested, so the finding is based on student perceptions rather than measured grades.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of learning and expected exam preparation benefits

paper_profiles.title: Impact of Social Relationships on Peer Assessment in E-Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether pre-existing social relationships between students affect the quality and perceived fairness of peer assessment in an online higher-education course. The authors are motivated by prior work showing that peer assessment can be accurate and scalable, but may be biased by friendship or dislike among students, especially in e-learning settings where students may know each other from prior coursework.

To study this, the authors built a Moodle plugin (PeerForum) for a master’s-level Multimedia Content Production course at the University of Lisbon and used it in a fully remote semester. Students nominated peers they liked most and least, completed rubric-based training before grading, and then assessed one another’s forum submissions; each post received five peer assessments, with reviewer assignment partially tailored by relationship status. The study analyzed peer-grade reliability, agreement with instructor grades, and differences in grading by relationship type, and also collected end-of-course survey responses about peer assessment perceptions.

The results suggest that peer assessment was reasonably reliable and accurate when at least three peer assessments were collected per post, with peer grades slightly higher than professor ratings overall. Relationship bias was detectable: students who liked an author tended to grade slightly higher and students who disliked an author slightly lower, but these differences were small and had little effect on the final aggregate peer grade. Survey data indicated that students generally viewed peer assessment as useful and fair, and most did not believe their relationships strongly affected the grades they gave or received. The authors conclude that, in this context, peer assessment can replace traditional evaluation when it is low-stakes and supported by rubrics and sufficient peer ratings.

finding.finding_summary: Peer assessment reduced reliance on instructor-only grading by allowing students to evaluate one another’s work in a Moodle-based workflow, and the authors argue this makes the process scalable for e-learning contexts. The paper does not report a formal efficiency effect size, but it concludes the system can replace traditional evaluation with manageable instructor oversight when at least three peer assessments are used.
finding.measure: Peer assessment workflow feasibility and scalability; instructor workload implications
finding.study_size: n=64 analyzed students; 2681 peer assessments; 588 posts with at least three peer assessments

finding.finding_summary: Students reported improved perceptions of peer assessment usefulness and fairness after the course, and most disagreed that relationships strongly influenced the feedback they gave or received. End-of-course survey responses showed 54.7% agreed peer assessment was helpful after the course (up from 43.4% before), and 52.8% agreed it was fair.
finding.measure: Likert-scale questionnaire on perceived usefulness, fairness, difficulty, and relationship influence
finding.study_size: n=53 survey respondents who had peer-graded at least one post

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds peer assessment supports collaboration and feedback-related practices, with students reporting that grading peers helped them learn the material, improve their own work, and stay engaged with course activities. Students’ open-ended comments emphasized that peer grading helped them give feedback, understand expectations, and collaborate with colleagues.
finding.measure: Self-reported engagement, collaboration, and learning benefits from peer assessment
finding.study_size: n=53 survey respondents; qualitative comments from open text box

paper_profiles.title: Assessment Formats and Student Learning Performance: What is the Relation?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether different assessment formats are associated with student learning performance in an undergraduate computer networking course. The authors argue that prior work on assessment and learning often lacks demographic detail, comparable course structures, or sufficient sample size, and they aim to address these issues by comparing sections with different final-exam formats while keeping content, assignments, and grading rubrics largely consistent.

The study was conducted in four sections of IT 341 at George Mason University in Fall 2016: three face-to-face sections and one distance-learning section, with 115 undergraduate students total. All sections used the same syllabus and similar home/lab assignments, but the final exams differed by section: one used essays only, one used MCQs plus essays, one used MCQs plus essays plus fill-in-the-blank and numerical problem items, and one used only MCQs plus a numerical problem. The analysis relied on Pearson correlations between assessment components and final course grades, along with descriptive comparisons across sections.

The authors conclude that assessment format is related to course performance and that more diverse, combined assessment formats are associated with better outcomes than a single-format exam. In particular, the section with the most varied final exam format had the highest median final score, while the essay-only section performed worst. The paper also reports that essay scores were the strongest predictor of the final exam score among the item types examined, though the overall interpretation is based on correlations rather than causal estimates. Because the design is correlational and confined to one undergraduate course, the findings should be read as suggestive rather than causal evidence.

finding.finding_summary: Across 115 undergraduate students in four sections of IT 341, assessment format was associated with course performance, but the pattern varied by item type and section. The section using a combined final exam format (MCQ, essay, fill-in-the-blank, and numerical problem) had the highest median final score, while the essay-only section had the lowest; however, essay questions were also the strongest predictor of final exam score (r=0.920, p=2.2e-16), ahead of MCQs (r=0.869), fill-in-the-blank (r=0.830), and numerical problems (r=0.430).
finding.measure: Final course grades and final exam scores by exam format; Pearson correlations between question types and final scores
finding.std_deviation: Section SDs reported for final grades: 11.79, 9.31, 18.06, 18.23

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames assessment formats as influencing students' ability to demonstrate knowledge, problem solve, and respond to different question types, which is most closely aligned with durable skills such as problem solving and higher-order reasoning. The strongest section performance was observed when multiple assessment formats were combined, suggesting students may better show competence when assessments allow varied ways to demonstrate understanding.
finding.measure: Course performance across mixed assessment formats; correlations of item types with final exam score

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Three Pivotal Concepts in K-12 Science State Standards and Maps of Conceptual Growth to Research in Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how three foundational physics concepts—Newton’s laws, conservation of energy, and geometrical optics—appear in K-12 science standards and why they are especially important for science learning. The authors compare concept maps from Project 2061 with science standards from four U.S. states (California, Colorado, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin) to identify concepts that are both widely represented in standards and central to later science understanding.

The paper then draws on physics education research to explain why these concepts are difficult for students to learn. For Newton’s laws and conservation of energy, the authors synthesize prior studies and provide multiple examples of common misconceptions, performance on conceptual inventories, and classroom difficulties. They also describe instructional approaches that have shown some success, such as prediction-based interactive demonstrations and research-based explorations that confront misconceptions directly.

The paper is not an intervention study and does not compare formative assessment against business-as-usual or summative-only instruction. Instead, it is a conceptual and standards-based synthesis aimed at helping teachers, teacher educators, and curriculum developers focus instruction on a smaller set of pivotal scientific ideas that are foundational, persistent, and difficult for students to master.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Newton’s laws and conservation of energy are foundational scientific concepts but are notoriously difficult for K-12 and introductory college students to learn. It summarizes multiple prior studies showing persistent misconceptions on conceptual instruments such as the Force Concept Inventory and energy-concept questions; for example, a majority of students in traditional instruction did not develop Newtonian views of force and motion, and only 36% answered one conservation-of-energy item correctly even after instruction.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding of force and motion and conservation of energy; performance on conceptual inventories and research-based multiple-choice items

paper_profiles.title: Effects of Popular Science Writing Instruction on General Education Student Attitudes Towards Science: A Case Study in Astronomy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a writing-intensive popular science / science journalism course can improve non-STEM undergraduates’ attitudes toward science and their confidence in engaging with science-related tasks. The authors focus on a general education astronomy seminar that combined reading and writing about science, scaffolded popular science article production, weekly writing journals, and in-class activities about audience, genre, and communication.

The study population was first-year undergraduates at a large public U.S. university, specifically students in a year-long GE science sequence who then took a final-quarter seminar on astrobiology and science journalism. The course was designed for non-STEM majors and used pre/post surveys, open-ended written responses, and a small number of interviews to examine changes in interest, perceived relevance and benefits of science, perceptions of scientists, and confidence in science-related abilities.

The main conclusion is that the course had its clearest effects on students’ perceived ability to engage with science: students reported greater comfort reading scientific papers, greater confidence explaining science concepts, and greater confidence writing about a new scientific discovery. Students also reported that writing helped them understand science more deeply, connect science to humanities interests, and see science as more accessible, communicative, and less rigid than they had previously thought. Changes in interest and general perceived benefits of science were smaller, and the quantitative survey results were descriptive rather than statistically significant.

finding.finding_summary: The writing-intensive course was associated with improved science-related literacy skills, especially the ability to write about a new scientific discovery and to translate technical science for a lay audience. Students reported that writing forced them to understand the material more deeply and better grasp audience, genre, and accessibility; qualitative coding showed clearer post-course confidence in writing tasks (e.g., 9 students more confident about writing about a new scientific discovery).
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses and interviews about writing about a new scientific discovery; weekly writing journals and popular science writing tasks
finding.study_size: n=19 (2022 survey respondents); also n=11 from 2021 evaluations and n=5 interviews

finding.finding_summary: Students reported increased confidence in explaining science concepts to others, suggesting improved spoken/explanatory communication related to science. In the coded pre/post responses, 9 students became more confident in explaining science, while 2 remained neutral and 2 were already confident, and interview data suggested that explaining ideas helped them clarify their own understanding.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey item on explaining science concepts to others; interviews

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that writing about science improved their understanding of scientific ideas, how science works, and how to evaluate science news and primary literature. The study’s qualitative evidence indicates that reading and writing tasks helped students better understand scientific processes, assess reliability, and connect evidence into coherent explanations; quantitative descriptive statistics also suggested increased interest and relevance, though not significant at p<0.05.
finding.measure: Pre/post open-ended survey responses and interviews about reading scientific papers, reading science news, and understanding the scientific process

finding.finding_summary: The course changed students’ views of science journalism and the role of science communication, an outcome outside literacy/fluent speaking but central to the course content. Students reported a better understanding of how science is portrayed to the public and of the media landscape around science, including the distinction between research articles and popular science writing and the importance of accessibility.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses and interviews about science journalism and portrayals of science

finding.finding_summary: The strongest and most consistent change was in students’ confidence, comfort, and willingness to engage with science. Students reported moving from feeling overwhelmed or intimidated by scientific writing toward feeling comfortable, challenged, and even excited; 8/14 improved in reading science news, 9/15 improved in reading research articles, and 9 became more confident explaining science, indicating increased self-efficacy and engagement.
finding.measure: Matched pre/post open-ended survey coding; descriptive statistics from ASSA survey items; interviews

finding.finding_summary: The intervention appeared to strengthen transferable skills such as critical thinking, synthesis, and metacognition. Students said writing about science forced them to understand material well enough to explain it, helped them synthesize evidence, and broadened their view of science by connecting it with ethics, communication, and humanities-based ways of thinking.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses and interviews about how writing about science impacted learning and what students took away from the course

finding.finding_summary: Students left with broader beliefs about who can participate in science and how science connects to public communication, outreach, and citizenship. Interview and survey responses suggested increased recognition of non-research pathways into science and stronger appreciation of science as accessible to general-education students, but the study does not test institutional change directly.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses and interviews about views of scientists, science as a field, and engagement with science beyond the course

paper_profiles.title: Closing the Gap between Teaching and Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual/position piece arguing that assessment should be integrated with instruction rather than treated as an end-of-course summative exercise. It frames evidence-based teaching as a cycle in which instructors clarify learning goals, identify students’ initial knowledge, design instruction to build on that prior knowledge, and use assessment data to provide feedback to both students and instructors.

The central approach advocated is formative assessment embedded throughout instruction: think-pair-share, clicker questions, tutorials with pre- and post-tests, collaborative problem solving, minute papers, concept maps, and other low-stakes tasks. These activities are presented as mechanisms for helping students understand course goals, receive timely feedback, stay engaged, and improve their understanding before the course ends.

The paper draws primarily on physics education research and discusses assessment in introductory and advanced university science courses, especially physics, chemistry, biology, and mathematics. It does not report a new empirical study or comparative effect estimate; instead, it synthesizes prior work and argues that formative assessment can improve learning and help instructors refine instruction. The paper also notes that assessment should align with explicit, measurable learning goals and students’ initial knowledge, but it does not provide subgroup analyses by grade, subject, or baseline achievement from a new dataset.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment embedded throughout instruction should improve students’ conceptual understanding and scientific reasoning by giving repeated feedback aligned to learning goals. However, it does not present original effect estimates; the claims are supported by cited prior research and examples from physics education research rather than a new comparative study.
finding.measure: conceptual understanding assessments; pre-tests/post-tests; course-goal aligned performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes problem solving, metacognition, self-monitoring, and collaborative work as important byproducts of formative assessment practices such as peer instruction, reflective activities, and small-group problem solving. It argues these practices help students develop useful skills, but no original quantitative results are reported in this paper.
finding.measure: problem-solving strategies; self-monitoring; reflection; collaborative engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper contends that frequent formative assessment can keep students active and engaged, reduce frustration by matching challenge to current knowledge, and improve motivation through timely feedback. These are presented as theoretical and research-based claims rather than findings from a new empirical comparison.
finding.measure: engagement; motivation; frustration/disengagement; self-efficacy-attitudes

paper_profiles.title: Selection of contributing factors for predicting landslide susceptibility using machine learning and deep learning models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether selecting a smaller, more informative set of landslide contributing factors improves the accuracy of landslide susceptibility prediction models. The authors compare several feature-selection approaches—filter (IGR), wrapper (RFE, PSO, HHO), embedded (LASSO), exhaustive search, and autoencoder-based selection—across six predictive models: SVM, logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, CNN, and LSTM.

The study is conducted on a Kerala, India landslide inventory containing 4,728 documented landslides, combined with 15 terrain, geological, land-cover, and hydrological predictors. The paper uses a train/validation/test split and five-fold cross-validation, evaluating models by accuracy, AUC, precision, recall, F1, and Kappa. For the machine-learning models, feature selection generally improves performance modestly over using all factors, with the best results coming from the exhaustive benchmark and strong nonlinear learners such as RF and XGBoost. For the deep-learning models, however, traditional factor selection usually hurts performance; the full-feature baseline performs better, while the autoencoder-based architecture improves predictive accuracy relative to other DL selection approaches.

The main conclusion is that the choice of prediction model matters more than factor selection alone. RF and XGBoost outperform SVM and logistic regression, and traditional feature-selection methods yield only small gains for ML models. In contrast, DL models already incorporate feature extraction internally, so external factor selection is less effective; the autoencoder-based approach is the most beneficial DL variant tested.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly shows that feature selection can improve landslide-susceptibility model efficiency and, in some cases, predictive performance relative to using all 15 inputs. For example, the exhaustive benchmark and selected-feature models often achieved slightly higher test accuracy than the all-factor baseline, and the authors note that LASSO was much faster than PSO and RFE (e.g., 0.3–0.7 s versus 452–1679 s for several wrapper methods).
finding.measure: Model training / feature-selection computational time and classification accuracy for landslide susceptibility prediction
finding.study_size: n=4728 landslides with matched non-landslide samples; 15 predictors

finding.finding_summary: The study has direct implications for landslide-risk modeling practice and decision support, showing that better model/model-selection choices can improve susceptibility mapping used for hazard mitigation. The best-performing models (RF and XGBoost, and the autoencoder-based DL variant) produced higher AUC/accuracy than baseline models, suggesting practical value for operational landslide assessment.
finding.measure: Landslide susceptibility map predictive performance (accuracy, AUC, Kappa) used for hazard assessment
finding.study_size: n=4728 landslides with matched non-landslide samples

paper_profiles.title: Qality Assessment of Online Automated Privacy Policy Generators: An Empirical Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates the quality of online Automated Privacy Policy Generators (APPGs), tools that help app developers create privacy policies for mobile applications. The authors argue that while APPGs are convenient, they can introduce legal risk if the generated policies are incomplete or inconsistent with the actual app behavior and developer input.

The study identifies 10 popular APPGs, analyzes the completeness of privacy policies from popular apps, and designs three boilerplate apps to test whether generated policies cover essential privacy-policy items and remain consistent with the simulated app functionality. The evaluation combines completeness analysis, a hand-coded scoring rubric for essential/recommended items, and TF-IDF/cosine similarity comparisons against original privacy policies.

Results show that many APPGs omit essential items or generate over-scoped terms that do not match the app inputs. Template-based generators are limited in versatility, while paid APPGs generally outperform free ones, though even paid tools still produce inconsistent or incomplete policies. The paper concludes that APPGs should better align questionnaire design with essential policy items and that developers should consult legal professionals before relying on generated policies.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that online APPGs improve developer convenience by quickly generating privacy policies, reducing the time and legal effort needed to draft them manually. However, the study also shows that efficiency gains come with quality tradeoffs: many generators are incomplete or inconsistent with app inputs, especially free tools and template-based systems.
finding.measure: APPG usability/quality assessment, questionnaire complexity, and policy-generation process
finding.study_size: n=10 APPGs; 3 boilerplate apps; 30 generated privacy policies

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that many APPGs may create institutional and legal risk because generated privacy policies can be incomplete, over-scoped, or inconsistent with user input and app behavior. The authors report that some generators lack privacy policies/disclaimers and that paid APPGs generally outperform free ones, but even the better tools are still not robust enough for safe legal reliance.
finding.measure: Completeness of privacy-policy content, consistency with boilerplate app inputs, and similarity to original policies
finding.study_size: n=10 APPGs; 3 boilerplate apps; 30 generated privacy policies

paper_profiles.title: Student Explanation Strategies in Postsecondary Mathematics and Statistics Education: A Scoping Review
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 27th Annual Conference on Research in Undergraduate Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This scoping review examines how student explanation strategies are used in postsecondary mathematics and statistics education and how the literature can be categorized. The authors searched English-language peer-reviewed research from 2014 to 2024 and identified 46 studies, focusing on three forms of student explanation: self-explanation, peer explanation, and explanation to fictitious others.

The review is not an intervention study itself, but it synthesizes prior work on how these explanation activities are implemented and what they appear to influence. Across the literature, self-explanation and explaining to fictitious others are described as supporting individual cognitive processing, while peer explanation adds collaborative and social dimensions. The authors conclude that effects vary by implementation, duration, and context, with some evidence that peer explanation can be beneficial but may also introduce drawbacks such as domination by more knowledgeable students.

The paper’s population focus is undergraduate/college students in mathematics, statistics, and related STEM contexts. Its main contribution is conceptual and descriptive: it maps the field, summarizes the theoretical foundations (retrieval practice, generative learning, and social presence), and notes that findings across studies are mixed rather than uniform. It does not provide a pooled effect size or a direct comparison against business-as-usual or summative-assessment-only instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Across 46 studies in postsecondary mathematics and statistics, student explanation strategies were generally associated with improved learning outcomes, but the review emphasizes that results vary substantially by implementation, duration, and context. The paper does not report a pooled effect size; instead, it synthesizes prior studies showing benefits for conceptual learning, proof comprehension, achievement, and problem solving, alongside some null or weaker findings.
finding.measure: Conceptual learning, proof comprehension, academic achievement, problem-solving performance in mathematics and statistics
finding.study_size: 46 studies reviewed; individual study ns not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that peer explanation and related student explanation activities have been linked to higher motivation and increased engagement/mental effort in prior studies. These effects are described qualitatively rather than quantitatively, and the review does not report a pooled effect size or confidence interval.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, mental effort, self-efficacy-related outcomes
finding.study_size: 46 studies reviewed; individual study ns not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally discusses durable skills such as self-explanation quality, metacognitive processing, collaboration, and perspective-taking in explanation activities. It concludes that self-explanation and explanation to fictitious others support generative thinking, while peer explanation adds collaborative learning benefits, though the review also notes that peer discussion can be dominated by more knowledgeable students.
finding.measure: Self-explanation quality, metacognitive processes, collaboration, perspective-taking, conceptual understanding
finding.study_size: 46 studies reviewed; individual study ns not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Attention-Guided Discriminative Region Localization and Label Distribution Learning for Bone Age Assessment
paper_profiles.venue: arXiv preprint (later presented as an IEEE-style journal manuscript)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses automated bone age assessment (BAA) from pediatric hand radiographs, a clinically important task used to diagnose growth, endocrine, and metabolic disorders and to estimate skeletal maturity. The authors focus on two key limitations of prior deep learning approaches: the need for expensive manual region annotations to localize informative parts of the hand, and the use of single-label regression/classification losses that ignore the ordinal structure of age labels.

The proposed method has two stages. First, an attention-guided localization network learns to identify discriminative regions from image-level labels only, including the full hand region, the carpal bones (Region-1), and the metacarpal bones (Region-2). Second, a regression network uses these localized regions for bone-age expectation regression, combining image and gender features and adding label-distribution regularization to encourage age predictions that follow a smooth Gaussian-like distribution around the true age.

Experiments are conducted on the RSNA Pediatric Bone Age Challenge dataset using random train/validation/test splits. The method is evaluated with mean absolute error (MAE) for bone age prediction and IoU/AP for region localization. Results show that the attention mechanism can localize clinically meaningful hand regions without extra annotations, and that using localized regions improves MAE over the full image. The best reported performance is 4.3 months MAE when combining regions with the proposed distribution-learning objective, competitive with prior state-of-the-art methods that rely on additional supervision or ensembling.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is a medical image analysis study, not an education intervention study. Its core empirical result is that attention-guided localization and label-distribution learning improve pediatric bone age estimation on the RSNA dataset, with the best reported MAE of 4.3 months when combining localized regions (H+R1+R2 or H+R1+E) and the proposed loss. Compared with using the original image alone, the proposed approach improves MAE from 7.3 to 4.3 months, and it localizes the hand/carpal regions with high overlap (e.g., hand mIoU=0.757, AP50=0.995 at τ=20).
finding.measure: Bone age estimation error (MAE in months) and region localization quality (mIoU, AP50)
finding.study_size: n=unknown (RSNA test split with 500 test images; 200 images manually labeled for localization evaluation)
finding.effect_size: 4.3 months MAE; improvement of 3.0 months over full-image baseline

paper_profiles.title: Coherence Learning using Keypoint-based Pooling Network for Accurately Assessing Radiographic Knee Osteoarthritis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically assessing radiographic knee osteoarthritis (OA) severity from plain X-ray images. The authors argue that existing clinical grading systems are subjective and that standard deep learning classifiers do not fully exploit the relationship between global OA severity scores and finer-grained compartment-level findings.

To improve performance, the paper proposes a multi-task computer-aided diagnosis model with two main components: a keypoint-based pooling network (KPN) that extracts image features from anatomically targeted knee keypoints, and a semi-supervised coherence-learning loss based on a Gaussian Mixture Model over the joint distribution of KL and OARSI grades. The model is trained on the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) dataset, a multi-center longitudinal observational study with 4,796 subjects, using both labeled and unlabeled knee radiographs.

Experiments compare the proposed method against ResNet baselines and show consistent improvements in grading accuracy and RMSE for the composite KL score and most compartment-level OARSI scores. Ablation analyses suggest that keypoint-based pooling is especially helpful for fine-grained compartmental grading, while coherence learning contributes more to composite KL grading and enables better use of unlabeled data. Overall, the paper concludes that the combined approach yields better OA severity assessment than standard whole-image classifiers, but it is a medical imaging paper rather than an education study.

paper_profiles.title: Cross-Scale: Multi-scale coupling in space plasmas
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report is an ESA assessment study for the Cross-Scale space mission, which was designed to investigate multi-scale coupling in collisionless plasma phenomena near Earth. The mission focuses on three fundamental processes—shocks, magnetic reconnection, and turbulence—and argues that understanding them requires simultaneous measurements across electron, ion, and fluid scales using a constellation of spacecraft.

The document is not an education study and does not evaluate any instructional intervention, formative assessment approach, or student learning outcome. Instead, it presents the scientific rationale, mission requirements, spacecraft configurations, payload concepts, operations, and programmatic considerations for a future space physics mission. The central conclusion is that multi-spacecraft in situ measurements are needed to resolve cross-scale plasma dynamics, with a 7-spacecraft ESA configuration presented as a feasible reduced mission relative to the larger 10–12 spacecraft concepts discussed for optimal science return.

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment II. Indications of Effectiveness in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the use of InkSurvey, a free web-based tool that supports real-time formative assessment through open-response questions on pen-enabled mobile devices. The authors argue that such assessment allows instructors to see student thinking immediately, identify misconceptions, and adapt instruction in time to improve understanding.

The paper presents seven vignettes from diverse educational settings, including high school algebra, undergraduate physics, engineering physics, food chemistry, chemical engineering, and graduate study in the United States and Mexico. The evidence is drawn from a combination of classroom observation, student feedback, instructor reflections, and comparisons of student performance before and after InkSurvey-based instruction or against similar classes without InkSurvey. Reported results suggest improved learning, greater participation, better metacognition, and stronger engagement, with some indications that female students in the high school example benefited especially strongly.

Because the article is a descriptive synthesis of multiple classroom examples rather than a single controlled study, its conclusions are suggestive rather than definitive. Still, the authors conclude that InkSurvey can be an effective tool for real-time formative assessment across a range of subjects, grade levels, and device types, especially when used to make student thinking visible and to guide immediate instructional response.

finding.finding_summary: In a Calculus III comparison, 87 students in an InkSurvey-supported lesson were later assessed on triple integrals, and only 1 student still showed the targeted misconception on any of three exam questions. In a comparison large-lecture section without InkSurvey, 12 of 103 students made the same mistake on the same exam questions, suggesting substantially better concept retention with real-time formative assessment.
finding.measure: Summative exam questions on triple integrals / conceptual understanding in Calculus III

finding.finding_summary: High school Algebra I students using InkSurvey reportedly gained traction on mastery of fundamental concepts as measured by standards-based assessments, compared with students not exposed to the intervention. The paper does not report a numeric effect size, but it notes that female students in particular showed much greater learning gains than the control group.
finding.measure: Standards-based assessments in Algebra I

finding.finding_summary: Across undergraduate and graduate Food Chemistry courses, formative assessment using Tablet PCs and InkSurvey was associated with higher performance on summative quizzes relative to the same courses four years earlier. Mean improvements were reported as 0.6 points out of 10 in the undergraduate course and 0.5 points out of 10 in the graduate course.
finding.measure: Summative quiz scores in Food Chemistry

finding.finding_summary: In an upper-level engineering physics course, students’ problem-solving skills showed steady improvement over the semester when InkSurvey was used for real-time formative assessment. The paper reports adjusted scores increasing over time as students responded to a standard three-question problem-solving sequence, indicating growth in applying a problem-solving strategy.
finding.measure: Problem-solving skill scores from open-response task sequence

finding.finding_summary: In chemical engineering courses using interactive simulations plus InkSurvey, student competence across six concepts increased from about 1.8 to about 2.3 after unguided simulation use, and then to about 3.1 after instructor-guided formative assessment on a 4-point scale. This indicates that real-time formative assessment helped students refine understanding and apply concepts more successfully during problem exploration.
finding.measure: Concept competence ratings on a 4-point scale across six topics

finding.finding_summary: Student survey responses in an undergraduate physics lab showed strong perceived benefits for engagement and self-monitoring: 86% of 63 students agreed that InkSurvey helped the instructor better understand what they did and did not understand, and 76% said creating InkSurvey responses helped them better understand the material or realize what they did and did not understand. The paper also reports stronger agreement from female students than males in the high school Algebra I vignette (70% vs. 48%) on a similar self-awareness item.
finding.measure: Student attitude survey on perceived understanding, engagement, and metacognition

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly reports that InkSurvey improved metacognition by making students analyze their own thinking, identify gaps, and revise understanding in real time. In one undergraduate physics survey, 48 of 63 students (76%) said the activity helped them better understand what was being covered or what they did and did not understand.
finding.measure: Metacognitive self-report survey items

finding.finding_summary: Students generally reported that InkSurvey made classes more active, increased motivation to participate, and kept them constantly thinking. In the graduate Food Chemistry vignette, students said it increased motivation to participate in class and improved learning with understanding, though the paper provides mainly qualitative evidence rather than controlled estimates.
finding.measure: Student qualitative feedback / classroom participation reports

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines formative assessment as a teaching and learning approach and asks how it can be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard Learning System. The authors argue that frequent, low-stakes assessment paired with immediate, detailed feedback can support learning more effectively than relying on only end-of-semester summative tests.

The paper describes a proposed implementation at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus), where weekly or fortnightly online tests were created in Blackboard using multiple-choice and true/false items, with immediate score display and explanatory feedback. The study also includes a student questionnaire on perceptions of continuous assessment and Blackboard-based testing, with moderate-to-high internal consistency on the survey subscales (alpha=0.67 and 0.81). Students generally supported the approach because it broke content into manageable pieces, provided flexibility and convenience, and gave immediate feedback; however, some also worried that frequent testing could increase stress and overemphasize grades.

Overall, the paper concludes that formative assessment is viewed positively by students and that Blackboard can operationalize it at scale through repeated online assessments and feedback. The evidence is primarily perception-based and descriptive rather than causal, but the authors suggest the approach may improve engagement with content over the semester and potentially support summative exam performance. The paper also notes that effectiveness depends on good feedback, structured implementation, and teacher follow-up.

finding.finding_summary: Students generally supported frequent online formative assessments because they perceived them as helpful for keeping up with the subject, checking progress, and receiving immediate feedback. However, they also reported concerns that too many tests could create stress and pressure to perform, so the net affective response was positive but not unqualified.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire on perceptions of continuous assessment, feedback, and Blackboard test implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames formative assessment as supporting metacognition and self-monitoring because students receive feedback, reflect on errors, and judge whether they are 'on track.' Students reported that the frequent small assessments helped them learn progressively and understand strengths and weaknesses, but no direct performance measure of metacognitive skill was reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of self-monitoring, strengths/weaknesses awareness, and progress tracking

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that weekly or fortnightly Blackboard formative assessments helped them learn in small steps, stay in touch with the subject throughout the semester, and prepare for the summative semester examination. The evidence is based on survey responses rather than achievement outcomes, but the paper argues that immediate feedback and detailed explanations made the learning process more effective.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment and perceived support for course learning/preparation for semester exams

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests Blackboard-based assessment improves instructional efficiency by enabling online administration of repeated tests, immediate scoring, and automated display of detailed feedback. It also notes that teacher follow-up can be enhanced with other Blackboard tools such as discussion forums and virtual classrooms, but it does not measure teacher workload directly.
finding.measure: Descriptive implementation features of Blackboard online tests and feedback delivery

finding.finding_summary: At the institutional level, the authors present formative assessment as a scalable continuous-assessment model within the university's Blackboard system and report that students favored the idea of splitting course work into 10-12 weekly assessments. The paper also found statistically significant differences by academic stream in attitudes toward the Blackboard test option (Cramer's V=0.236, p<0.05) and toward open-book continuous assessment (Cramer's V=0.206, p<0.05), indicating variation in implementation acceptance across subgroups.
finding.measure: Student survey attitudes toward continuous assessment and Blackboard test implementation; subgroup comparisons by academic stream

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: Not reported; the paper is a narrative review focused on K-12 and higher-education formative assessment contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review and practical guide on how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback. The authors frame formative assessment around three core questions: where learners are going, where they currently are, and how to move them forward. They argue that LLMs may help with each component by rewriting learning objectives into student-friendly language, generating sample work and discussion prompts, creating questions and checks for understanding, and producing feedback that is more actionable than generic comments.

The paper is not an empirical intervention study; instead, it synthesizes prior work and offers example prompts and classroom use cases. It discusses generic LLMs, domain-specialized LLMs, and LLM-integrated educational platforms, emphasizing that AI should augment rather than replace expert pedagogy. The authors repeatedly note that current evaluation metrics often miss formative-assessment quality, especially the distinction between task-level, process-level, and self-regulatory feedback.

The review also highlights limitations and implementation challenges at scale. These include prompt sensitivity and output variability, the need for teacher expertise to vet AI-generated content, concerns about overreliance on AI, privacy and transparency issues with proprietary systems, and the fact that many tools are benchmarked in ways that do not reflect real classroom formative assessment. The main conclusion is that LLMs may improve scalability and reduce teacher workload, but only if used with strong pedagogical judgment, context-sensitive prompting, and robust evaluation criteria.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or speeding up tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating diagnostic questions, creating sample work, and drafting feedback. The evidence presented is illustrative rather than experimental, so no effect size is reported; the claim is that these tools can save time and make frequent formative assessment more feasible at scale, especially in large or resource-constrained classrooms.
finding.measure: Teacher time/workload; feasibility of generating formative-assessment materials

finding.finding_summary: A central claim is that LLM-supported formative assessment can promote durable skills such as metacognition, critical thinking, and self-regulation when used to co-construct goals, generate exemplars, and provide process-level feedback. The paper also warns that poorly designed AI use may encourage passive reliance rather than reflection, so the benefit depends on whether prompts and tasks require students to think about their reasoning.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognitive reflection, self-regulation, and analysis of exemplars/feedback

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests that formative assessment supported by LLMs may improve engagement and motivation by making feedback faster, more personalized, and more accessible, but it also highlights a risk of overreliance that could reduce active participation. Because this is a conceptual review, the evidence is theoretical and no quantitative effect estimate is provided.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, and learner participation in formative assessment activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs could help overcome systemic and cultural barriers to formative assessment by making assessment supports more accessible, especially in large classrooms and in low- and middle-income contexts where specialized edtech may be costly or unavailable. At the same time, it notes institutional concerns around proprietary systems, privacy, transparency, and the need for culturally and pedagogically appropriate prompt templates.
