finding.measure: Scalability/access to formative assessment; barriers related to cost, training, and institutional adoption

paper_profiles.title: Data Synthesis and Adversarial Networks: A Review and Meta-Analysis in Cancer Imaging
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews and synthesizes research on generative adversarial networks (GANs) and related adversarial training methods for cancer imaging. The authors focus on how these methods may address key clinical and technical challenges such as data scarcity, class imbalance, privacy, annotation burden, cross-modality translation, segmentation, diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring. They screen 164 publications and organize the literature into five cancer-imaging challenge categories.

A second contribution is the SynTRUST framework, a meta-analysis tool for assessing the validation rigor of medical image synthesis studies. Using SynTRUST, the authors evaluate 16 promising cancer-imaging synthesis studies and find generally high validation rigor, while also identifying areas where evaluation practices could improve. The paper is not an intervention study in education; rather, it is a methodological review of AI image synthesis in adult medical imaging contexts, with the main conclusion that GANs are promising but still require stronger validation, better evaluation metrics, and more attention to failure modes such as hallucinations, dataset shift, and fairness issues.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that GAN-based synthesis and adversarial training can reduce data curation burden, annotation effort, and imaging workflow constraints by generating synthetic data, harmonizing multi-center datasets, and improving reconstruction/super-resolution. However, the paper is a synthesis of prior studies rather than a single empirical test, so no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Data curation, annotation burden, reconstruction/super-resolution utility, and workflow efficiency in cancer imaging
finding.study_size: 164 reviewed publications; 16 studies assessed with SynTRUST

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies broader institutional implications of adversarial networks for cancer imaging, including improved data sharing under privacy constraints, multi-center harmonization, and fairness considerations for underrepresented groups. It also introduces the SynTRUST framework as a proposed standard for trustworthiness assessment, but does not provide a quantitative institutional effect size.
finding.measure: Privacy-preserving data sharing, multi-center standardization, fairness, and trustworthiness assessment framework
finding.study_size: 164 reviewed publications; framework applied to 16 studies

paper_profiles.title: Embedded Formative Assessment in the Undergraduate Engineering Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses the pedagogical role of embedded formative assessment in undergraduate engineering classrooms, with an emphasis on how technology has reduced the clerical burden of collecting student responses. The authors frame formative assessment as a classroom practice that reveals student thinking so instructors can adjust instruction in real time or in the next class, and they contrast traditional multiple-choice clicker use with open-format questions that better expose reasoning.

Rather than testing a single intervention, the paper is largely a conceptual and practice-oriented discussion grounded in examples from undergraduate engineering physics and references to prior engineering education studies. It argues that technology such as clickers, text messaging, and InkSurvey can make formative assessment more scalable, but notes important limitations: instructor response is often the critical missing link, teachers may be reluctant or unable to adapt instruction on the fly, and multiple-choice formats can constrain creativity and diagnostic value. Open-format responses are presented as a richer alternative because they reveal misconceptions, support higher-order thinking, and can be used even in large classes, though they may require new workflows and tools such as digital ink capture or automated text analysis.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that embedded formative assessment supports deeper conceptual understanding in STEM by making student thinking visible and allowing instruction to be adjusted. In the undergraduate electromagnetics example (n=60), open-format prompts after instruction on Gauss’s law revealed major misconceptions in deriving the law and in graphing the electric field, suggesting the approach can diagnose and refine scientific reasoning in real time.
finding.measure: Open-format formative assessment responses on electromagnetics problems (derivation and graphing tasks)

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that open-format formative assessment can strengthen higher-order thinking, metacognition, and critical thinking by requiring students to explain reasoning rather than select answers. The student work described showed gaps in reasoning, symmetry use, and calculus fluency, and the authors interpret the process as helping students focus on the problem-solving journey rather than just the answer.
finding.measure: Quality of reasoning and student thinking revealed in open-ended written/drawn responses

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the paper is that technology-assisted formative assessment reduces the instructor’s clerical burden and enables real-time collection and review of student responses. The authors also note that tools like clickers, texting systems, InkSurvey, Google Docs, and automated text analysis can make implementation more feasible at scale, though open-response workflows may still require quick visual inspection or delayed analysis turnaround.
finding.measure: Instructor clerical burden, speed of collecting and inspecting student responses, and turnaround time for analysis

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that embedded formative assessment can increase student engagement, metacognition, and confidence by helping learners see what they know and do not know. It also notes that anonymous response options may reduce embarrassment and encourage participation, although these claims are presented as pedagogical benefits rather than as directly measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Student engagement, metacognition, confidence, and willingness to reveal thinking

paper_profiles.title: FOUNDATIONS FOR AI-ASSISTED FORMATIVE ASSESSMENT FEEDBACK FOR SHORT-ANSWER TASKS IN LARGE-ENROLLMENT CLASSES
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether natural language processing can support scalable formative assessment for short-answer tasks in large-enrollment statistics courses. The motivating problem is that constructed-response formative assessment can provide richer evidence of learning than selected-response formats, but it becomes difficult for instructors to score and provide timely feedback when classes are very large. The authors therefore explore human-machine collaboration as a way to preserve the educational value of open-ended formative assessment while reducing instructor burden.

Using de-identified responses from 1,935 post-secondary students across 29 class sections in 16 introductory statistics courses, the study examines the reliability of human scoring and compares it to an NLP-based automated scorer. Four raters used a detailed rubric to score six short-answer tasks, and the paper reports substantial inter-rater agreement among human raters (pairwise QWK mostly 0.79-0.83; Fleiss’ kappa 0.70) and strong agreement between the best algorithm (SFRN) and humans (pairwise QWK 0.74-0.82; four-way Fleiss’ kappa 0.68). The algorithm also outperformed an LSTM baseline on classification accuracy (83% vs. 72%).

The paper additionally pilots clustering approaches intended to group semantically similar student responses so instructors can interpret common patterns and potentially deliver more targeted feedback at scale. The central technical tradeoff identified is that representations optimized for classification are not necessarily optimal for clustering, and the authors note the challenge of balancing high-dimensional models for scoring with low-dimensional representations for meaningful clusters. Overall, the study concludes that AI-assisted formative assessment for short-answer tasks appears feasible and promising in large classes, but that future work is needed to connect reliable automated scoring with high-quality feedback design and classroom implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that AI-assisted scoring can make short-answer formative assessment more feasible at scale in large-enrollment courses. Human raters showed substantial agreement (pairwise QWK > 0.74 for most comparisons; Fleiss’ kappa = 0.70), and the best automated model (SFRN) matched human scoring fairly well (pairwise QWK = 0.7403-0.8151; four-way Fleiss’ kappa = 0.678) while outperforming an LSTM baseline in classification accuracy (83% vs. 72%). The paper argues this human-machine collaboration could reduce instructor burden for scoring and enable more timely feedback, but it does not test workload directly.
finding.measure: Inter-rater reliability, classification accuracy, and clustering consistency for short-answer scoring workflows

paper_profiles.title: A Review of Tools and Techniques for Optimization of Workload Mapping and Scheduling in Heterogeneous HPC System
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic literature review of workload mapping and scheduling optimization in heterogeneous high-performance computing (HPC) systems. Its central question is how to model, optimize, evaluate, and implement resource-allocation and scheduling methods for modern heterogeneous compute continua that span sensors, edge devices, clouds, and data centers.

The review synthesizes 66 papers published from 2017 to 2024 and organizes them by problem type, optimization approach, metrics, tools, and benchmarking practices. The paper argues that classic job-shop formulations are not expressive enough for modern HPC environments, and that most real-world scheduling problems remain NP-hard or NP-complete, leading researchers to rely heavily on heuristics, meta-heuristics, ILP/MILP, AI/ML, and quantum-inspired methods. It concludes that hybrid, adaptable, and energy-aware approaches are most promising, but that scalability, dynamic adaptation, benchmarking standardization, and integration into operational HPC/cloud systems remain major challenges.

The context is not a human learner population or school setting; it is adult-facing computational infrastructure research. The paper’s findings are based on a broad review rather than a single intervention study, and its main contribution is a structured synthesis of techniques, gaps, and best practices for HPC workload management rather than an estimate of educational or social outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Across the 66 reviewed papers, the dominant objective was improving operational efficiency through better workload mapping and scheduling. The review reports that most studies pursued lower execution time, better resource utilization, and reduced makespan/cost, but also notes that many methods are limited by scalability and dynamic adaptation challenges; no single method comprehensively solves resource management at scale.
finding.measure: Execution time, makespan, resource utilization, cost, efficiency, throughput

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that heterogeneous HPC scheduling research is moving toward hybrid optimization frameworks that combine heuristics, meta-heuristics, ILP/MILP, AI/ML, and quantum methods, with implications for HPC/cloud system design and research practice. It also identifies benchmarking standardization, tool integration, and scalable validation as important institutional challenges and recommends broader systematic reviews and standardized evaluation frameworks.
finding.measure: Distribution of methods, benchmarking and validation practices, integration considerations, research trend analysis

paper_profiles.title: Optical Flow Method for Measuring Deformation of Soil Specimen Subjected to Torsional Shearing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether an optical flow image-analysis method can measure small surface deformations of cylindrical soil specimens during torsional shearing tests. The authors are motivated by a measurement problem in geotechnical laboratory testing: standard torsional shear (TS) procedures infer strain from a single twist measurement near the top of the specimen and assume deformation is linearly distributed along the full specimen height, which may hide local deformation anomalies and bias calculated stiffness.

The study applies a SIFT-based optical flow algorithm to image sequences captured during TS tests on dry, non-cohesive silica sand specimens under two confining pressures. The optical flow results are validated against digital PIV variants. The analysis shows that displacement along the specimen height is not linear and differs across loading stages and confining pressures, implying an 'active height' smaller than the full specimen height. This means conventional TS calculations may substantially underestimate shear strain and overestimate shear modulus G.

The paper also compares the practicality of the optical flow approach with PIV. Optical flow is more sensitive enough to detect very small deformations and local anomalies, while some PIV configurations struggle with very small displacements or produce NaN errors depending on interrogation-area settings. The authors conclude that side-surface displacement tracking should accompany TS tests to improve interpretation of small-strain soil behavior and stiffness estimation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper demonstrates that SIFT-based optical flow can accurately measure small deformations in a geotechnical laboratory context and reveal non-linear deformation mechanisms that standard TS interpretation misses. Validation against PIV showed close agreement (e.g., RMSE for specimen A as low as 7.3106×10^-4 and for specimen B as low as 3.5910×10^-4), supporting the method’s measurement credibility for small-strain deformation analysis.
finding.measure: Measured horizontal displacement fields / deformation distribution on soil specimen side surfaces during torsional shearing, validated against PIV
finding.study_size: n=34 specimens tested; detailed validation shown for 2 specimens (A, B)

finding.finding_summary: The optical flow approach has practical advantages and limitations for lab workflows. The paper reports that processing 500 images took about 3-4 hours for both optical flow and PIV, but optical flow required careful image acquisition, correction, and parameter tuning; the authors note that recording and environmental control were critical because reflections or nearby movement could corrupt results.
finding.measure: Computation time and implementation burden for image-based deformation analysis

paper_profiles.title: Identification of error sources in high precision weight measurements of gyroscopes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates why prior studies on spinning gyroscopes reported conflicting weight-change results, including claims of anomalous mass reduction and numerous null replications. The authors do not study an education intervention; instead, they build two high-precision experimental setups to measure gyroscope weight under different orientations and rotation directions, aiming to identify measurement artifacts and error sources.

The paper compares a counter-balance weighing method with a direct electronic-scale method. The authors argue that the counter-balance configuration is highly vulnerable to torque and precession artifacts, making it unsuitable for precise weighing of rotating bodies. In the electronic-scale setup, they find that vibration interactions between the spinning gyroscope and the scale’s active feedback system can create apparent mass anomalies; after adding damping, these anomalies are reduced and the data become consistent with a null effect.

Overall, the paper concludes that previously reported gyroscope weight anomalies are best explained by measurement errors rather than a real mass-change phenomenon. Their damped measurements yield no anomaly within Δm/m < 2.6×10^-6 across horizontal and vertical orientations, and they recommend mechanical decoupling and careful control of vibration as essential precautions in high-precision weighing experiments.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in digital pathology: a diagnostic test accuracy systematic review and meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review and meta-analysis examines whether artificial intelligence (AI) applied to whole slide images (WSIs) in digital pathology can accurately detect disease or classify disease subtypes. The paper was motivated by the rapid growth of pathology AI and the need to assess whether reported performance is strong enough for safe clinical use.

The review included diagnostic accuracy studies of AI models applied to WSIs for any disease, with histopathology and/or immunohistochemistry as the reference standard. Searches were conducted in PubMed, EMBASE, and CENTRAL through June 2022; 100 studies met inclusion criteria and 48 provided data for meta-analysis. The studies covered a wide range of pathologies, were international in scope, and collectively represented more than 152,000 WSIs.

Overall, the meta-analysis found high reported diagnostic accuracy, with mean sensitivity of 96.3% and mean specificity of 93.3%. However, the evidence base had major limitations: study designs were highly heterogeneous, raw performance data were often missing, only 48 studies could be meta-analyzed, and 99% of included studies had at least one domain at high or unclear risk of bias. The authors conclude that AI shows promise for assisting pathologists, but substantially more rigorous study design, external validation, and transparent reporting are needed before routine clinical use.

finding.finding_summary: Across 48 studies in the meta-analysis, AI applied to WSIs showed high diagnostic accuracy, suggesting potential to assist and automate pathology workflows. Mean sensitivity was 96.3% (CI 94.1-97.7) and mean specificity was 93.3% (CI 90.5-95.4) across more than 152,000 WSIs, although the paper emphasizes that these are research performance estimates rather than evidence of real-world workflow gains.
finding.measure: Diagnostic accuracy of AI on whole slide images (sensitivity and specificity)
finding.study_size: n=100 studies in review; n=48 studies in meta-analysis; >152,000 WSIs

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that AI has high reported diagnostic accuracy across multiple disease areas in digital pathology, but that translation to routine clinical use is limited by substantial risk of bias, incomplete reporting, and lack of external validation. Of 100 included studies, 99% had at least one area at high or unclear risk of bias, indicating that the main institutional implication is a need for stronger evidence standards before deployment.
finding.measure: Study-level risk of bias, applicability concerns, and diagnostic accuracy reporting across included AI pathology studies
finding.study_size: n=100 studies in review; n=48 in meta-analysis

paper_profiles.title: Quantum feedback: theory, experiments, and applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad review of quantum feedback control, surveying the theory, mathematical machinery, experiments, and applications developed for controlling quantum systems. It explains the historical development from classical feedback and quantum continuous measurement theory to measurement-based feedback, Bayesian feedback, Markovian feedback, and coherent feedback.

The review focuses on how continuous measurements are converted into state estimates through quantum filtering or quantum trajectories, and how those estimates or measurement streams can be used to control quantum systems in real time. It also compares measurement-based and coherent feedback, emphasizing practical tradeoffs such as measurement back-action, detection inefficiency, amplification requirements, processing delay, and environmental noise in controllers.

Although the paper is not an education study, it provides a technical synthesis of experiments in quantum optics, trapped atoms and ions, superconducting circuits, and opto-/electro-mechanical systems. The main conclusions are that quantum feedback can reduce noise, stabilize states, generate squeezing and entanglement, improve estimation and cooling, and that coherent feedback can outperform measurement-based feedback in some settings because it avoids the need to convert quantum information into classical signals.

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how formative assessment could be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard, in a university setting. The authors frame formative assessment as a way to provide ongoing feedback, improve learning, and support better performance on end-of-semester summative exams, especially in a technology-enabled environment.

The proposed approach was a series of weekly or fortnightly online tests on Blackboard, including question types such as multiple choice, true/false, and other item formats. The implementation emphasized immediate feedback, detailed explanations of answers, and the possibility of using additional Blackboard tools such as discussion forums and virtual classrooms to support feedback and correspondence.

To explore student perceptions, the authors surveyed university students with a 16-item questionnaire and analyzed both closed and open-ended responses. Students generally supported frequent small-topic assessments and valued immediate feedback, flexibility, and the ability to monitor strengths and weaknesses. However, they also raised concerns that frequent testing could create stress and that learning might be overemphasized relative to grades. The paper concludes that Blackboard-based formative assessment appears workable and potentially helpful for maintaining engagement and improving learning, but it is not an experimental impact study and provides no direct evidence of gains in achievement.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent small-topic online assessments and immediate feedback helped them stay in touch with the subject, monitor strengths and weaknesses, and feel more confident about their standing. At the same time, some students worried that too many tests would create stress/pressure to perform and that learning was being overemphasized relative to grades.
finding.measure: Student perception survey and open-ended responses about frequent assessment, feedback, stress/pressure, and engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognition and self-monitoring by helping students identify errors, reflect on feedback, and determine whether they are on track. Students endorsed the value of feedback for checking strengths and weaknesses and for learning topics progressively.
finding.measure: Student perception survey on feedback usefulness and self-monitoring; conceptual discussion of metacognition

finding.finding_summary: The Blackboard implementation was presented as a practical way to deliver frequent assessments with immediate automated feedback and flexible access, reducing delay compared with traditional classroom-based assessment. The paper also notes that Blackboard tools such as discussion forums and virtual classrooms could supplement lecturer correspondence, but it does not quantify teacher workload or efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of Blackboard test option, flexibility/convenience, and immediate feedback; descriptive implementation analysis

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative/practice-oriented review of how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback. The authors organize the discussion around a formative assessment framework: clarifying where learners are going, determining where learners are now, and providing guidance on how to move them forward. They argue that LLMs can help with tasks such as rewriting learning objectives into student-friendly language, generating success-criteria discussion prompts, creating sample work for critique, automatically generating questions, and producing feedback that is more scalable than what teachers can do manually.

The paper is not an empirical evaluation of an intervention; instead, it uses examples, prior research, and illustrative prompt templates to show how accessible LLMs might be used in classrooms. The context is primarily K-12 and higher education teaching practice, with examples ranging from high school biology to undergraduate fMRI coursework. The authors emphasize that LLMs can save time and expand access, but only when educators apply them with pedagogical judgment and subject-matter expertise.

The main conclusion is that LLMs should augment rather than replace expert pedagogy. The paper highlights several limitations of current LLM use in formative assessment, including variability in outputs, weak alignment of existing evaluation metrics with formative feedback quality, over-reliance risks, and implementation challenges such as prompt quality, privacy, transparency, and contextual fit. It also calls for future research on robust metrics for LLM-generated feedback, AI-aware assessment design, and ways to reduce systemic and cultural barriers to formative assessment at scale.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by helping generate student-friendly objectives, questions, exemplars, and feedback at scale. This is presented as a practical, time-saving support for formative assessment, especially in large classes and contexts where providing timely personalized feedback is difficult; no quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload / time required to create formative assessment materials and feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper contends that LLM-supported formative assessment can promote higher-order skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, and self-regulation when used to co-construct success criteria, generate exemplars for critique, and provide process-level feedback rather than direct answers. It also warns that poorly designed use may encourage over-reliance on AI and reduce critical engagement; no empirical effect size is reported.
finding.measure: critical thinking, metacognition, self-regulation, and reflective engagement in formative tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses LLMs as tools for improving the clarity and usability of formative assessment materials across subjects, including rewriting objectives, generating sample work, and creating diagnostic questions. The focus is on general academic task support rather than a single subject-specific achievement outcome, and the paper does not present direct empirical measurement.
finding.measure: quality and accessibility of formative assessment materials across academic subjects

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance for Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can serve as a useful, scalable teacher coach for classroom observation and instructional feedback. The authors focus on a practical problem in teacher professional development: expert coaching is valuable but scarce, inconsistent, and expensive, so an automated system might complement human coaching if it can provide accurate, actionable feedback.

The study evaluates GPT-3.5/ChatGPT in three zero-shot teacher-coaching tasks using elementary mathematics classroom transcripts from the NCTE dataset. Task A asks the model to score transcript segments on observation rubrics (CLASS and MQI). Task B asks it to identify highlights and missed opportunities for instruction, and Task C asks it to generate actionable suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning. Expert math teachers rate the outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

Results show that ChatGPT has substantial room for improvement. On rubric scoring, correlations with human ratings are low across items and prompt variants, and added rubric detail or reasoning does not reliably help. For qualitative feedback tasks, teachers judge many responses as insufficiently insightful or relevant, and for suggestions, 82% repeat something the teacher already did in the transcript. The paper concludes that ChatGPT may have promise as a complement to coaching, but current performance is not yet strong enough to replace expert feedback and raises concerns about hallucination, novelty, and context sensitivity.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT could eventually provide scalable, cost-effective teacher coaching and reduce the need for scarce expert feedback, but the empirical results show it is not yet reliable enough for this role. In qualitative evaluation, teachers rated many outputs as relevant or actionable, yet scoring accuracy was poor and 82% of suggestions were redundant, indicating limited current utility despite potential efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Human teacher ratings of ChatGPT-generated rubric scores, highlights/missed opportunities, and actionable suggestions; qualitative assessment of scalability/cost-effectiveness potential
finding.study_size: n=100 transcript segments for scoring; n=216 CLASS items; n=288 MQI items; n=36 suggestions; 2 human teacher raters

paper_profiles.title: Equity in College Physics Student Learning: a Critical Quantitative Intersectionality Investigation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether introductory college physics courses reproduce or reduce inequities in student learning across intersecting race/racism and gender/sexism categories. The authors use a critical quantitative intersectionality framework to question how equity should be measured and argue that different operationalizations of equity can lead to different conclusions about the same data.

The study analyzes pretest and posttest scores from research-based concept inventories, primarily the Force Concept Inventory (FCI) and Force and Motion Conceptual Evaluation (FMCE), drawn from the LASSO national database. After cleaning and multiple imputation, the final dataset included 13,857 students in 187 first-semester college physics courses across 31 institutions. Hierarchical linear models estimated differences in preparation and learning by gender, race/ethnicity, and course type (lecture vs. collaborative learning).

Findings show substantial pretest and gain gaps by race and gender, with White male students predicted to score highest and Black female students lowest on pretests. After controlling for pretest scores, White male students still had the largest predicted gains, and collaborative learning increased gains for all groups by about 3.06 percentage points relative to lecture. However, collaborative learning did not reduce gaps between demographic groups, so it did not achieve Equality of Learning; it did achieve Equity of Individuality because all groups benefited in absolute terms. The paper concludes that collaborative learning improves learning overall but is insufficient on its own to eliminate inequities in physics outcomes, and that equity claims depend strongly on how equity is defined and measured.

finding.finding_summary: The study found substantial differences in conceptual physics learning, measured by gains on research-based concept inventories (FCI and FMCE). White male students had the highest predicted gains, while several marginalized groups had smaller gains even after controlling for pretest scores; collaborative learning increased gains for all groups by about 3.06 percentage points relative to lecture (e.g., 20.1% to 30.8% proportional increases for marginalized groups).
finding.measure: Conceptual physics learning gains on the Force Concept Inventory (FCI) and Force and Motion Conceptual Evaluation (FMCE), calculated as posttest minus pretest percentage correct

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that collaborative physics instruction changes equity conclusions depending on the equity definition used. Under Equity of Individuality, collaborative courses improved outcomes for marginalized groups; under Equality of Learning, course-type differences did not close racial/gender gaps, indicating that instructional transformation alone did not eliminate institutional inequities.
finding.measure: Comparative equity operationalizations applied to course-level and demographic learning-gain models
finding.effect_size: 3.06 percentage-point gain increase in collaborative vs. lecture courses

paper_profiles.title: Comparing Few-Shot Prompting of GPT-4 LLMs with BERT Classifiers for Open-Response Assessment in Tutor Equity Training
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research / AAAI 2025 Workshop iRAISE
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether modern large language models can automatically score open-ended learner responses in an ill-defined educational domain: scenario-based equity training for future tutors. The authors ask whether few-shot prompting of GPT-4o and GPT-4 Turbo can match or exceed a fine-tuned BERT classifier when judging whether tutor responses are correct and adequate across two equity-training lessons.

The study uses 291 human-labeled responses from 243 undergraduate tutors in the northeastern United States who were completing online training to become middle-school tutors. Each response was binary coded by human raters, and model performance was compared using stratified 5-fold cross-validation. BERT was fine-tuned offline on annotated examples, while GPT models were prompted with 2-3 few-shot examples and asked to output a binary decision.

Results show that fine-tuned BERT outperformed both GPT models across the four prediction tasks, with average accuracy of 0.837 and F1 of 0.886, versus 0.726/0.720 for GPT-4o and 0.549/0.550 for GPT-4 Turbo. The authors conclude that few-shot prompting alone is not sufficient for nuanced open-response assessment in this domain and that smaller, fine-tuned models may be more accurate, more stable, and more resource-efficient for scalable automated assessment of tutor equity training.

finding.finding_summary: Fine-tuned BERT was more resource-efficient and operationally practical than commercial GPT models for automated scoring of open responses. The paper reports average accuracy/F1 of 0.837/0.886 for BERT versus 0.726/0.720 for GPT-4o and 0.549/0.550 for GPT-4 Turbo, indicating that offline fine-tuning achieved better performance with lower deployment cost and less dependence on commercial APIs.
finding.measure: Model classification performance for automated open-response scoring; resource-efficiency/cost discussion

paper_profiles.title: The Rise of Artificial Intelligence in Educational Measurement: Opportunities and Ethical Challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This white paper surveys how artificial intelligence is being used across educational measurement and the ethical concerns that arise from those uses. The paper is organized around major assessment functions—automatic item generation, automated scoring, and score reporting/feedback—and also discusses related issues such as automation bias, fairness, transparency, privacy, and environmental impact.

Rather than reporting a single empirical study, the paper synthesizes existing research and gives illustrative examples from current AI assessment practice, including automated scoring challenges and automated writing evaluation. It argues that AI can increase efficiency, provide rapid feedback, and support more personalized assessment, but only if developers and users address validity, reliability, bias, representativeness, explainability, and human oversight.

The authors emphasize that many AI assessment applications are promising but still carry substantial risks at scale, especially for underrepresented groups and other priority populations. They repeatedly recommend human-in-the-loop design, better validation evidence, better documentation, and more careful monitoring of subgroup effects before operational use. The paper is best understood as a conceptual and policy-oriented synthesis rather than a study of a specific intervention in one school or classroom context.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-supported assessment can reduce educator workload and speed feedback generation, especially for automated scoring and feedback systems, but it also introduces implementation burdens related to validation, monitoring, privacy protection, and bias checking. No single empirical effect size is reported because this is a conceptual white paper; the claims are based on prior studies and illustrative examples rather than a new experiment.
finding.measure: Educator workload, speed of feedback delivery, assessment processing efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper reviews automated writing evaluation and related AI feedback tools as supports for writing development, noting reported improvements in writing quality in prior studies (effect sizes ranging from 0.38 to 0.98 in tertiary and L2 settings). It also highlights limitations: AWE can be less effective for younger students, may demotivate high-achieving writers, and can provide feedback that is misaligned with a student’s curriculum or developmental stage.
finding.measure: Writing quality, automated writing feedback usefulness, revision outcomes
finding.effect_size: 0.38-0.98 (from prior studies summarized in the paper)

finding.finding_summary: The paper summarizes prior AWE research showing that automated feedback can improve motivation and self-efficacy in some contexts, but effects on students’ writing-related beliefs and affect are mixed. It notes that some high-achieving students may feel demotivated when automated systems evaluate their work less positively than teachers do.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-efficacy, writing-related beliefs and affect

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is the institutional and governance implications of deploying AI in assessment at scale, including validity, reliability, fairness, transparency, test security, privacy, and accountability. The authors argue that operational deployment without rigorous subgroup analysis and human oversight can perpetuate inequities, but that standards, documentation, and responsible-AI practices can mitigate these risks.
finding.measure: Validity, fairness, subgroup bias, policy and governance considerations for assessment systems

paper_profiles.title: How Teachers Can Use Large Language Models and Bloom’s Taxonomy to Create Educational Quizzes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models (LLMs) can support teachers in writing better educational quizzes, and whether pedagogically structured generation is preferable to generic generation. The authors focus on question generation for quiz writing, comparing a simple prompt that asks GPT-3.5 to generate six questions from a passage with a controlled prompting strategy that generates six questions aligned to Bloom’s taxonomy levels (remembering through creating).

The study uses passages from two domains, biology and machine learning, and recruits 24 teachers (12 per domain) to create quizzes under three conditions: handwritten from scratch, with simple generated candidates, and with Bloom’s-taxonomy-controlled generated candidates. Teachers’ quiz-writing time, their use of generated questions, and their preference were measured; independent annotators rated resulting quizzes on coverage, structure, redundancy, usefulness, relevancy, fluency, and answerability. Overall, the quizzes produced with generated questions were comparable in quality to handwritten quizzes, and some metrics suggested improvement—especially coverage. Teachers strongly preferred the controlled Bloom’s-taxonomy condition and copied/edit generated questions more often there, suggesting that pedagogically targeted generation can better support classroom quiz creation at scale.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers used automatically generated questions to create quizzes of comparable or slightly better quality than handwritten quizzes. Across 24 teachers and 72 quizzes, coverage improved significantly when teachers used generated questions, and in the machine-learning cohort the controlled Bloom’s-taxonomy condition also improved usefulness relative to handwritten quizzes.
finding.measure: Quiz quality metrics: coverage, structure, redundancy, usefulness; question-level relevancy, fluency, answerability
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CIs reported for figures, but exact numeric values not reported in the text

finding.finding_summary: Using generated questions did not produce a consistent change in quiz-writing time. Mean completion times were similar across handwritten, simple-generation, and controlled-generation conditions, and the authors report no distinct difference in efficiency; time seemed more dependent on the teacher and passage than on the candidates themselves.
finding.measure: Time taken to write each quiz
finding.confidence_interval: 95% confidence intervals shown in figure; exact numeric values not reported

finding.finding_summary: The controlled Bloom’s-taxonomy prompting strategy improved quiz content quality by helping teachers produce more diverse, higher-coverage quizzes with better alignment to pedagogical goals. Teachers also reported that the taxonomy-aligned questions were especially useful for writing questions that targeted deeper understanding, which suggests support for instructional planning and higher-order questioning.
finding.measure: Structure, redundancy, usefulness, coverage; teacher preference and reported rationale

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Peer, Self, and Teacher Assessments for Generative AI-Enhanced Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teacher, peer, and self-assessments align within the AICoFe system, a GenAI-enhanced feedback environment used in an undergraduate engineering course. The central problem is the difficulty of providing timely, meaningful formative feedback at scale in higher education, especially when feedback must balance human judgment, scalability, and pedagogical validity.

The study analyzes 46 complete evaluation sets from 46 final-year undergraduate engineering students at Universidad Autonoma de Madrid. Each student gave an oral presentation that was assessed with the same validated 15-item rubric by the teacher, two randomly assigned peers, and the student themselves; the teacher also assigned an independent global grade. The authors computed inter-rater agreement, correlations, and paired tests to examine reliability and bias across evaluators.

Results showed moderate to substantial agreement when using Gwet’s AC2 and Kendall’s W, though weighted Cohen’s kappa was lower. Teacher rubric scores were most strongly aligned with the teacher’s own overall grade (r=0.88), peer scores were moderately aligned (r=0.69), and self-assessments were least aligned (r=0.59). The teacher scored rubric items more strictly than peers and her own global grades, while peers and self-assessments tended to be slightly more lenient. Based on these findings, the paper proposes an enhanced GenAI feedback design that gives weighted influence to different evaluators, detects bias/divergence, and generates context-aware explanations rather than simply averaging scores.

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies oral presentation performance in engineering education using a validated 15-item rubric covering delivery, content, and design. Across 46 presentations, peer assessments correlated moderately with the teacher’s overall grade (r=0.69) and self-assessments were weaker (r=0.59), while agreement varied from weak κw (0.22-0.30) to moderate/substantial AC2 (0.58-0.63).
finding.measure: Rubric-based oral presentation assessment (content, design, delivery) and teacher’s independent overall grade

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines evaluative judgment, self-assessment, and peer assessment as durable skills tied to metacognition and reflective practice. Self-assessments aligned only moderately with teacher grades (r=0.59), and the authors interpret the pattern as evidence of calibration/self-perception bias alongside meaningful metacognitive value.
finding.measure: Self-assessment rubric scores, peer assessment scores, agreement indices, and correlations with teacher grades

finding.finding_summary: A major motivation and implication of the paper is scaling formative feedback while managing teacher workload in a large course. The authors argue that GenAI-enhanced aggregation of teacher, peer, and self-assessment can support personalized feedback and reduce the burden of manually synthesizing feedback, although this study itself measures reliability/bias rather than workload directly.
finding.measure: Design analysis of an AI-based collaborative feedback workflow and discussion of workload/scalability implications

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames self-assessment as supporting reflection, self-regulated learning, and student responsibility, but also finds only moderate alignment with teacher grading, suggesting imperfect calibration. Peer and self-scores were slightly more lenient than teacher rubric scores, indicating a mild positive bias but not large divergence.
finding.measure: Self-assessment rubric scores and their correlations with teacher grades; bias comparisons across evaluator types
finding.effect_size: r=0.59; mean difference teacher vs self=+0.36 on rubric scale; mean difference teacher vs peers=-0.49

paper_profiles.title: Equity-Aware Geospatial AI for Forecasting Demand-Driven Hospital Locations in Germany
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of inequitable hospital access in the Saarland region of Germany and asks how demand forecasting and geospatial optimization can be combined to guide future hospital placement through 2030. The authors argue that existing approaches often treat spatial accessibility, demographic forecasting, deprivation mapping, and facility location optimization as separate problems, leaving policymakers without an integrated planning tool.

To address this, the paper proposes EA-GeoAI, an equity-aware geospatial AI pipeline that combines district-level demographic projections, elderly population density, travel-time matrices, deprivation measures, and hospital capacity data. The system computes an Equity Index and accessibility-related metrics, then uses an interpretable agentic optimization framework (including linear programming and CMA-ES weight tuning) to recommend new hospital sites and bed allocations under travel-time, equity, and capacity constraints.

The study is set in Saarland, Germany, and uses publicly available regional datasets on hospital locations, population demographics, disease incidence, and travel times; no surveys or primary data collection were conducted. The model is evaluated against the status quo, a population-weighted heuristic, and ablation variants using metrics such as equity score, travel time, hospital-demand ratio, over-served count, and a Gini coefficient.

The main conclusion is that the integrated agentic planner outperforms the baselines on the paper’s central objectives, especially equity and capacity balance, while also improving accessibility in underserved districts. The authors note limitations including static demand assumptions, incomplete real-world constraints, and dependence on data quality, and they suggest future work on dynamic forecasting, stakeholder input, and additional practical constraints.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed equity-aware geospatial AI pipeline improved hospital planning outcomes relative to the status quo and a population-weighted heuristic. The authors report that the main model achieved an equity score of 0.117 and was described as near the best (almost the lowest) equity score while also improving hospital-facility demand balance, indicating more equitable and better-targeted hospital placement.
finding.measure: Equity score, accessibility score, hospital-facility demand ratio (HFDR), travel time, Gini coefficient, over-served count

paper_profiles.title: PMU measurements based short-term voltage stability assessment of power systems via deep transfer learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of short-term voltage stability assessment (STVSA) in power systems using phasor measurement unit (PMU) data. The goal is to improve the ability of an online assessment model to generalize across different fault types and system topologies, which is difficult when training data are limited to a narrow set of operating conditions.

The authors propose a deep transfer learning framework built around a Transformer-based classifier, together with data augmentation using semi-supervised learning and generative modeling techniques. The approach first expands and restructures the training data using temporal ensembling and synthetic sample generation, then transfers a pre-trained model to target fault datasets and fine-tunes it for the new domain. The workflow is evaluated offline and then mapped to an online monitoring pipeline that uses PMU measurements to classify system states as stable or unstable.

Experiments compare the proposed method against LSTM, decision tree, SVM, and other baselines using accuracy, AUC, MCC, and F1-score. The reported results show that transfer learning substantially improves performance over training without transfer, and that the method remains robust under added noise and across multiple fault datasets. The paper concludes that deep transfer learning can support accurate, adaptable, real-time STVSA from PMU data.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies a technical classification task in power systems: short-term voltage stability assessment from PMU measurements. The proposed transfer-learning Transformer achieves very high classification performance, improving from ACC=0.7862, AUC=0.7553, MCC=0.7026, F1=0.7135 before transfer learning to ACC=0.9847, AUC=0.9983, MCC=0.9661, F1=0.9847 after transfer learning.
finding.measure: Short-term voltage stability classification performance on PMU-based test data (ACC, AUC, MCC, F1-score)

paper_profiles.title: Teacher Learning of Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports on a five-year project studying how science and mathematics teachers learn to enact Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment (TEFA), a pedagogy centered on classroom response systems (“clickers”), rich question cycles, whole-class discussion, and teacher adjustment based on student thinking. The main research problem is not whether TEFA improves student test scores directly, but how teachers change over time, what makes the pedagogy difficult to learn, and what kinds of professional development support that change.

The intervention combined CRS technology, the TEFA pedagogy, and intensive professional development. The PD began with a four-day summer workshop and continued with frequent after-school meetings, on-site support, journals, surveys, classroom video, interviews, and implementation logs. The study involved approximately 39 science and mathematics teachers across multiple western Massachusetts middle and high school sites, with staggered entry and delayed intervention design to allow longitudinal observation and mid-course corrections.

The paper is primarily a set of teacher-change case narratives for four teachers, followed by cross-case observations. Across cases, the authors conclude that TEFA is difficult but learnable, that teachers typically move through tensions around technology use, question design, discourse orchestration, and time constraints, and that many gradually become more student-centered and more skilled at using formative information to adjust instruction. The paper also highlights implementation tradeoffs: TEFA can improve insight into student thinking and increase student discussion, but it requires substantial preparation time, class time, and professional development support; teachers may also adapt TEFA in highly individualized ways, sometimes diverging from the canonical model.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds substantial implementation burden and workload tradeoffs. Teachers repeatedly reported that TEFA required considerable time to craft effective questions, use class time for discussion, manage technology, and integrate the approach into their curricula; however, some teachers also became more efficient over time as they learned the pedagogy and technology. No effect size was reported; evidence comes from implementation logs, journals, interviews, and case narratives across approximately 39 teachers.
finding.measure: Teacher prep time, class time used for TEFA, implementation logs, journals, interviews, and classroom observations

finding.finding_summary: In the mathematics cases, TEFA is reported to support students’ review and understanding of math concepts, especially through discussion, questioning, and real-time adjustment of instruction. The strongest evidence is qualitative and teacher-reported rather than standardized achievement data; for example, Kim and Gina used TEFA to surface misunderstandings and guide review for upcoming math exams, and Kim reported that a well-designed TEFA question led to unusually strong student reasoning and discussion. No effect size or standardized outcome data were reported.
finding.measure: Student mathematical understanding as inferred from discussion quality, teacher observations, and exam review practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper positions TEFA as a means of improving scientific reasoning and conceptual understanding in science classes, and teachers reported that it helped them elicit and respond to students’ thinking about concepts. Across cases, teachers increased the time spent in discussion, the frequency of student-student interaction, and their use of more varied discussion formats, suggesting stronger engagement with reasoning about scientific ideas. No standardized science test scores or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Student reasoning and conceptual discussion in science classrooms, as observed in video, interviews, and teacher reports

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests positive effects on engagement, participation, confidence, and persistence, though evidence is qualitative. Teachers reported that TEFA could increase student participation and change classroom atmosphere, and several teachers noted that students became more willing to discuss, while teachers themselves became more comfortable and persistent in learning the pedagogy over time. No effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student participation, engagement, and teacher persistence/confidence as described in journals, surveys, and interviews

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that TEFA supported metacognition, student discussion, and teachers’ own instructional agility and understanding of students’ thinking. Teachers reported gaining better insight into student thinking and changing lessons based on formative information; classroom discussions became more dialogic, with increased student-student exchange and reduced IRE patterns. No effect size was reported, and the evidence is based on mixed qualitative and descriptive quantitative sources.
finding.measure: Metacognitive/reflective teaching practice, classroom discourse patterns, and teacher adjustment based on student responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that TEFA has potential for scalable implementation and that the project is developing scalable instrumentation and knowledge for future controlled studies, but it also documents significant institutional constraints. These include technology infrastructure gaps in some districts, the need for intensive on-site PD, attrition, and strain on project personnel as the number of participating sites grew. No effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Feasibility of large-scale professional development, school infrastructure readiness, and implementation sustainability

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Bias and Prediction Metrics to Characterise the Fairness of Machine Learning for Equity-Centered Public Health Decision-Making: A Narrative Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the literature on algorithmic bias and fairness metrics for machine learning (ML) in public and population health. The authors ask what types of bias are prevalent in ML systems used for public health decision-making and what quantitative metrics can be used to identify and measure these biases from an equity perspective.

Using a narrative review approach, the authors searched PubMed, MEDLINE, IEEE, ACM Digital Library, ScienceDirect, Springer Nature, and Nature Portfolio for English-language articles published from 2008 to 2023. They identified 72 articles and synthesized common bias sources across the ML lifecycle, including data quality/diversity problems, algorithmic processing issues, cultural and social context mismatches, human-AI interaction problems, feedback loops, access and digital divide issues, regulatory/ethical oversight gaps, and temporal drift.

The paper also compiles a set of fairness and performance metrics used in public health ML, including disparate impact ratio, false positive/negative rates, equalized odds, calibration, predictive parity, balanced accuracy, and related measures. The main conclusion is that fairness must be assessed throughout the ML lifecycle, and that future work should improve ground-truth validity, use context-specific fairness metrics, and ensure access to equity-relevant variables such as race, income, and gender. The review is about public health ML rather than education, so it does not study formative assessment models or K-12 learning outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: A Unified Framework for Pricing Credit and Equity Derivatives
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a unified quantitative finance framework for jointly pricing credit and equity derivatives for the same firm. The authors ask whether a single risk-neutral model with stochastic interest rates, stochastic volatility, and stochastic default intensity can be calibrated to both corporate bond term structures and equity option implied volatility surfaces, and then used to predict credit default swap (CDS) spreads.

The approach combines a Vasicek interest-rate model, a multiscale stochastic default intensity, and a stochastic volatility model for the stock price that jumps to zero at default. Using asymptotic expansions, the authors derive explicit approximate pricing formulas for defaultable bonds, European options, and CDS spreads. They then calibrate the model to Ford Motor Company bond and option data, along with Treasury yield-curve and historical stock/spot-rate data, and compare the resulting model-implied CDS spreads to observed market CDS data.

The paper is not an education study; it does not examine formative assessment or any K-12 outcome. Its main contribution is methodological and financial: the model fits Ford’s implied volatility surface reasonably well, produces CDS spread term structures that match observed CDS data closely even out of sample, and shows that incorporating stochastic interest rates materially improves fit relative to earlier models. The authors also show that, for index options, accounting for stochastic interest rates can perform comparably to adding a slow volatility factor in other benchmark models.

paper_profiles.title: Participation and Performance on Paper- and Computer-Based Low-Stakes Assessments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether low-stakes research-based assessments (RBAs) administered online outside of class produce data comparable to traditional in-class paper-and-pencil administration. The authors are especially interested in two practical issues relevant to formative/low-stakes assessment at scale: whether computer-based testing changes student participation rates and whether it changes student performance scores.

The study was conducted in 25 sections of three introductory college physics courses at a large public Hispanic-Serving Institution over two semesters (n=1,310 after exclusions). Using a stratified random assignment within each course section, students were assigned so that each student completed one assessment online via the LASSO platform and the other in class on paper; the instruments were the FCI, CSEM, and CLASS. The authors modeled participation with hierarchical generalized linear models and performance with hierarchical linear models, and also examined instructor practices intended to improve participation on online assessments.

The main conclusion is that performance on low-stakes assessments was essentially equivalent across online and paper administration: differences were very small, inconsistent in direction, and not statistically significant. Participation, however, was lower for online assessments when instructors did little to support completion; participation on CBT posttests matched paper participation when instructors used the full set of recommended practices (multiple email reminders, multiple in-class announcements, and participation credit for both pretests and posttests). The paper therefore argues that online low-stakes assessment can reduce instructor/class time while preserving measurement quality, but that participation at scale depends strongly on implementation supports and may otherwise overrepresent higher-achieving students.

finding.finding_summary: Performance on low-stakes concept inventories administered as CBTs versus PPTs was equivalent. Across the CI models, adding assessment condition did not reduce variance; the total variance changed only trivially (e.g., 270.79 to 272.7 in Model 2, 266.24 in Model 3), and none of the CBT coefficients were statistically significant. Observed score differences were small and inconsistent, ranging from about -2.1% to 2.2%.
finding.measure: Concept inventory scores on the FCI and CSEM (0-100% scale)

finding.finding_summary: Participation in low-stakes assessments was lower for online CBT administration than for in-class PPT administration when instructors did not use participation supports. Raw posttest participation was 54%-59% for CBT versus 74%-75% for PPT, and models showed that female students were slightly more likely to participate than male students, though gender differences were not statistically significant.
finding.measure: Assessment participation/completion rates

finding.finding_summary: The online LASSO platform was designed to simplify administration, scoring, interpretation, and instructor monitoring of low-stakes assessments, and the authors conclude that it can save class and instructor time while producing data equivalent to paper assessments. Instructors could track participation in real time and send reminder emails, and papers were scanned and matched automatically to online data.
finding.measure: Assessment administration/scoring workflow and instructor effort (qualitative implementation outcome)

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that scalable online assessment infrastructure can expand institutional data collection and research use by aggregating, anonymizing, and sharing student RBA data across courses. At the same time, the authors warn that low-stakes assessments can systematically overrepresent higher-achieving students unless participation is actively supported, creating a potential data-quality and equity limitation for institutional decision-making.
finding.measure: Participation bias / representativeness of assessment data at scale

paper_profiles.title: Fail, flip, fix, and feed – Rethinking flipped learning: A review of meta-analyses and a subsequent meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether flipped learning actually improves student learning, and whether its benefits come from the theoretical elements often claimed for it: pre-class preparation, active in-class learning, formative assessment, and feedback. The authors first review 46 existing meta-analyses to show that previously reported effects vary widely, then conduct their own meta-analysis of 173 quasi-experimental studies (192 independent samples; 532 effect sizes) published through 2019.

The review codes the nature of the pre-class and in-class activities, as well as confounds such as extra instructional time, formative assessment, and instructor consistency. The main conclusion is that flipped learning shows a positive overall effect on academic achievement, but the effect appears to be driven more by extra exposure/time-on-task and by in-class lecture after pre-class preparation than by active learning per se. When active learning is more common in the comparison condition, the advantage of flipping shrinks or reverses; formative assessment/feedback did not meaningfully change the overall effect. The paper argues for a revised model of flipping—"Fail, Flip, Fix, and Feed"—where students attempt problems before instruction so that subsequent teaching can target misconceptions.

finding.finding_summary: Across 173 studies (192 independent samples; 532 effect sizes; 43,278 participants), flipped learning produced a positive overall effect on academic achievement of g=0.37 (SE=0.025, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.41). The same conclusion held in the per-study average (g=0.41, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.48) and a three-level meta-analysis (g=0.41), although heterogeneity was very high (I2=91.27%).
finding.measure: Academic achievement, primarily mid-term or final quizzes and examinations

paper_profiles.title: Innovating transfusion training: a BOPPPS-based blended learning model to enhance nursing interns’ specialized competency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examined whether a structured BOPPPS-based blended learning model could improve nursing interns’ transfusion training compared with traditional rotational instruction. The authors motivated the study by noting that standard clinical internship training often provides unstructured, opportunistic exposure to specialty procedures, leaving gaps in transfusion knowledge, procedural preparation, and self-directed learning (SDL).

Using a prospective, nonrandomized, nonsimultaneous controlled quasi-experimental design with a mixed-methods component, the study compared 40 interns in the intervention group with 38 in the control group during a 4-week internal medicine rotation in a tertiary teaching hospital in China. The experimental group received online/offline BOPPPS instruction built around bridge-in, objectives, pre-test, participatory learning, post-test, and summary phases, while the control group received standard didactic rotational training. Outcomes included transfusion theoretical knowledge, operational skill scores, and SDL ability, with follow-up interviews from the intervention group to explain quantitative results.

Quantitatively, the BOPPPS blended model produced significantly higher theoretical knowledge scores and SDL scores, but did not significantly improve standardized transfusion operational skill scores relative to control. Qualitative interviews suggested that interns found the model engaging, clearer, and more helpful for understanding transfusion procedures and adverse reaction management, while also increasing interest in further specialty learning. Overall, the paper concludes that BOPPPS-blended specialty training is a promising supplement to conventional internship education, especially for strengthening theoretical mastery and SDL, though more intensive practice and better skill assessments may be needed to produce larger procedural gains.

finding.finding_summary: The BOPPPS-based blended training significantly improved transfusion-related theoretical knowledge compared with traditional training. The experimental group scored 68.91±10.53 versus 60.47±17.04 in the control group (n=40 vs n=38; p=0.010), indicating better mastery of specialty transfusion content after the intervention.
finding.measure: Transfusion theoretical knowledge exam score (0-100)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention significantly improved self-directed learning (SDL) ability. Post-intervention total SDL scores were 105.88±7.30 in the experimental group versus 94.84±8.17 in the control group (n=40 vs n=38; p<0.001), suggesting stronger learning autonomy, engagement, and self-regulation.
finding.measure: Nursing College Students’ Independent Learning Ability Scale total score

finding.finding_summary: The qualitative results indicate improved clinical thinking, problem-solving, and learning initiative, but the paper does not report a direct quantitative effect size for these durable skills. Interview themes described clearer understanding of procedures, better confidence in transfusion tasks, and increased interest in exploring other specialties, consistent with gains in metacognition and independent learning.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes; self-reported learning benefits and competence improvements

paper_profiles.title: Peer instruction improves comprehension and transfer of physiological concepts: a randomized comparison with self-explanation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether peer instruction (PI), an interactive learning strategy, improves medical students’ understanding of physiology more than self-explanation (SE), a constructive but individual learning strategy. The authors frame the work around the active-constructive-interactive (ICAP) framework and specifically address the gap in direct head-to-head evidence comparing interactive learning with another active/constructive method, rather than with business-as-usual instruction.

The experiment was conducted with first-year medical students in a physiology course at Leiden University Medical Center. Students were randomly assigned to PI or SE in a pre-post design. They completed baseline recall questions, pre-tests, the intervention on one of two physiology concepts, post-tests, and near/far transfer questions. PI involved paired discussion of multiple-choice concept questions; SE required silent individual reflection and explanation generation.

Results showed that both PI and SE improved comprehension from pre- to post-test, but PI produced a larger gain than SE (post-test improvement +35% vs. +23%, p=0.006). PI also increased the likelihood of turning incorrect answers into correct ones and reduced correct-to-incorrect switching. For transfer, both interventions outperformed the no-intervention comparison on congruent questions, but PI and SE did not differ significantly overall on near or far transfer. The authors conclude that interactive peer discussion is especially effective for conceptual understanding in medical physiology, while transfer benefits are present for both methods and are not clearly superior for PI.

finding.finding_summary: Peer instruction improved first-year medical students’ comprehension of physiological concepts more than self-explanation. Post-test scores increased by 0.27 points in the PI group versus 0.16 in the SE group on a 2-point scale, with the between-group difference significant (F(1,619)=7.671, p=0.006; partial η²=0.012).
finding.measure: Multiple-choice physiology comprehension pre-test/post-test scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper also examined transfer performance as an indicator of applying knowledge to new contexts. Both PI and SE produced higher transfer scores than the control condition on congruent questions (p=0.006), but there was no significant overall difference between PI and SE on near or far transfer (B=0.004, p=0.904).
finding.measure: Near and far transfer multiple-choice questions

paper_profiles.title: Retrieval Practice in Classroom Settings: A Review of Applied Research
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate, Adult
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews applied research on retrieval practice (testing effect) in real classroom settings, asking whether low-stakes tests improve learning beyond simple restudy or no-activity controls, and whether the effect depends on test format, learner age, and feedback. The motivation is practical: while laboratory work strongly supports retrieval practice, classroom recommendations require evidence from authentic educational contexts.

The authors systematically identified 23 empirical classroom studies conducted from elementary school through medical school and organized them by retrieval format: multiple-choice, fill-in-the-gaps, short-answer, free-recall, and comparisons among test types. Across the reviewed studies, retrieval practice was generally beneficial relative to rereading or no activity, especially when corrective feedback was provided. However, the review repeatedly notes that the strongest evidence is against weak control conditions; evidence is less conclusive when retrieval practice is compared with more active alternatives such as concept mapping, copying, or other instructional strategies already used in classrooms.

Overall, the paper concludes that retrieval practice is promising and often effective in classroom environments, but the literature is not yet strong enough to establish that it is superior to alternative active learning strategies. The review also suggests that feedback may be important for younger learners and for some test formats, and that multiple-choice and short-answer tests can both improve later achievement, with some mixed evidence depending on age, feedback, and comparison condition.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review synthesized 23 classroom studies of retrieval practice across age groups and subject areas. Overall, retrieval practice usually improved later performance on quizzes, unit exams, and delayed tests relative to rereading or no-activity controls, but benefits were less consistent when compared with more active learning strategies such as copying or concept mapping, and some studies found no advantage without feedback.
finding.measure: Delayed achievement on classroom tests, unit exams, and course exams following retrieval practice versus control conditions
finding.study_size: n=23 studies (review-level synthesis); individual studies varied

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies used science content, including biology, physiology, probability, light and sound, and general science concepts, and found that retrieval practice improved later science exam performance. Effects were observed on unit exams and delayed retention tests in studies with 8th- and 9th-grade students, undergraduates, and medical students, though some benefits depended on feedback or comparison condition.
finding.measure: Science concept and exam performance (e.g., unit exams, delayed tests, course exams)
finding.study_size: multiple studies; individual n not consistently reported in the review text

finding.finding_summary: One reviewed study focused on probability calculation for high-school students and found that short-answer retrieval practice improved retention of both factual knowledge and application of probability principles one week later. Performance on factual and application questions was equivalent, but both were better than restudy.
finding.measure: Short-answer posttest on probability facts and principle-application questions

paper_profiles.title: The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper revisits the evidence on educational feedback by conducting a meta-analysis of primary studies on feedback effects on student learning. The authors aimed to test and refine the influential Visible Learning conclusions, which had previously been based on meta-syntheses rather than a direct meta-analysis of primary studies. They focused on whether feedback improves learning outcomes overall and which characteristics moderate its effectiveness.

Across 435 studies and 994 effect sizes (N > 61,000), the authors found a positive overall effect of feedback on student learning (random-effects d = 0.55; d = 0.48 after excluding extreme outliers), but with very high heterogeneity. Moderator analyses showed that feedback is more effective when it is high-information, and that feedback aimed at cognitive and physical outcomes tends to outperform motivational and behavioral outcomes. Teacher-to-student feedback was more common and generally more effective than student-to-teacher feedback, while feedback channel was not a significant moderator.

The study spans educational contexts from kindergarten through university, but most evidence came from classroom and school settings, with some higher-education studies included in the feedback-direction moderator. The paper does not analyze subgroup moderators specifically for prior achievement, English learners, disability status, socioeconomic status, or postsecondary students as separate populations; rather, it provides broad moderator evidence about feedback characteristics and study design. Overall, the authors conclude that feedback is beneficial on average, but it is not a single uniform treatment and its effectiveness depends strongly on what the feedback contains and how it is delivered.

finding.finding_summary: This meta-analysis synthesized 994 effect sizes from 435 studies (N > 61,000) and found that feedback improved student learning overall. The random-effects mean effect was d = 0.55 (95% CI 0.48–0.62), and after removing 35 extreme outliers the effect was d = 0.48 (95% CI 0.44–0.51).
finding.measure: Student learning outcomes, including achievement and cognitive performance

finding.finding_summary: The review also analyzed motivational and behavioral outcomes as distinct dependent variables. Feedback showed a smaller positive effect on motivational outcomes (d = 0.33, 95% CI 0.23–0.42; k = 109) and a mixed-to-uncertain effect on behavioral outcomes (d = 0.48, 95% CI -0.09–1.06; k = 30), indicating that feedback was less consistent for these domains than for cognition.
finding.measure: Motivation, locus of control, self-efficacy, persistence, and classroom behavior/discipline
finding.study_size: k=109 motivational effects; k=30 behavioral effects

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats cognitive outcomes broadly, including achievement, retention, and cognitive test performance, and reports a positive overall effect for this category.
