Cognitive outcomes comprised the largest outcome subgroup (k = 597) with d = 0.51 (95% CI 0.46–0.55), suggesting feedback supports higher-order understanding and information processing beyond immediate task performance.
finding.measure: Cognitive outcomes, including achievement, retention, and cognitive test performance

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics appears within the included evidence base, but only as part of the broader cognitive/academic outcome set rather than as a separately pooled math-specific moderator. The paper reports examples of math-test studies in the outlier discussion and confirms an overall positive cognitive learning effect, but it does not provide a dedicated math-specific effect size.
finding.measure: Math test performance as part of cognitive achievement outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Classroom assessment and pedagogy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that formative and summative assessment cannot be fully understood apart from the broader theory of pedagogy. Drawing on prior literature and the authors’ earlier formative-assessment work, it proposes that classroom assessment should be embedded in a model of teaching that includes aims, planning, dialogue, feedback, and summative purposes.

The article is a conceptual/theoretical synthesis rather than an empirical intervention study. It reviews major strands of pedagogy and assessment scholarship, including classroom dialogue, teacher responsiveness, peer- and self-assessment, and the use of summative tests for formative purposes. The authors argue that effective classroom assessment depends on eliciting evidence from all students, using that evidence to adapt instruction, and balancing formative and summative demands rather than sharply separating them.

The paper also examines teacher-generated summative assessment, especially issues of validity, reliability, moderation, and accountability. Using examples such as GCSE science and the King’s-Oxfordshire Summative Assessment Project, it concludes that teacher assessment can contribute meaningfully to summative judgments if supported by clear criteria, sampled tasks, moderation, and professional training. More broadly, the paper contends that high-stakes accountability systems can undermine learning unless assessment design supports both instructional improvement and credible summative reporting.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that teacher summative assessment and moderation can improve rigour, consistency, and confidence, but also adds workload and requires training and support. In the King’s-Oxfordshire Summative Assessment Project, moderation was described as ‘incredibly valuable’ for assessment quality, but the article does not report a quantitative effect size or sample-based workload estimate.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, moderation utility, assessment rigour and consistency

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central claim is that assessment design, accountability, and moderation practices shape classroom pedagogy and institutional assessment systems. It argues that systems relying solely on external tests can undermine learning, while teacher-involved summative assessment with moderation and contextual value-added accountability can support more valid and useful institutional judgments.
finding.measure: Assessment system validity, accountability effects, moderation structures, school-level summative assessment practices

finding.finding_summary: A major theme is that dialogue, peer assessment, self-assessment, and formative feedback support metacognition, collaboration, and critical review. The paper synthesizes prior evidence rather than presenting new estimates, and it does not report an effect size; its conclusion is that these classroom practices are more effective than rote recitation for developing durable learning capacities.
finding.measure: Dialogue quality, metacognition, collaboration, critical thinking, peer/self-assessment processes

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses formative feedback and classroom dialogue as supporting learners’ motivation, engagement, and sense of agency, especially when feedback focuses on improvement rather than grades. It also notes that praise, recasting, or high-stakes accountability can have negative motivational effects, but the paper does not provide a quantitative estimate.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, learner agency, response to feedback and praise

paper_profiles.title: A review of predictive factors of student success in and satisfaction with online learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews research on factors associated with student success, satisfaction, and persistence in online learning, with a particular focus on adult learners in postsecondary settings. The review asks what learner characteristics, course design features, and instructional practices predict stronger outcomes in online environments, and whether online learning is as effective as traditional face-to-face instruction.

The paper synthesizes prior comparative studies, course design studies, and correlational studies of learner attributes. It discusses evidence that online learning can be comparable to traditional learning on achievement outcomes, especially when courses are well structured and interactive, but that satisfaction is strongly tied to clear design, instructor feedback, collaboration, and practical relevance. It also highlights learner traits linked to online success, including self-regulation, time management, motivation, emotional intelligence, and reflective/visual learning preferences, while noting that some commonly assumed differences such as learning style or technology self-efficacy do not reliably predict performance.

The review emphasizes that many studies relied on self-report and GPA, and that important moderation questions remain unresolved, especially for students with disabilities and students from different socioeconomic backgrounds. It concludes that institutions should provide explicit support for both students and instructors, design courses with alignment and feedback, and continue research on readiness, course size, and accessibility in online learning.

finding.finding_summary: Across the studies reviewed, online learning was often comparable to or better than face-to-face instruction on achievement measures, but results varied by course design and context. A US Department of Education meta-analysis cited in the review reported a modest advantage for online/blended learning outcomes versus traditional instruction (online d=0.20 overall; blended d=0.35, fully online d=0.05), while individual studies sometimes found no significant differences in course passing rates or GPA.
finding.measure: Course grades, GPA, course passing rates, course tests, midterm/final exam scores

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies self-regulation, self-discipline, motivation, persistence, and time management as key predictors of success and persistence in online learning. Several cited studies found these traits to be associated with better outcomes, while barriers such as low motivation and poor time management were repeatedly linked to dropout and lower performance.
finding.measure: Self-report surveys of motivation, persistence, time management, self-regulation; course success/retention indicators

finding.finding_summary: The review treats reflective learning, collaboration, communication, organization, planning, and metacognitive/self-evaluative skills as central to online success. It reports that well-designed online courses can foster self-directed learning and community building, and that independent-learning abilities were among the strongest predictors of online readiness in the reviewed literature.
finding.measure: Learner surveys, readiness scales, course participation/discussion indicators, self-directed learning measures

finding.finding_summary: The review notes that reading and writing proficiency are important for online learning success because communication and course participation occur primarily in writing. It cites the development of the TOOLS instrument and related work indicating that reading and writing proficiency was crucial to student performance in online courses, although the review does not report a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Reading and writing proficiency / literacy readiness

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of Peer Assessment on Academic Performance: A Meta-analysis of Control Group Studies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether peer assessment improves students’ academic performance, and whether its effects vary by educational level and several implementation features. The authors note that prior work on peer assessment has largely relied on narrative reviews and correlational evidence, so they synthesize only experimental and quasi-experimental control-group studies to estimate causal effects on achievement.

The meta-analysis includes 54 studies (k = 141 effect sizes; 55 articles in the full search flow) across primary, secondary, and tertiary settings and across subjects such as writing, science, IT, language, and statistics. The outcome is academic performance measured with non-self-reported tasks and grades. The overall effect of peer assessment is positive and small-to-medium (g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.18, 0.44]), with benefits versus no assessment (g = 0.31) and teacher assessment (g = 0.28), and no significant difference versus self-assessment (g = 0.23, ns).

finding.finding_summary: Peer assessment produced a small-to-medium positive effect on literacy-related outcomes, especially writing. Across the meta-analysis, the writing subgroup showed g = 0.30 to 0.35 depending on the analysis, with significant gains in academic performance compared with control conditions. The effect was present across a mix of elementary, secondary, and tertiary writing studies, though the review did not isolate a single standardized writing measure across all studies.
finding.measure: Writing performance / academic performance in writing tasks
finding.study_size: n=54 studies; writing subgroup n=22 studies, k=48 effect sizes (descriptive table shows 36 studies and 81 effects for written-component analyses)
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI = 0.18 to 0.44 (overall); writing subgroup CI not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Across non-writing academic subjects, peer assessment also improved performance. The overall meta-analytic effect on academic performance was g = 0.31 (95% CI [0.18, 0.44]), and the effect did not meaningfully differ between writing and other subjects (b = -0.003, p = .979). This suggests peer assessment benefits transfer across disciplines such as science, IT, language, medicine, statistics, accounting, and arts.
finding.measure: Non-self-reported academic performance across subjects (e.g., science, IT, language, statistics, medicine, accounting, arts)

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively discusses peer assessment as a formative practice that may affect learning-related motivation and perceptions, but the quantitative synthesis did not directly measure these constructs as primary outcomes. Evidence reported here is indirect: the review notes that peer assessment is theorized to influence motivation and engagement, yet the meta-analysis itself focuses on academic performance only. No pooled effect size for social-emotional outcomes is reported.
finding.measure: Not directly measured in the meta-analysis; discussed as a theoretical mechanism and implementation factor

finding.finding_summary: The review centrally engages with skills such as critical engagement, comparison, evaluation, and self-review as plausible mechanisms of peer assessment, but these were not directly meta-analyzed as outcomes. The paper argues that peer assessment may improve students’ evaluative judgment and metacognitive processing, yet the empirical synthesis reported achievement outcomes rather than direct durable-skill measures. No pooled effect size for durable skills is provided.
finding.measure: Not directly measured; discussed in relation to evaluative judgment, metacognition, and critical engagement

paper_profiles.title: Twins’ Early Development Study (TEDS): A Multivariate, Longitudinal Genetic Investigation of Language, Cognition and Behavior Problems from Childhood Through Adolescence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the Twins’ Early Development Study (TEDS), a large longitudinal twin cohort in the United Kingdom designed to examine the genetic and environmental origins of cognitive, language, academic, and behavioral development from early childhood through adolescence. The article is primarily a study profile/methods paper rather than an evaluation of an educational intervention, and it summarizes the sample, measures, assessment waves, and major findings from the broader TEDS program.

TEDS follows twins assessed repeatedly from ages 2 through 14 using parent report, in-home testing, telephone testing, teacher ratings, and later web-based assessments. Core academic measures include reading, mathematics, and teacher-assessed National Curriculum performance, alongside language and cognitive batteries. The paper emphasizes that both genetic and environmental factors shape performance, with genetic influences showing substantial overlap across language, reading, and mathematics, and environmental influences tending to be more domain-specific.

The article does not focus on formative assessment as an intervention, nor does it report moderator analyses by English learner status, disability status, socioeconomic status, or postsecondary participation. However, it does document the use and validity of teacher assessments and other educational measures within a large population sample. Overall, the main contribution is methodological and descriptive: it establishes the TEDS resource and summarizes evidence that learning abilities and disabilities are influenced by shared genetic liability and developmental continuity across time.

finding.finding_summary: The paper summarizes multiple TEDS findings showing substantial genetic and environmental contributions to reading development and reading difficulty. In one cited 7-year-old twin study, teacher-reported reading performance and low performance were substantially influenced by genetic factors, and web/teacher reading measures were used to support longitudinal prediction from preschool language and nonverbal ability to later reading. No single effect size is reported in this article for reading outcomes, but the broader program is described as showing high heritability and meaningful environmental influence.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension, word reading efficiency, teacher-assessed reading performance, reading difficulty

finding.finding_summary: TEDS includes extensive language assessment and the paper summarizes evidence for both genetic and environmental influence on early language development. Prior TEDS studies cited here found strong overlap among lexical, grammatical, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics skills, with correlations such as r=.54 between parent-based PARCA and standardized nonverbal language-related composites in validation work; however, the article itself is a program description and does not present a new primary language effect estimate.
finding.measure: Vocabulary, grammar, semantics/pragmatics, syntax, language impairment

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that TEDS has investigated mathematics in middle childhood and found high heritability with moderate shared environmental influence in the first studies of mathematics. It also reports that a web-based composite of five mathematics tests correlated r=.58 with teacher-assessed mathematics composite based on UK National Curriculum criteria, indicating good concurrent validity of the assessment approach rather than an intervention effect.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement, teacher-assessed mathematics composite, web-based mathematics composite

paper_profiles.title: The evaluation of an evidence-based model of feedback implemented on an undergraduate dental clinical learning environment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examined whether introducing a structured, evidence-based model of feedback (MOF) could improve the feedback experience in an undergraduate dental clinical learning environment. The authors were responding to a common problem in clinical education: feedback is important, but it is often inconsistent, rushed, and difficult to operationalize in busy settings. Their model was designed to make feedback more dialogic, individualized, and future-oriented, while also adding a preparatory step to support patient safety in the dental clinic.

The intervention was implemented in a Dublin Dental University Hospital with third- and fourth-year undergraduate dental students. Forty-four students participated in a 4-week trial of the six-step feedback model, first through an anonymous online survey and then through six focus groups. The model emphasized learning goals at the start of the session, examples of good work, reflective dialogue, individualized performance feedback, action planning, and peer discussion.

Overall, students responded positively to the new model. Survey results showed that 64% viewed it as a good intervention, 83% wanted to continue using it, and 77% linked feedback to improved performance. Qualitative themes indicated that the model enhanced learning opportunities, supported future-oriented improvement, improved alignment with individual competency goals, created space for feedback, and encouraged peer feedback. The study concluded that structured, evidence-based feedback practices can support self-regulation and learning in clinical education, though time constraints and student reluctance to seek feedback remain important barriers.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that the feedback model improved their learning experience, helped them feel supported, and was associated with improved individual performance. In the survey, 83% preferred to continue using the model, 98% said regular feedback was important, and 77% linked feedback to better performance on clinical sessions (n=44).
finding.measure: Student survey responses about feedback value, preference to continue, perceived performance improvement, and qualitative perceptions of learning support

finding.finding_summary: The model was intended to strengthen reflective ability, self-assessment, self-regulation, and goal-directed improvement, and students described it as helping them identify what went well, what to improve, and how to apply prior learning to future sessions. The qualitative data strongly supported gains in reflection, feedback literacy, and peer learning, although no standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Survey and focus group evidence on reflection, self-assessment, goal-setting, and peer feedback

finding.finding_summary: The intervention aimed to improve the structure and consistency of feedback delivery in a busy clinical setting, but time pressure remained the most common barrier. Students valued having dedicated time for feedback and 66% reported time constraints as limiting feedback access, indicating that the model improved organization but did not eliminate workflow challenges.
finding.measure: Student survey responses and qualitative reports about time constraints and feedback delivery process

finding.finding_summary: At the institutional level, the study suggests that adopting a standardized feedback model can improve consistency and clarity in clinical teaching practices. Students described the previous approach as non-standardized, while the new model was viewed as a more coherent and sustainable institutional feedback process; however, the evidence is limited to one school and one short implementation period.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of standardization, consistency, and sustainability of the feedback process

paper_profiles.title: Assessment as a positive influence on 21st century teaching and learning: A systems approach to progress
paper_profiles.population: Not explicitly bounded; general K-12 and broader educational systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual/perspective piece arguing that educational assessment, when properly designed and used, can positively support 21st-century teaching and learning goals. Pellegrino frames the problem as the mismatch between current assessment practices and the deeper learning competencies needed for college, careers, and civic life, such as critical thinking, communication, collaboration, and problem solving.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the paper synthesizes prior research and policy reports to propose a systems view of assessment. It discusses three core frameworks: assessment as reasoning from evidence, learning progressions, and evidence-centered design (ECD), and it explains how these should guide classroom and large-scale assessment design. The paper also emphasizes that assessments should be aligned with curriculum and instruction, provide formative information to teachers and students, and support a balanced assessment system.

The context is primarily K-12 education in the United States, though the author notes that the principles apply broadly across educational systems and levels. The main conclusion is that assessments should be instructionally sensitive, valid, reliable, fair, and part of coherent systems that use multiple measures over time. The article does not report original empirical data; instead, it argues that better-designed assessments can improve learning and reduce the harmful effects of narrow, high-stakes testing.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that coherent, balanced assessment systems can improve educational practice by aligning curriculum, instruction, and assessment, and by making assessment more instructionally useful and fair. It does not report original effect sizes or experimental estimates; instead it synthesizes conceptual and policy arguments that assessment should support learning rather than merely audit it.
finding.measure: Conceptual/policy analysis of assessment system design

finding.finding_summary: The article centers on higher-order competencies such as critical thinking, problem solving, collaboration, metacognition, and communication as key targets for 21st-century assessment. It argues that assessments should directly measure these competencies, but provides no empirical estimates of their effects.
finding.measure: Conceptual treatment of higher-order competencies and assessment targets

finding.finding_summary: The paper mentions motivation, engagement, and learning support as intended benefits of formative and improved assessment systems, especially when assessments are used to assist learning. However, these are discussed conceptually rather than as measured outcomes, and no empirical results are reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of motivation/engagement in assessment use

paper_profiles.title: Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This meta-analysis examines how instructional support helps learners in higher education develop diagnostic competences in medical and teacher education. The paper focuses on whether problem-solving and several forms of scaffolding—examples, prompts, role assignments, and reflection phases—improve diagnostic performance, and whether these effects differ by learners’ prior professional knowledge and by contextual features of the diagnostic task.

The review synthesizes 35 empirical studies conducted with postsecondary learners, including medical students, nursing students, teacher education students, and related in-service samples. Across the studies, diagnostic competence was measured using objective outcomes such as diagnostic accuracy, expert ratings of reasoning, knowledge tests, scenario/video-case assessments, and related performance measures. The meta-analysis finds a moderate positive overall effect of instructional support on diagnostic competences (g = 0.39, 95% CI [0.22, 0.56]), with notable heterogeneity.

Moderator analyses show that prior knowledge matters: learners with lower prior professional knowledge benefit more from highly guided scaffolds, while more advanced learners benefit more from scaffolds that require higher self-regulation, such as reflection-oriented supports. Problem-solving itself appears beneficial regardless of prior knowledge base, and the effects vary by scaffold type and context. Overall, the paper concludes that instructional support can effectively facilitate diagnostic competence in higher education, especially when aligned with learners’ developmental stage and the structure of the diagnostic task.

finding.finding_summary: Instructional support had a moderate positive effect on diagnostic competences across 35 studies (n=3472, k=35; g=0.39, 95% CI [0.22, 0.56]). The outcome is captured through diagnostic reasoning, professional vision, clinical reasoning, and related competence measures rather than a single uniform test.
finding.measure: Diagnostic competence / diagnostic reasoning / professional vision / clinical reasoning performance

paper_profiles.title: A Review of Feedback Models and Theories: Descriptions, Definitions, and Conclusions
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual review; no single study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of major feedback models and theories in education. The authors aimed to clarify how feedback has been conceptualized over time, what mechanisms are proposed to explain its effects, and how the most influential models differ in their assumptions about learners, tasks, and instructional context.

Rather than evaluating one intervention in a single sample, the paper identifies and compares 14 prominent publications, including theoretical pieces, narrative reviews, and meta-analytic reviews. The review traces the field from early behaviorist and systems perspectives through cognitive and self-regulated learning frameworks, and it emphasizes recurring themes such as discrepancy reduction, learner engagement with feedback, self-assessment, and the importance of task, learner, and instructional factors.

The authors conclude that feedback is no longer best understood as information simply delivered to students; instead, it is an interactive process in which learners interpret, generate, and act on feedback. They highlight the evolution toward more comprehensive and context-sensitive models, and they propose that future work should integrate shared elements across models. Because this is a conceptual review, it does not test a new intervention or report a new empirical effect on students.

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how formative assessment might be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard (BB), in a university setting. The authors frame the problem as a need for more frequent, feedback-rich assessment in a technology-driven higher education environment, arguing that formative assessment can improve learning by giving students timely information about their progress and mistakes.

The proposed approach was a series of weekly or fortnightly online tests delivered through Blackboard, with immediate automated feedback and explanations. The paper describes the test design and the Blackboard features used, then reports survey data on students’ perceptions of continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and the BB test option. Students generally supported frequent online assessment and valued the immediate feedback, flexibility, and ability to study smaller topic units; some also reported concern that too many tests could increase stress and overemphasize learning over grades.

The study was conducted with university students at Swinburne University of Technology’s Sarawak campus, and it compares perceptions across Business, Engineering, and IT streams. The authors conclude that Blackboard-based formative assessment is workable and can support ongoing learning, particularly by providing immediate feedback and helping students monitor their understanding. The paper is largely descriptive and perception-based; it does not report achievement gains from an experimental comparison, but it argues that formative assessment may improve summative performance and be especially helpful for lower achievers.

finding.finding_summary: Students generally supported frequent internal assessments delivered as open-book online tests through Blackboard. The paper reports that a majority favored splitting course work into 10–12 weekly BB assessments because it helped them study small topics, check learning step by step, and receive immediate feedback, but it did not report objective achievement gains.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment and Blackboard online tests

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined student perceptions related to motivation, confidence, and stress under formative assessment. Students valued immediate feedback and said it helped them identify strengths and weaknesses and stay on track, though some worried that frequent assessments created stress/pressure to perform.
finding.measure: Survey responses on motivation, feedback value, and stress/pressure associated with frequent assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes metacognitive benefits of formative assessment, especially helping students reflect on feedback and correct mistakes without delay. Students reported that the process helped them understand individual topics progressively and monitor whether they were on track, but no direct test of metacognitive skill gains was reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of feedback, self-monitoring, and progressive learning

finding.finding_summary: The Blackboard implementation was presented as an efficient way to administer frequent assessments and return immediate feedback with less delay than traditional classroom tests. The paper argues that online tests and automated review screens can improve the speed and convenience of assessment delivery, but it does not measure workload or productivity outcomes quantitatively.
finding.measure: Perceived convenience and immediacy of online assessment/feedback delivery

paper_profiles.title: Student Explanation Strategies in Postsecondary Mathematics and Statistics Education: A Scoping Review
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 27th Annual Conference on Research in Undergraduate Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This scoping review examines how student explanation strategies are used in postsecondary mathematics and statistics education. The authors reviewed 46 peer-reviewed studies published from 2014 to 2024 and organized the literature into three categories: self-explanation, peer explanation, and explanation to fictitious others.

The paper asks how this literature can be categorized and what patterns emerge across study types, instructional settings, and theoretical explanations for why student explanation might improve learning. Rather than testing a single intervention, it synthesizes evidence from prior studies on retrieval practice, generative learning, and social presence to explain why these strategies may support learning in higher education STEM courses.

Across the reviewed studies, self-explanation and explaining to fictitious others were described as supporting individual cognitive processing and generative thinking, while peer explanation added collaborative benefits but also risks such as domination by stronger students or reinforcement of misconceptions. The review concludes that the effectiveness of these strategies varies by implementation, duration, and context, and suggests that explanation to fictitious others may reduce some downsides of peer explanation. Overall, the paper provides a conceptual synthesis of postsecondary explanation-based learning research rather than new primary outcome data.

finding.finding_summary: Across 46 postsecondary mathematics and statistics studies, student explanation strategies were generally associated with improved learning outcomes, but the review emphasizes that results varied by strategy and implementation. Self-explanation and explanation to fictitious others often supported conceptual learning and transfer, while peer explanation sometimes improved achievement but could also introduce misconceptions or unequal participation.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes, academic achievement, conceptual learning, transfer, proof comprehension, problem-solving performance, and statistics performance

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that peer explanation and related collaborative approaches were associated with higher motivation, social presence, and engagement in postsecondary mathematics and statistics settings. However, these benefits were context-dependent and could be undermined when more knowledgeable students dominated discussions.
finding.measure: Motivation, social presence, arousal, and engagement-related outcomes

finding.finding_summary: A central theme of the review is that student explanation supports durable skills such as metacognition, cognitive elaboration, and collaborative sense-making. The authors argue that self-explanation and explanation to fictitious others foster generative thinking, while peer explanation can additionally promote discussion and perspective-taking.
finding.measure: Metacognitive processes, generative thinking, collaboration, and explanatory quality

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (educator-facing review; primarily discusses undergraduate and K-12 examples rather than studying a specific participant population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative, practice-oriented review that examines how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback. The authors organize their discussion around a formative assessment framework: clarifying where learners are going, understanding where learners are, and identifying how to move learners forward.

The paper does not report a new empirical study. Instead, it synthesizes prior research and provides examples of prompts and use cases for educators, including rewriting learning objectives into student-friendly language, co-constructing success criteria, generating sample work at varying quality levels, and creating formative questions and feedback. The discussion emphasizes that LLMs can help scale formative assessment and reduce teacher workload, but should augment rather than replace expert pedagogy.

The paper is written for educators and researchers and uses illustrative examples from high school biology and undergraduate fMRI instruction, alongside broader comments on classroom implementation. Its main conclusion is that accessible LLMs can support formative assessment when used with pedagogical judgment, but current evaluation benchmarks and prompt practices need to be better aligned with formative-assessment principles. The authors also highlight concerns about student overreliance, prompt quality, contextual fit, and the need for future work on robust evaluation metrics and AI-aware assessment design.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can save educators time by automating or accelerating tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating formative questions, and producing sample work and feedback. This is a conceptual/practice claim rather than an empirical effect estimate; no sample size, effect size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / time saved in formative assessment tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review claims LLM-supported formative assessment can foster metacognition, self-regulation, and critical thinking by helping students interpret learning goals, evaluate exemplars, and reflect on feedback. These are presented as pedagogical benefits supported by prior literature and examples, not as direct empirical findings from this paper.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-regulation, critical thinking in formative assessment activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses LLM use in generating and simplifying learning objectives and sample work for subjects such as biology and fMRI/neuroimaging, with the goal of improving clarity of instruction and alignment to course goals. This is an instructional synthesis with illustrative examples rather than a direct study of student academic outcomes.
finding.measure: Quality/clarity of learning objectives and exemplar work for subject-specific instruction

paper_profiles.title: SocioEconomicMag Meets a Platform for SES-Diverse College Students: A Case Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a multi-phase case study of SocioEconomicMag (SESMag), an emerging usability inspection method designed to help software practitioners identify socioeconomic inclusivity bugs in educational technology. The authors ask whether SESMag can reveal real access, literacy, risk, self-efficacy, and authority-related barriers that disproportionately affect low-SES users, and whether redesigns based on those findings improve a learning platform.

The case study followed a team building a learning management platform for college students over 16 months. In Phase 1, the team used SESMag with a low-SES persona to inspect four scenarios and identified inclusivity bugs in 76% of evaluated questions. In Phase 2, interviews with a college instructor and a recent low-SES student validated all identified bugs except one, and the interview data repeatedly aligned with the SESMag facets. In Phase 3, the team redesigned the prototype using the facet explanations as guidance. In Phase 4, seven SES-diverse first-year CS students from a community college and a public university used the revised prototype in think-aloud sessions; the fixes eradicated 45%–54% of the previously identified bugs overall, with some bug types eliminated at rates of 80% or higher.

Overall, the paper concludes that SESMag is useful for surfacing and localizing socioeconomic inclusivity problems in educational software and that facet-based redesigns can improve inclusivity for SES-diverse college students. The study is primarily a methodological case study rather than an effectiveness trial of a student learning intervention, but it provides evidence that inclusive design changes can reduce barriers tied to SES-related differences in access, literacy, time constraints, and trust in technology.

finding.finding_summary: The SESMag-informed redesign reduced the prevalence of previously identified inclusivity bugs in a learning platform used by SES-diverse college students. In the think-aloud study with seven participants, the revised prototype eradicated 45%–54% of the bugs overall, and some bug types were eradicated at rates of 80% or higher.
finding.measure: Think-aloud task completion on redesigned learning platform; bug eradication / presence of SES-inclusivity bugs across scenarios

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that a socioeconomic inclusivity inspection method can help a development team identify, validate, and fix platform barriers that affect low-SES college students. Across the case study, practitioners identified SES-inclusivity bugs in 76% of evaluated questions, and interviews with an instructor and student validated all but one of those bugs, indicating potential institutional value for improving educational technology design and accessibility.
finding.measure: SESMag evaluation bug detection and stakeholder validation of platform inclusivity issues
finding.study_size: n=4 evaluation team in Phase 1; n=2 interviewees in Phase 2; n=7 think-aloud participants in Phase 4

paper_profiles.title: The Development of the College Park Tornado of 24 September 2001
paper_profiles.venue: University of Maryland, Department of Meteorology (Master of Science thesis)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This thesis investigates the synoptic, mesoscale, radar, satellite, and numerical-model conditions associated with the F3 College Park, Maryland tornado of 24 September 2001. The central question is not about schooling or instruction, but about how atmospheric features combined to produce a long-track tornadic supercell that caused substantial urban damage across the Washington, DC–Maryland region.

The author analyzes GOES satellite imagery, WSR-88D and TDWR radar data, upper-air soundings, and MM5 mesoscale model output initialized at 1200 UTC on 24 September 2001. The study describes a negatively tilted upper-level trough, strong vertical wind shear, warm moist low-level flow, and mesoscale instability as key ingredients supporting severe convection and tornadogenesis. Radar analyses show a hook echo, a high-reflectivity knob, tornadic cyclone signatures, and eventual evolution toward a bow echo as the storm weakened.

A major conclusion is that the MM5 model reproduced many observed features of the event and provided useful operational guidance hours in advance, including a previously unobserved solitary wave/density current that may have triggered deep convection. Overall, the paper argues that coordinated use of numerical model guidance, satellite imagery, and radar data can help forecasters anticipate and monitor severe convective outbreaks and tornado development.

paper_profiles.title: A Method for Estimating Individual Socioeconomic Status of Twitter Users
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint addresses the problem of measuring individual socioeconomic status (SES) from digital trace data, where direct income, education, and occupation information is usually unavailable. The authors argue that the commercial and entertainment brands Twitter users follow can function as behavioral indicators of economic and cultural capital, and they adapt correspondence analysis from political-ideology estimation to construct a continuous SES scale for users.

The study uses the Twitter followings of 339 U.S. consumer and media brands and a very large sample of 3,482,652 U.S. Twitter users. The method is validated in several ways: brand-level SES is compared with Facebook Marketing API audience education profiles, user-level SES is compared with self-reported job titles and salaries for 42,099 users, and individual SES estimates are compared with education and income in a survey sample of 200 (education) and 182 (income) respondents.

The main conclusion is that the proposed SES measure shows meaningful convergent validity: higher estimated SES corresponds to higher educational attainment, higher salaries, and more advantaged occupational classes, especially at the aggregate level. However, individual-level correlations are modest, indicating that the method captures a real SES signal but also substantial noise. The authors also report weak or non-significant associations with age, gender, race, political ideology, and urban/rural residence, suggesting the measure is not simply proxying those other demographics.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes a scalable measurement method for estimating individual socioeconomic status (SES) from Twitter followings, enabling new large-scale research on inequality when direct SES data are unavailable. Validation analyses show the measure correlates with established SES proxies, including education (Spearman ρ=0.269 for n=200 survey respondents), income (ρ=0.188 for n=182), mean salary for job titles (ρ=0.673 for n=42,099), and occupational class (ρ=-0.640 for n=42,099), suggesting institutional usefulness for social-science research and data collection.
finding.measure: Validity of a Twitter-following-based SES estimation method; correlations with education, income, salary, and occupational class
finding.study_size: n=3,482,652 users (main estimation); validation subsamples n=42,099, n=200, n=182

paper_profiles.title: The Digital Divide in Generative AI: Evidence from Large Language Model Use in College Admissions Essays
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether the rapid spread of large language models (LLMs) changed how college applicants write admissions essays and whether those changes are distributed equitably across socioeconomic groups. The authors ask three linked questions: how essay language changed over time, whether estimated LLM use differed by socioeconomic status (SES), and whether the association between essay characteristics and admissions outcomes shifted after ChatGPT became widely available.

The study analyzes a de-identified longitudinal dataset of 81,663 applications submitted to a highly selective U.S. university across five admission cycles (2019–2020 through 2023–2024). SES is proxied using fee-waiver status. The authors estimate essay-level LLM use with a distribution-based detector trained on human essays and synthetic GPT-4o essays, then compare linguistic features, LLM-use patterns, and admissions outcomes using descriptive analyses, difference-in-differences models, stratified logistic regressions, interaction models, and a mediation-style change-in-coefficient analysis.

The main findings are that essays converged linguistically after 2023, especially among lower-SES and rejected applicants; estimated LLM use rose sharply in 2024 for all groups but more so for lower-SES applicants; and LLM use was negatively associated with admissions, with a substantially larger penalty for lower-SES applicants than for higher-SES applicants. The authors interpret this as evidence of a digital divide in generative AI: lower-SES students appear to adopt LLMs at higher rates, yet they do not receive equal returns from that use in a high-stakes admissions setting. The paper is explicitly observational and cautions that it cannot establish causal effects of LLM availability on admissions decisions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds substantial post-2023 convergence in essay writing features, including lexical diversity and complexity, with larger changes among lower-SES and rejected applicants. Among post-GPT LLM users, lower-SES applicants produced shorter essays with slightly lower lexical diversity (e.g., MTLD 90.88 vs. 95.78, d not reported) and higher repetition (Yule’s K 112.00 vs. 108.42), suggesting improved surface polish but persistent or greater inequities in writing quality indicators.
finding.measure: Admissions essay linguistic features (type-token ratio, Maas TTR, MTLD, HDD, Yule’s K, average word length, sentence length, complexity)
finding.study_size: n=81,663 overall; post-GPT LLM-user comparison n=10,626 (7,377 higher SES; 3,249 lower SES)
finding.effect_size: d=0.15 (for mean estimated LLM usage by SES); other effect sizes not_reported
finding.std_deviation: Reported in tables for some measures (e.g., MTLD SD=21.39 higher SES, 19.79 lower SES; ˆα SD=0.169 lower SES, 0.119 higher SES)

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that the socioeconomic admissions gap widened in the post-GPT period. In the difference-in-differences model, the lower-SES × post-GPT interaction was negative and statistically significant (β=-0.170, OR=0.844, 95% CI [0.727, 0.979], p=0.025), indicating an additional 15.6% reduction in admission odds for lower-SES applicants relative to higher-SES applicants after LLMs became widely available.
finding.measure: Binary college admissions decision and admission-rate gap by SES across pre- vs. post-GPT eras

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s strongest outcome result is in college admissions, where estimated LLM usage is negatively associated with admission probability. In the post-GPT interaction model, higher-SES applicants show a negative association between LLM use and admission odds (β=-0.922, OR=0.398), but the penalty is significantly larger for lower-SES applicants (interaction β=-1.028, OR=0.358), yielding a total lower-SES association of β=-1.949 (OR=0.142).
finding.measure: Predicted admission probability / binary admission outcome from logistic regression using estimated LLM usage
finding.effect_size: β=-0.922 (higher SES baseline); β=-1.028 interaction; total lower-SES β=-1.949
finding.confidence_interval: Higher SES OR [0.264, 0.600]; interaction OR [0.147, 0.868]; total OR [0.065, 0.313]

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs may function as a substitute for scarce writing support and may lower barriers to essay production, especially for lower-SES students. However, this is inferred from adoption patterns rather than directly measured productivity: lower-SES applicants were 28% more likely to fall into the high-intensity LLM-use category, suggesting perceived efficiency or access gains in writing support.
finding.measure: Estimated LLM usage category and essay generation patterns
finding.study_size: n=17,654 post-GPT sample for SES comparisons
finding.effect_size: d=0.15 for mean estimated LLM usage difference by SES; high-use category 22.7% lower SES vs. 18.7% higher SES
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.169 lower SES, 0.119 higher SES for estimated LLM usage

paper_profiles.title: Embedded Formative Assessment in the Undergraduate Engineering Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues for the pedagogical value of embedded formative assessment in undergraduate engineering classrooms and explains how technology has made real-time collection and analysis of student responses more feasible. The authors frame formative assessment as a way to make student thinking visible, help instructors adjust instruction, and promote active learning, metacognition, and conceptual change.

The paper is primarily a conceptual and practitioner-oriented overview rather than an empirical study. It discusses classroom response systems, mobile polling, and open-format tools such as InkSurvey as ways to reduce clerical burden and make formative assessment easier to implement in large engineering classes. The paper also emphasizes that the instructional benefit depends on instructor responsiveness to student feedback and on using questions that reveal reasoning, not just right-or-wrong answers.

Examples are drawn from an undergraduate electromagnetics course with 60 third-year engineering physics majors, where students responded to open-format questions about Gauss’s law using digital ink. These examples are used to illustrate common student misconceptions, limited calculus fluency, and the value of seeing student work in real time. Overall, the paper concludes that embedded formative assessment can improve undergraduate engineering learning, but it has greater potential when instructors use the feedback to adapt teaching and when questions are designed to expose student thinking.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that embedded formative assessment supports metacognition, critical thinking, and deeper reasoning by making student thinking visible and prompting students to reflect on what they know and do not know. In the classroom examples, open-format questions revealed students’ reasoning processes, misconceptions, and shortcut strategies, but no quantitative effect size or formal outcome analysis was reported.
finding.measure: Classroom open-format responses and qualitative inspection of student reasoning processes; metacognition and critical thinking discussed conceptually

finding.finding_summary: A central claim is that technology-assisted formative assessment reduces the clerical burden on instructors by streamlining the collection and immediate review of student responses. The paper does not report a quantified workload reduction, but it repeatedly emphasizes that clickers, texting, and tools like InkSurvey make real-time formative assessment more practical in large classes.
finding.measure: Instructor burden / ease of collecting and reviewing student responses

paper_profiles.title: On Using Chatbots to Promote Smoking Cessation Among Adolescents of Low Socioeconomic Status
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of youth smoking cessation among adolescents of low socioeconomic status (SES), who face structural barriers to accessing in-person treatment such as transportation, family obligations, and limited provider availability. The authors argue that because smartphone and texting use are very common among adolescents, mobile interventions may be a promising way to deliver more accessible cessation support.

The paper is not an intervention trial; rather, it is a brief review and position paper that synthesizes prior work on adolescent smoking cessation and on conversational agents. It discusses motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioral therapy as promising counseling approaches, reviews existing mobile and chatbot-based cessation tools, and highlights limitations of current systems (e.g., limited conversational flexibility and weak evidence of long-term efficacy). The paper suggests that AI chatbots could be used to simulate human-like support, extend treatment over longer periods, and improve access for low-SES adolescents.

Overall, the authors conclude that chatbots are a plausible future delivery mechanism for adolescent smoking cessation, but existing evidence is limited and current systems are not yet sufficient. The paper emphasizes the need for data-driven chatbot design, evaluation of long-term outcomes, and integration with clinical care rather than replacement of providers.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not report a direct evaluation of a chatbot intervention or any measured change in motivation, persistence, or self-regulation. It only argues, based on prior literature, that mobile conversational support may help adolescents engage in smoking cessation and that current tools may improve accessibility for low-SES youth.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment II. Indications of Effectiveness in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.population: High School; Undergraduate; Graduate; Community college
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether InkSurvey, a free web-based tool for real-time formative assessment using pen-enabled mobile devices, can support learning across a range of educational settings. The authors frame the problem as the need for an efficient, robust way to collect open-ended student responses during instruction and to use them immediately to diagnose misconceptions and adjust teaching.

The paper presents seven vignettes from diverse contexts, including high school algebra, undergraduate and graduate university courses, community college, and engineering/physics classrooms in the United States and Mexico. Across these cases, instructors used InkSurvey to pose open-format questions and students responded with digital ink, sketches, graphs, and written solutions. Reported evidence is largely descriptive and comparative, drawing on exam results, quiz performance, class observations, and student surveys.

The main conclusion is that InkSurvey appears to be effective for real-time formative assessment across varied disciplines, devices, and educational levels. Reported benefits include improved learning gains, greater student engagement and metacognition, quicker identification of misconceptions, and more responsive instruction. Because the paper is primarily a set of case illustrations rather than a controlled causal study, its evidence is suggestive rather than definitive.

finding.finding_summary: In a high school Algebra I setting, students receiving regular formative feedback through InkSurvey showed stronger mastery of fundamental concepts than students not exposed to the intervention, as measured by standards-based assessments. The paper does not report effect sizes, but it notes especially strong gains for female students; survey items also found 70% of females vs. 48% of males agreed InkSurvey helped them know what they understood and what needed further help.
finding.measure: Standards-based Algebra I assessments; student attitude survey item about understanding

finding.finding_summary: Across physics, engineering physics, chemical engineering, and food chemistry examples, InkSurvey was associated with improved conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. One physics vignette reports that after a lesson on triple integrals, only 1 of 87 students later showed the misconception on exam questions, compared with 12 of 103 in a comparison section without InkSurvey; another engineering physics course reported steady improvement in problem-solving skills over the semester, and chemical engineering students increased from about 1.8 to 3.1 on a 4-point competence scale after guided simulation plus InkSurvey probing.
finding.measure: Summative exam questions on conceptual understanding; problem-solving skill scores; 4-point competence ratings
finding.study_size: n=87 and n=103 for one comparison; other vignette samples not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Student surveys and focus-group comments indicate improved engagement, motivation, and perceived usefulness of feedback. In an advanced laboratory class (n=63), 86% agreed that InkSurvey gave the instructor a better understanding of what they did and did not understand, and 76% said creating InkSurvey responses helped them better understand the material or realize what they did not understand.
finding.measure: Anonymous student survey; focus-group feedback; attitude items

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports gains in metacognition, self-assessment, and problem-solving. In the advanced laboratory survey (n=63), 76% of students said InkSurvey helped them better understand what was being covered or what they did and did not understand; elsewhere, the authors describe improved student reflection on their own processes as learners and steady improvement in problem-solving skill scores across the semester.
finding.measure: Student survey items on understanding/metacognition; analyzed problem-solving responses over time
finding.study_size: n=63 for the survey; other samples not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that InkSurvey helps instructors identify common difficulties quickly and tailor instruction in real time, improving classroom efficiency and responsiveness. Student comments and instructor reflections emphasize that immediate feedback lets the class move on when understanding is adequate and revisit concepts promptly when it is not, but no formal workload or efficiency metric is reported.
finding.measure: Instructor observations; student comments on immediacy of feedback and pacing

paper_profiles.title: Disability data futures: Achievable imaginaries for AI and disability data justice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how AI and data systems can reproduce disability exclusion and ableism, and argues for disability-led approaches to create more just data futures. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, it offers four reflective, disciplinary perspectives on how AI and disability data might be redesigned to support disability justice.

The paper is organized as a collective writing piece by four scholars/advocates, each proposing a different “imaginary” for change: rethinking records as collaborative and multilateral, improving disability data collection and accessibility, synthesizing inclusive design and participatory methods for disability-centered AI, and reshaping institutional leadership and governance. The context is broad and cross-sectoral, with particular emphasis on health, public systems, and AI/data infrastructures.

The main conclusion is normative and conceptual: current disability data practices are often exclusionary and can amplify harm when embedded in AI, but more inclusive futures are achievable if disabled people are involved in all phases of data and AI work. The chapter does not report original empirical results, but instead synthesizes prior literature and proposes actionable principles for disability data justice, accessibility, community engagement, and institutional leadership.

paper_profiles.title: Community College Articulation Agreement Websites: Students’ Suggestions for New Academic Advising Software Features
paper_profiles.venue: Community College Journal of Research and Practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study examines the user experience problems community college transfer students encounter when using ASSIST, California’s centralized articulation-agreement website. The paper asks what new academic-advising software features students would want in order to make transfer planning, course selection, and articulation-agreement interpretation easier.

The authors surveyed and interviewed 24 California community college transfer students enrolled at UC or CSU campuses, using open-ended survey responses and semi-structured interviews conducted in late 2021. They analyzed the data with structural coding and thematic analysis to identify recurring feature requests.

Students’ suggestions clustered into four broad themes: automating laborious advising tasks, reducing ambiguity in articulation agreements, preventing mistakes in term-by-term planning, and supporting online advising and peer communication. Specific proposed features included finding equivalent courses at other community colleges, identifying programs close to completion, labeling requirements as mandatory vs. recommended, notifying students of report updates, tracking progress toward transfer requirements, showing prerequisites and historical course offerings, and adding advisor/peer communication tools.

The main conclusion is that transfer students see substantial value in a more interactive, transparent, and planning-oriented ASSIST platform. The study does not test whether these features improve transfer outcomes; rather, it provides design requirements and user needs evidence suggesting that current articulation-agreement websites are difficult to use and may contribute to planning errors, confusion, and extra effort for students.

finding.finding_summary: Students consistently described ASSIST-related and transfer-planning tasks as time-consuming and error-prone, and they wanted software features to automate these tasks. The paper reports qualitative evidence from n=24 transfer students that features like querying equivalent courses, tracking requirements, and notifying users of report changes could reduce manual searching, repetitive checking, and planning mistakes; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative student suggestions and reported time/effort burdens in academic advising and transfer planning

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on institutional features of the ASSIST articulation-agreement system and the broader transfer infrastructure, emphasizing how website design, report updating practices, and communication mechanisms shape student access to transfer information. Based on interviews with n=24 students, the paper argues that clearer labeling, annual report publication, change notifications, and advisor access could improve institutional transparency and reduce transfer confusion; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions of articulation-agreement website design, report governance, and transfer-system transparency

paper_profiles.title: Bayesian Hierarchical Models with Calibrated Mixtures of G-Priors for Assessing Treatment Effect Moderation in Meta-Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint addresses the statistical problem of estimating treatment effect moderation in individual participant data meta-analysis (IPD-MA). The authors argue that standard Bayesian shrinkage priors can over- or under-shrink moderator effects when trials differ in size, variability, sparsity, and correlation structure, making it difficult to identify which baseline characteristics genuinely moderate treatment response.

To address this, they propose calibrated mixtures of g-priors (CMG), which combine moderator-level shrinkage with trial-level sample-size tuning. They compare CMG against flat priors, horseshoe priors, stochastic search variable selection, and several standard mixtures of g-priors through simulation studies and then illustrate the approach on an IPD-MA of four randomized controlled trials comparing duloxetine and vortioxetine for adults with major depressive disorder.

The simulation results show that CMG methods generally reduce error and improve estimation risk, especially under high between-trial variability, high sparsity, weak moderation, and correlated predictors. In the depression case study, CMG and related shrinkage methods yield much narrower posterior distributions than the flat model and suggest age, smoking status, diabetes, anxiety, and antidepressant use may be the most plausible moderators, although no interaction has a 95% credible interval excluding zero. The paper is methodological rather than educational, so it does not study student outcomes or formative assessment.

paper_profiles.title: Consistent Bayesian meta-analysis on subgroup specific effects and interactions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a statistical problem in meta-analysis: how to obtain subgroup-specific treatment effects and subgroup interactions that remain consistent with each other when subgroup prevalence varies across studies. The authors argue that conventional subgroup pooling can produce mismatches between subgroup effects and interaction estimates because of differing subgroup contributions across trials, leading to aggregation bias and non-collapsibility problems.

To solve this, the paper proposes Contribution-adjusted Meta-analysis by Subgroup (CAMS), a Bayesian framework that adjusts subgroup analyses using study-specific information fractions (a proxy for subgroup prevalence). CAMS is shown to recover the same interaction inference as a within-trial contrast-based Bayesian Interaction Meta-analysis (BIM) while retaining interpretable subgroup effect estimates, and the method can also be implemented in frequentist or likelihood frameworks.

The paper is demonstrated on published randomized trial subgroup data in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, comparing treatment effects by age and disability (EDSS) subgroup. The examples show that unadjusted subgroup pooling can differ from within-trial interaction estimates, whereas CAMS aligns with BIM and appropriately handles influential studies with unusual subgroup composition. The main conclusion is that subgroup and interaction analyses should be contribution-adjusted when subgroup prevalences differ, and that reporting subgroup effects at an information-fraction-based prevalence can improve coherence and interpretability.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes a method intended to improve how subgroup effects and interactions are reported in meta-analyses, reducing aggregation bias and improving coherence between subgroup and overall estimates. In the MS example, CAMS reproduced BIM-equivalent interaction estimates (e.g., RR ratio interaction 1.45, 95% CrI 1.11–1.87 for age; 1.35, 95% CrI 1.06–1.73 for EDSS) and showed how reporting at an overall information fraction can make subgroup summaries more stable and interpretable.
finding.measure: Methodological consistency of subgroup and interaction meta-analysis; posterior interaction estimates and credible intervals in an MS example
finding.study_size: n=7 trials in the main example (EDSS analysis also included one additional small study)

paper_profiles.title: A tutorial for propensity score weighting for moderation analysis: An application examining smoking disparities among sexual minority adults
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a methodological tutorial on how to estimate and test moderation effects in observational data using propensity score (PS) weighting. The authors focus on the practical problem that standard interaction or stratified regression analyses can produce biased estimates of effect heterogeneity when treated and comparison groups are not comparable within levels of a moderator.

The paper presents a step-by-step workflow: checking overlap, estimating PS weights within moderator strata, assessing covariate balance, fitting doubly robust weighted outcome models, and conducting sensitivity analyses for unobserved confounding. Although the tutorial is broadly generalizable, the worked example uses data from 41,832 adults in the 2019 National Survey on Drug Use and Health to examine whether gender moderates the association between sexual minority status and past-month smoking.

In the illustrative application, the authors find successful covariate balance after weighting and significant moderation. The estimated smoking risk difference for lesbian/gay/bisexual (LGB) versus heterosexual adults is 0.15 for females and 0.05 for males, with the interaction term indicating moderation (coefficient 0.65, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.04). Sensitivity analysis suggests the female estimate is relatively robust to unobserved confounding, whereas the male estimate is more sensitive and should be interpreted cautiously.

finding.finding_summary: The paper demonstrates a practical analytic workflow for estimating moderation effects with propensity score weighting, showing that weighting can improve covariate balance within moderator strata and support more credible subgroup-effect estimation. In the case study (n=41,832 adults), balance diagnostics after weighting showed all absolute SMDs and KS statistics below 0.10, indicating successful balance; the interaction term for gender was significant (0.65, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.04).
finding.measure: Propensity score balance diagnostics (standardized mean differences and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics) and moderated treatment-effect estimation in a weighted logistic regression

paper_profiles.title: Disability data futures: Achievable imaginaries for AI and disability data justice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how artificial intelligence and data systems can reproduce disability exclusion and ableism, and argues for disability-led approaches to data justice. Rather than testing an intervention, it offers a set of normative, future-oriented “social imaginaries” for rethinking how disability data are collected, interpreted, governed, and used in AI systems.

The paper is organized as a collective writing piece by four scholars and disability advocates, each contributing a perspective on a different leverage point: records and documentation, disability data measurement, inclusive design and participatory methods, and leadership/culture in institutions. Across these sections, the authors argue that current disability data practices often undercount or misclassify disabled people, exclude them from datasets, and limit AI accountability. They propose emancipatory futures grounded in disability justice, universal design, human-centered design, community-based participatory research, and disability representation in governance and leadership.

The chapter is conceptual and advocacy-oriented, centered on health, data, and institutional systems rather than educational interventions or student outcomes. Its main conclusion is that disability data justice requires disabled people’s participation across the full lifecycle of data and AI systems, and that meaningful inclusion depends on redesigning both technical infrastructures and organizational cultures.

paper_profiles.title: Sociodemographic inequalities in student achievement: An intersectional multilevel analysis of individual heterogeneity and discriminatory accuracy (MAIHDA) with application to students in London, England
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how student achievement varies across intersecting sociodemographic characteristics, and whether those differences are better explained by additive main effects or by higher-order interaction effects. The authors argue that conventional analyses of achievement gaps can miss important heterogeneity because they focus on single characteristics or average group differences, rather than multiple overlapping forms of disadvantage.

Using an intersectional multilevel analysis of individual heterogeneity and discriminatory accuracy (MAIHDA), the study analyzes administrative data from the National Pupil Database for two cohorts of London students in the 2018/19 academic year: 90,744 students at age 11 and 71,321 students at age 16. Intersectional strata were defined by combinations of age-in-year, gender, free school meal (FSM) eligibility, special educational needs (SEN) status, and ethnicity. The outcome was standardized achievement in English and mathematics at age 11 and standardized achievement across English, mathematics, and other GCSE subjects at age 16.

The main conclusion is that intersectional strata explain a substantial portion of achievement variation in the unadjusted models (about 30% at age 11 and 25% at age 16), but this is driven overwhelmingly by additive effects of the sociodemographic characteristics rather than by interaction effects. After adjusting for main effects, only a very small amount of stratum-level variation remains (about 1.3% VPC), although some specific intersections—especially combinations involving FSM, ethnicity, and SEN—show meaningful deviations from additivity. The authors conclude that educational inequality in this setting is strongly socially patterned, that multiply marginalized students should remain a policy focus, and that intersectional MAIHDA is a useful tool for studying educational disparities.

finding.finding_summary: The paper's central outcome is standardized student achievement, measured at age 11 and age 16. In the unadjusted MAIHDA models, intersectional strata explained about 30% of variance at age 11 and 25% at age 16, indicating substantial between-stratum differences in achievement. After adding main effects for age-in-year, gender, FSM, SEN, and ethnicity, about 97% of the age-11 stratum variance and 96% of the age-16 stratum variance was explained, leaving only a small residual role for interaction effects.
finding.measure: Standardized achievement scores from Key Stage 2 English and mathematics tests (age 11) and GCSE English, mathematics, and other subject examinations (age 16)

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that intersectional MAIHDA can improve how education systems identify and understand achievement inequalities, especially for multiply marginalized students. The authors conclude that policy should pay greater attention to intersecting sociodemographic disadvantage and suggest that targeted or proportionately targeted support may be more effective than relying on single-factor indicators such as FSM alone.
finding.measure: Variance partitioning coefficient (VPC), proportional change in variance (PCV), and predicted intersectional stratum effects used to infer policy-relevant inequality patterns

paper_profiles.title: A novel density-based approach for estimating unknown means, distribution visualisations and meta-analyses of quantiles
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a statistical problem in meta-analysis: many studies report only quantiles such as medians, quartiles, and ranges rather than means and standard deviations, making conventional inverse-variance meta-analysis difficult. The authors propose a density-based approach that fits flexible quantile-based distributions to summary data so that unknown means, standard deviations, and approximate densities can be estimated without assuming a fixed parametric form upfront.

The paper develops two main tools. First, it uses the generalized lambda distribution and the skew logistic distribution to reconstruct distributions from three-point and five-point summaries, enabling estimation of means/SDs and visualizing underlying distribution shapes. Second, it introduces meta-analytic methods directly for quantiles and functions of quantiles, including confidence intervals and pooled comparisons of medians, quartiles, and IQR ratios.

The methods are evaluated with simulations and a real data example from COVID-19 age summaries across studies of survivors and non-survivors. The results show that the proposed approaches estimate means at least as well as, and often better than, commonly used methods from the literature, while also providing useful distribution visualizations and quantile meta-analysis capabilities. The real example demonstrates substantial heterogeneity in age distributions and statistically significant differences in quartiles and dispersion between groups.

paper_profiles.title: Moderator Simulation for the Compact Positron Source at NLCTA
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how to maximize slow-positron production for a compact positron source planned for the NLCTA at SLAC. The authors use G4beamline/GEANT4-based simulations to study the target, adiabatic matching device (AMD), radiofrequency (RF) decelerating cavity, and multiple moderator geometries, with the goal of improving the number of positrons that are slowed and reemitted from tungsten moderators.

The work first optimizes the target material and thickness for a 100 MeV electron beam, finding that 7 mm tungsten performs about as well as tantalum while being more practical. The authors then show that an AMD plus a five-cell L-band RF cavity substantially increases the fraction of positrons entering the moderator at low energy, which in turn raises moderator yield. They also derive and fit a modified stopping-distribution model for thin foils and compare traditional polycrystalline foils, a grid moderator, and a single-crystal tungsten moderator.

Overall, the single-crystal tungsten moderator is reported as the best design among those tested, especially when paired with the AMD and RF cavity. In the simulated setup, the full system achieves a 39.3× improvement in moderated positron output relative to a simple polycrystalline foil moderator without the cavity. The paper is therefore primarily an accelerator/particle-physics engineering optimization study rather than an education study.

paper_profiles.title: Moderator: Moderating Text-to-Image Diffusion Models through Fine-grained Context-based Policies
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of moderating text-to-image diffusion models so they are less able to generate harmful or policy-violating images. The authors argue that existing moderation approaches are too coarse and fail to account for context, diverse prompts, and interactions among multiple moderation goals.

To solve this, they introduce Moderator, a policy-based model management system that lets administrators specify fine-grained moderation rules using a semi-structured policy language (method, object/action/style, and purpose).
