Moderator uses self-reverse fine-tuning to derive task vectors from model-generated examples, then modifies model weights to suppress target content while preserving unrelated generation quality. The system also includes automatic policy expansion, multiple moderation methods (remove, replace, mosaic), and multi-policy interference handling.

The paper evaluates the system on Stable Diffusion and Stable Diffusion XL using harmful prompts, CLIP-based image-text similarity, and LLM-as-judge harm ratings, and compares against baseline moderation methods. It also includes a usability study with 14 adult participants acting as administrators and an experiment with 32 Stable Diffusion users. The main conclusion is that Moderator can substantially reduce harmful generations, can be authored reasonably quickly by non-expert admins, and can enforce multiple policies with manageable side effects on non-target content.

finding.finding_summary: Moderator improved administrative policy-authoring efficiency: 14 participants produced policies that passed unit tests in an average of 2.29 iterations and 2.11 minutes per policy. Participants also reported a mean System Usability Scale score of 80.71, indicating the interface was easy to use for policy creation and debugging.
finding.measure: Policy authoring iterations, task completion time, and SUS usability score

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that a policy-based moderation system can be operationalized for managing TTI model behavior at the system level. In user testing with 32 Stable Diffusion users, Moderator prevented 65% of users from generating moderated content within 15 attempts and increased the remaining users' attempts by an average of 8.3x, suggesting meaningful governance/control impact over model misuse.
finding.measure: Success in generating moderated content under repeated attempts; number of attempts required
finding.effect_size: 65% prevented; 8.3x more attempts for remaining users

paper_profiles.title: Definition drives design: Disability models and mechanisms of bias in AI technologies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines how definitions of disability shape the design of AI systems used for decision-making. Rather than evaluating a specific deployed intervention, the authors develop a critical framework for analyzing bias in AI through the stages of problem formulation: defining scope, selecting data, deciding the system’s use, and specifying operational definitions. They argue that bias is not inherent to AI itself but emerges from sociotechnical design choices that encode particular disability ideologies.

The paper centers on two illustrative decision-making contexts: healthcare priority-setting and government benefits eligibility review. Using these settings, the authors contrast three conceptual models of disability—the medical, social, and relational models—to show how different definitions lead to different information requirements, outputs, and downstream harms or benefits. The discussion is grounded in critical disability studies, HCI, and sociotechnical AI research, and emphasizes the need for disability-led, participatory design.

The population discussed is disabled people, especially people with mobility-related disabilities such as spinal cord injuries and wheelchair users, in North American and UK contexts. The paper does not report empirical testing of an intervention or dataset; instead, it is a conceptual/theoretical analysis intended to guide more equitable AI development and assessment in disability-related decision-making systems.

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that AI systems used in healthcare and government benefits can reproduce or reduce institutional bias depending on how disability is defined at design time. Rather than reporting an empirical effect size, it provides a conceptual framework showing that operational definitions of disability shape downstream decisions, with potential harms such as exclusion, curative violence, and inequitable eligibility determinations.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of AI problem formulation in healthcare and government benefits decision-making

paper_profiles.title: Student self-management, academic achievement: Exploring the mediating role of self-efficacy and the moderating influence of gender—insights from a survey conducted in 3 universities in America
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether students’ self-management is associated with academic achievement, and whether self-efficacy mediates that relationship while gender moderates it. The paper is motivated by prior work suggesting that students who plan, monitor, and regulate their learning tend to perform better academically, but it specifically tests the role of self-efficacy and gender within this pathway.

The authors surveyed 289 students from three universities in the United States. Self-management was measured with a Likert-scale questionnaire, self-efficacy with the General Academic Self-Efficacy Scale, and academic achievement with a self-reported Likert measure. The sample was mostly undergraduate students (56.4%), with master’s and PhD students also included. The study reports positive correlations between self-management and academic achievement, and between self-management and self-efficacy, as well as between self-efficacy and academic achievement.

Mediation analysis suggests that self-efficacy carries part of the relationship between self-management and academic achievement, with a bootstrap confidence interval reported as not including zero. By contrast, gender does not significantly moderate the self-management–achievement association. Overall, the paper concludes that strengthening students’ self-management may improve academic achievement partly by increasing self-efficacy, but this relationship appears similar across genders in this sample.

finding.finding_summary: Self-management was strongly and positively associated with academic achievement in the sample of n=289 university students. The reported Pearson correlation was r=0.987 (p<0.01), and the regression model also found a positive association between self-management and academic achievement (t=103.027, p=0.000).
finding.measure: Academic achievement (self-reported Likert-scale measure)

finding.finding_summary: Self-management was positively related to self-efficacy (r=0.870, p<0.01) in the survey of n=289 students. The authors interpret this as evidence that students who better regulate their learning and behavior also report stronger academic self-efficacy.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy (General Academic Self-Efficacy Scale)

finding.finding_summary: Self-efficacy was positively associated with academic achievement (r=0.787, p<0.01). In the mediation model, the indirect pathway self-management ⇒ self-efficacy ⇒ academic achievement was reported as significant because the bootstrap interval did not include zero (BootLLCI=0.369, BootULCI=0.558).
finding.measure: Academic achievement and self-efficacy
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI 0.369 to 0.558 (reported for bootstrap interval); indirect effect CI not clearly reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats self-management as a core durable skill and finds it is positively related to academic achievement. In the sample of n=289 university students, self-management showed a very strong positive correlation with achievement (r=0.987, p<0.01).
finding.measure: Self-management (Likert-scale self-management survey)

paper_profiles.title: Sensitivity analysis for an unobserved moderator in RCT-to-target-population generalization of treatment effects
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a generalizability problem in randomized trials: how to estimate treatment effects for a target population when treatment effect moderators differ between the trial sample and the population, and some moderators are not observed in the target population dataset. The authors frame this as a sensitivity-analysis problem for RCT-to-population transportability, focusing on two cases: a specific moderator observed in the RCT but missing from the target dataset (V), and a broader unobserved composite moderator not even measured in the RCT (U).

Methodologically, the paper develops several sensitivity-analysis approaches, including outcome-model-based, weighting-based, and hybrid weighted-outcome-model methods for the V case, and bias-formula-based plus weighting-plus-bias-formula methods for the U case. These methods are designed for situations where the outcome is not observed in the target population and where researchers want to bound how much the target average treatment effect (TATE) could vary under plausible assumptions about the missing moderator(s). The paper also includes simulation studies comparing the methods under correct and misspecified outcome models.

The empirical application is a smoking cessation RCT (CTN9) conducted with adults in community substance use treatment programs, generalized to U.S. adults seeking substance use treatment who smoke at least 10 cigarettes per day. The authors identify baseline cigarette addiction severity as a key moderator measured in the RCT but not in the target population dataset (NSDUH), and use the proposed sensitivity analyses to show that the treatment effect remains negative across plausible target-population values of that missing moderator. Overall, the paper concludes that the intervention would likely reduce smoking in the target population, while demonstrating how sensitivity analysis can quantify uncertainty from unobserved effect modifiers.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main empirical application is not an educational intervention but a transportability analysis applied to a smoking cessation RCT in adult substance use treatment programs. Using outcome-model-based and weighted-outcome-model-based sensitivity analyses, the authors estimated target-population treatment effects ranging from about -9.87 to -5.13 cigarettes/day across plausible values of the missing moderator, and from about -8.36 to -4.83 cigarettes/day under the weighted approach, indicating reduced smoking in the target population.
finding.measure: Mean number of cigarettes smoked per day over the 8 weeks after the target quit date
finding.confidence_interval: Outcome-model-based: 95% CI from (-12.51, -7.23) to (-7.98, -2.28); weighted-outcome-model-based: 95% CI from (-12.50, -4.23) to (-8.76, -0.90)

paper_profiles.title: How Can Predictive Learning Analytics and Motivational Interventions Increase Student Retention and Enhance Administrative Support in Distance Education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether predictive learning analytics (PLA) can be used to identify undergraduate students at risk of not completing their studies and to target them with low-cost motivational interventions. The central question is whether combining a Student Probabilities Model (SPM) with proactive contact from Student Support Teams can improve retention and course completion in distance education.

The intervention was tested at the Open University UK with undergraduates who had a 31–40% predicted probability of completing their course. Students were randomly assigned to a control group or an intervention group; the intervention consisted of an initial text message, followed by a phone call, or an email if the student could not be reached. The study compares retention at multiple course milestones, from course start through 25%, 50%, 100%, and completion.

Results showed statistically significant retention advantages for the intervention group at all milestone points when analyzed as a combined intervention, with the largest difference at course completion. However, when phone and email interventions were compared separately to control, the differences at course completion were not statistically significant, suggesting that the short early intervention improved progression and retention but may not have been sufficient by itself to guarantee long-term completion for all students. The paper concludes that PLA can help institutions target support more efficiently and at scale, improving administrative support while positively affecting retention outcomes in distance education.

finding.finding_summary: The targeted motivational intervention improved student retention and progression, indicating better persistence/engagement among at-risk undergraduates. In the combined intervention analysis (control n=318; intervention n=312), retention was higher at course start (87.7% vs 94.2%, p=.004), 25% FLP (86.8% vs 93.9%, p=.002), 50% FLP (73.6% vs 88.1%, p=.001), 100% FLP (65.7% vs 77.6%, p=.001), and course completion (45.9% vs 56.1%, p=.010).
finding.measure: Course retention / continuation at milestones; course completion

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the predictive model and targeted outreach improved the administration of student support at scale and low cost by helping Student Support Teams focus limited resources on students most at risk. The Student Probabilities Model identified at-risk students more accurately than single indicators (55% correctly identified as non-completers vs. 34–42% for some existing indicators), supporting more efficient allocation of outreach effort.
finding.measure: Accuracy of at-risk student identification; scalability/low-cost administrative support
finding.study_size: n=1,968 selected as at-risk by SPM; study intervention n=630

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that predictive learning analytics can strengthen institutional retention practices by enabling more systematic identification and support of at-risk students. The SPM was presented as a more reliable institutional process than existing ad hoc indicators, and the authors argue it can be adopted by other institutions to guide retention and support strategies.
finding.measure: Institutional retention practice / targeting of student support

paper_profiles.title: Emotional Intelligence and Academic Performance Among College Students: A Quantitative Analysis
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Education and Human Development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether emotional intelligence (EI) is associated with academic performance and student retention among undergraduate students. The authors focus on five Bar-On EQ-i dimensions—intrapersonal skills, interpersonal skills, stress management, adaptability, and general mood—and ask which aspects of EI are most strongly related to college GPA and continued enrollment.

Using a convenience sample of 200 undergraduates from a mid-sized university, the study collected self-reported EI scores, current and high school GPA, demographics, and retention status in a cross-sectional correlational design. The main findings were that stress management and general mood were the strongest and most consistent predictors of both GPA and retention, while adaptability showed a smaller positive association with GPA. Intrapersonal and interpersonal scores were not significantly related to GPA. Logistic regression also showed that higher stress management and general mood modestly increased the odds of retention.

The authors conclude that emotional regulation and positive affect may be more important for persistence and academic success than EI as a broad construct. They suggest higher education institutions should incorporate stress-management, resilience, and emotional wellness supports into student services and first-year programming to improve retention and success. Because the study is cross-sectional and based on self-report, the findings are correlational rather than causal, but they point to potentially actionable student-support strategies in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: Higher emotional intelligence, especially stress management and general mood, was associated with better college GPA in a sample of n=200 undergraduates. Stress management correlated most strongly with GPA (r=.31, p<.01) and remained a significant predictor in regression (β=0.25, p<.01), while general mood also predicted GPA (r=.28, p<.01; β=0.21, p<.01).
finding.measure: Self-reported college GPA

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies emotional intelligence subdomains tied to self-regulation, stress management, mood, and persistence. In this n=200 undergraduate sample, stress management (r=.31, p<.01) and general mood (r=.28, p<.01) were positively related to academic outcomes, and both also predicted retention (OR=1.09 and OR=1.07, respectively).
finding.measure: Bar-On EQ-i subscales; self-reported retention status; self-reported GPA

finding.finding_summary: The study examined college retention as an institutional outcome and found that emotional intelligence variables predicted continued enrollment. In logistic regression, general mood (OR=1.07, p<.05) and stress management (OR=1.09, p<.05) significantly increased the odds of retention, while age and ethnicity were not significant predictors.
finding.measure: Self-reported retention status (continuously enrolled from previous term)

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Review on Student Engagement in Undergraduate Mathematics: Conceptualization, Measurement, and Learning Outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review examines how student engagement (SE) has been conceptualized, defined, measured, and linked to learning outcomes in undergraduate mathematics. The authors were motivated by the widespread claim that engagement supports achievement, course completion, persistence, and related outcomes, but noted that prior mathematics-specific evidence was fragmented and often focused narrowly on particular instructional approaches or measurement tools.

Using PRISMA guidelines, the review screened 1,584 records and included 48 empirical papers published between 2009 and 2024. The papers covered a range of undergraduate mathematics contexts, including statistics, algebra, calculus, developmental mathematics, and complex analysis, and used quantitative, mixed-methods, and qualitative designs. Across the literature, the most common research aims were evaluating instructional methods/tools, understanding learning behavior, and examining factors of academic success.

The review found substantial heterogeneity in SE definitions and measurement. Only 23 papers explicitly defined SE, and measurement relied mainly on process data (especially log files), self-reports, product data, and attendance records. SE was most often studied as behavioral engagement, while cognitive and affective dimensions were less frequently and less consistently operationalized. For learning outcomes, the review reports that less than half of the studies examined links between SE and outcomes, and that the evidence generally supported positive associations, but the paper is primarily a mapping/synthesis review rather than a pooled effects meta-analysis.

Overall, the paper concludes that undergraduate mathematics SE research would benefit from clearer conceptual boundaries, more transparent measurement choices, and stronger alignment between theory, context, and outcome measurement. The review emphasizes that engagement is activity-specific and dynamic, and recommends more coherent and longitudinal approaches to studying how engagement relates to achievement and other learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed undergraduate mathematics studies, student engagement was generally positively associated with mathematics learning outcomes such as grades, performance, and mastery-related measures. The review does not report a pooled effect size, but it summarizes that less than half of the included studies examined this relationship and that the overall pattern in the corpus was positive.
finding.measure: Mathematics grades, performance scores, quiz/homework/formative assessment scores, mastery-related outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review primarily synthesizes student engagement as a social-emotional/behavioral construct and reports that many studies found engagement to be higher under instructional approaches that supported autonomy, interaction, or active participation. Where engagement itself was measured over time, one pre-post study reported increases in most engagement indicators across a semester, though attentiveness and achievement orientation did not change.
finding.measure: Self-reported engagement scales, observation-based engagement indicators, log-file engagement indicators
finding.study_size: n=48 papers in review; one longitudinal study discussed as pre-post

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies linked engagement with processes relevant to durable skills such as self-regulation, persistence, and strategic learning, and the review notes that behavioral engagement indicators often included perseverance, time on task, and sustained effort. The synthesis indicates that these dimensions were commonly treated as part of engagement and were generally improved by active or supportive instructional designs, but the review does not provide pooled estimates.
finding.measure: Persistence, effort, time on task, self-regulatory strategy use, strategic engagement indicators

paper_profiles.title: The Employer Potential of MOOCs: A Mixed-Methods Study of Human Resource Professionals’ Thinking on MOOCs
paper_profiles.venue: International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how employers, specifically human resource (HR) professionals, perceive massive open online courses (MOOCs) as tools for recruiting, hiring, and professional development. The authors note that although MOOCs had received substantial media attention, there was very little peer-reviewed evidence on how employers value them or whether they could serve as signals of employee skill, motivation, or continued learning.

To address this gap, the Finding and Developing Talent study used a mixed-methods design: a web survey of 103 employers in North Carolina and follow-up interviews with 20 HR respondents. The survey examined awareness of MOOCs and employer openness to using them for recruitment, hiring, and employee professional development; the interviews explored perceived pros, cons, and implementation barriers. The population was workplace HR professionals across a range of industries, not students directly, and the context was early-MOOC adoption in 2013–2014.

The main conclusion is that employer awareness of MOOCs was still relatively low, but receptivity was fairly strong once respondents understood the concept. Employers were especially open to using MOOCs for professional development, and many viewed MOOC completion positively in hiring because it signaled motivation, initiative, and a desire to keep learning. However, interviewees repeatedly emphasized the need for stronger evidence of MOOC quality, verified completion, and, importantly, proof of longer-term learning retention and job-performance gains before they would use MOOCs more broadly in recruitment, hiring, or workforce development.

finding.finding_summary: The study found substantial employer openness to MOOCs as an institutional tool, especially for professional development. Among 103 surveyed organizations, 83% were using, considering using, or could see their organization using MOOCs for professional development, while 59% were using, considering using, or open to using them for recruitment; however, actual current use was low (7% for professional development, 1 organization for recruitment).
finding.measure: Employer awareness, willingness, and reported use of MOOCs for recruitment and professional development
finding.study_size: n=103 organizations; interviews with n=20 HR professionals

finding.finding_summary: HR professionals viewed MOOCs as potentially useful for low-cost, flexible professional development and for filling specific training gaps, especially in technical or specialized areas. No formal effect size was reported, but respondents consistently described MOOCs as a practical way to expand training options, reduce direct training costs, and provide scalable learning opportunities, albeit with concerns about labor time and completion.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness of MOOCs for professional development, training breadth, and cost/time efficiency
finding.study_size: n=103 organizations; interviews with n=20 HR professionals

finding.finding_summary: Employers often interpreted MOOC completion as evidence of positive personal attributes rather than direct job-specific competence. In hiring contexts, 73% of organizations viewed MOOC coursetaking positively or very positively, with respondents describing it as a signal of motivation, dedication, ambition, self-motivation, and willingness to keep learning.
finding.measure: Employer perceptions of MOOC completion as a signal of motivation, dedication, and ongoing learning in hiring decisions
finding.study_size: n=103 organizations; interviews with n=20 HR professionals

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights employers’ interest in MOOCs for building transferable skills such as leadership, management, communication, and specialized technical competencies. Interviewees said MOOCs could help employees “stay up to date” and develop skills for promotion or new roles, but they also wanted evidence that these skills were actually learned and retained beyond course completion.
finding.measure: Perceived value of MOOCs for skill development, especially leadership/management and specialized technical training
finding.study_size: n=103 organizations; interviews with n=20 HR professionals

paper_profiles.title: 2020 EDUCAUSE Horizon Report: Teaching and Learning Edition
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report surveys major macro-level trends and emerging technologies shaping higher education teaching and learning. Rather than testing a single intervention, it synthesizes expert panel judgments, supporting evidence, and scenario-based forecasting to identify what is likely to matter most for institutions in the near future.

The report highlights six emerging technologies/practices (adaptive learning, AI/machine learning applications, analytics for student success, instructional design/learning engineering/UX, open educational resources, and XR technologies) alongside social, technological, economic, higher education, and political trends. Its core purpose is to inform institutional decision making, helping leaders anticipate changes in student populations, funding, privacy, equity, and workforce needs.

Because the document is primarily a horizon-scanning and policy-oriented synthesis, it does not report original experimental or quasi-experimental data. It does, however, describe examples from institutions where adaptive learning and AI tools are associated with improved course success, student satisfaction, support efficiency, and student services. The main conclusion is that higher education institutions should plan for more flexible, data-informed, and student-centered models, while attending to costs, privacy, equity, and faculty receptiveness.

finding.finding_summary: The report cites adaptive-learning implementations in college algebra that improved course outcomes. At Oregon State University, pass rates increased from 65% to 77% over two years while withdrawal rates fell from 11% to 4%; at Arizona State University, a self-paced algebra course raised success rates (course completion with a C or better) from 54% in 2015 to 84% after combining adaptive instruction with a stretch-semester model.
finding.measure: College algebra pass rates, withdrawal rates, and course completion with a C or better

finding.finding_summary: The report indicates positive student affect and persistence-related outcomes associated with adaptive learning and related supports. For example, in UCF’s redesigned Spanish courses, preliminary data showed more positive student perception of instruction surveys, and the report argues that adaptive/active redesigns can improve student success and reduce withdrawal, which are persistence-relevant outcomes.
finding.measure: Student perception of instruction surveys; course withdrawal rates; course success/completion

finding.finding_summary: The report describes AI/chatbot and adaptive systems as improving support efficiency and extending service availability. Northwestern’s Canvas support chatbot and similar tools are presented as enabling 24/7 student/faculty support, while AI and ML applications are framed as helping institutions surface student-success data and reduce routine workload.
finding.measure: Helpdesk support availability, chatbot interactions, and routine support queries handled by AI systems

finding.finding_summary: A central finding of the report is that adaptive learning, AI/ML, analytics, and related practices are reshaping institutional design, budgeting, and student-success strategies. The report argues that institutions adopting these technologies can redesign curricula, use data for intervention, and reconfigure learning ecosystems, but must also contend with cost, privacy, equity, and faculty-receptiveness challenges.
finding.measure: Institutional course redesign, student-success initiatives, data/analytics use, and service redesign

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper examines the rationale for formative assessment and explores how it could be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard Learning System, in a university setting. The authors argue that frequent low-stakes assessment with immediate, detailed feedback can improve learning by helping students identify errors quickly, reflect on performance, and stay engaged with course content throughout the semester.

The paper combines a conceptual discussion of formative assessment with a small implementation example and a student perception survey conducted at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus). Students were asked about continuous assessment and the proposed Blackboard online test format. Results indicated broad student support for frequent online assessments, especially because they broke content into manageable units, provided immediate teacher feedback, and offered flexibility and convenience.

The study is not a controlled outcome evaluation of achievement gains; rather, it focuses on perceived benefits and implementation feasibility. Students believed the approach would help them learn progressively, keep up with the subject over the semester, and prepare better for semester examinations, though some expressed concern that too many tests could create stress and overemphasize learning over grades.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that the proposed frequent Blackboard-based formative assessments were helpful because they provided immediate feedback, helped them monitor strengths and weaknesses, and kept them engaged with the subject throughout the semester. The paper reports student perceptions only, with no achievement effect size; the main evidence is that students believed the approach would support ongoing learning and reduce the risk of falling behind.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment, feedback, and engagement/persistence in a questionnaire survey

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues and reports student perceptions that formative assessment with immediate feedback supports metacognition and self-monitoring by helping students assess what they know, identify mistakes, and understand how to improve. Students said the approach would help them learn individual topics progressively and check whether they were on track, but the study does not provide direct performance measures for these skills.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of self-monitoring, reflection, and metacognitive support

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on formative assessment implementation in a university course context and reports that students believed weekly or fortnightly Blackboard tests with detailed feedback would improve subject learning and likely prepare them better for the summative semester examination. The evidence is perceptual rather than experimental, so no numeric effect on grades or retention is reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of subject learning and preparation for semester examinations

paper_profiles.title: Learning Assistant Supported Student Outcomes (LASSO) study initial findings
paper_profiles.venue: American Physics Society / Physics Education Research conference proceedings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports initial findings from the Learning Assistant Supported Student Outcomes (LASSO) study, a multi-institution effort examining how features of Learning Assistant (LA)-supported STEM courses relate to student outcomes. The authors focus on whether student characteristics, course characteristics, and patterns of interaction with LAs predict performance on concept inventories administered at the start and end of a term.

The study drew on more than 4,500 students and 17 instructors from 13 LA Alliance institutions, with data collected across biology, chemistry, and physics courses. Students completed discipline-specific concept inventories such as the FMCE, BEMA, CINS, GCA, IMCA, and CCI; hierarchical linear models were used to estimate pre-to-post effect sizes and relate them to gender, race, student-LA interaction time, student-to-LA ratio, faculty meeting time with LAs, and instructor experience using LAs.

The main conclusion is that LA-supported courses showed positive pre/post gains overall, and that more sustained LA engagement was associated with larger gains. Specifically, students who interacted with LAs for 16–30 minutes per week had the largest gains, and larger gains were also associated with lower student-to-LA ratios, more faculty planning time with LAs, and more instructor experience teaching the course with LAs. The paper also reports inequitable patterns by gender and race in these correlational data, with male students showing larger gains than female students and mixed race differences across groups. The authors frame these as preliminary, correlational findings from the first term of a multi-year study rather than causal evidence.

finding.finding_summary: Across 3,315 usable pre-post pairs, students' average effect size on concept inventories was 0.845 standard deviations, indicating substantial gains from the start to end of the term. By discipline/instrument, average effect sizes ranged from 0.052 on the Chemistry Concept Inventory to 1.248 on CINS, with FMCE (1.230) and BEMA (1.130) also showing large gains.
finding.measure: Pre/post concept inventory scores on FMCE, BEMA, CINS, GCA, IMCA, CCI, and GCIICS

finding.finding_summary: The paper uses student weekly interaction time with LAs as a predictor and finds a positive association with learning gains. Students who spent 16-30 minutes/week with LAs had the highest average effect size (0.873), compared with 0.369 for students reporting 0 minutes/week; the 16-30 minute group was the only category statistically different from the 0-minute group.
finding.measure: Student weekly interaction time with LAs (min/week) and post-pre concept inventory effect size
finding.study_size: n=1,284 in the categorical interaction-time model
finding.effect_size: 0.873 vs 0.369 (16-30 min/week vs 0 min/week); model effect not reported as standardized coefficient

finding.finding_summary: Greater faculty and organizational support for LAs was associated with better student outcomes. In the continuous model, student-to-LA ratio had a negative association with effect size (-0.005 per additional student per LA), faculty meeting time with LAs had a small positive association (+0.004 per additional minute/week), and prior instructor experience teaching the course with LAs was positively associated with gains (+0.154 per additional term, p<0.05).
finding.measure: Student-to-LA ratio, faculty meeting time with LAs, and number of times instructor had taught the course with LAs
finding.effect_size: -0.005 per additional student/LA; +0.004 per additional faculty meeting minute/week; +0.154 per additional prior term taught with LAs

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: Educators / teachers (with examples spanning elementary, high school, and undergraduate contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative/practical review that asks how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback in pedagogically sound ways. The authors organize the discussion around a classic formative assessment framework: clarifying where learners are going, where learners are now, and how to move them forward. They argue that current AI uses often emphasize technical performance metrics, but do not sufficiently align with the core instructional purposes of formative assessment.

The paper does not report a primary empirical study or intervention. Instead, it synthesizes existing literature and provides illustrative prompting examples for teachers, including rewriting learning objectives into student-friendly language, generating prompts for co-constructing success criteria, creating sample work of varying quality, and producing formative questions or feedback. The context is mainly classroom teaching across K-12 and undergraduate settings, with examples from biology and fMRI coursework used to demonstrate how LLMs might be applied.

The main conclusion is that LLMs can augment, but should not replace, expert teaching. The authors emphasize that educators need to use professional judgment, check outputs for accuracy and appropriateness, and design AI-aware formative assessments that support deep learning, transferable skills, and self-regulation while reducing overreliance on AI-generated responses. The paper also highlights future research needs, including better evaluation metrics for LLM-generated feedback and more context-sensitive prompt repositories.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can save teachers time by automating or streamlining tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating formative questions, creating exemplars of different quality, and drafting feedback. However, this is a conceptual claim supported by examples and cited prior work rather than a direct empirical comparison, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher task efficiency / workload in generating formative-assessment materials

finding.finding_summary: The authors emphasize that LLM-supported formative assessment can be designed to promote transferable skills, critical thinking, and metacognition, particularly when students critique AI-generated outputs or co-construct success criteria. This is presented as a pedagogical recommendation and synthesis of prior research, not as a measured outcome in the paper itself.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognitive engagement, and transferable skills (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that formative assessment supported by LLMs may improve student self-regulation by clarifying goals, providing actionable feedback, and prompting reflection on learning progress. The paper discusses these outcomes conceptually and does not present direct student-level empirical evidence.
finding.measure: Self-regulation and learning engagement (conceptual/pedagogical outcomes)

paper_profiles.title: Transferring Knowledge from Large Foundation Models to Small Downstream Models
paper_profiles.venue: ICML (Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a machine learning transfer-learning problem: how to transfer task-relevant knowledge from very large foundation models into much smaller downstream models that are cheaper to train and deploy. The authors argue that standard fine-tuning only passes along a limited initialization signal and cannot easily combine multiple pretrained sources or selectively transfer only the most useful information.

They propose Adaptive Feature Transfer (AFT), a feature-space regularization method that encourages the downstream model to rely on knowledge already present in frozen pretrained features while discouraging learning irrelevant new features. AFT uses a kernel-based objective and a learned diagonal weighting of pretrained features, with precomputed pretrained representations cached during training to keep overhead low.

Across vision, language, and multimodal benchmarks, AFT is reported to improve downstream accuracy and error relative to standard transfer learning, knowledge distillation, and B-Tuning, especially when transferring from stronger pretrained models or multiple complementary pretrained models. The paper also shows that AFT is robust to irrelevant/noisy features and reduces inference cost by enabling smaller downstream models to perform well without deploying the large teacher model. This is a methodological paper in computer science, not an education study, so it does not address retention, course completion, or other learner outcome measures relevant to educational persistence.

paper_profiles.title: Flow patterns and heat transfer around six in-line circular cylinders at low Reynolds number
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines low-Reynolds-number fluid flow and forced-convection heat transfer around six in-line circular cylinders arranged in a row. The authors use direct numerical simulation to study how changing the center-to-center spacing ratio between cylinders (s/d = 3.6 versus 4.0) alters wake patterns, vortex shedding, drag, and heat transfer.

The computational approach uses the Gerris solver with adaptive mesh refinement, and the simulations are validated against known single-cylinder and two-cylinder benchmark cases. For the six-cylinder array, the authors identify two distinct flow regimes: a stable shear layer (SSL) mode at s/d = 3.6 and a shear layer secondary vortices (SLSV) mode at s/d = 4.0.

The main conclusion is that flow topology strongly affects both drag and thermal performance. Decreasing spacing from 4.0 to 3.6 reduces total drag by about 30% and increases total mean Nusselt number by about 25%, largely because counter-phase shedding at the smaller spacing entrains cooler fluid toward downstream cylinders and boosts heat transfer. The paper is a fluid mechanics/heat transfer simulation study rather than an education study, so it does not address the requested educational outcome categories beyond this engineering context.

paper_profiles.title: Predicting Long-Term Student Outcomes from Short-Term EdTech Log Data
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether short-horizon log data from educational technology can predict delayed, end-of-year outcomes as well as longer-horizon usage data. The motivation is practical: schools and tutors often want early signals about students’ likely performance on sparse external assessments, but waiting for months of product use or end-of-year tests makes timely intervention difficult.

The authors analyze three datasets from different contexts: Can’t Wait to Learn reading game data from 739 students in Uganda, iReady math data from 428 Grade 7 students in the U.S., and MATHia math tutoring data from 2,644 middle school students in the U.S. They extract interpretable count, timing, and persistence features from the first 1–5 hours of usage (and compare against full-horizon logs), then train linear regression, support vector regression, and random forest models to predict external post-test scores. They also examine subgroup prediction quality and the added value of pre-test scores when available.

The main finding is that 2–5 hours of log data can predict long-term outcomes nearly as well as the full multi-month log horizon, with only minor differences across models and datasets. Random forest is often slightly best, but differences among algorithms are small. Important predictive features are consistent across settings, especially percent success and average attempts per problem; adding pre-test scores generally improves prediction further. The models are not highly accurate for individual-level subgroup classification, but they are relatively precise at the extremes, suggesting possible use for early alerts or support targeting rather than high-stakes individual decisions.

finding.finding_summary: Using short-horizon log data from Can’t Wait to Learn reading, the models predicted later reading post-test performance with meaningful accuracy. The best short-horizon model (random forest with 5 hours of data) achieved RMSE=0.13 and R2=0.34, which the authors describe as near the full-horizon performance; adding pre-test scores further improved fit to R2=0.44 in the short+pre-test condition.
finding.measure: Reading post-test score averaged from letter knowledge, phonemic awareness, reading fluency, and reading comprehension subtask scores

finding.finding_summary: In MATHia and iReady mathematics, short-horizon log data predicted delayed math outcomes with performance similar to full-horizon logs. For MATHia, 2 hours of log data gave the best early-horizon results, with RMSE around 0.119 for GBDR (reported in a note) and similar performance across LR/SVR/RF; for iReady, 3 hours of log data produced strong predictive performance, with the best model achieving RMSE=0.16 and R2=0.41, and with pre-test scores the R2 rose to 0.66 for SVR in the short+pre-test setting.
finding.measure: End-of-year math post-test scores / state standardized test scores (MATHia) and SBAC math scores (iReady)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies persistence-related behavioral features in log data, especially unproductive persistence (wheel-spinning), as predictors of later achievement. Features such as the number of long idle events, time to first unproductive persistence, and counts of consecutive failed attempts were among the selected top predictors across datasets, indicating that persistence-related behavior carries signal for later performance, but the paper does not test an intervention to improve persistence itself.
finding.measure: Log-based persistence and wheel-spinning indicators, including num unproductive persistence thres 5/10 and time first unproductive persistence

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that a small set of generalizable behavioral features extracted from short-term log data can predict later outcomes across multiple platforms and contexts, suggesting that these features capture broader learning-related processes rather than system-specific quirks. In particular, percent success per problem and average attempts per problem were repeatedly selected as important predictors across datasets and horizons, and using the full feature set outperformed single-feature models (for example, in iReady short-horizon LR, R2 increased from 0.074 with percent success alone to 0.369 with the full feature set).
finding.measure: Feature importance and predictive performance of interpretable log-derived features across datasets

finding.finding_summary: A central result is that only 2–5 hours of early log data were often enough to approximate the predictive performance of full multi-month usage logs, implying a more efficient way to estimate delayed outcomes. Across all three datasets, a short-horizon model was nearly as effective as a full-horizon model, and in some cases short-horizon performance was slightly better, which could reduce data requirements and speed up evaluation or early-warning use cases.
finding.measure: Prediction accuracy for delayed external assessments using short-horizon versus full-horizon log data (RMSE and R2)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that early prediction from product logs could support school- and system-level decisions, such as identifying students likely to need support months before an external assessment and helping educators allocate resources. Empirically, the models showed reasonable precision at the extremes, though subgroup classification was not highly accurate overall, so the institutional benefit is framed as promising but not ready for high-stakes deployment.
finding.measure: Prediction quality for quintile-based performance subgroups and on-track/not-on-track classification

paper_profiles.title: Reinterpretation and Long-Term Preservation of Data and Code
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This Snowmass community planning report addresses the problem of how to preserve experimental data, simulations, analysis outputs, and analysis code so they can be reused after the end of a project’s active operations. The authors argue that long-term preservation maximizes scientific return by enabling future reinterpretation, recasting, global combinations, and new analyses that were not possible at the time the original data were collected.

The report synthesizes community discussions, contributed white papers, and existing infrastructure examples from high-energy physics and astronomy, including CERN Open Data Portal, HEPData, Zenodo, and domain-specific archives. It emphasizes that the technical challenge is only part of the problem: sociological barriers, incentive structures, and resource allocation for post-operations preservation are major obstacles, especially for smaller and non-collider projects. The report recommends dedicated funding, shared cyberinfrastructure, better standards for analysis preservation, and recognition mechanisms for researchers who contribute to preservation work.

The report is not an empirical study of an educational intervention or learning outcome. Its only educationally adjacent discussion is that public data can be used to train the next generation of scientists and support equity, diversity, and inclusion through access to datasets, documentation, and computing resources. Overall, the paper is a field-level policy and infrastructure recommendation document focused on scientific data stewardship rather than measured outcomes in education or student learning.

paper_profiles.title: On the long-term archiving of research data
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how research data should be managed over the long term as datasets age and become less frequently used. The authors argue that repositories cannot sustainably keep every dataset in hot, immediately accessible storage, because of monetary and ecological costs, and they propose a framework for deciding when data should move to cold archival storage rather than being deleted.

The article is a conceptual and policy-oriented discussion grounded in an observational analysis of OpenNeuro usage patterns. The authors examine download counts for 167 datasets deposited since January 2020 and show that a small fraction of datasets accounts for a disproportionate share of downloads, while lower-use datasets tend to show declining access over time. They use these patterns to motivate recommendations for cold archiving, metadata preservation, interoperable repository transfer, and clear responsibility assignments for long-term access.

The paper is not about instructional intervention or student outcomes. Its primary audience is data repository managers, researchers, and institutions responsible for scientific data stewardship. The main conclusion is that repositories should preserve cold data by default when feasible, maintain metadata and retrieval mechanisms, and plan for long-term integrity and transfer across repositories.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues for institutional policies that preserve research data through cold archiving rather than destruction, emphasizing that repositories should maintain metadata, retrieval mechanisms, and integrity safeguards for long-term access. Based on an observational look at 167 OpenNeuro datasets, the authors note that a small subset of datasets accounts for over 16% of downloads and that lower-use datasets show declining access over time, supporting a tiered storage policy.
finding.measure: Dataset download counts / repository access frequency; policy recommendations for archiving and preservation

paper_profiles.title: Persistence in Nonequilibrium Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a theoretical review of the persistence problem in nonequilibrium statistical physics. Persistence refers to the probability that a fluctuating field does not change sign over time, and the paper surveys results for single-particle and many-body systems, including Brownian motion, random acceleration, diffusion from random initial conditions, Ising coarsening, and related Gaussian stationary processes.

The author focuses on how to convert a variety of non-stationary stochastic processes into stationary Gaussian processes via a log-time transformation, which then allows analysis of zero-crossing probabilities. The review also discusses approximate methods such as the independent interval approximation, series expansions, perturbation theory near Markov processes, and variational approximations for non-Markovian systems. Although the paper is not an educational study, it synthesizes key theoretical results and cites experimental measurements of persistence exponents in physical systems such as liquid crystals, soap bubbles, and breath figures.

Overall, the paper concludes that persistence exponents are nontrivial and highly sensitive to the full temporal correlation structure of the process, especially in non-Markovian settings. It also highlights several generalizations, including global persistence, block persistence, residence-time distributions, and persistence in disordered systems and interface growth models, while emphasizing that many open questions remain.

paper_profiles.title: Long-term Large-scale Mapping and Localization Using maplab
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a robotics mapping and localization problem: how to build and maintain a large-scale visual-inertial map across multiple recording sessions and then reuse that map months later for localization. The authors focus on the open-source maplab framework, describing the pipeline for multi-session map construction, optimization, landmark filtering, and efficient 2D-3D localization against an existing 3D model.

The experiments were conducted in the Zurich Old Town area using more than 16 km of trajectories collected across 45 sessions over two days. The study then revisited the area about 6 months later with an additional 521 m trajectory (1,796 frames) to test long-term localization against the previously built map. The system processed the map in under 10 hours on a single PC, produced a map with 435k landmarks and 21k keyframes, and was able to localize over 20% of the later query frames with no false positives within a 10 m radius.

Overall, the paper concludes that large-scale, long-term map reuse is feasible with maplab and that the framework can support correct co-registration even after months have passed. The paper is primarily a systems/robotics evaluation rather than an education study, so it does not report outcomes related to learning, retention, or formative assessment in the K-12 sense.

paper_profiles.title: Laminar convective heat transfer of shear-thinning liquids in rectangular channels with longitudinal vortex generators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how channel geometry and working-fluid rheology affect laminar convective heat transfer in a rectangular channel heat sink. The authors ask whether adding longitudinal vortex generators (LVGs) and using shear-thinning carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) aqueous solutions can improve heat transfer performance relative to a plain channel and water, while also accounting for pressure-loss penalties.

Using three-dimensional numerical simulations in OpenFOAM, the study compares a plain channel and a channel with five pairs of LVGs across Reynolds numbers 25–200, three LVG angles of attack (30°, 45°, 60°), three lateral spacings, and four CMC concentrations (200–2000 ppm). The model treats the flow as steady, laminar, and single-phase, and evaluates Nusselt number, pumping power, friction factor, and an overall performance metric.

The simulations show that LVGs substantially increase heat transfer but also increase pumping power. Relative to the plain channel, mean Nusselt number improvements of about 24.17–134.83% are reported for channels with LVGs, and 38.52–188.43% for CMC solutions relative to water. Overall performance improves by 6.82–31.18% for CMC aqueous solutions versus water, with better performance generally associated with higher CMC concentration, larger LVG angle of attack, and larger LVG spacing, though these gains come with greater pressure losses.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central scientific finding is that longitudinal vortex generators and shear-thinning CMC fluids improve heat-transfer performance in laminar channel flow by intensifying secondary flow and disrupting the thermal boundary layer. Relative to a plain channel, mean Nusselt number increased by 24.17–134.83% with LVGs, and by 38.52–188.43% for CMC solutions relative to water, across Re=25–200 and the tested geometries.
finding.measure: Mean Nusselt number (heat transfer performance), pumping power, friction factor, overall performance metric

paper_profiles.title: Sustainability of Developed Self-Regulation by Means of Formative Assessment Among Young Adolescents: A Longitudinal Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This longitudinal study asks whether the benefits of formative assessment for students’ self-regulation persist after the transition from primary to secondary school. The authors were motivated by prior evidence that self-regulation often declines in early secondary grades and by the lack of longitudinal studies examining whether formative assessment can produce durable changes beyond the immediate intervention period.

The intervention was conducted with 695 Dutch sixth graders from 17 primary schools. Schools were randomly assigned to peer-assessment, self-assessment, or control conditions, and students completed writing tasks over several months in primary school, followed by a 10-week follow-up after summer break at the start of secondary education. The formative assessment conditions embedded criteria clarification, checklists/rubrics, and evaluation activities into writing instruction; the control condition received conventional writing instruction.

The study found that peer- and self-assessment produced positive effects on self-regulation and intrinsic motivation during the intervention, and those gains persisted at follow-up after the transition to secondary school. External regulation did not change meaningfully across conditions. Extrinsic motivation increased at the transition for all students, and self-efficacy showed no robust intervention-related persistence. Overall, the paper concludes that formative assessment can support durable self-regulation development in upper primary education, with effects lasting into secondary school.

finding.finding_summary: The formative assessment intervention had sustained positive effects on self-regulation and intrinsic motivation after the transition to secondary school. In multilevel analyses of 695 students, self-assessment and peer-assessment groups showed significant gains at posttest that remained at the 10-week follow-up, with no significant decline from Time 2 to Time 3. The paper reports no effect size, but means increased from about 2.68-2.70 pretest to 3.31-3.41 follow-up for self-regulation in the intervention groups.
finding.measure: Self-regulation and motivation questionnaire scores (Inventory Learning Style Questionnaire: self-regulation, intrinsic motivation, external regulation, extrinsic motivation)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was embedded in writing instruction, and the paper reports that formative assessment improved outcomes tied to writing-task learning processes rather than standardized literacy achievement. Students in the self- and peer-assessment conditions completed repeated writing assignments with criteria, checklists/rubrics, revision, and feedback, and these supports were associated with better self-regulation and motivation during writing tasks and after the school transition. No direct writing achievement effect size or standardized writing score is reported in the paper text provided.
finding.measure: Writing assignment process within formative assessment intervention

paper_profiles.title: Kahoot: A Promising Tool for Formative Assessment in Medical Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether Kahoot, a game-based quiz platform, is perceived by medical students as a useful formative assessment tool. The authors focus on student perceptions of Kahoot’s usefulness for feedback, motivation, engagement, learning, and knowledge retention, and also test whether perceptions differ by gender.

The study was conducted in a Malaysian public medical school with first-year undergraduate medical students. Data were collected through a 12-item survey administered immediately after a Kahoot-based formative assessment session. The sample included 113 students, most of whom were female. The instrument asked students to rate Kahoot on dimensions such as focus, motivation, fun, engagement, understanding, knowledge retention, simplification of complex subjects, corrective feedback, reflective learning, and preference relative to the school’s existing e-learning portal.

Overall, students responded positively to Kahoot as a formative assessment tool: it was seen as fun, effective for feedback, and better than the existing e-learning platform for feedback. Students also perceived that Kahoot could support motivation and knowledge retention, although it was not viewed as effective for simplifying complex subjects. Gender differences were found for motivation and perceived knowledge retention, with male students rating those items higher than female students. The paper concludes that Kahoot is feasible and practical for formative assessment in medical education, but its benefits are based on perceptions rather than direct outcome measures.

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived Kahoot as fun, motivating, engaging, and useful for feedback in a formative assessment session. In the 113-student survey, items on fun and feedback were rated highly (median 4), and motivation was also rated positively (median 3); male students rated motivation higher than female students (3.5 vs 3.0, p=0.016).
finding.measure: Student perception survey items on motivation, fun, engagement with feedback, and feedback effectiveness

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes student perceptions that Kahoot helps retain knowledge and enhances understanding of the subject matter. Knowledge retention was rated positively overall (median 3), and male students scored higher than female students on this item (p=0.027), but this is a perceived rather than direct retention measure.
finding.measure: Student perception survey item on knowledge retention

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper examines how formative assessment might be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard Learning System, in a university setting. The authors argue that frequent low-stakes testing paired with immediate, detailed feedback can improve learning by helping students identify mistakes early, monitor their progress, and stay engaged throughout the semester.

The paper combines a conceptual discussion of formative assessment with a student perception survey conducted at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus). The proposed implementation involved weekly or fortnightly online tests with automated and/or instructor feedback, using Blackboard tools such as online tests, discussion forums, and virtual classrooms. Students generally supported the approach, especially because it broke course work into smaller topic assessments, provided immediate feedback, and offered flexibility and convenience.

Empirically, the study reports descriptive survey results and a few statistical comparisons across student streams (Business, Engineering, IT). Students favored continuous assessment and the Blackboard test option, and many believed the approach would help them keep in touch with the subject, correct mistakes without delay, and perform better on the semester examination. The authors conclude that formative assessment supported by e-learning can create a 'culture of success' and may improve summative grades, though the paper does not directly measure learning gains or long-term outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent online formative assessments and immediate feedback helped them stay in touch with the subject throughout the semester and check whether they were on track. The survey also suggested that students preferred the method because it reduced the penalty of any single bad test and supported ongoing engagement, though some students worried about stress from too many tests.
finding.measure: Student perception survey on continuous assessment, feedback, and Blackboard test implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognition and self-monitoring by helping students recognize strengths and weaknesses, reflect on feedback, and learn progressively across smaller topic assessments. Students specifically endorsed immediate feedback as useful for correcting mistakes without delay and for understanding their standing in the course.
finding.measure: Student perception survey and conceptual discussion of formative assessment processes

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on course-level academic learning in a university business, engineering, and IT context, with students indicating that frequent Blackboard-based formative tests were useful for learning course content in steps and preparing for semester examinations. However, no direct achievement scores or retention/transfer measures were reported; the evidence is based on perceived usefulness and expected benefits for grades.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment and expected performance on semester examinations

paper_profiles.title: Improving Students’ Understanding of Quantum Mechanics by Using Peer Instruction Tools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that quantum mechanics is difficult for students to learn conceptually, even at the junior-senior undergraduate level. The authors argue that traditional physics instruction overemphasizes quantitative problem solving and underemphasizes conceptual understanding, leaving students with fragile or incorrect mental models.

To support learning, the authors developed about 500 research-based multiple-choice concept tests for use with peer instruction as a formative assessment strategy in junior-senior quantum mechanics courses. The concept tests were designed iteratively from prior research on student difficulties, used multiple representations (verbal, graphical, mathematical), and were embedded in lectures at 10–15 minute intervals with peer discussion and instructor feedback.

The paper reports classroom examples of concept-test sequences on bound and scattering states, and a preliminary evaluation comparing three experimental classes using concept tests (n=25, 13, and 20 across 2008–2010) with a traditional instruction comparison group (n=18). Students in the concept-test classes performed substantially better on a conceptual quiz about the infinite square well, and performance improved across years as the concept tests were refined. The authors conclude that peer-instruction concept tests can improve students’ understanding of quantum mechanics and help instructors monitor and adjust teaching in real time.

finding.finding_summary: Students in classes using research-based concept tests with peer instruction showed significantly better understanding of quantum-mechanical concepts than students receiving traditional instruction. On a 10-point conceptual quiz about the 1D infinite square well, the experimental groups averaged 5.5 (n=25), 7.0 (n=13), and 7.6 (n=20) across 2008–2010, compared with 1.8 for the traditional comparison group (n=18); the difference was reported as significant at p<0.0001. The authors also report that performance improved over time as the concept tests were refined.
finding.measure: Conceptual quiz on basic quantum-mechanical concepts related to a 1D infinite square potential well
finding.study_size: n=76 total across four groups (experimental n=25, 13, 20; comparison n=18)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that peer instruction increased students’ active engagement, discussion, and willingness to resolve discrepancies in their thinking during class. However, this outcome is supported mainly by classroom description and observational evidence rather than a dedicated validated measure, so no numeric effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Classroom participation/discussion during peer instruction

finding.finding_summary: The authors claim that the concept-test sequence helped students organize, extend, and monitor their knowledge, which aligns with metacognition and critical-thinking skills. This is supported by students' improved conceptual quiz performance and by descriptions of students revising their ideas during discussion, but the paper does not report a direct standalone measure of durable skills.
finding.measure: Students’ ability to organize, repair, extend, and monitor their knowledge during concept-test work

paper_profiles.title: Flipping Linear Algebra using a MOOC platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes a three-year implementation of a flipped classroom model in a standard undergraduate Linear Algebra course at Instituto Superior Técnico, University of Lisbon. The authors used an institutional MOOC platform to deliver videos, quizzes, formative assessment, and other online materials for the final five weeks of a 14-week course, aiming to shift class time toward interactive problem solving and peer discussion.

The intervention was implemented with roughly 100 first-year Computer Science engineering students per year from 2017 to 2019. The study draws on multiple sources of evidence, including questionnaire responses, MOOC completion data, final course grades, and classroom observations, to examine how students responded to the model and whether it supported course performance and engagement.

The paper reports encouraging descriptive trends across the three years: online assessment completion increased, student satisfaction with the flipped model was generally positive, and final pass rates in Linear Algebra rose from a pre-intervention baseline of 67% to 74%, 81%, and 83% across the three implementation years. The authors conclude that the approach appears promising for STEM higher education, especially when paired with well-designed online materials and learning spaces that support collaboration, though the evidence is descriptive rather than causal.

finding.finding_summary: Across three years, the flipped Linear Algebra course was associated with higher course approval rates than the pre-intervention baseline. Final approval rates were 74% in 2017/2018, 81% in 2018/2019, and 83% in 2019/2020, compared with 67% in 2016/2017. The paper also reports that most participating students were able to write correct mathematical statements, solve conceptual exercises, and produce short proofs in written tests.
finding.measure: Final course approval rate; written test performance in Linear Algebra
finding.study_size: n≈100 students per year; questionnaire subsamples n=45, n=48, n=59

finding.finding_summary: Student responses suggest improved engagement, confidence, and self-management during the flipped implementation. The paper reports that students felt more self-confident and had greater freedom in time management, and that the approach helped them become more engaged with course content. Questionnaire results also showed that 70% (2017/2018), 56.3% (2018/2019), and 67.7% (2019/2020) appreciated or appreciated a lot the flipped model.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire ratings; reported self-confidence and time-management perceptions

finding.finding_summary: The flipped design appears to have supported collaboration, problem solving, and independent learning behaviors. The paper describes lively group discussions, peer commentary on mathematical solutions, and students' development of learning strategies; it also notes that one student later volunteered to prepare and conduct a flipped session, suggesting increased autonomy and ownership. These outcomes are reported qualitatively and through class observations rather than via standardized measures.
finding.measure: Classroom observations; qualitative descriptions of group work, problem solving, and learning strategies

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved the usability of class time for interactive work, though the paper does not quantify teacher workload or efficiency. The authors report that moving from lecture to group discussion made sessions more dynamic and that the specially adapted room was crucial for running the flipped and tutorial sessions effectively.
finding.measure: Observed classroom use and instructional format changes

finding.finding_summary: The work was recognized as a good practice by the IST Observatory of Good Practices in 2018, suggesting institutional approval and potential scalability within the department. The authors also frame the model as a promising response to student-centered reforms in STEM higher education, but this is presented as an institutional implication rather than a measured system-level outcome.
finding.measure: Institutional recognition / good-practice designation

paper_profiles.title: How Well Can You Articulate that Idea? Insights from Automated Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines automated formative feedback for middle school science explanation essays in a roller coaster physics unit. The authors study how well the PyrEval system can detect whether students included six target science ideas in their essays, and how detection accuracy varies by both the distinctiveness of the ideas themselves and the clarity of students’ writing.

The intervention/approach is not a classroom experiment comparing learning gains across conditions; rather, it is an error-analysis and validation study of an AI-supported essay feedback tool. The authors use manually labeled essay datasets from a 2-3 week digital curriculum on energy and energy transfer, compare several semantic vector methods for PyrEval, and analyze the cosine-similarity structure that drives automated matching. They report that WTMF performed best on their tuning set, that overall feedback accuracy on the classroom dataset was reasonably good but uneven across ideas, and that some ideas such as the law of conservation of energy were much easier for the system to detect than others because they were more formulaic and distinctive.

A second main conclusion is that student writing clarity affects the tool’s accuracy: essays or clauses that are more vague or that match multiple ideas at similar levels of similarity are more likely to be misclassified. The paper argues that even imperfect feedback may still support learning by prompting students and teachers to reflect on how ideas are articulated more clearly. Because the paper focuses on model accuracy and writing clarity rather than learning outcomes such as retention, transfer, or completion, it provides limited evidence about downstream educational effects beyond immediate essay revision support.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that automated formative feedback can help students improve their revised science explanation essays, but its own primary analysis is on feedback accuracy rather than learning gains. In the classroom dataset of 60 students (120 essays and revisions), PyrEval’s total accuracy was 74.44% on GT2 and 75.47% overall across the 159-essay set, with revised essays being evaluated as more accurate when the system matched ideas correctly; however, the paper does not provide a direct effect size for writing improvement in this article, only referring to separate work showing revision gains.
finding.measure: Science explanation essay revision quality / automated detection of main ideas in essays
finding.study_size: n=60 students (120 essays and revisions) for GT2; n=159 essays overall

finding.finding_summary: The intervention is situated in a middle school roller coaster physics curriculum about energy, potential energy, kinetic energy, and conservation of energy, and the feedback rubric is built around six science ideas that students are expected to articulate. The study finds that automated feedback accuracy is highest for more formulaic scientific statements, especially the law of conservation of energy (main idea 4; 89.30% accuracy overall) and the initial-drop idea (main idea 5; 83.01%), and lower for more flexible conceptual relations such as PE/KE relationships (main ideas 1 and 2; 66.66% and 64.77%).
finding.measure: Accuracy of detecting science ideas in explanatory essays; science explanation articulation
finding.study_size: n=159 essays overall; n=60 students in classroom validation set

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that writing clarity and articulation are central to how well the AI feedback works, and it uses clause-level cosine similarity patterns as an indirect probe of students’ expressive clarity. It reports that clauses in high- and mid-accuracy essays matched an average of 1.63 main ideas (sd=0.84), while low-accuracy essays matched 1.73 main ideas (sd=0.78), suggesting that vaguer statements are more confusable and less clearly articulated.
finding.measure: Clarity / distinctiveness of student statements in essay writing (proxied by cosine similarity overlap with multiple main ideas)
finding.study_size: n=117 essays analyzed for clarity patterns; 42 additional essays used as consistency check

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Auto-Grading and Feedback System for Constructive Geometry Tasks Using Large Language Models on an Online Math Platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether a large language model (LLM)-based auto-grading and feedback system can support formative assessment in constructive geometry tasks on an online mathematics platform. The authors focus on open-ended and construction-based geometry problems that are difficult to score with traditional answer matching, especially when student responses vary in wording or solution path.

The intervention combines rule-based grading for closed-ended and geometry-construction items with GPT-4-based grading and feedback for open-ended explanations. The feedback is teacher-authored, attempt-aware, and personalized to students’ prior submissions, with up to three retries per item.
