The system was implemented on Algeomath and piloted with 79 South Korean middle school students across four classes on an 18-question sequence centered on triangle circumcenter/circumcircle concepts and applied geometry tasks.

Main findings show strong agreement between automated grading and teacher judgments for closed-ended and geometry-construction items (100%), and substantial agreement for open-ended explanations overall (agreement rate 0.866, Cohen’s κ = 0.737). Feedback was judged moderately good on average by an expert reviewer (pooled mean 3.98/5, SD 1.78), but quality varied by item and issues included answer leakage, imprecise terminology, and overly generic or harsh prompts. Student work improved within attempts: 36.7% of initially incorrect responses were corrected on the next try (260/708), but evidence for longer-term transfer to later questions was not statistically significant. The study concludes that LLMs can feasibly support scalable formative assessment in middle-school geometry, though better feedback design is needed to support deeper transfer and avoid revealing answers.

finding.finding_summary: The system supported iterative correction on geometry tasks and showed strong grading alignment with teachers. Across the 18-item middle-school geometry sequence (n=79 students), open-ended grading achieved 0.866 agreement with teachers (Cohen’s κ = 0.737), and 36.7% of initially incorrect responses were corrected on the next attempt (260/708).
finding.measure: Geometry task correctness, grading agreement with teacher judgments, post-feedback correction rate
finding.study_size: n=79 students; 878 open-ended judgments; 708 incorrect responses eligible for conversion analysis

finding.finding_summary: The feedback system was designed to encourage persistence through multiple retries, and the data show that many students revised answers after feedback. Attempt-level learning curves rose from about 0.60 correct by the first attempt to about 0.73 by the second attempt, suggesting that the feedback/retry cycle supported persistence and re-engagement on difficult geometry tasks.
finding.measure: Attempt-level retry success / cumulative proportion solved by attempt

finding.finding_summary: The paper examined whether feedback-driven correction promoted transfer to later, more complex questions, but evidence was inconclusive. For three target questions (Q10, Q11, Q18), prior experience with a feedback-driven correction was not significantly associated with better later performance (all p > 0.05), suggesting no clear measurable transfer in this dataset.
finding.measure: Performance on later target questions following prior feedback-driven correction; first-attempt correctness and eventual success
finding.study_size: n=79 students; target-question analyses reported with subgroup counts including Q10, Q11, Q18

finding.finding_summary: The system automated grading and feedback delivery for complex geometry responses, reducing reliance on teacher scoring in the pilot. For closed-ended and CGT items, grading agreed 100% with teacher judgments, and for open-ended explanations the overall agreement rate was 0.866, indicating substantial feasibility for scalable use in formative assessment workflows.
finding.measure: Agreement between automated and teacher grading; automated feedback delivery in an online platform

paper_profiles.title: Changes in Coding Behavior and Performance Since the Introduction of LLMs
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 15th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK 2026)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how the widespread availability of large language models (LLMs) has changed students’ coding behavior and downstream learning outcomes in a graduate-level cloud computing course. The authors are especially interested in whether changes in submission patterns and edit behavior are associated with longer-term outcomes beyond immediate task completion, such as performance on other course projects.

Using a quasi-longitudinal observational design, the study analyzes 2,066 source-code submissions from 721 enrollments across 10 semesters at Carnegie Mellon University, spanning five semesters before ChatGPT and five after. The main focal task is a repeated PageRank programming assignment that stayed essentially unchanged across semesters, allowing comparison of number of submissions, edit distances between submissions, and final auto-graded task scores. The authors also use two broader performance measures: a student’s aggregate score on the top five individual projects and the team project score.

The paper finds that after the introduction of ChatGPT, students’ submissions became longer and more heavily edited: median number of submissions rose, total edit distance increased sharply, and average edit distance increased substantially. However, the final PageRank task score did not improve, and performance on individual projects slightly decreased, while team project scores increased modestly. The authors interpret the pattern as consistent with greater reliance on LLM-generated code that may reduce learning efficiency, though they caution that the study cannot directly verify LLM usage. Overall, the paper argues that traditional task scores may mask changes in learning behavior and that LLMs may be altering both individual learning and collaborative performance in computing education.

finding.finding_summary: Coding-related performance on the focal PageRank task did not materially improve after ChatGPT's release: nearly all students still received perfect scores in most semesters, indicating no clear gain in immediate task performance. However, broader course performance showed a small decrease in Individual Projects (IP) score (correlation with Average Edit Distance: r=-0.16, p<0.001), while Team Project (TP) score increased after f22, suggesting mixed downstream effects on programming coursework.
finding.measure: Auto-graded PageRank task score; Individual Projects (IP) score; Team Project (TP) score
finding.study_size: n=721 enrollments attempting the PageRank task
finding.effect_size: r=-0.16 for IP score vs Average Edit Distance; r=0.240 for IP score vs TP score

finding.finding_summary: The paper interprets the increase in number of submissions and edit distance together with lower average score improvement between consecutive submissions as evidence of reduced learning efficiency and potentially less structured, less strategic problem-solving behavior. While not directly measuring persistence or motivation with surveys, the authors use submission patterns as behavioral proxies suggesting diminished self-regulation/learning efficiency after LLM availability.
finding.measure: Number of submissions; total edit distance; average edit distance; average submission effect

finding.finding_summary: Students' coding behavior changed substantially after ChatGPT's release: median number of submissions increased by about 50%, median average edit distance rose by about 300%, and median total edit distance rose by about 500% between f22 and s25. These behavioral changes were associated with slightly lower individual project performance, suggesting that the way students approached iterative coding and problem-solving became less efficient and may reflect weaker independent debugging and incremental development skills.
finding.measure: Number of submissions; average edit distance; total edit distance; score changes between consecutive submissions; IP score
finding.effect_size: r=-0.16 for IP score vs Average Edit Distance

finding.finding_summary: Coding efficiency declined markedly after the introduction of LLMs. Median number of submissions increased by roughly 50%, median average edit distance by 300%, and median total edit distance by 500% from f22 to s25, while average submission effect steadily decreased since s24, meaning students made more and larger edits without comparable score gains. The paper frames this as reduced productivity and less effective iteration in programming work.
finding.measure: Number of submissions; average edit distance; total edit distance; average submission effect; task score changes between consecutive submissions

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLM adoption may be changing how computing courses should assess student learning, because conventional auto-graded task scores remained stable even as underlying coding behavior shifted substantially. The authors suggest that institutions may need to revise evaluation methods to better detect genuine expertise and account for AI-assisted work, especially in project-based courses.
finding.measure: Observed course assessment patterns across semesters; task score stability versus behavioral change

paper_profiles.title: Did the Model Change? Efficiently Assessing Machine Learning API Shifts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether commercial machine learning prediction APIs change their behavior over time when the input data distribution is held constant. The authors frame this as an API shift problem: rather than asking whether a model’s reported accuracy changes, they ask how the full confusion matrix changes across time, which can reveal class-specific degradations or improvements that overall accuracy hides.

To study the problem, they evaluate commercial APIs from providers such as Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and IBM on fixed benchmark datasets across two time points (spring 2020 and spring 2021). Across 36 API–dataset combinations, they find 12 cases with greater than 1% performance change, including both improvements and degradations. They then propose MASA, an adaptive sampling method that clusters the dataset by label and difficulty, queries the API strategically, and estimates confusion-matrix shifts with far fewer samples than uniform sampling.

The empirical work is on adult-accessed machine learning services for classification tasks in sentiment analysis, facial emotion recognition, and speech recognition. The main conclusion is that silent model updates in commercial APIs are common and can materially alter downstream application behavior, and that MASA can estimate these shifts much more efficiently than standard sampling—often reducing query cost by more than 70% and sometimes up to 90% while maintaining similar estimation accuracy.

finding.finding_summary: MASA substantially improves the efficiency of estimating API shifts. Across real-world API–dataset combinations, it achieved estimation errors an order of magnitude smaller than uniform sampling at the same sample size, and it often reduced the number of required API queries by more than 70% to reach 1% Frobenius norm error (e.g., 4.5K vs 19.7K for Amazon/YELP; 1.1K vs 18.5K for Google/AMNIST).
finding.measure: Frobenius norm error of estimated confusion-matrix shift; number of API queries/samples required to reach 1% error
finding.study_size: n=36 API-dataset combinations for shift detection; 12 cases with >1% performance change; experiments averaged over 1500 runs

paper_profiles.title: Benchmark Environments for Multitask Learning in Continuous Domains
paper_profiles.venue: Lifelong Learning: A Reinforcement Learning Approach Workshop @ ICML
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of standardized benchmark environments for studying multitask, transfer, and lifelong learning in continuous control domains. The authors argue that, unlike Atari in discrete domains, continuous-control research has relied on disparate environment sets that make fair comparison difficult. To improve comparability, they introduce an expandable open-source framework built on OpenAI Gym and define more than 50 environment variants spanning gravity changes, body-part morphology changes, sensor and wall perturbations, goal/start randomization for arm tasks, Humanoid multitask variants, and new 2D navigation tasks.

The paper is not an educational intervention study; it is a machine-learning benchmark paper. The main empirical component is a baseline evaluation using Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) trained sequentially across the benchmark task groups and then evaluated on previously seen and final tasks. The reported results show both catastrophic forgetting in some settings (especially Hopper and some morphology/gravity variants) and positive forward transfer in others (notably HalfCheetah and Walker2d variants). For navigation tasks, the baseline fails to learn under the reported setup, remaining at the lowest reward, suggesting that these environments are challenging and may require better exploration and memory mechanisms.

Because the paper focuses on reinforcement-learning environments and not on learners, classrooms, or formative assessment, it does not study K-12 educational outcomes such as literacy, language fluency, mathematics, or social-emotional skills. Its relevance to the retrieval sub-question is indirect at best: it provides benchmarks for transfer and lifelong learning, but not downstream educational outcomes like retention, course completion, or persistence in schooling.

paper_profiles.title: Remember This Event That Year? Assessing Temporal Information and Understanding in Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can retain and reason about temporal information, especially when answering questions that require knowing how facts change over time. The authors argue that temporal grounding is important for real-world applications, but existing LLMs often fail on time-sensitive and numerically changing information.

To study this, the authors introduce TempUN, a large temporal dataset built from Our World in Data and focused on eight United Nations-related issue areas such as climate, health, economic development, and peace/war. They also create a smaller filtered subset, TempUNs, and evaluate 12 LLMs in zero-shot settings as well as after three fine-tuning paradigms: yearwise fine-tuning, continual learning, and random fine-tuning. The tasks include next-word prediction and six multiple-choice question types designed to probe date-based recall, comparisons across years, sequences over time, ranges, min-max reasoning, and trend understanding.

The main finding is that current LLMs perform poorly at temporal retention and temporal reasoning. Zero-shot accuracy is low, incorrect answers are common, and open-source models generally produce more wrong answers than closed-source models, though closed-source models more often admit when information is unavailable. Fine-tuning changes behavior somewhat by reducing incorrect generations and increasing “information not available” responses, but it also lowers correct answer rates, suggesting that these training approaches are not yet effective solutions for numerical-temporal understanding in LLMs.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates numerical-temporal reasoning on a dataset of country- and issue-level quantitative facts. In zero-shot evaluation, average correct rates were low (e.g., 27% for open-source and 28% for closed-source models on date-based MCQs), with high incorrect rates (61% and 59%, respectively). Fine-tuning reduced incorrect outputs and increased “information not available” responses, but often reduced correctness, indicating mixed effects on numerical reasoning.
finding.measure: Accuracy on date-based, comparative, window-based, range-based, min-max, and trend-based multiple-choice questions; next-word prediction on numerical temporal values
finding.study_size: n=12 models; TempUNs n=1,907 instances / 104,130 samples for MCQs; TempUN n=462,894 instances / 9,497,502 samples

paper_profiles.title: Studying physics during the COVID-19 pandemic: Student assessments of learning achievement, perceived effectiveness of online recitations, and online laboratories
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This descriptive survey study examines how undergraduate physics students experienced the abrupt shift to online instruction during the COVID-19 pandemic, with a focus on problem-solving recitations and laboratory courses. The authors developed a multilingual questionnaire and administered it to 578 physics students from five universities in Germany, Austria, and Croatia. The survey asked about students’ self-organization, communication, learning environment, attitudes toward online learning, perceived learning achievement, and the organization and perceived effectiveness of online recitations and laboratories.

The paper does not test an intervention; instead it analyzes relationships among student characteristics, course formats, and self-reported outcomes. Students who reported stronger self-organization, better communication, and a more study-friendly environment also reported higher perceived learning achievement, while more positive attitudes toward online learning were associated with higher expected achievement. First-year students reported lower perceived learning achievement than more advanced students.

For recitations, students preferred live discussion and feedback on their own solutions over receiving worked-out handouts, and students who submitted their own solutions for feedback rated recitations as more effective. For laboratories, students rated online labs more favorably when they gathered data themselves rather than using simulated or handed-out data, with benefits reported for both experimental skills and content reinforcement. Overall, the paper concludes that communication, self-regulation, feedback, and active data generation are central to students’ perceived success in emergency online physics instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that online physics laboratories were perceived as more effective for scientific/experimental learning when students gathered data themselves rather than working with simulated data or handed-out data. This was significant for both acquisition of experimental skills, F(2, 198)=14.2, p<0.001, and reinforcement of content, F(2, 216)=3.50, p=0.03, based on 220 students in lab courses.
finding.measure: Perceived acquisition of experimental skills and reinforcement of physics content in online laboratory courses

finding.finding_summary: Perceived learning achievement was positively associated with self-organization during the COVID-19 semester (r=0.63, p<0.001) and with self-organization in general (r=0.33). The paper also reports positive correlations with communication (r=0.50) and a negative correlation with attitudes toward online learning (r=-0.58), indicating that self-regulation and related behavioral factors were strongly linked to students’ subjective success.
finding.measure: Self-organization, communication, attitudes toward online learning, and perceived learning achievement

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds strong relationships between perceived learning achievement and durable skills such as self-organization and communication. Self-organization during COVID-19 showed the strongest association with perceived achievement (r=0.63), and communication was also positively correlated (r=0.50), suggesting that metacognitive and collaborative skills were central to students’ reported success in emergency online physics learning.
finding.measure: Self-organization and communication scales correlated with perceived learning achievement

finding.finding_summary: In online recitations, students who submitted their own solutions for correction and feedback rated the recitations as more effective than students who did not submit solutions, F(1, 393)=6.74, p=0.01. This finding is based on 401 recitation participants and suggests that feedback on students’ own problem solving improved perceived usefulness of the course format.
finding.measure: Perceived effectiveness of online recitations

paper_profiles.title: Web-based Database Courses E-Learning Application
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Computing Sciences Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the development of a web-based e-learning application for database courses at Bulacan State University’s College of Information and Communications Technology. The project was motivated by a mismatch between the number of students needing database instruction and the limited number of faculty experts, alongside the increased need for online learning during the pandemic.

The application includes lessons on SQL for MySQL and SQL Server, quizzes, examinations, and an entity-relationship diagram (ERD) simulator with drag-and-drop functionality. The authors followed an Agile software development process and a cross-sectional developmental approach to gather requirements, design, and develop the system. The system was then evaluated by 50 second-year IT students, 10 faculty members, and 10 IT experts using ISO/IEC 25010:2011 software quality criteria.

Results indicate that respondents rated the application positively overall, with mean scores of 4.24 from students, 4.41 from faculty, and 4.33 from experts on a five-point scale, all interpreted as "Very Good." Faculty rated compatibility and usability as "Excellent," while experts rated performance efficiency highest. The study concludes that the application functions well as a supplemental teaching and learning tool, but it does not report learning gains, retention, transfer, completion, or other downstream educational outcomes beyond acceptability and software quality perceptions.

finding.finding_summary: The developed web application was judged to function well as a supplemental teaching tool, with overall ISO/IEC 25010 ratings of 4.24 (students), 4.41 (faculty), and 4.33 (IT experts) on a 5-point scale, each interpreted as "Very Good." Faculty members specifically saw it as useful for teaching database courses because it consolidates lessons, quizzes, and assessments in one platform.
finding.measure: ISO/IEC 25010:2011 software quality evaluation ratings; perceived usefulness/acceptability of the web application
finding.study_size: n=70 total respondents (50 students, 10 faculty members, 10 IT experts)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the application addresses an institutional need at BulSU-CICT by providing an additional teaching and learning tool for database courses when faculty expertise and student demand are mismatched. Respondents’ ratings suggest the system is acceptable for potential integration into course delivery, though no institutional implementation outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: ISO/IEC 25010:2011 acceptability ratings and stakeholder perceptions of institutional usefulness
finding.study_size: n=70 total respondents (50 students, 10 faculty members, 10 IT experts)

paper_profiles.title: Embedding Formative Assessment: Evaluation report and executive summary
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This evaluation asks whether a whole-school formative assessment professional development programme improves secondary students’ GCSE attainment. The report was produced for the Education Endowment Foundation and focuses on whether Embedding Formative Assessment (EFA) led to better end-of-secondary-school outcomes than business-as-usual practice.

EFA was a two-year, school-wide intervention delivered in 140 secondary schools in England during 2015/2016 and 2016/2017. The programme combined monthly Teacher Learning Communities (TLCs), peer lesson observations, and ongoing support from SSAT Lead Practitioners, with materials organized around five formative assessment strategies developed by Dylan Wiliam and Siobhan Leahy. All classroom teachers in treatment schools were expected to participate. The control group received a £300 payment and otherwise continued usual practice.

The trial used a cluster randomized controlled design with school-level randomization and externally validated GCSE outcomes from the National Pupil Database. The primary outcome was Attainment 8, with Maths and English GCSE scores as secondary outcomes. The main result was a small positive impact on Attainment 8 (Hedges g=0.10, 95% CI -0.01 to 0.21, n=25,393), equivalent to about two months’ additional progress, but there was no evidence of improvement in Maths or English specifically. Process findings suggest schools generally increased use of formative assessment and teacher dialogue, though implementation varied substantially and prior exposure to the related TEEP programme may have influenced delivery and impact.

finding.finding_summary: The primary outcome, GCSE Attainment 8, improved modestly in the EFA group relative to control. The precise model estimated Hedges g=0.10 (95% CI -0.01 to 0.21; p=0.088) for all pupils, based on n=25,393, which the report translates to about two additional months of progress.
finding.measure: GCSE Attainment 8 score

finding.finding_summary: There was no significant effect on Maths GCSE attainment. The precise model reported Hedges g=0.02 (95% CI -0.08 to 0.12; p=0.74) for all pupils, based on n=22,935.
finding.measure: Numerical Maths GCSE grades

finding.finding_summary: There was no significant effect on English GCSE attainment. The precise model reported Hedges g=0.02 (95% CI -0.08 to 0.11; p=0.72) for all pupils, based on n=22,628.
finding.measure: Numerical English GCSE grades

finding.finding_summary: The process evaluation found that schools generally implemented the programme in ways that increased formative assessment use and teacher dialogue, indicating institutional uptake of the model. However, implementation varied substantially across schools, and some prior exposure to TEEP appeared to shape how EFA was delivered and understood.
finding.measure: Process evaluation evidence from case study visits, surveys, and implementation/fidelity reports
finding.study_size: 10 case study schools; end-of-project survey: 40 treatment schools; control survey: 39 schools

paper_profiles.title: The effects of self-monitoring and self-reflection in A1 adult learners in an English blended learning environment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This thesis examines whether self-monitoring and self-reflection strategies could improve the learning experience of adult A1 English learners in a blended learning course. The central question is not a comparison among different formative assessment models, but rather whether two self-assessment strategies, embedded within a blended course, would help learners become more aware of their progress, identify areas for improvement, and engage more actively in learning.

The study was conducted as action research with a group of adult distance tutors at Universidad Nacional Abierta y a Distancia (UNAD) in Bucaramanga, Colombia, enrolled in an elementary English blended-learning course. The intervention integrated self-assessment activities such as checklists, surveys, and student journals, along with scaffolded instruction across face-to-face and online sessions. The thesis frames self-monitoring and self-reflection as components of formative self-assessment and self-regulated learning, and the data analysis is qualitative.

The main conclusions are that participants responded positively to the self-assessment practices. The reported effects were increased awareness of the language learning process, greater involvement in individual learning, better recognition of strengths and weaknesses, and more intentional goal-setting and progress monitoring. The study also reports positive reactions to the blended modality and to scaffolded instruction, suggesting that these supports helped learners engage productively with self-assessment in a non-credit-bearing course context.

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported more involvement in their individual learning process, greater awareness of progress, and more positive reactions to the self-assessment activities. The thesis concludes that self-monitoring and self-reflection affected learners in positive ways by increasing engagement and helping them identify specific areas for improvement and set goals.
finding.measure: Checklists, surveys, and students’ journals; reported learner perceptions and reflections

finding.finding_summary: The study directly focuses on metacognitive self-assessment skills, especially self-monitoring and self-reflection. Findings indicate that learners became more aware of the language learning process, monitored their learning and progress, identified areas for improvement, and planned learning goals, all of which are consistent with gains in metacognition and self-regulation.
finding.measure: Checklists, surveys, and students’ journals; thematic analysis of reflections

finding.finding_summary: Although not a test-based outcomes study, the paper is situated in an English blended-learning course and reports that learners became more aware of their progress in language learning and monitored their development in language skills. The evidence is qualitative and does not report standardized speaking or listening scores, but the study substantively concerns English learning progress in a basic-language course.
finding.measure: Learner reflections on English learning progress in a blended course

paper_profiles.title: An Evaluation of an Innovative In-Service Teacher Training Model in Turkey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates an in-service teacher training model developed within a UNICEF- and Ministry of National Education-supported inclusive education project in Turkey. The specific module examined, "Teaching and Assessment," was designed to help teachers develop skills for differentiated instruction and formative assessment as part of broader inclusive education practice.

The study asks whether a one-shot workshop format can still produce meaningful teacher change when the training is designed around active learning, collaboration, reflection, and teachers’ own classroom problems. The authors collected data from four focus group discussions with 27 teachers from different school levels and teaching experience groups who completed the module across Turkey.

Teachers generally reported that the training was useful for their professional and personal development and led to changes in their beliefs, awareness, and classroom practices. Reported gains included greater recognition of the limits of lecture-based teaching, more attention to disadvantaged learners, increased use of hands-on and student-centered activities, and improved communication and empathy with students.

The paper also notes implementation weaknesses, especially uneven organization across local sites, timing problems, and some repetition or overuse of worksheets. Overall, the study concludes that even a one-shot in-service model can support teacher change when it is well structured, practice-based, and collaborative, though it would benefit from better logistics and more subject- and level-specific follow-up.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported improved motivation, feeling valued, and greater enthusiasm for professional learning after the training. In the focus groups (n=27), many participants said the collaborative format increased their engagement and made them feel more supported and willing to participate.
finding.measure: Focus group reports of motivation, engagement, and sense of value/support

finding.finding_summary: Participants described gains in reflective practice, collaboration, problem solving, and metacognitive awareness about their own teaching. The training was designed around active reflection and group production of materials, and teachers reported that it helped them question prior beliefs and develop new strategies.
finding.measure: Focus group reports of reflection, collaboration, problem solving, and professional learning

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported practical gains in lesson planning, material development, and more efficient use of collaborative work, but also identified organizational inefficiencies such as late start times, fatigue, and uneven delivery across sites. The paper emphasizes both improved training utility and logistical drawbacks, rather than a single clear efficiency effect.
finding.measure: Focus group reports on training organization, planning/material development, and usability

finding.finding_summary: The study found that the training shifted teachers’ perceptions and practices toward inclusive education and formative assessment, suggesting institutional value for in-service teacher development. Across four FGDs (n=27), participants described broader changes in classroom culture, collegial networking, and adoption of more inclusive practices.
finding.measure: Focus group reports of teacher change, inclusive education perceptions, and practice change

paper_profiles.title: Assessing and Learning Alignment of Unimodal Vision and Language Models
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable / machine learning models (no human participant population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how well pretrained unimodal vision models and language models can be aligned for downstream vision-language tasks, and which properties of those unimodal representations most strongly predict alignment. The authors argue that common proxy evaluations of cross-modal alignment do not directly reflect practical use in vision-language systems, so they introduce an "alignment probing" method that freezes both backbones and trains a lightweight alignment layer on image-text pairs. They use this probing setup to compare multiple self-supervised vision encoders and several language embedders, and they examine how representation quality, model size, and training objective relate to image-text retrieval and reasoning.

The paper then proposes SAIL (Swift Alignment of Image and Language), an efficient transfer-learning framework that combines frozen pretrained vision and language backbones with a lightweight non-linear alignment layer, a sigmoid-based contrastive loss, and higher-quality captions. The authors evaluate SAIL on image classification, retrieval, open-vocabulary segmentation, Winoground-style compositional reasoning, and multimodal LLM integration. Across these benchmarks, SAIL generally outperforms CLIP and other baselines while using substantially less paired image-text data (about 6% of CLIP-scale training data in some comparisons), and it improves the language-compatibility of vision encoders for downstream multimodal models. The main conclusions are that clustering quality of SSL vision representations is more predictive of alignment than linear separability, strong language encoders matter greatly for complex reasoning, and efficient alignment training can yield strong multimodal performance without end-to-end training from scratch.

finding.finding_summary: SAIL is substantially more compute- and data-efficient than training CLIP-style models from scratch. The paper reports that SAIL needs only about 6% of the paired image-text data required by CLIP, can train with a single A100 GPU in roughly 5 hours, and supports batch sizes up to 32,768 while freezing the backbones.
finding.measure: Training compute, wall-clock time, batch size, and amount of paired image-text data required for alignment training

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies complex visio-linguistic reasoning, a durable-skill-like capability, through Winoground and related compositional benchmarks. SAIL-L-NV2 improves Winoground scores over CLIP-L (Text 40.25 vs 30.5, Image 18.75 vs 11.5, Group 15.0 vs 8.75), indicating better compositional reasoning, but the paper also shows that gains depend strongly on the language model and task type.
finding.measure: Winoground text, image, and group scores; related compositional retrieval/reasoning benchmarks

finding.finding_summary: Although not an education study, the paper evaluates general visual and language understanding tasks that map most closely to broad academic reasoning rather than a specific school subject. Across zero-shot ImageNet classification, retrieval, open-vocabulary segmentation, and multimodal benchmarks, SAIL improves over CLIP-like baselines; for example, SAIL-L-NV2 reaches 73.4% zero-shot top-1 accuracy on ImageNet and outperforms CLIP-L (72.7%) while using far less paired data.
finding.measure: Zero-shot image classification accuracy, retrieval recall@1/R@10, segmentation mIoU, multimodal benchmark scores

paper_profiles.title: Improve bone age assessment by learning from anatomical local regions
paper_profiles.population: Pediatric patients undergoing hand radiography for bone age assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses automated skeletal bone age assessment from pediatric hand radiographs, focusing on whether incorporating anatomical local regions can improve prediction accuracy and interpretability. The authors note that standard end-to-end deep learning models largely use global hand appearance, while clinical bone age assessment methods such as Tanner-Whitehouse (TW2) rely on localized analysis of specific hand bones.

To address this, the paper proposes Anatomical Local-Aware Network (ALA-Net), which combines a global ResNet-50 backbone with a local extraction module that learns anatomical regions via region proposal networks and ROI align. The model also adds an anatomical patch training strategy that uses detected regions as additional training crops, serving as a regularizer inspired by TW2-style local evaluation. The approach is evaluated on the RSNA Pediatric Bone Age Challenge dataset (12,611 training images, 1,425 validation images, 200 test images), with performance measured by mean absolute error (MAE) in months.

The main finding is that ALA-Net improves over the authors’ ablations and prior single-model methods, achieving 3.91 MAE on the test set versus 4.92 for a ResNet-50 baseline, 4.53 with local extraction only, and 4.49 with patch training only. Compared with the previous state of the art (BoNet, 4.14 MAE), the proposed method reports a 0.23 MAE improvement. The paper concludes that leveraging anatomical local information improves accuracy and interpretability for pediatric bone age assessment.

finding.finding_summary: ALA-Net improved automated pediatric bone age assessment on the RSNA dataset, reaching 3.91 MAE on the test set. This was better than the ResNet-50 baseline (4.92 MAE), local extraction only (4.53 MAE), patch training only (4.49 MAE), and the previous SOTA BoNet (4.14 MAE), indicating a meaningful accuracy gain from combining anatomical local extraction with patch-based training.
finding.measure: Mean absolute error (MAE) in months for bone age prediction on pediatric hand radiographs
finding.study_size: n=14,236 total images (12,611 train; 1,425 validation; 200 test)

paper_profiles.title: Domain Knowledge-Informed Self-Supervised Representations for Workout Form Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses automated assessment of workout form in real-world gym videos, where subtle exercise errors are difficult to detect because of camera angle changes, occlusions from equipment, lighting variation, and unusual body poses. The authors argue that off-the-shelf 2D/3D pose estimators are too unreliable in these conditions and propose replacing pose features with domain knowledge-informed self-supervised visual representations learned from unlabeled exercise videos.

The paper introduces two self-supervised approaches: cross-view cross-subject pose contrastive learning (CVCSPC), which learns pose-sensitive embeddings from quasi-synchronized videos, and motion disentangling (MD), which separates global exercise motion from local anomalous motion. To support training and evaluation, the authors also curate Fitness-AQA, a new in-the-wild dataset covering BackSquat, BarbellRow, and OverheadPress, with expert annotations for multiple exercise errors. They then finetune small labeled classifiers for error detection and compare against pose-based baselines and general self-supervised methods.

Experiments show that the proposed representations outperform off-the-shelf pose estimators and several generic self-supervised baselines, especially in complex real-world gym settings. In simpler controlled settings, gains are smaller and sometimes comparable to existing pose-based methods. Overall, the paper’s main contribution is methodological for action-quality assessment: it shows that domain-specific self-supervision can improve workout form error detection when pose estimation is brittle, and that the learned representations transfer to other tasks such as pose retrieval and dive quality assessment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies automated assessment of exercise/workout form, a vocational/physical-skill quality assessment task rather than a conventional academic subject. On the in-the-wild Fitness-AQA benchmark, the proposed self-supervised representations improved error detection over pose-based and general SSL baselines, including F-scores such as 0.5195 vs 0.4143 for knees-inward error (KIE) with CVCSPC, and 0.5263 for KIE when combining MD + CVCSPC. On the Waseda Squat controlled benchmark, the method achieved 89.92 average accuracy vs 89.08 for the HMR-TDM baseline.
finding.measure: Workout form / exercise error detection performance (F-score, accuracy)

paper_profiles.title: NetBench: A Large-Scale and Comprehensive Network Traffic Benchmark Dataset for Foundation Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces NetBench, a benchmark dataset and evaluation suite for network traffic analysis models. The authors argue that prior work in encrypted traffic classification and generation often used inconsistent datasets, incompatible preprocessing pipelines, and sometimes leakage-prone train/test splits, making model comparisons unfair and difficult to reproduce.

To address these issues, the paper constructs a unified benchmark from seven public network-traffic datasets spanning 20 tasks: 15 classification tasks and 5 generation tasks. The benchmark standardizes preprocessing by splitting data before extraction, anonymizing sensitive header fields, converting traffic to hexadecimal, and applying WordPiece tokenization; it also supports both flow-level and packet-level evaluation. The authors evaluate eight state-of-the-art models, including foundation models ET-BERT and YaTC, plus two generative models, STAN and NetShare. Across the classification tasks, the foundation models substantially outperform traditional deep learning baselines, while generation results show task-specific strengths for STAN and NetShare. The main contribution is therefore methodological: a unified benchmark for fair comparison, not a study of an educational intervention or learner outcome.

paper_profiles.title: Monitoring the Evolution of Behavioural Embeddings in Social Media Recommendation
paper_profiles.venue: SIGIR ’24 (Proceedings of the 47th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how item embeddings used in a large-scale short-video recommender system evolve over time under two update strategies: batch learning and real-time learning. The motivating problem is operational rather than educational: short-video platforms receive a continuous stream of new content, and recommender systems must rapidly learn useful content representations from sparse and delayed feedback.

Using production data from ShareChat, the authors analyze embeddings for Hindi-language video posts over one week, focusing primarily on the view signal and comparing how quickly embeddings mature, how informative successive updates are, and how embedding norms relate to popularity bias. They compute embedding-distance metrics from Field-aware Factorization Machines (FFMs) and compare batch updates every six hours with per-interaction real-time updates.

The main findings are that real-time embeddings mature much faster than batch embeddings, reaching maturity with about 20% of the interactions and achieving saturation roughly three times sooner. The paper also reports that real-time updates improve user engagement metrics such as video click rate and successful video play rate in low-view buckets, while batch training produces substantially larger embedding norms and stronger popularity bias. Overall, the paper argues that monitoring embedding evolution can help diagnose recommender performance and guide system design choices.

finding.finding_summary: Real-time updating of content embeddings was substantially more efficient than batch updating in terms of learning speed. The paper reports that real-time embeddings matured with only about 20% of the user interactions required by batch learning, and that the saturation point was reached about 3x faster (around 1,500 views versus 3,500 views) on the analyzed short-video dataset.
finding.measure: Embedding maturity / convergence speed measured by cosine distance between successive embeddings and the converged embedding

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved user engagement under real-time embedding updates, especially for items in lower view buckets. Compared with batch updates, real-time training showed better video click rate and successful video play percentage, indicating stronger engagement with recommended content in the early lifecycle of posts.
finding.measure: Video click rate and successful video play percentage across view buckets

paper_profiles.title: Embedding Formative Assessment: Evaluation report and executive summary
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report evaluates whether the Embedding Formative Assessment (EFA) programme improved secondary school pupils’ attainment when implemented at scale in ordinary school conditions. The core question was whether a whole-school professional development model focused on formative assessment strategies could raise GCSE outcomes compared with business-as-usual practice.

EFA was a two-year, whole-school intervention for secondary schools in England. It combined monthly Teacher Learning Community (TLC) workshops, peer lesson observations, school-based lead teachers, an initial training day led by Dylan Wiliam, and ongoing support from SSAT. The intervention materials targeted five broad formative assessment strategies, but schools could choose specific techniques to try within each strategy, meaning the programme was a bundled professional development and implementation package rather than a single isolated component.

The trial randomized 140 secondary schools to intervention or control, with outcomes measured using National Pupil Database GCSE data for 25,393 Year 10 pupils at baseline. The primary outcome was Attainment 8; secondary outcomes were GCSE Maths and English. The main finding was a small positive effect on Attainment 8 (Hedges g = 0.10, 95% CI -0.01 to 0.21), equivalent to about two additional months’ progress, but no significant effects on Maths or English separately. A subgroup analysis suggested somewhat larger effects for lower prior attainers and for schools not previously exposed to the related TEEP programme, while compliance analysis produced a similar overall estimate. Overall, the report concludes that EFA had modest positive effects on broad GCSE attainment, but that implementation varied across schools and subject-specific effects were not detected.

finding.finding_summary: The primary outcome was Attainment 8 GCSE scores. In the main precise ITT model, the intervention produced a small positive effect of Hedges g = 0.10 (95% CI -0.01 to 0.21; p = 0.088) for all pupils (n = 25,393). This was interpreted by the evaluators as roughly two additional months’ progress, indicating a modest positive impact on broad GCSE attainment.
finding.measure: Attainment 8 GCSE score

finding.finding_summary: For GCSE Maths, the precise model estimated a very small effect size of g = 0.02 (95% CI -0.08 to 0.12; p = 0.74) for all pupils (n = 22,935). The report found no significant evidence that EFA improved maths attainment, and subgroup analyses for FSM pupils were also null (g = -0.01, 95% CI -0.12 to 0.10; n = 6,564).
finding.measure: GCSE Maths numerical grade

finding.finding_summary: For GCSE English, the precise model estimated a very small effect size of g = 0.02 (95% CI -0.08 to 0.11; p = 0.72) for all pupils (n = 22,628). The report found no significant evidence that EFA improved English attainment, and the FSM subgroup analysis was also null (g = 0.00, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.12; n = 6,489).
finding.measure: GCSE English numerical grade

paper_profiles.title: Scaffolding in Teacher–Student Interaction: A Decade of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines a decade of research on scaffolding in teacher–student interaction, focusing on three questions: how scaffolding is conceptualized, what forms it takes in classrooms, and whether it is effective. The authors argue that scaffolding is often used too broadly and propose three key characteristics that should define it: contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility. They also synthesize prior work into a framework that distinguishes scaffolding intentions (e.g., metacognitive, cognitive, affective) from scaffolding means (e.g., feedback, hints, modeling, questioning).

The review searched SSCI, ERIC, and PsycINFO for English-language articles published from 1998 to 2009 on human scaffolding in face-to-face primary and secondary education. Of 66 included articles, most were theoretical or descriptive; only eight were effectiveness studies. The empirical literature was concentrated in literacy, with fewer studies in math and science, and most studies used qualitative or small-scale observational methods. The review concludes that scaffolding appears effective in the limited set of effectiveness studies, especially for students’ metacognitive and cognitive outcomes, but that the field suffers from major measurement problems and inconsistent operationalizations.

A central conclusion is that future scaffolding research should move beyond descriptive accounts and adopt clearer, more systematic measurement that captures both teacher and student behavior, as well as the dynamic qualities of scaffolding. The paper is not a direct comparison of formative assessment models; rather, it notes formative assessment as one diagnostic strategy related to contingency within scaffolding.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that scaffolding research was most developed in literacy, and descriptive studies frequently documented literacy-related scaffolding practices such as modeling, questioning, and explanation. In the effectiveness literature, literacy was one of the main domains in which scaffolding was associated with improved performance, though the review does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Literacy practices, text comprehension, reading discussions, and related classroom literacy outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Several effectiveness studies in mathematics found benefits from contingent scaffolding. In Murphy and Messer (2000), more children in the scaffolding condition advanced in representation level on a balance-scale task than children in the comparison groups, and in Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998), students receiving contingent support solved significantly more long-division problems than peers in other conditions at immediate and follow-up testing.
finding.measure: Balance scale performance and long-division problem solving
finding.study_size: n=41, n=40, n=41; and n=8 per condition in Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998)

finding.finding_summary: Science-focused studies generally found scaffolding to be beneficial for conceptual understanding and reasoning. For example, Mercer et al. (2004) reported better use of talk for reasoning and greater gains on reasoning measures in the scaffolded condition, and Azevedo et al. (2005) found that adaptive human scaffolding was associated with more shifts in mental models and greater knowledge gains than fixed or no scaffolding.
finding.measure: Reasoning talk, mental model shifts, and knowledge of science content (e.g., circulatory system, chemical equilibrium)
finding.study_size: n=109 vs n=121; n=38, n=34, n=37; and n=20 vs n=10 in the cited studies

finding.finding_summary: The review includes evidence that scaffolding can support engagement, motivation, enjoyment, and involvement. Turner et al. (1998) found that classrooms with more intrinsic support and transfer of responsibility had higher student involvement, while Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998) found no condition differences in enjoyment except that the no-support group scored lower than the supported groups.
finding.measure: Student involvement, motivation/emotion, and enjoyment questionnaires
finding.study_size: n=42 across 34 math lessons; and n=40 total across five support conditions in Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998)

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the review is on metacognitive and collaborative/interactive aspects of scaffolding, including transfer of responsibility, self-regulation, and reasoning together. Studies reported improved self-regulating behavior, more constructive interaction, better diagnostic accuracy by tutors, and higher transfer-question performance when scaffolding was more contingent or interactive.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning behaviors, collaborative reasoning, transfer questions, and diagnostic/interactive tutoring behaviors

finding.finding_summary: The review does not substantively evaluate productivity or workload outcomes, but it does discuss that contingent scaffolding may make diagnosis more accurate and interactions more constructive. These are process benefits rather than direct efficiency outcomes, so evidence for this category is weak and indirect.
finding.measure: Teacher diagnosis accuracy and interaction constructiveness

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and postgraduate students in higher education; higher education institutions and educators as the unit of analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI) has been studied in higher education, who is producing that research, and what kinds of applications are being investigated. The authors conducted a systematic review of 146 peer-reviewed journal articles published from 2007 through November 2018, drawn from Web of Science, Scopus, and EBSCO Education Source, and coded them for publication patterns, conceptualization of AI, ethical reflection, and application types.

The review finds that the literature is dominated by computer science and STEM authors, with relatively little involvement from educators, and that most studies are quantitative. The reviewed AI work clusters into four application areas: profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalization. Across the set, the authors note a striking lack of explicit definitions of AI and very limited critical discussion of privacy, ethics, cost, and pedagogical implications.

Substantively, the paper is a map of the field rather than an evaluation of one intervention. It reports that many AI systems are used for prediction/classification, automated grading, feedback, and tutoring, often showing high accuracy or generally positive preliminary results, but the evidence base is uneven and frequently short-term. The authors conclude that AI in higher education has grown quickly, but educators are underrepresented and more theoretically grounded, ethically informed, and pedagogically relevant research is needed.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed higher-education AI studies, many applications were explicitly designed to automate or streamline tasks such as admission decisions, course scheduling, grading, feedback, plagiarism/academic integrity checking, and some advising or support functions. The review concludes that AI applications can perform assessment and evaluation tasks at very high accuracy and efficiency levels, and that such systems could reduce staff workload, especially in large-enrollment contexts, although the paper does not report a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Accuracy/efficiency of AI systems for grading, prediction, and administrative decision support; workload reduction implications
finding.study_size: n=146 reviewed articles; outcome-specific studies vary

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies a substantial body of work using AI for institutional and administrative purposes, including profiling and prediction, admission decisions, course scheduling, retention, career services, and alignment of student competencies with labor-market needs. These studies generally suggest that AI can support institutional decision-making and student management, but the evidence is descriptive and heterogeneous rather than an evaluated institutional reform with a pooled impact estimate.
finding.measure: Institutional decision-making applications (admissions, retention, advising, course planning, competency matching)
finding.study_size: n=146 reviewed articles; outcome-specific studies vary

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies focused on academic learning tasks outside the core literacy/math/science categories, especially automated essay scoring, writing feedback, and subject-specific tutoring in computer science, business, medicine, physics, and language learning. The review reports generally positive or satisfactory preliminary results for many of these systems, but also notes important limitations such as genre appropriateness for automated essay scoring and concerns about feedback quality.
finding.measure: Essay scoring accuracy, tutoring performance, and subject-specific learning support in higher education
finding.study_size: n=146 reviewed articles; outcome-specific studies vary

finding.finding_summary: The review includes studies that used AI to predict student engagement, academic motivation, and dropout risk, and it notes that these systems can identify low-engaged or at-risk students for intervention. Findings are mostly positive about predictive utility, but the paper does not synthesize a causal effect on motivation or engagement outcomes, and some studies reported negative or limited support for particular learner groups.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, dropout/retention risk, and related student-behavior indicators
finding.study_size: n=146 reviewed articles; outcome-specific studies vary

finding.finding_summary: A smaller set of reviewed studies addressed skills such as collaboration, self-regulation, and metacognitive support through intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive systems. The review reports that these applications generally aimed to support collaborative learning, self-regulated learning, and problem solving, with mostly positive preliminary results, but the evidence base is limited and short-term.
finding.measure: Collaborative learning support, self-regulatory support, and problem-solving assistance
finding.study_size: n=146 reviewed articles; outcome-specific studies vary

paper_profiles.title: AI Literacy as a Key Driver of User Experience in AI-Powered Assessment: Insights from Socratic Mind
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how undergraduate students’ AI literacy and prior exposure to AI technologies shape their experiences with Socratic Mind, an AI-powered oral formative assessment tool. The paper asks whether students who are more AI-literate perceive the system as more usable, satisfying, engaging, and effective for learning, and whether mere prior exposure to generative AI predicts similar outcomes.

The intervention/context is Socratic Mind, an interactive oral assessment system embedded in Computer Science and Business courses at a research university. Students used the tool across a semester as a practice quiz and then completed UX and AI literacy surveys; the analysis included 309 valid responses. The authors used PLS-SEM, group comparisons by AI literacy and AI exposure, and analyses by demographics to study relationships among AI literacy, usability, satisfaction, engagement, and perceived learning effectiveness.

Results show that AI literacy was a strong predictor of usability, satisfaction, and engagement, and it indirectly predicted perceived learning effectiveness through usability and satisfaction. In contrast, prior AI exposure alone did not significantly predict perceptions of the tool. Students with higher AI literacy reported more favorable UX and higher perceived effectiveness, while generative-AI usage showed only limited differences on some AI-literacy subcomponents. The study concludes that functional AI competence matters more than simple familiarity, and that adaptive, user-centered design can improve the effectiveness of AI-powered formative assessment.

finding.finding_summary: Students with higher AI literacy reported significantly better engagement, satisfaction, and usability when using Socratic Mind. In the PLS-SEM model, AI literacy positively predicted engagement (β = .160, p < .001), usability (β = .301, p < .001), and satisfaction (β = .212, p < .001) among 309 undergraduates.
finding.measure: Engagement survey, satisfaction items, usability survey

finding.finding_summary: AI literacy was associated with higher perceived learning effectiveness through indirect pathways, and it was not directly significant for effectiveness (β = .041, p = .324). Usability and satisfaction strongly predicted perceived learning effectiveness, with the model explaining substantial variance in effectiveness (R² = .616) across 309 undergraduates.
finding.measure: Perceived learning effectiveness survey

paper_profiles.title: CS1-LLM: Integrating LLMs into CS1 Instruction
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM Symposium on Computer Science Education (paper text indicates arXiv preprint and conference-style format)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This experience report describes a redesign of an introductory programming course (CS1) around large language models (LLMs), specifically GitHub Copilot, at a research-intensive university. The authors ask what students can do now with LLM support that they could not do before, and they restructure the course to reduce emphasis on syntax and writing code from scratch while increasing emphasis on code reading, tracing, explanation, testing, debugging, problem decomposition, and prompt engineering.

The course is built around frequent formative assessments, supervised and unsupervised uses of Copilot, and three large open-ended projects in data science, image processing, and games. The student population is standard undergraduate CS1 enrollment with many non-majors and substantial representation of women, first-generation students, Pell-eligible students, and students from multiple racial/ethnic groups. The paper uses survey data from 315 of 552 students (57% response rate), course artifacts, and instructor observations, but explicitly states that it did not conduct formal quantitative or qualitative analysis at this stage.

Main conclusions are that most students reported feeling comfortable using GenAI tools and that a slight majority felt Copilot helped their learning of fundamental programming concepts, though a notable minority worried about over-reliance and reduced confidence working without Copilot. Students frequently read, tested, and modified Copilot output, and they valued the open-ended projects. The authors conclude that integrating LLMs into CS1 is feasible and potentially beneficial, but requires clearer expectations about when students should and should not rely on LLM support and more careful alignment of assessments with learning goals.

finding.finding_summary: The course redesign shifted emphasis away from writing code from scratch and toward code reading, tracing, explanation, debugging, problem decomposition, and prompt engineering in an undergraduate CS1 setting. The paper does not report a controlled comparison or effect size, but it describes that students were able to complete larger and more open-ended programming projects than typical CS1 assignments and that exam performance mostly mirrored previous CS1 offerings, with code-writing-from-scratch performance slightly lower anecdotally.
finding.measure: Course performance on exams, projects, and formative assessments focused on Python programming, code reading, tracing, debugging, and project completion

finding.finding_summary: Student survey results suggested generally positive attitudes toward learning with Copilot: 79% reported being comfortable using GenAI tools to program, and 59% said Copilot helped their learning of programming concepts. However, some students reported feeling over-reliant on Copilot or less confident working without it, indicating a mixed social-emotional response rather than uniformly positive effects.
finding.measure: End-of-course survey items on comfort using GenAI, perceived learning impact, and confidence working without Copilot

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes durable skills such as problem decomposition, testing, debugging, code explanation, and collaboration/pair programming as core course goals and formative-assessment targets. Survey and artifact evidence indicate that students commonly read Copilot-generated code, tested it, and modified it, suggesting engagement with metacognitive and debugging practices, but the paper reports no formal outcome analysis or effect size for these skills.
finding.measure: Survey self-reports on interacting with Copilot; completion of decomposed project diagrams and debugging/testing tasks
finding.study_size: n=315 survey respondents; course artifacts from enrolled students

finding.finding_summary: Operationally, the course design used Copilot and PrairieLearn to increase the scale and openness of programming tasks students could complete in CS1. The paper reports that projects were graded in about 10–15 minutes each by instructional assistants and that students were able to attempt larger projects and a large Copilot-supported final-exam task, but it does not compare workload or productivity against a baseline with quantitative effects.
finding.measure: Instructor/grader time for project grading; ability to complete larger programming tasks with Copilot support

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues for a broader institutional redesign of CS1 around LLMs and reports that nearly every course element was changed, including lectures, labs, homework, quizzes, projects, and the final exam. The main institutional finding is that a full CS1 redesign integrating LLMs is feasible in a research-intensive university context, but the authors also note implementation challenges such as unclear expectations, assessment alignment, and login/credential issues during exams.
finding.measure: Course redesign implementation, assessment structure, and instructional lessons learned

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the value of formative assessment and how it can be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard Learning System, in a university context. The authors frame formative assessment as a way to provide continuous feedback during instruction, contrasting it with summative assessment that occurs at the end of a course.

The implementation described uses weekly or fortnightly online tests in Blackboard, with immediate detailed feedback after each attempt. The paper also reports a student survey (16-item questionnaire plus open-ended responses) on perceptions of continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and the Blackboard test option. Students generally supported the approach because it broke content into smaller topic-based assessments and provided immediate feedback, flexibility, and a clearer sense of progress.

The sample came from Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus) students across Business, Engineering, and IT streams. The main conclusions are that frequent online formative assessments were viewed positively, particularly for their feedback function and ease of studying smaller units, and that the Blackboard option could support a culture of success and may help improve learning and summative performance. However, the paper is largely descriptive and perception-based rather than a controlled effectiveness study.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent online formative assessments were helpful because they provided immediate feedback, helped them monitor strengths and weaknesses, and kept them on track during the semester. The paper reports majority support for frequent internal assessments and teacher feedback, but does not provide an overall effect size on motivation or engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Student perception survey on continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard test implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues and reports student perceptions that formative assessment supports metacognitive processes such as checking progress, reflecting on mistakes, and learning topics progressively. Students indicated that the approach helped them understand where they stood in the course and improve over time, but no standardized metacognition measure or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of progress monitoring, reflection, and self-evaluation

finding.finding_summary: Students viewed the Blackboard-based formative assessment as a useful way to learn course content in smaller units and prepare for semester examinations. The study reports that frequent weekly or fortnightly assessments with immediate feedback were perceived as supporting learning and likely improving summative grades, but it does not report objective achievement scores.
finding.measure: Perceived course learning and preparation for summative semester examinations

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: Mixed (teachers and students across K-12 and higher education examples)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative/practical review that asks how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support core formative assessment functions in education. The authors frame formative assessment around three recurring questions: where learners are going, where they currently are, and how to move them forward. They argue that LLMs may help scale common formative practices such as rewriting learning goals into student-friendly language, generating discussion prompts and exemplars, producing feedback, and creating quick checks for understanding.

The paper is not an empirical evaluation of a specific AI intervention. Instead, it synthesizes existing work on formative assessment, prompt engineering, automatic question generation, and AI-assisted feedback, and then provides examples and classroom-oriented prompting templates. The examples span school and university settings, with frequent illustrations from high school biology and undergraduate fMRI instruction. The authors emphasize that LLMs can augment but not replace teacher expertise, and that outputs should be checked for accuracy, pedagogical fit, and cultural/contextual appropriateness.

The main conclusion is that LLMs are potentially useful for reducing teacher workload and making formative assessment more scalable and accessible, but current evaluation metrics and much of the existing AI literature do not adequately capture formative-assessment quality. The paper also highlights risks such as over-reliance on AI, limitations in generic LLM-generated MCQs and feedback, and the need for teacher assessment literacy to guide effective use. It argues for future research that links pedagogical theory with AI tool design and develops stronger formative-assessment-specific benchmarks.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher time and effort by automating or assisting with routine formative-assessment tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating discussion prompts, creating exemplars, and producing formative questions. No empirical effect size is reported because this is a narrative review rather than an evaluation study.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / task efficiency (conceptual discussion, not empirically measured)

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests LLM-supported formative assessment can foster metacognition, self-regulation, and critical thinking by prompting students to reflect on learning goals, evaluate exemplars, and engage with feedback at the process and self-regulation levels. These claims are theoretical and illustrative rather than empirically tested in this paper.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-regulation, critical thinking (theoretical discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that formative assessment can support student engagement and motivation, and it argues that LLMs may help by making goals clearer and feedback more immediate and personalized. However, the paper does not present direct empirical evidence for these outcomes in this study.
finding.measure: Engagement / motivation (discussion only)

paper_profiles.title: Average Is Not Enough: Caveats of Multilingual Evaluation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines a methodological problem in multilingual natural language processing (NLP): evaluation practices that rely on simple aggregate statistics, especially average performance across languages, can hide important patterns and bias conclusions in favor of dominant language families. The authors argue that multilingual results should be interpreted with the help of qualitative analysis grounded in comparative linguistics and typological information, rather than only by summary scores.

To illustrate the issue, the paper proposes a visualization approach built on the URIEL typological database and UMAP projection of language features. The authors apply this approach in case studies on previously published multilingual NLP papers, showing that aggregate averages can overstate the value of cross-lingual transfer for some language groups while obscuring better performance for other languages or clusters. The analysis highlights that languages in dominant European clusters often benefit more from cross-lingual supervision, while many non-European languages and some non-Latin-script languages show different patterns that are hidden by averages.

The paper is not an intervention study and does not involve a student or school sample. Its contribution is methodological: it recommends richer evaluation practices for multilingual systems and demonstrates that visualization-based qualitative analysis can uncover linguistic bias in published results. The main conclusion is that average performance alone is insufficient for fair multilingual evaluation and can mislead interpretation.

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Bilingual: Multi-sense Word Embeddings using Multilingual Context
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of learning multi-sense word embeddings when a word has different meanings in different contexts. The authors argue that bilingual signals are often insufficient for disambiguating polysemous words because senses can survive translation, and they propose a multilingual extension that leverages parallel corpora from multiple languages to improve sense induction in English.

The method is a multi-view Bayesian non-parametric embedding model built on a skip-gram-like objective with a Dirichlet process prior over senses. It jointly learns English sense vectors and foreign-language word vectors from aligned parallel corpora, using English as a bridge language so that multilingual contexts help cluster senses more accurately. The model can infer a variable number of senses per word and is trained with stochastic variational inference.

Experiments are conducted on parallel corpora in English paired with French, Chinese, Spanish, and Russian, using word sense induction benchmarks (Semeval-2007, Semeval-2010, and WWSI) and contextual word similarity (SCWS). Results show that multilingual training generally improves word sense induction over monolingual and bilingual baselines, with the best performance coming from multilingual models; however, performance on contextual word similarity is mixed and not consistently improved. The paper also reports that using more distant language families can provide slightly better disambiguation signals, and that crosslingual window size affects performance.

finding.finding_summary: The multilingual model improves word sense induction compared with monolingual and bilingual baselines. On the main WSI benchmarks, the FULL multilingual model outperforms the MONO baseline (e.g., average ARI .082 vs .073 for En-Fr; .075 vs .067 for En-Zh; .093 vs .082 for En-FrZh), with the strongest gains coming from multilingual training. The paper also reports that using non-Indo-European languages yields slightly larger average ARI improvements than Indo-European languages in controlled-domain experiments.
finding.measure: Word sense induction performance (Adjusted Rand Index, ARI) on Semeval-2007, Semeval-2010, and WWSI

paper_profiles.title: Towards Global, Socio-Economic, and Culturally Aware Recommender Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of recommender systems that do not adequately account for cultural identity and socio-economic context when predicting user preferences. The author argues that standard recommenders, which often rely mainly on interaction history or item metadata, can produce less accurate or less relevant recommendations when deployed across diverse markets and countries.

To address this gap, the paper reviews recommender-system literature and proposes an ontology and modelling approach for incorporating cultural and socio-economic indicators into recommendation pipelines. The method is illustrated with a streaming-media subscription-plan selection scenario, where country-level data are combined with domain-specific subscription data to build and evaluate machine-learning models. The paper emphasizes using publicly available country indicators, cultural indices, demographic variables, and infrastructure measures to construct context-aware recommendation features.

The empirical demonstration focuses on predicting subscription-plan preference at the country level, rather than on educational settings or learners. The paper reports that a highly tuned artificial neural network using domain-specific data plus selected cultural and socio-economic factors achieved 95% accuracy, 94% precision, 92% F1, and 90% recall in the illustrated scenario. Overall, the paper concludes that socio-economic and culturally aware recommender systems may improve recommendation accuracy and relevance in global markets, but it is primarily a conceptual and modelling paper rather than a school-based evaluation.

paper_profiles.title: Notes on socio-economic transparency mechanisms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual and position-style review of socio-economic transparency mechanisms.
