It asks how systems can make the implications of socio-economic choices more transparent, with emphasis on the inference problem: how to turn many individual reports into useful summaries or answers for an inquirer. The paper frames transparency systems as instruments that support both inquiry and reporting, and it organizes the design space around four challenges: language, inference, truth/gaming, and privacy.

Rather than evaluating a specific intervention in an empirical study, the author surveys established examples from practice such as product reviews, salary databases, web platforms, and whistleblowing systems. The paper discusses how limited vocabularies enable aggregation, how machine learning and natural language processing might support inference, how mechanisms can expose discrepancies to reduce gaming, and how anonymity and privacy-preserving methods can protect reporters and those mentioned in reports.

The main conclusion is that existing transparency systems only occupy points along a much broader possible spectrum, and that future progress will likely depend on better inference methods, stronger trustworthiness and anti-gaming tools, and privacy-preserving designs. The paper is exploratory and forward-looking, with no empirical evaluation, and it argues that these mechanism design questions remain open, including financing and broader deployment.

paper_profiles.title: Multilingual Event Linking to Wikidata
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of multilingual event linking: given an event mention in text, identify the corresponding event in Wikidata. The authors argue that event grounding is a useful complement to event coreference because it can scale to large multilingual corpora and provide a shared, global representation of event identity across languages and documents.

To study this, they automatically compile a large dataset from multilingual Wikipedia and Wikidata, with 1.8M mentions across 44 languages linked to 10.9K events. They define two benchmark settings: a multilingual task, where mention and event descriptions are in the same language, and a crosslingual task, where event descriptions are always in English. They evaluate BM25+ and multilingual retrieve-and-rank systems based on mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa, finding that the neural biencoder/crossencoder models substantially outperform BM25+ and that crosslingual linking is harder than multilingual linking.

The paper also creates a smaller Wikinews-based evaluation set to test out-of-domain generalization and reports that performance drops in the zero-shot setting, especially for unseen events in newswire. The analysis highlights specific challenges such as temporal reasoning, temporal/spatial mentions, and the relative informativeness of language-specific versus English event descriptions. The work is primarily a benchmark/dataset and modeling paper for multilingual NLP, not an educational intervention study.

paper_profiles.title: Multilingual Email Zoning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of email zoning, i.e., segmenting email text into functional zones such as greetings, quotations, signatures, code blocks, and technical content. The authors note that prior email zoning research was largely English-centric, despite email being a multilingual communication medium and despite downstream NLP applications needing robust segmentation across languages.

To address this gap, the paper introduces a new multilingual benchmark, Cleverly zoning corpus, containing 625 annotated emails in Portuguese, Spanish, and French, all labeled with a 15-zone schema adapted from prior work. The annotations were produced by two bilingual annotators, and the paper reports inter-annotator agreement as well as zone distributions across languages. The authors also propose OKAPI, a multilingual email segmentation model built from a frozen XLM-RoBERTa sentence encoder plus a BiLSTM-CRF segmentation module.

The evaluation shows that OKAPI generalizes reasonably well in zero-shot multilingual testing when trained on English and applied to the new multilingual corpus, and that it is competitive with prior English zoning systems on several established benchmarks. The model also performs well in domain adaptation settings, outperforming QUAGGA in the reported cross-corpus experiments. Overall, the paper’s main contribution is methodological and benchmark-oriented: it expands email zoning beyond English and demonstrates that multilingual transformer-based segmentation can be effective for this task.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that OKAPI can automatically segment emails into functional zones with strong accuracy, which supports downstream NLP workflows and reduces the need for manual preprocessing. In multilingual zero-shot evaluation, the model achieved global accuracy of 0.91 (pt), 0.93 (es), and 0.93 (fr); on English benchmarks it reached 0.96 on the 15-zone Gmane task and 0.99/0.95 on 2-zone and 5-zone cross-domain settings, respectively.
finding.measure: Email zoning accuracy / zone classification accuracy
finding.study_size: n=625 multilingual benchmark emails; plus reported evaluations on prior English corpora (sizes not reported in the table excerpt for all comparisons)

finding.finding_summary: The paper contributes a new multilingual email zoning corpus and shows that multilingual annotation and evaluation are feasible beyond English-centric resources. It releases the Cleverly zoning corpus with 625 emails across Portuguese, Spanish, and French, which is positioned as infrastructure for future research rather than an individual-task intervention.
finding.measure: Corpus creation and inter-annotator agreement; benchmark availability

paper_profiles.title: Socio-economic Segregation in a Population-Scale Social Network
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether socio-economic segregation is more pronounced when measured through social networks rather than through standard spatial neighborhood boundaries. The authors ask whether the common neighborhood-based lens underestimates segregation and whether a network-based approach can reveal “hidden” segregation across multiple social contexts.

To address this, they use population-scale administrative register data from the Netherlands covering 17.2 million residents and 1.3 billion ties, aggregated to 7.7 million households connected through family, school, work, and next-door-neighbor relations. They measure segregation using income assortativity and compare it across the multilayer social network and administrative neighborhoods. They also decompose segregation by network layer and by municipality.

The main conclusion is that segregation is substantially higher in the social network than in spatial neighborhoods: overall income assortativity is about 0.22 in the network versus 0.10 in administrative neighborhoods. Segregation is present across family, school, work, and neighbor layers, with next-door neighbors most segregated and family least segregated. The paper also finds higher segregation in larger municipalities, challenging the assumption that cities necessarily promote socio-economic mixing. The study argues that spatial measures alone can substantially underestimate social segregation and inequality.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that measuring segregation through a population-scale social network reveals substantially more socio-economic segregation than standard administrative-neighborhood measures. Overall income assortativity is 0.217 in the social network versus 0.103 in neighborhoods, indicating that spatial indicators systematically understate the degree of segregation present in social structure.
finding.measure: Income assortativity comparing multilayer social network vs administrative neighborhoods
finding.study_size: n=17.2 million residents; n=7.7 million households

finding.finding_summary: The school layer is one of the constituent social contexts analyzed and shows moderate income segregation (ρ=0.16), though less than work and neighbor ties. The paper further reports heterogeneous patterns by school type, with higher exposure to low-income households in higher education and stronger rich-poor segregation in primary and secondary schooling.
finding.measure: Income assortativity within the school network layer; within-decile concentration of contacts by school type
finding.study_size: n=2.2 million school-network nodes (households) for the school layer

finding.finding_summary: Operational efficiency is not a substantive outcome of the study, but the paper does report that the work layer is the largest network layer and makes the largest incremental contribution to overall segregation when layers are added sequentially. This is an institutional/network-structure finding rather than an efficiency outcome, so evidence for operational efficiency is limited and indirect.
finding.measure: Layer contribution to overall assortativity; average degree of work layer
finding.study_size: n=4.6 million household nodes in the work layer

paper_profiles.title: Tracing Multilingual Representations in LLMs with Cross-Layer Transcoders
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how multilingual large language models internally represent and process multiple languages, with a focus on whether they build shared language-agnostic representations and how they recover the correct output language. The authors ask why multilingual models often perform better in English than in other languages, even when trained on multilingual data.

To study this, they train several GPT-2-style multilingual models and TinyStories-based multilingual models across five languages (English, German, French, Arabic, and Chinese), and also analyze a larger off-the-shelf LLaMA model. They use Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) and attribution graphs to trace feature circuits across layers, plus intervention and model-diffing experiments to test causal mechanisms behind language decoding and language-specific failures.

The main finding is that multilingual models develop a shared multilingual space in middle layers, while early and late layers are more language-specific. Language identity is decoded in later layers using a small set of high-frequency features, and targeted interventions on these features can change the model’s output language. The paper also finds that performance gaps across languages are linked less to missing shared representations and more to tokenization bias, weaker late-layer activations, and language-specific decoding failures, especially for Arabic.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies multilingual language generation and decoding behavior in LLMs across English, German, French, Arabic, and Chinese. It finds that models can generate and route outputs in multiple languages through shared middle-layer representations, but performance remains better in English; non-English failures are associated with weak late-layer features and tokenization issues rather than absence of multilingual circuits.
finding.measure: Language modeling / next-token prediction performance, validation cross-entropy loss, logit rank, output-language decoding behavior

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment II. Indications of Effectiveness in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.venue: arXiv (Technology in Practice Strand; companion paper to WIPTTE 2013 proceedings)
paper_profiles.population: High School, Undergraduate, Graduate, Community College
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether InkSurvey, a free web-based tool for collecting open-ended, real-time formative assessment responses via pen-enabled mobile devices, can support learning across diverse educational settings. The motivation is practical and pedagogical: instructors need an efficient way to embed formative assessment in instruction and receive immediate information about student thinking so they can adjust teaching before misconceptions become entrenched.

The paper synthesizes seven vignette-style cases from multiple instructors and contexts, including high school algebra, undergraduate physics and engineering, chemistry, biology, and graduate courses in the United States and Mexico. Across these settings, instructors used InkSurvey to pose open-ended questions, view student work in real time, and provide immediate feedback or follow-up instruction. The evidence presented is mostly observational and comparative rather than experimental, but it suggests improved conceptual understanding, stronger problem-solving, greater student engagement, and positive instructor perceptions when formative assessment is integrated with InkSurvey.

The clearest quantitative examples include reduced persistence of a triple-integrals misconception in a calculus course (1/87 students vs. 12/103 in a comparison lecture section), higher Algebra I mastery in a high school setting relative to students not exposed to InkSurvey, mean quiz score gains of 0.6 points in an undergraduate course and 0.5 points in a graduate course on a 10-point scale, and an increase in simulation-based conceptual competence from about 1.8 to 2.3 to 3.1 on a 4-point scale after guided InkSurvey prompting. The paper concludes that InkSurvey is effective as a real-time formative assessment tool across varied disciplines and educational environments, while also noting that successful implementation depends on instructor skill in question design and responsive teaching.

finding.finding_summary: In a Calculus III setting, InkSurvey was used to reveal and repair a misconception about triple integrals over general regions. Two weeks later, only 1 of 87 students on the InkSurvey-supported lesson still made the error on exam questions, compared with 12 of 103 students in a comparable large-lecture section without InkSurvey. The evidence is comparative and suggestive of improved mathematical understanding, though the paper reports no effect size or statistical test.
finding.measure: Summative exam performance on triple-integral concept questions / misconception persistence

finding.finding_summary: In upper-level engineering physics and chemical engineering contexts, InkSurvey-supported formative assessment was associated with improved problem-solving and conceptual competence. One study reported steady improvement over a semester in problem-solving skills as new problems were introduced; another reported competence rising from about 1.8 to 2.3 after unguided simulation use and to about 3.1 after InkSurvey-guided questioning on a 4-point scale across six concepts.
finding.measure: Problem-solving strategy scores; conceptual competence ratings on a 4-point scale

finding.finding_summary: In undergraduate and graduate food chemistry courses redesigned around frequent formative assessment, students showed improved performance on summative quizzes compared with cohorts from four years earlier. The paper reports mean gains of 0.6 points in the undergraduate course and 0.5 points in the graduate course out of 10 possible points, alongside increased participation in class discussions and problem-solving activities.
finding.measure: Summative quiz scores; classroom participation in discussions/problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: Student attitudes toward InkSurvey were generally favorable, with evidence of increased engagement, motivation, and perceived usefulness for understanding material. In one survey of 63 junior-level physics students, 54 (86%) agreed that InkSurvey gave the instructor a better understanding of what they did and did not understand, and 48 (76%) said creating InkSurvey responses helped them better understand course content or realize what they did not understand.
finding.measure: Student survey responses about engagement, motivation, and metacognitive usefulness

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that InkSurvey supported metacognition and problem-solving by prompting students to think through and articulate their reasoning in real time. In the surveyed physics class (n=63), 48 students (76%) said constructing responses helped them better understand what was being covered or recognize what they did not understand, and instructors observed improved ability to display conceptual understanding through sketches, graphs, and written solutions.
finding.measure: Student self-reports of metacognition; instructor observations of problem-solving and reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that InkSurvey improves instructional efficiency by giving instructors immediate access to student responses, allowing rapid identification of common difficulties and faster adjustment of instruction. Instructors reported being able to tailor teaching in real time, provide immediate feedback, and manage classroom pacing more effectively; however, no workload measures or formal efficiency statistics were reported.
finding.measure: Instructor-reported ability to identify difficulties and adjust instruction in real time

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment. I. Applications in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.population: High School; Undergraduate; Graduate; Community College
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues for the pedagogical value of real-time formative assessment using InkSurvey, a free web-based system that lets instructors pose open-response questions and receive students’ handwritten or sketched answers immediately on pen-enabled mobile devices. The central problem addressed is that formative assessment is often delayed, cumbersome, and limited by multiple-choice formats, which can prevent instructors from seeing student thinking in time to respond to misconceptions.

The paper presents seven qualitative vignettes across diverse settings: a university honors calculus course, a high school algebra class, community college biology, university food chemistry, introductory physics, chemical engineering and physics courses using simulations, and a creativity-in-physics course. Across these contexts, instructors used InkSurvey to ask open-ended questions, review student responses in real time, discuss misconceptions, and adjust instruction on the spot.

The main conclusion is that InkSurvey appears broadly useful for engaging students, revealing misconceptions, and supporting immediate instructional adaptation across subjects and settings. However, this paper is descriptive and does not report controlled outcome data; it refers readers to a companion paper for evidence of effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: In the honors calculus vignette (n=87 enrolled; 83 responses to one item), InkSurvey helped the instructor identify a common misconception about setting up inequalities for triple integrals. After class discussion informed by student responses, a follow-up question showed improvement: all students responded, only 4 still showed a one-dimensional misconception, and none used all constant bounds. No standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Open-ended calculus problem solving on triple-integral inequalities
finding.study_size: n=87 enrolled; 83 responses on one question

finding.finding_summary: Several science/engineering vignettes describe InkSurvey being used to probe conceptual understanding, reveal faulty reasoning, and support immediate instructional adjustment in physics, biology, and food chemistry. The paper reports qualitative improvement in students’ ability to articulate reasoning and in instructors’ capacity to diagnose misconceptions, but it provides no quantitative effect size or inferential analysis.
finding.measure: Open-ended conceptual understanding and explanation tasks in physics, biology, and food chemistry

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly describes InkSurvey as supporting metacognition, justification of answers, and collaborative idea generation. In the creativity-in-physics vignette, the tool was used to gather ideas, questions, critical comments, and solution metrics from students anonymously, explicitly aiming to improve independent thinking, metacognition, and constructive participation; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Metacognition, independent thinking, and collaborative brainstorming in a creativity-focused physics course

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that InkSurvey increased engagement and participation, especially because all students could respond and receive immediate feedback. In the creativity vignette, anonymity was also described as reducing evaluation apprehension and encouraging participation regardless of gender or race; however, these claims are qualitative and unquantified.
finding.measure: Student engagement, participation, and evaluation apprehension in classroom activities

finding.finding_summary: The instructors report that InkSurvey made it easier to collect and scan student responses in real time, allowing rapid identification of misconceptions and immediate instructional adjustment. The paper suggests improved efficiency compared with calling on a few students or using delayed formative assessment, but it does not quantify time savings or workload reduction.
finding.measure: Real-time collection, review, and instructional adjustment using open-response formative assessment

paper_profiles.title: Student’s Video Production as Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.venue: ICPE 2013 – International Conference on Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether student-produced short videos can serve as a reliable formative assessment tool in high school physics. The authors argue that video tasks may reveal students’ conceptual understanding, misunderstandings, and broader skills better than traditional tests, while also giving teachers information they can use to adjust instruction during the term.

The activity was implemented in a Brazilian federal high school (Colégio Pedro II, Rio de Janeiro) with 232 students across grades 1–3 (ages 14–17). After formal instruction in physics topics such as mechanics, optics, heat, waves, and electricity, students worked in self-selected groups of up to five to produce a 1–10 minute video and a short written explanation. Teachers reviewed the videos and used class discussions to provide feedback and revisit learning activities.

The paper reports descriptive analysis of 55 student videos from 2011. Most videos showed at least partial correctness in physics content, and many had clear structure and a logical sequence. The authors report a strong correlation between technical quality and content quality, with technically strong videos being much more likely to be conceptually correct. They conclude that student video production is a useful and reliable formative assessment resource because it surfaces misconceptions, encourages planning and collaboration, and helps teachers understand how students are interpreting the content.

finding.finding_summary: Student-produced videos functioned as a formative assessment for physics learning by revealing both correct and incorrect conceptual understandings. Among 55 videos, 19 (35%) were judged correct and 25 (45%) partially correct in physical content; 47% were clear, 75% had a satisfactory connection between proposal and product, and 87% had a logical sequence. The paper concludes that this format helps teachers diagnose student understanding of physics concepts in time to adjust instruction.
finding.measure: Teacher analysis of student video content for physical correctness, clarity, coherence, and alignment with the assignment

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents video production as a task that elicited metacognitive planning, replanning, and collaborative work. The authors report that students often chose technically demanding production formats and that higher technical quality was strongly associated with stronger content quality, suggesting that planning and sustained effort were linked to better products. No effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative/analytic review of video production processes and product features (planning, collaboration, technical quality)

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that the activity supported student engagement and participation by using familiar media formats and allowing students to create amusing, age-appropriate presentations. They describe the process as encouraging active participation in learning and note that students appeared to spend time preparing the videos, but they do not report a direct quantitative measure of motivation or engagement.
finding.measure: Descriptive observation of student participation and engagement during video creation and discussion

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of Student Learning Styles on the Learning Gains Achieved When Interactive Simulations Are Coupled with Real-Time Formative Assessment via Pen-Enabled Mobile Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether the learning gains produced by a classroom model that combines interactive computer simulations with real-time formative assessment differ by students’ learning styles. The authors were motivated by the idea that visually rich, hands-on simulation activities might advantage some learners more than others, particularly in undergraduate STEM settings.

The intervention, called the Coupled Model, used one pen-enabled mobile device per student so that learners could interact with simulations and answer open-format formative questions in real time through InkSurvey. The study was conducted in an undergraduate engineering physics laboratory course across two sections, with 41 students in total, and learning styles were measured with the Felder-Soloman Index of Learning Styles.

Student learning was assessed using pre-tests and end-of-semester summative assessments on five simulation-based topics, and learning gains were correlated with learning style dimensions. The main finding is that students made statistically significant learning gains across all five simulations, but these gains were not meaningfully related to learning style; correlations between learning gains and the four learning-style dimensions were all near zero and not statistically significant. The paper concludes that the Coupled Model appears effective across a broad range of learning styles rather than being selectively beneficial for any particular style.

finding.finding_summary: Students achieved statistically significant learning gains on all five simulation activities after the Coupled Model was used, with class-average normalized gains ranging from 60% to 75% across the reported simulations. For example, the circuits simulation had n=41 and an average gain of 63%, and paired tests for the pre/post assessments were all p<0.001.
finding.measure: Pre-test vs. summative assessment scores on physics/statistics simulation tasks; normalized learning gain
finding.study_size: n=41 (overall class; simulation-specific n ranged from 30 to 41)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly tests whether learning gains from the Coupled Model vary by learning style, using Pearson correlations between gain and the four Index of Learning Styles dimensions. Across the five simulations, correlations were near zero (e.g., ACT-REF from -0.13 to 0.25; SEN-INT from -0.28 to 0.04; VIS-VRB from -0.06 to 0.14; SEQ-GLO from -0.15 to 0.06), and none were statistically significant.
finding.measure: Correlation between normalized learning gains and Index of Learning Styles dimensions
finding.effect_size: r values near zero; range reported across simulations
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI for correlations reported in table, e.g. ACT-REF -0.28 to 0.32 for circuits; overall all near zero

paper_profiles.title: Measuring the Effectiveness of Learning Resources Via Student Interaction with Online Learning Modules
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how instructors can measure the effectiveness of online learning resources at high resolution using data generated by students’ interactions with the resources themselves. The authors argue that conventional pre/post testing and typical LMS analytics are too infrequent or too disconnected from the instructional materials to attribute learning gains to a specific resource.

To address this, they created a sequence of 10 online learning modules (OLMs) for a first-semester calculus-based physics course. Each module used a mastery-learning structure in which students first attempted an assessment component, then optionally interacted with instructional materials, and then could make additional attempts. The study analyzed time-stamped log data from 230 students to infer pre-learning and post-learning performance, test-taking effort, and learning effort, and then combined these into sunburst visualizations and correlation analyses.

The main conclusion is that this OLM design can yield detailed, instructor-friendly evidence about which modules are effective, which assessments may be too easy or poorly discriminating, and where disengagement or insufficient instructional support appears to be limiting outcomes. The paper finds substantial module-to-module variation: some modules appear to have effective instruction and adequate assessment, while others show signs of weak instructional materials, overly easy assessment items, or student disengagement. The authors emphasize that the method is useful for iterative improvement of online physics instruction, but they also note that the study is descriptive and based on one course context rather than a causal experiment.

finding.finding_summary: The study evaluates students’ performance on physics concept and calculation problems across 10 mastery-learning online modules. Module-level results show that some modules supported learning well (e.g., module 6: almost all students passed after learning), while others were less effective or appeared to have weak assessment quality or inadequate instructional support (e.g., module 7: most normal and even extensive learners still failed after learning).
finding.measure: Pass/fail on physics assessment attempts before learning (ABL) and after learning (AAL) within each online learning module
finding.study_size: n=230 students attempted at least one module; module-specific N ranged from 223 to 230

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly analyzes student engagement and learning effort using time-on-task and interaction logs, classifying learners into brief versus normal engagement modes and identifying disengagement patterns. Module 10, in particular, showed a much larger fraction of brief-brief-brief behavior and overall non-completion, suggesting substantial disengagement, whereas other modules showed stronger engagement with learning resources.
finding.measure: Duration of major learning sessions (MLS), assessment attempt duration, and engagement-mode classification from log data
finding.study_size: n=230 students (module-level analyses vary from n=223 to n=230)

finding.finding_summary: Although not a direct intervention study of durable skills, the paper explicitly interprets differing learning durations as reflecting qualitatively different learning behaviors, such as skimming versus careful reading and problem solving. The analysis uses these behaviors to infer how students regulate effort during mastery learning, but the paper does not directly measure critical thinking or metacognition with a validated instrument.
finding.measure: Time-on-task during major learning sessions and assessment attempts, used as proxies for learning behavior

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Auto-Grading and Feedback System for Constructive Geometry Tasks Using Large Language Models on an Online Math Platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing timely, individualized grading and feedback for complex constructive geometry tasks in online mathematics learning environments. The authors argue that open-ended and multi-step geometry work is difficult to assess with conventional answer-based systems, especially when students use diverse valid solution strategies and need feedback that supports revision rather than just correctness judgments.

To address this, the study develops a personalized auto-grading and feedback system on the Korean Algeomath platform that combines rule-based evaluation for closed-ended and geometry-construction tasks with GPT-4–based few-shot grading and feedback generation for open-ended explanations. Teacher-authored exemplars and attempt-aware prompting are used to generate short, supportive feedback that changes across retries, aiming to scaffold student learning within up to three retries per item.

The system was piloted in four middle school classes in South Korea with 79 students across 18 geometry items. Results showed perfect agreement with teacher grading for rule-based items and substantial agreement for open-ended explanatory items (overall agreement 0.866, Cohen’s κ = 0.737). Expert review suggested the feedback was generally usable but sometimes weakened by answer leakage, imprecise terminology, and overly directive tone. Student response data indicated that feedback often supported immediate correction: 36.7% of initially incorrect responses were revised to correct answers on the next attempt, though evidence for longer-term transfer to later items was not statistically significant.

finding.finding_summary: The system substantially supported learning and performance in constructive geometry tasks. In a field study with 79 middle school students across 18 items, 36.7% of initially incorrect responses were corrected on the next attempt after feedback, and first-attempt correctness increased from about 0.60 to 0.73 by the second attempt, with smaller gains thereafter.
finding.measure: Correctness on geometry tasks; attempt-level learning curves; post-feedback conversion rate

finding.finding_summary: The feedback system appears to have supported persistence and iterative engagement, as many students revised incorrect answers after receiving feedback and the authors observed short-term corrections to be frequent. The system was designed to encourage retry behavior with supportive, polite prompts, and student survey responses about the activity were generally favorable (ratings around 4.1–4.5 on a 5-point scale).
finding.measure: Retry behavior, post-feedback revision, learner self-assessment survey

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides evidence that feedback supported iterative reasoning and refinement of geometric explanations, but not uniformly. Qualitative examples showed students moving from vague responses to more precise, conceptually grounded justifications, yet statistical tests found no significant evidence that prior feedback-driven corrections transferred to later complex questions.
finding.measure: Iterative answer refinement; transfer to later target questions; qualitative response changes

finding.finding_summary: The system was highly effective as a scalable grading tool. Rule-based grading for closed-ended and geometry-construction items matched teacher judgments perfectly (100% agreement), and LLM grading for open-ended explanations achieved substantial overall agreement with teachers (0.866 agreement; Cohen’s κ = 0.737), suggesting meaningful potential to reduce grading workload while supporting real-time formative assessment.
finding.measure: Agreement between automated grading and teacher judgments
finding.study_size: n=878 open-ended responses across 7 items; 18 questions total

paper_profiles.title: Assessing Mobile Learning System Performance in Indonesia: Reports of the Model Development and Its Instrument Testing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a measurement-development problem rather than testing a learning intervention. The authors seek to build and preliminarily validate a mobile learning (m-learning) success model for Indonesia, using the DeLone and McLean information systems success framework extended with mobile-learning-specific constructs for system content and user motivation.

The study is presented as an early-stage model development and instrument-testing report. The researchers collected online survey data from about 50 respondents using snowball purposive sampling and analyzed the questionnaire with PLS-SEM (SmartPLS) to examine indicator reliability and validity. Across 31 proposed indicators, 10 were rejected and 21 retained, leading the authors to conclude that the instrument showed acceptable psychometric properties for further study, while also noting that the questionnaire should be revised before later stages.

The paper is situated in Indonesia and focuses on end-user perceptions of m-learning systems rather than student achievement or classroom implementation. Its main contribution is methodological: it demonstrates how the model was constructed, operationalized into indicators, and statistically screened. The paper does not evaluate effects on learning outcomes, nor does it provide evidence about formative assessment moderators such as prior achievement, multilingual status, disability, socioeconomic status, class size, or teacher assessment literacy.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that the proposed m-learning system measurement instrument was mostly reliable and valid, supporting the model-development process. Using PLS-SEM on about 50 respondents, the authors retained 21 of 31 indicators and rejected 10 (including INQ1, NBF1, SVQ1, SYQ1, SYQ2, SYQ5, SYU1, SYU2, USF1, and USF4), indicating that the remaining items adequately captured perceived system performance and related constructs.
finding.measure: Indicator reliability, composite reliability (CR), average variance extracted (AVE), discriminant validity, and item cross-loadings for an m-learning success questionnaire

paper_profiles.title: Transition Matrices: A Tool to Assess Student Learning and Improve Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes a spreadsheet-based analysis tool called a transition matrix for interpreting pre-/post-instruction multiple-choice assessment data. The authors argue that dichotomous scoring on common diagnostic tests can hide meaningful shifts in student thinking, especially when incorrect answer choices represent intermediate misconceptions rather than random errors.

Using college-level physics data from the Force Concept Inventory (FCI), primarily from Rice University calculus-based introductory mechanics courses taught by the lead author between 2000 and 2003, the paper shows how to rank answer choices by item response curve analysis and then display pre-to-post movements among choices. The resulting matrices show not only how many students become correct, but also how many move from one misconception to a better misconception or regress to a worse one.

The main conclusion is that transition matrices provide instructors with richer formative feedback than traditional pre/post score differences or normalized gain, helping them identify which misconceptions are most persistent and where instruction may be partially effective. The paper also notes that the tool could be adapted for other assessments and disciplines, but it does not present evidence on K-12 formative assessment moderators such as prior achievement, multilingual status, disability, socioeconomic status, class size, or teacher assessment literacy.

finding.finding_summary: The transition matrix analysis showed that instruction improved students' physics understanding beyond what dichotomous scoring revealed. On Question 18 of the FCI, 50.0% of students answered correctly post-instruction, and 72.7% of those initially incorrect moved either to the correct answer or to a better incorrect answer, indicating partial conceptual gains in Newtonian reasoning.
finding.measure: Force Concept Inventory item responses; transition matrix of pre-/post-instruction answer choices
finding.study_size: n not fully reported; example item analysis used approximately 500 Rice student tests for IRCs, with Table 1 based on Rice University students from 2000-2003

paper_profiles.title: British Columbia Healthy Connections Project process evaluation: a mixed methods protocol to describe the implementation and delivery of the Nurse-Family Partnership in Canada
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a study protocol for a process evaluation nested within the British Columbia Healthy Connections Project (BCHCP), which is evaluating the Nurse-Family Partnership (NFP) in Canada. The central question is not whether the intervention works on child or maternal outcomes, but how it is implemented and delivered across five regional Health Authorities, and what contextual factors shape fidelity, dosage, reach, and adaptation.

The NFP is a nurse home-visitation program for first-time, socially and economically disadvantaged pregnant women and mothers with young children. The protocol describes a convergent parallel mixed-methods design that combines quarterly fidelity reports, supervision records, meeting summaries, field observations, and repeated interviews/focus groups with public health nurses, supervisors, managers, and the provincial coordinator. The study is situated in British Columbia, where the program is being delivered in both urban and rural/remote contexts, with some sites participating in an RCT and others in process evaluation only.

The paper emphasizes that implementation fidelity, dosage, and local adaptation are essential for interpreting trial outcomes and for understanding whether the Canadian context requires modifications to the original U.S. model. Planned quantitative analyses will summarize enrollment timing, caseloads, visit frequency, dosage received, and time allocation across visit domains, while qualitative analyses will examine acceptability, supervision, contextual influences, and strategies used to support delivery. Because this is a protocol rather than results paper, it reports planned measures and analytic approaches rather than empirical findings.

finding.finding_summary: This is a protocol paper and therefore does not report outcome results. It plans to measure implementation efficiency-related indicators such as caseloads, supervision burden, time spent across visit domains, number of home visits, and the timing/frequency of visits using quarterly fidelity reports and supervision records.
finding.measure: Program fidelity reports, supervision records, team meeting and case conference summaries, interview/focus group data
finding.study_size: n=71 planned primary participants (11 supervisors + provincial coordinator; 60 PHNs) plus 5-15 managers

finding.finding_summary: This protocol focuses substantively on system-level implementation of a public health intervention across five Health Authorities, including governance, organizational adoption, inter-site variation, policy feedback loops, and program sustainability. No results are reported, but the study is explicitly designed to inform provincial decision-making, future program adaptation, and implementation policy.
finding.measure: Process evaluation of implementation, delivery, contextual factors, and organizational practices across Health Authorities
finding.study_size: n=71 planned primary participants plus 5-15 managers

paper_profiles.title: Diabetes and hypertension MobileHealth systems: a review of general challenges and advancements
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Engineering and Applied Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review surveys mobile health (mHealth) systems for self-management of diabetes and hypertension, with a particular emphasis on the challenges that limit adoption and sustained use. The paper brings together fragmented literature on user concerns, system limitations, and design expectations, aiming to provide a more comprehensive view of what diabetes and hypertension mHealth solutions need to address.

A second major aim of the article is to review how machine learning (ML) has been applied to diabetes and hypertension management, including prediction, diagnosis, blood glucose monitoring, blood pressure estimation, and support for non-pharmacological self-management approaches such as physical activity, dietary therapy, and sleep/restfulness. The review synthesizes 20 diabetes-focused ML papers and 10 hypertension-focused ML papers, highlighting that ML is used most often for prediction and diagnosis, while only a small fraction of studies integrate ML into actual mHealth systems.

The paper concludes that while mHealth and ML show promise for chronic disease self-management, practical benefits have not fully translated into robust real-world systems. For diabetes, random forest was the strongest-performing algorithm across the reviewed metrics; for hypertension, random forest and support vector machine were generally the top performers depending on the metric. The authors also identify major usability and implementation issues, including adherence, cost, interoperability, privacy/security, and lack of clear feedback and monitoring workflows.

finding.finding_summary: This review primarily synthesizes how mHealth and ML systems may reduce clinician workload and support self-management, but it does not test an intervention directly. Across the reviewed literature, only 25% of diabetes ML studies were integrated into mHealth systems and none of the hypertension ML studies showed integration, indicating limited operational uptake despite potential efficiency benefits.
finding.measure: Proportion of reviewed studies integrating ML into mHealth systems; reported system functionality and workload-reduction claims
finding.study_size: diabetes ML review n=20 papers; hypertension ML review n=10 papers

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies system-level barriers and expectations relevant to adoption, including interoperability with EHRs, security of personal and health information, cost, and sustainability. It is a review rather than an outcomes study, so the evidence is descriptive: the main finding is that these institutional and implementation issues remain unresolved and are central to successful deployment.
finding.measure: Qualitative synthesis of user expectations and implementation challenges

finding.finding_summary: User engagement and adherence-related issues are discussed as key challenges for mHealth self-management, including prescription non-adherence, abandonment driven by cost, and the need for notifications, motivation, and user-friendly design. The paper does not report a direct intervention effect size, but it emphasizes that these engagement factors are central to sustained use.
finding.measure: Reported user challenges and app features linked to engagement, adherence, and sustained use

paper_profiles.title: Replicating or franchising a STEM afterschool program model: core elements of programmatic integrity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether the NE STEM 4U afterschool STEM program can be replicated across different institutional and geographic contexts while preserving programmatic fidelity. The authors are especially interested in what core elements must remain stable during scale-up, and how much adaptation can occur without turning the program into something fundamentally different.

NE STEM 4U is a faculty-guided, post-secondary student-led outreach and professional development model that combines STEM teaching, mentorship, and research experiences for undergraduate mentors while providing inquiry-based afterschool STEM activities for youth in grades K–8. The study used qualitative focus groups, interviews, reflection surveys, participant observation, and program quality assessments (notably YPQA and Dimensions of Success) across the originating R2 site and two expansion sites (an R1 and a PUI) in urban and rural settings.

The paper concludes that the model is replicable, but fidelity depends on four core elements: intentional programming, staff quality, effective partnerships, and program evaluation/continuous improvement. Qualitative themes across mentor participants emphasized flexibility, student engagement, classroom management, and communication, while site leaders described the need for ongoing training, mentoring, and local adaptation. Overall, the authors argue that the program can be franchised successfully with minor contextual changes, as long as core components and evaluation routines are preserved.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that NE STEM 4U supports mentor and youth engagement, flexibility, and classroom management, with post-secondary mentors repeatedly identifying student engagement as a major theme across sites (overall 19.53% of coded coverage). The authors interpret the qualitative and program quality evidence as showing that the afterschool model helps sustain engagement and positive participation, but no causal effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative focus groups, reflection surveys, and program quality observations (YPQA/DoS) capturing student engagement, classroom management, and related mentoring experiences
finding.study_size: n=16 focus group participants; n=12 reflection surveys

finding.finding_summary: The program is presented as strengthening durable skills among undergraduate mentors, especially flexibility, communication, collaboration, networking, leadership, and professional development. Across all sites, flexibility (21.22%), communication (15.71%), and collaboration-related themes were prominent, and site leaders reported that mentors gained leadership, oral/written communication, and teamwork skills through participation.
finding.measure: Qualitative theme coding from focus groups, surveys, and faculty reflections about mentor development
finding.study_size: n=16 focus group participants; n=12 reflection surveys

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that the replicated sites could maintain program quality while adapting locally, indicating operational viability for scale-up. Evidence includes YPQA averages that were broadly similar across the original and expansion sites (e.g., Supportive Environment 4.72 vs 4.51; Interaction 3.25 vs 3.13), though Engagement was lower at expansion sites (2.99 vs 2.21), suggesting a modest implementation challenge rather than failure.
finding.measure: Youth Program Quality Assessment (YPQA) scores; Dimensions of Success observations; attendance and mentor recruitment indicators
finding.study_size: original site n=16 YPQA observations; expansion sites n=4 YPQA observations

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that the NE STEM 4U model can be replicated as a franchise-like network across institutions with different missions, sizes, and settings, provided that core elements and shared evaluation practices are preserved. The study identifies programmatic integrity, partnership structure, and continuous improvement as necessary for institutional scale-up and reports that the expansion sites had operated for at least 1.5–2 years, with one site already showing general replication of program quality.
finding.measure: Cross-site qualitative analysis, faculty leader reflections, and program quality comparisons across institutions
finding.study_size: 3 sites total (1 origin site, 2 expansion sites)

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation of the nutrition education for limited resource audiences in Iowa
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This thesis evaluates two Iowa nutrition education curricula for limited-resource audiences: Buy. Eat. Live Healthy. (BELH), a nine-lesson program, and Plan Shop Save and Cook (PSSC), a four-lesson pilot curriculum. The central question is whether the curricula improve participants’ food- and nutrition-related behaviors and whether the shorter PSSC series can produce meaningful change despite lower dosage.

The study uses a mixed-methods approach. Quantitatively, program graduates (n=92 BELH; n=42 PSSC) completed pre/post Food and Physical Activity Questionnaires, and the author compared changes in diet quality, physical activity, food safety, food security, and food resource management. Qualitatively, the researcher conducted structured observations of a PSSC lesson and a focus group with six PSSC participants to examine curriculum fidelity and participant perceptions.

Findings indicate that both curricula produced short-term behavior change, with BELH showing significant improvements across more food resource management items than PSSC. BELH was associated with broader gains in diet quality, physical activity, food safety, and food security change, while PSSC improved three of five food resource management items. The qualitative component suggested lower fidelity in the observed lesson, yet participants still viewed the content as useful; overall, the thesis concludes that behavior change can occur even with fewer lessons, though dosage appears related to the breadth of outcomes improved.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines implementation fidelity and program dosage in nutrition education delivery. Structured observations of a PSSC lesson found lower curriculum fidelity, but the focus group suggested the lesson remained robust in providing useful knowledge and skills. The thesis also reports that the nine-lesson BELH curriculum produced broader behavior change than the four-lesson PSSC curriculum, implying dosage mattered for breadth of impact even though both programs showed some improvement.
finding.measure: Structured observations of curriculum fidelity; comparison of behavior change across BELH (9 lessons) and PSSC (4 lessons); focus group discussion
finding.study_size: n=1 observed lesson; n=6 focus group participants; program graduates n=92 BELH and n=42 PSSC

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes participant perceptions of the PSSC curriculum and reports that focus group members identified 13 common themes, with reading labels most frequently mentioned. Although not a direct psychosocial outcome study, the qualitative findings indicate participants perceived the curriculum as helpful and engaging, which supports a positive interpretation of participant engagement with the instruction.
finding.measure: Focus group discussion themes and participant perceptions

paper_profiles.title: Scaffolding in Teacher–Student Interaction: A Decade of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article reviews a decade of research on scaffolding in teacher–student interaction, focusing on how scaffolding has been defined, how it appears in classroom practice, and whether it is effective. The authors argue that scaffolding research has suffered from inconsistent conceptualizations and measurement problems, especially around distinguishing scaffolding from generic support. They identify three core characteristics of scaffolding: contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility.

The review synthesizes 66 English-language articles published between 1998 and 2009, drawn from SSCI, ERIC, and PsycINFO. Most included studies were descriptive and concentrated on literacy, with smaller bodies of work in mathematics and science; a smaller set of studies examined effectiveness. Across these studies, scaffolding was commonly enacted through means such as modeling, questioning, hints, explaining, and feedback, and often aimed at metacognitive, cognitive, or affective support.

The review concludes that scaffolding appears to be effective in the available experimental and quasi-experimental studies, especially for metacognitive and cognitive outcomes, but the evidence base is limited and methodologically uneven. The authors emphasize that future research needs clearer operationalization, better coding of teacher and student interaction, and stronger measurement instruments that capture contingency, fading, and responsibility transfer together.

finding.finding_summary: Literacy was the most fully developed domain in the reviewed literature, and the review reports that scaffolding in literacy classrooms was commonly associated with richer descriptions of effective teacher support and, in the effectiveness studies cited, positive learning outcomes. However, the review is largely synthesizing prior studies rather than reporting a single pooled effect size, so no meta-analytic estimate is provided here.
finding.measure: Literacy-related classroom interactions, reading comprehension, text understanding, and literacy performance outcomes across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies in mathematics found positive effects of contingent scaffolding on task performance and transfer. For example, Murphy and Messer (2000) reported that more children in the scaffolding condition advanced in representation level on a balance-scale task, and Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998) found students with contingent support solved significantly more long-division problems than peers in other conditions at immediate and follow-up testing.
finding.measure: Math problem-solving, balance-scale reasoning, and transfer on long-division tasks
finding.study_size: n=41,40,41 (Murphy and Messer 2000); n=8 per condition (Pratt and Savoy-Levine 1998)

finding.finding_summary: Science-focused studies in the review generally suggest scaffolding supports learning and reasoning, especially when it is contingent and interactive. Mercer et al. (2004) found that students in the Thinking Together condition were better able to use talk for reasoning and made greater gains on non-verbal reasoning; Azevedo et al. (2005) also found adaptive human scaffolding associated with more shifts in mental models and greater knowledge gains in a hypermedia science task.
finding.measure: Science reasoning, conceptual change, mental models, knowledge gains, and reasoning talk
finding.study_size: n=109 vs n=121 (Mercer et al. 2004); n=38 adaptive, n=34 fixed, n=37 no scaffolding (Azevedo et al. 2005)

finding.finding_summary: The review includes studies on student engagement, motivation, enjoyment, and affect, with overall positive associations for scaffolding that promotes interest, motivation, and involvement. Turner et al. (1998) found that whole-class intrinsic support and transfer of responsibility were more common in high-involvement mathematics classes, while Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998) found no difference in enjoyment across most support conditions but lower enjoyment in the no-support control group.
finding.measure: Student involvement/engagement, enjoyment, motivation, and affect questionnaire ratings
finding.study_size: n=42 students across 34 lessons (Turner et al. 1998); n=40 total across five conditions (Pratt and Savoy-Levine 1998)

finding.finding_summary: A central conclusion of the review is that scaffolding supports durable skills such as metacognition, reasoning, collaboration, and transfer of responsibility. Several effectiveness studies showed gains in reasoning together, self-regulated learning, diagnostic accuracy, and transfer performance, and the authors explicitly frame scaffolding as aiding metacognitive and cognitive activities.
finding.measure: Metacognitive activity, reasoning talk, self-regulated learning behaviors, diagnostic/transfer performance, and responsibility-taking
finding.study_size: Multiple studies; examples include n=109 vs n=121, n=38/34/37, n=41/40/41, n=11

finding.finding_summary: Operational efficiency is not a primary outcome of the review, but it is discussed indirectly through measurement and implementation fidelity issues. Chi et al. (2001) and Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998) checked intervention fidelity and found that more contingent, interactive tutoring elicited more evidence of student understanding and more scaffolding episodes, but the paper does not report direct productivity or workload effects.
finding.measure: Intervention fidelity, frequency of scaffolding episodes, and tutoring interaction patterns

paper_profiles.title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews and compares six influential models of self-regulated learning (SRL): Zimmerman, Boekaerts, Winne and Hadwin, Pintrich, Efklides, and Hadwin, Järvelä, and Miller. The central purpose is not to test a single intervention, but to synthesize the conceptual structure of SRL research, summarize the empirical support for each model, and identify future directions for the field.

The review examines how each model organizes phases of SRL, how it conceptualizes cognition, motivation, emotion, top-down versus bottom-up regulation, automaticity, and context, and what instruments or methodologies have been built around each framework. It also discusses educational implications, emphasizing that SRL models provide an integrative framework for teaching students to become more strategic and successful learners.

The paper is based on theoretical and empirical literature rather than a single population study, so its population is best characterized as adult researchers/educators and the broader educational psychology field. It does not report a new dataset, intervention effect, or direct learner outcomes; instead, it concludes that SRL models are coherent and useful for educational practice, and that different models may be more relevant at different developmental stages or educational levels.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that SRL is strongly linked to motivation, emotion, self-efficacy, and self-regulation processes, but it does not report a single new effect estimate because it synthesizes prior studies. Across the reviewed literature, models such as Boekaerts, Pintrich, Efklides, and Hadwin et al. emphasize that motivation and affect shape goal pursuit, monitoring, and adaptation, and that these processes vary by task, context, and developmental level.
finding.measure: Motivation, affect, self-efficacy, self-regulation, and related SRL constructs across prior studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main educational claim is that SRL supports durable skills such as metacognition, planning, monitoring, adaptation, and collaboration. It synthesizes evidence across models showing that students can be taught to regulate their learning more strategically, and that SRL interventions and measurements target these higher-order learning processes rather than content mastery alone.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning, metacognition, planning, monitoring, adaptation, and collaborative regulation constructs across reviewed studies

paper_profiles.title: What Works in Early Grade Literacy Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This RTI Press occasional paper synthesizes lessons learned from nearly 30 early grade literacy programs implemented by RTI International in low- and middle-income countries. The paper asks what instructional components and implementation practices are most consistently associated with improved early grade literacy instruction and learner outcomes, with a focus on alphabetic and alphasyllabic languages in the early primary years.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention with a formal experimental design, the paper presents a practice-oriented synthesis of RTI’s approach to early grade literacy: Teach, Text, Time, Test, and Tongue. Across the discussion, the authors emphasize explicit, systematic instruction in phonological awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension; the importance of learner materials and structured lesson routines; efficient use of instructional time; formative assessment to guide instruction; and mother-tongue or otherwise appropriate language-of-instruction decisions.

The paper is grounded in RTI implementation experience across diverse contexts, including Nigeria, Kenya, Egypt, Liberia, Haiti, Indonesia, Malawi, Uganda, and Ethiopia. It highlights the need for local adaptation, differentiated and inclusive instruction, and teacher support. The main conclusion is that effective early grade literacy programs require a balanced, context-sensitive combination of explicit skill instruction, abundant practice, feedback, assessment, and instructional adjustment—not a one-size-fits-all model.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that RTI’s early grade literacy approach improves learner literacy outcomes by combining explicit, systematic instruction in phonological awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension with frequent practice and feedback. However, it is a synthesis of implementation lessons rather than a single impact study, so it does not report a unified effect size, confidence interval, or study-level estimate for literacy outcomes.
finding.measure: Early grade literacy skills (phonological awareness, phonics/decoding, fluency, vocabulary, comprehension, and writing)

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes the role of oral language, listening comprehension, and vocabulary development in supporting reading comprehension, and it recommends frequent oral interaction, songs, storytelling, and comprehension activities. These are presented as instructional practices drawn from program experience, but no study-level estimate is reported for speaking or listening outcomes.
finding.measure: Oral language, listening comprehension, and vocabulary-related classroom activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes learner motivation, engagement, and positive attitudes toward reading as important components of early literacy instruction. It presents these as design principles supported by classroom examples (e.g., songs, gestures, interactive activities), but it does not report quantitative evidence for social-emotional outcomes.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, and attitudes toward reading

finding.finding_summary: A major theme of the paper is improving the efficient use of instructional time through structured lesson plans, pacing guidance, guided reading routines, and sequencing that allows regular practice and quick movement toward mastery. The paper includes examples such as lesson timing guidance and differentiated guided-reading frequency, but it does not provide a formal effect estimate on teacher workload or efficiency.
finding.measure: Instructional time use, pacing, lesson structure, and guided-reading routines

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that RTI worked with Ministries of Education to develop and implement literacy programs, adapt materials to local contexts, and build teacher-support systems and inclusion plans. These system-level efforts are described as important to successful implementation, but the paper does not report a quantified institutional impact estimate.
finding.measure: Ministry-supported program development, teacher training systems, and inclusion-oriented implementation

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and Mathematics Education: the Perspective of In-Service Mathematics Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how applicable general formative assessment (FA) practices are in the specific context of secondary mathematics education. The authors ask how often in-service mathematics teachers use 26 FA practices drawn from Wiliam’s model, which practices are less frequent, what additional practices teachers report, and what obstacles they encounter when implementing FA.

The study uses a mixed-methods design with a 26-item Likert questionnaire completed by 30 in-service secondary mathematics teachers in Uruguay, plus in-depth interviews with 3 teachers. The paper focuses on teachers’ reported frequency and feasibility of FA practices such as eliciting evidence of learning, giving feedback, collaborative peer learning, clarifying goals, and promoting self-regulation. Quantitative descriptive results are combined with thematic analysis of interview data to explain why some practices are common and others are rare.

Findings indicate that most FA practices are reported as frequent and feasible, especially those related to collecting evidence, feedback, collaboration, and self-regulation. However, clarifying and sharing learning goals needs adaptation in mathematics, and peer co-assessment is relatively uncommon despite being viewed as valuable. Teachers also report several context-specific practices not in the original repertoire, including iterative feedback cycles and small-group feedback sessions. The main barriers are laborious planning, time constraints, and tensions between formative and summative assessment, suggesting that implementation fidelity in mathematics depends heavily on time, classroom conditions, and alignment with assessment purposes.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that 26 formative assessment practices were generally frequent in secondary mathematics classrooms, with mean ratings above the midpoint of the 1-7 scale. The highest-rated practices involved eliciting evidence of learning (e.g., encouraging questions, coming near students to know what they did) and providing feedback that helps students improve (e.g., M=6.63 for encouraging questions; M=6.17 for feedback explaining why they were wrong), but clarifying learning goals was less consistently enacted and often required adaptation to mathematics.
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of formative assessment practices in mathematics teaching

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described FA practices as supporting student engagement, confidence, persistence, and willingness to participate. For example, self-regulation-related practices such as encouraging students to feel competent (M=6.47) and to make an effort even when tasks are difficult (M=6.43) were reported as frequent, and interviews emphasized motivation, trust, and persistence as important elements of implementation.
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of self-regulation/persistence-oriented FA practices and interview themes

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined practices tied to collaboration, dialogue, and self-regulation, including peer discussion, explaining to classmates, and reflecting on different problem-solving paths. Teachers rated collaborative and metacognitive practices as frequent overall, though peer correction of each other’s work was the least frequent practice in the set (M=4.2), despite being viewed as valuable and feasible.
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of collaboration, peer learning, and self-regulation practices

finding.finding_summary: A major substantive finding is that formative assessment was perceived as laborious to implement and time-consuming. Teachers reported that planning and carrying out FA requires substantial extra time outside class, with obstacles including laborious planning/implementation, time shortage, and classroom routines; these barriers were repeatedly emphasized in interviews and were the most salient implementation constraints.
finding.measure: Interview-coded obstacles to implementing formative assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that FA implementation is shaped by institutional tensions, especially the conflict between formative and summative assessment functions. Teachers reported that grading requirements, assessment logbooks, and institutional routines can limit the extent to which formative feedback can be used, indicating that school assessment structures affect uptake and fidelity.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of interview reports on barriers and assessment-function tensions

paper_profiles.title: Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) Using R: A Workbook
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book is an introductory workbook on partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) using the R environment and the SEMinR package. It explains the conceptual foundations of SEM, contrasts PLS-SEM with covariance-based SEM, and walks readers through model specification, estimation, measurement-model evaluation, structural-model evaluation, mediation, and moderation.

The text is designed for readers who have already had some exposure to PLS-SEM or who are learning it through a structured workbook format. It emphasizes a didactic, hands-on approach with a single running case study, examples using R markdown, and companion learning materials and video courses. The target audience is students and researchers in business/management and related fields, not a K-12 population.

The main contribution is methodological: it argues for when and why PLS-SEM is appropriate, highlights its advantages for prediction, small samples, complex models, and formative measurement, and provides practical guidance for using SEMinR in R. It does not report an empirical study of an educational intervention or learner outcomes; instead, it is a methods textbook focused on statistical analysis and software use.

paper_profiles.title: Theory and Practice of Online Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book is a second-edition edited volume that surveys theory, design, infrastructure, delivery, and student support in online learning and distance education. Rather than testing a single intervention, it synthesizes scholarship and practitioner perspectives on how online learning should be designed and delivered, including foundational learning theories, media and technology choices, course development, quality control, and support services.

The retrieved text includes the book’s introduction and the beginning of Chapter 1, which argue that technology alone does not improve learning; instead, instructional design, feedback, interaction, and learner support are the key determinants of effectiveness. The chapter outlines how behaviorist, cognitivist, constructivist, and connectivist perspectives can inform online course design, and it gives practical implications such as sequencing content, embedding assessment and feedback, chunking information, and supporting learner autonomy.

Because this is a conceptual and edited reference work, it does not report a single empirical study, sample, or statistical effect estimate. Its main contribution is a broad synthesis of theory and practice intended for educators, administrators, and designers working in higher education and distance learning contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The book argues that online learning can increase flexibility and make tutoring, updating materials, and directing learners to resources more efficient, but it also requires commitment, resources, and careful instructional design. The text is conceptual rather than empirical, so no effect sizes, sample sizes, or statistical estimates are reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of course delivery, tutoring, updating materials, and support processes

finding.finding_summary: The chapter explicitly frames online learning as supporting higher-order thinking, metacognition, reflection, and the ability to apply, analyze, synthesize, and evaluate information. It recommends strategies such as information mapping, contextual learning, and learner-generated summaries to deepen processing and support transfer, but no empirical outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual treatment of higher-order thinking, metacognition, and deep processing

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Adoption: A New Framework for Theorizing and Evaluating Nonadoption, Abandonment, and Challenges to the Scale-Up, Spread, and Sustainability of Health and Care Technologies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses why promising health and social care technologies are often not adopted, are abandoned, or fail to scale up and sustain over time. The authors argue that many prior implementation frameworks focus too narrowly on initial adoption and do not sufficiently capture the dynamic interaction among the condition, technology, value proposition, users, organizations, and wider context.

To develop a more comprehensive framework, the study combined a hermeneutic systematic review of prior implementation frameworks with six empirical case studies of technology-supported health and social care programs in the UK. The case studies included video outpatient consultations, GPS tracking for cognitive impairment, pendant alarms, remote biomarker monitoring for heart failure, care-organizing software, and an integrated data warehouse for case management, using ethnography, interviews, document analysis, and action research over up to three years.

The resulting NASSS framework (Nonadoption, Abandonment, Scale-up, Spread, Sustainability) consists of seven domains and emphasizes that technologies are embedded in complex sociotechnical systems that change over time. The authors conclude that implementation success depends not only on technical features but also on alignment with clinical work, organizational routines, user capabilities, supply models, and adaptation over time; technologies characterized by complexity across multiple domains rarely became mainstreamed.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that technology-supported health and care programs can improve efficiency in some contexts, but implementation was often slow, required multiple workarounds, and sometimes led to abandonment or suspension. In the case studies, video consultations reached around 20% of follow-up visits in two services, but were abandoned in one service and put on hold in another; other technologies required substantial tinkering, support, and adaptation to work in practice.
finding.measure: Implementation success, service uptake, workflow fit, and sustainability of health/social care technologies
finding.study_size: 6 case studies; over 400 hours of ethnographic observation, 165 interviews, 200 documents

finding.finding_summary: The central finding is that adoption and sustainability depend on interactions across organizational, policy, and wider institutional contexts, not just local usability. Across the six cases, complexity in multiple NASSS domains was associated with failure to mainstream, whereas simpler or better-aligned programs were more likely to persist or spread.
finding.measure: Framework development and cross-case analysis of institutional, organizational, and contextual influences on adoption, spread, and sustainability
finding.study_size: 6 case studies plus review of 28 frameworks

paper_profiles.title: A view on drug resistance in cancer
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual review that explains why drug resistance remains the central barrier to curing cancer. The authors break resistance into several biological determinants, including tumor burden and growth kinetics, tumor heterogeneity, physical barriers to drug delivery, immune and microenvironmental factors, undruggable drivers, and the effects of therapeutic pressure. They argue that resistance should be understood as a dynamic, time-dependent process rather than a simple intrinsic-versus-acquired binary.

The article does not evaluate a single intervention or report original empirical data. Instead, it synthesizes evidence from oncology research to propose four broad strategies for overcoming resistance: earlier detection and interception, achieving deeper initial responses, real-time monitoring with adaptive treatment changes, and mapping cancer dependencies through screening and computational modeling. The paper highlights examples such as ctDNA-based screening and monitoring, dose-dense chemotherapy, antibody–drug conjugates, checkpoint blockade combinations, and synthetic lethality/CRISPR screening.
