The intended population is cancer patients and the clinical oncology ecosystem rather than an education setting. Its main conclusion is that combining early detection, stronger upfront treatment, ongoing monitoring, and data-driven adaptive therapy may eventually enable more durable responses and higher cure rates, but the authors frame these as a forward-looking framework rather than tested claims from a single study.

paper_profiles.title: A Critical Review of Research on Student Self-Assessment
paper_profiles.population: K-20 students (elementary through higher education); review spans classroom and postsecondary contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper critically reviews research on student self-assessment, with a focus on work published largely between 2013 and 2018. The author first refines the conceptual definition of self-assessment, arguing that it should be understood primarily as a formative feedback process that helps students monitor their competence, processes, and products in order to improve learning and performance.

The review synthesizes 76 empirical studies and organizes them around four main themes: consistency with external judgments, student perceptions, achievement, and self-regulated learning. It argues that summative self-assessment is often inconsistent and can be distorted when it counts toward grades, whereas formative self-assessment supported by rubrics, scripts, criteria, and feedback is more likely to improve learning outcomes. The paper also highlights that self-assessment is positively associated with achievement and self-regulated learning, especially when students are trained and given clear standards.

The review includes studies across K-20 settings, with many studies in elementary, secondary, and higher education classrooms, including college students in psychology and writing courses. Rather than testing one intervention directly, the paper evaluates patterns across the literature and concludes that future research should move beyond accuracy/consistency toward understanding the cognitive and affective mechanisms through which formative self-assessment affects learning.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, formative self-assessment was consistently associated with better writing quality. A meta-analysis by Graham et al. (2015), included in the review, reported an average weighted effect size of 0.62 on writing quality (10 studies). The review also describes quasi-experimental studies in which rubric-guided self-assessment and revision improved students' written work.
finding.measure: Writing quality / scores on written assignments

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that formative self-assessment improved performance across a range of non-literacy academic tasks, including dart throwing, map-making, speaking English, exams, and vocational performance. For the non-meta-analytic achievement studies, treatment groups generally outperformed comparison/control groups, while one summative self-assessment experiment showed no improvement and another showed improvement.
finding.measure: Task performance and course/exam achievement across multiple academic domains
finding.study_size: 25 studies on achievement; exact sample sizes vary/not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that self-assessment, especially when formative, was associated with stronger self-regulated learning, motivation, and related motivational beliefs. Studies using scripts or rubrics showed statistically significant gains in self-regulation with very small to moderate effects (eta^2 = 0.06–0.42), and one dart-throwing study found improvements in self-efficacy, attributions, and self-satisfaction.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning questionnaires, think-aloud protocols, motivational beliefs (self-efficacy, attributions, self-satisfaction)
finding.study_size: 12 studies on SRL; one cited study n=70; another n=39

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the review is the relationship between self-assessment and self-regulated learning/metacognition. The paper reports that students using rubrics or scripts were more self-regulated than comparison groups, and one study found self-assessment was associated with all three phases of SRL: forethought, performance, and reflection. The review emphasizes that formative self-assessment develops metacognitive monitoring and judgment, which in turn supports learning.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning, metacognition, forethought-performance-reflection phases, task selection and study strategy use
finding.study_size: 12 SRL studies; one study n=70; one qualitative study not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review includes evidence from higher-education and other classroom studies suggesting that self-assessment can improve speaking-related performance, including studies cited as showing gains in speaking English. These findings are summarized as part of the broader achievement literature, which overall favored formative self-assessment.
finding.measure: Speaking English / oral performance
finding.study_size: Included within the 25 achievement studies; exact n not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Students’ perception of Kahoot!’s influence on teaching and learning
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate students perceived the use of Kahoot!, a game-based student response system, in a third-year Information Systems Strategy and Governance course at a research-intensive university in New Zealand. The authors were interested in whether Kahoot! influenced classroom dynamics, student engagement, motivation, and learning, especially in a higher-education setting where participation can be limited and lecture-based teaching may produce boredom and disengagement.

The study used a qualitative case-study approach. Fourteen students from a class of 48 participated in semi-structured interviews conducted at the end of the semester-long course. Kahoot! was used in seven lectures in several ways: to check prior knowledge, review material after delivery, support student-created quizzes, and provide occasional fun/off-topic activities. The analysis was based on inductive content analysis of interview transcripts.

Students generally reported that Kahoot! improved attention, focus, interaction, engagement, motivation, and the perceived quality of learning. The strongest benefits were associated with classroom interaction, timely feedback, revision, and post-Kahoot discussion, which students said helped them understand and retain course content. The paper also notes some mixed effects: competition and humorous naming could distract from learning, and off-topic or overly game-like uses were sometimes seen as inefficient. Overall, the authors conclude that Kahoot! can enrich learning experiences in university classrooms when it is well aligned to course content and followed by discussion, though the evidence is perceptual rather than causal and does not test delayed outcomes with a counterfactual.

finding.finding_summary: All 14 interviewed students reported that Kahoot! improved attention, focus, engagement, and motivation during lectures. Students described the tool as fun, attention-grabbing, and useful for sustaining interest in 2-hour lectures; 13/14 said it increased interaction and involvement in class. The evidence is based on self-reported interview perceptions rather than a controlled comparison, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview perceptions of attention, focus, engagement, and motivation

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that Kahoot! supported deeper engagement, discussion, reflection, and knowledge checking, which students associated with learning and remembering course material. Nine participants explicitly described Kahoot! as useful for revision, and 11 said the post-Kahoot discussion was where the most valuable learning occurred, indicating perceived gains in metacognition and collaborative classroom interaction. No quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Interview themes concerning revision, post-quiz discussion, reflection, and perceived learning/retention

paper_profiles.title: Learning strategies: a synthesis and conceptual model
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review asks which learning strategies are most effective, and under what learning conditions they work best. Hattie and Donoghue argue that learning strategies cannot be evaluated as stand-alone techniques because their effectiveness depends on where students are in the learning cycle and whether the goal is surface learning, deep learning, or transfer.

To organize the evidence, the authors propose a conceptual model with three inputs/outcomes (skill, will, thrill), success criteria, and three phases of learning (surface, deep, transfer), each with acquisition and consolidation phases. They synthesize 228 meta-analyses (302 effects) drawn from more than 18,000 studies and conclude that strategy effectiveness is highly conditional on timing and content: lower-level strategies are stronger for acquiring surface knowledge, while higher-level metacognitive and collaborative strategies are more useful for deep learning and transfer.

The paper is not an intervention study but a meta-synthesis of prior evidence across school and postsecondary contexts. It emphasizes that strategies should be embedded in subject content rather than taught as generic study skills courses. The authors also find that prior achievement, self-efficacy, and success-criteria knowledge are important, and that transfer is most likely when students are explicitly taught to detect similarities and differences between contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Across the synthesized meta-analyses, several learning strategies improved reading and writing outcomes. The paper reports positive effects for self-regulation training in reading and writing (effect sizes around d=0.44 to 0.55) and for reading comprehension (d=0.36), with stronger effects when strategies were embedded in content instruction.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension and writing outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The synthesis found positive effects for mathematics outcomes across multiple meta-analyses. For self-regulation teaching methods, the reported effects were large in mathematics (d=0.96 and d=1.21), and problem-solving/transfer-oriented strategies were also presented as beneficial when students learned to detect similarities and differences across tasks.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement / problem solving

finding.finding_summary: Science outcomes improved with self-regulation interventions. The paper reports an overall effect of d=0.73 in science from one meta-analysis of self-regulation training, indicating substantial gains in science achievement when learners were taught effective strategies.
finding.measure: Science achievement

finding.finding_summary: This paper centrally studies achievement outcomes across many domains beyond literacy, math, and science, including prior achievement, content learning, and transfer. The overall average effect across 302 effects was d=0.53, with strong effects for success criteria (up to d=1.13), surface learning strategies such as outlining and mnemonics (e.g., d=0.85, d=0.76), and transfer strategies (d=0.80 to d=1.32).
finding.measure: Academic achievement, content learning, and transfer across subjects
finding.study_size: n=18,956 studies; estimated 11,006,839 participants reported across meta-analyses

finding.finding_summary: The review shows meaningful positive effects for several affective and motivational outcomes, especially self-efficacy, task value, reducing anxiety, and attitude to content. Reported effects include self-efficacy d=0.90, task value d=0.46, reducing anxiety d=0.45, and attitude to content d=0.35; the paper also notes that performance/surface motivation is weak or negative, while deep/achieving motivation is more favorable.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy, task value, anxiety, attitude, motivation
finding.effect_size: d=0.19 to d=0.90 depending on construct

finding.finding_summary: Durable learning skills are a major focus of the paper. The synthesis finds positive effects for success-criteria knowledge (e.g., d=1.13 for success criteria; d=0.76 for planning and prediction), surface-learning strategies like summarization, note taking, and mnemonics, deep-learning strategies like elaboration and self-regulation, and transfer skills such as detecting similarities and differences (d=1.32) and far transfer (d=0.80).
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-regulation, help-seeking, strategy use, transfer, planning, and concept mapping
finding.effect_size: d=0.53 overall; up to d=1.32 for transfer-related strategies

finding.finding_summary: Some strategies were evaluated in terms of study efficiency or managing learning conditions, but these were not the central focus. The paper reports small to modest effects for environmental structuring (d=0.41), time management (d=0.40), and student control over learning (d=0.02), suggesting limited but sometimes positive operational benefits.
finding.measure: Environmental structuring, time management, student control over learning

paper_profiles.title: Online Instruction in Higher Education: Promising, Research-based, and Evidence-based Practices
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Education and e-Learning Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews empirical research on online learning in higher education to identify instructional practices associated with effective learning. The authors narrowed the corpus to 104 studies published from 2014–2019 and focused on undergraduate and graduate students in online, blended, and face-to-face comparison contexts. Rather than testing a single intervention, the paper synthesizes evidence across course design, student support, faculty pedagogy, student engagement, and student success factors.

The review concludes that many practices associated with stronger outcomes in online instruction are familiar from face-to-face teaching, including multiple pedagogies, high instructor presence, quality faculty-student interaction, academic support, and classroom cohesion/trust. Online-specific supports such as user-friendly technology, orientation to online learning, synchronous sessions, and social media were sometimes promising, but evidence was mixed and often correlational. The authors identify faculty feedback as the only clearly evidence-based practice and emphasize that few studies used designs strong enough to support causal claims, limiting confidence in broad prescriptions for online instruction.

Because this is a literature review of higher-education online instruction, the paper is most relevant to understanding what practices may improve student learning, satisfaction, engagement, and persistence in college settings. Its strongest empirical takeaway is that instructor feedback and presence matter, but the paper does not report a single pooled effect size and frequently notes mixed or limited evidence across the reviewed studies.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, online learning factors such as motivation, engagement, self-efficacy, satisfaction, and persistence were repeatedly associated with success, but findings varied by construct and study. Examples include retention differences favoring blended and face-to-face over fully online formats (e.g., 1.2 to 1.6 times greater odds of retention in some groups) and multiple correlational findings linking motivation, self-efficacy, and support to better course outcomes.
finding.measure: Course satisfaction, engagement, motivation, self-efficacy, persistence/retention, withdrawal, and course grades
finding.study_size: 104 studies reviewed; individual studies ranged from n=19 to n=33,844

finding.finding_summary: The review found recurring evidence that durable skills such as self-regulation, time management, collaboration, help-seeking, and metacognition are important in online courses. Several studies reported positive associations between these skills or supports and achievement, including better collaboration when feedback/help-seeking and group trust were present, and improved metacognitive/self-regulation scores when metacognitive support was added in flipped learning.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning, metacognition, collaboration/teamwork, help-seeking, and related course outcomes
finding.study_size: 104 studies reviewed; individual studies ranged from n=19 to n=33,844

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports mixed findings for general academic outcomes in higher education online learning, including course grades, achievement tests, knowledge acquisition, and course completion. Across many comparisons of online, blended, and face-to-face delivery, results often showed no significant differences in learning, while some specific supports (e.g., feedback, orientation, learning partners, metacognitive support) improved performance; a few contexts, such as developmental English and some supports, showed worse outcomes online.
finding.measure: Course grades, achievement tests, knowledge acquisition, course completion, and final exam scores
finding.study_size: 104 studies reviewed; individual studies ranged from n=19 to n=33,844

finding.finding_summary: A smaller portion of the review addresses instructional efficiency-related issues such as feedback delivery, use of clickstream data to modify instruction, and technology-supported course design. The authors conclude that timely, useful faculty feedback and data-informed instructional adjustments can improve learning processes, but they do not report a pooled effect or direct productivity outcome.
finding.measure: Feedback use, clickstream-informed instruction, instructional processes

finding.finding_summary: The review has a clear institutional lens because it synthesizes evidence relevant to online-program design, student support services, retention, and progression in higher education. Findings suggest institutions should provide orientation, academic and technical support, and trusted faculty interaction, but the evidence base is too limited for strong policy claims and the review explicitly notes the scarcity of causal studies.
finding.measure: Retention, withdrawal, completion, articulation to undergraduate study, and institutional support conditions
finding.study_size: 104 studies reviewed; one cited institutional dataset included n=9,820 enrollments over 10 years

finding.finding_summary: The review includes evidence that feedback and online instructional supports can improve writing-related outcomes, especially for less proficient writers. One cited study found significant writing improvement with online peer and instructor feedback, while another reported that feedback immediacy and usefulness had the greatest impact on improvement on similar tasks.
finding.measure: Writing skills / writing performance

paper_profiles.title: Detecting Learning Strategies with Analytics: Links with Self-Reported Measures and Academic Performance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether learning strategies inferred from digital trace data can be interpreted in terms of established approaches to learning, and whether those inferred strategies relate to academic performance. The authors address a gap in learning analytics research: most studies infer behavior from logs without linking those patterns to validated self-report instruments or to outcomes grounded in learning theory.

The study was conducted in a first-year undergraduate engineering course in computer systems at an Australian research-intensive university using a flipped classroom design. Students completed the Study Process Questionnaire (SPQ) at the start of the course, and the researchers analyzed LMS trace data from preparatory learning activities, including watching videos, reading materials, formative MCQs, and summative exercises. They clustered learning sequences and then grouped students into deep- versus surface-approach profiles based on those clusters.

The findings suggest that trace-based learning strategies can be meaningfully mapped onto deep and surface approaches to learning. Students classified as deep-approach learners showed significantly higher self-reported deep strategy and deep approach scores, and they also earned significantly higher midterm and final exam scores than surface-approach students. Effect sizes were small for the self-report differences (d≈0.18-0.23) and small-to-moderate for exam performance (d≈0.36-0.38). The study concludes that learning analytics can offer useful proxies for learning approaches, but that motivational constructs measured by a beginning-of-course survey may not align well with realized behavior captured in logs.

finding.finding_summary: Students identified as following a deep approach to learning achieved significantly higher academic performance than students classified as surface-approach learners. Deep-approach students scored higher on both the midterm exam (Z=4.3133, p<0.0001, d=0.3594) and the final exam (Z=4.5136, p<0.0001, d=0.3761) in the undergraduate engineering course (deep group n=55; surface group n=89).
finding.measure: Midterm and final exam scores

finding.finding_summary: The trace-based deep-approach group differed significantly from the surface-approach group on self-reported deep strategy and deep approach scores, but not on surface strategy, surface approach, or motivation scales. Deep approach students had higher DS scores (Z=2.7206, p=0.006, d=0.2267) and DA scores (Z=2.2106, p=0.027, d=0.1842), while DM, SM, SA, and SS showed no significant differences.
finding.measure: Study Process Questionnaire (SPQ): deep motive, deep strategy, surface motive, surface strategy, deep approach, surface approach

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies learning strategies, self-regulation, and metacognitive/strategic engagement as expressed in LMS traces. Students in the deep-approach clusters showed higher overall activity and more balanced use of effective strategies such as formative self-testing, with the authors interpreting these patterns as better regulation of learning; the surface clusters showed lower engagement and more performance-oriented or passive behavior.
finding.measure: Clustered learning sequences from LMS trace data (e.g., formative assessment use, reading, video watching, summative trial-and-error patterns)

paper_profiles.title: Teaching in Blended Learning Environments: Creating and Sustaining Communities of Inquiry
paper_profiles.venue: au Press / Issues in Distance Education series
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book addresses how to design, facilitate, direct, and assess blended learning in higher education. Its central question is how instructors can intentionally combine face-to-face and online learning so that students experience a purposeful community of inquiry rather than a simple add-on of technology to traditional teaching.

The authors ground the book in the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework, emphasizing social presence, cognitive presence, and teaching presence. They argue that effective blended learning requires deliberate design choices around course structure, climate, interaction, facilitation, direct instruction, and assessment, with an emphasis on open communication, critical discourse, reflection, and shared responsibility for learning.

The intended context is college and graduate education, though the authors note the principles may also be adapted for K-12 and workplace settings. The book is primarily conceptual and practice-oriented, drawing on prior research and illustrative examples rather than reporting a new empirical study. Its main conclusion is that blended learning can enhance engagement, reflection, and educational quality when it is carefully designed around inquiry and aligned assessment practices.

finding.finding_summary: The book argues that blended learning supports higher-order thinking, critical reflection, discourse, and metacognitive responsibility when designed around a community of inquiry. It does not report new primary effect estimates, but repeatedly cites prior research and illustrates that the intended educational outcome is deeper inquiry, collaboration, and shared responsibility in higher education.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reflection, discourse, metacognitive responsibility, collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The text presents social presence as essential for trust, open communication, cohesion, engagement, and persistence in blended courses. It states that thoughtful course design and facilitation create conditions that support perceived learning and persistence, but it does not provide original quantitative estimates in this book.
finding.measure: Engagement, social presence, persistence, perceived learning

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that blended learning can produce administrative advantages such as access, retention, campus-space flexibility, and teaching-resource efficiencies. However, these are presented as general benefits of the model rather than as outcomes from a specific empirical evaluation.
finding.measure: Access, retention, campus space, teaching resources

finding.finding_summary: The book frames blended learning as a broader institutional response to changing conditions in higher education, including redesign of teaching roles, course structures, and assessment practices. Its claims are normative and conceptual, emphasizing institutional change and the need to update teaching principles for the internet age rather than reporting a measured institutional effect.
finding.measure: Institutional teaching practices and course design change

paper_profiles.title: Student engagement and wellbeing over time at a higher education institution
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate student engagement and wellbeing vary over time in a campus-based UK higher education setting. The authors were interested in whether engagement is multi-dimensional, how it changes across a term, whether assessment periods alter engagement, and how self-reported engagement relates to wellbeing and academic performance.

The study used a longitudinal self-report survey of first- and second-year undergraduates at a research-intensive UK university, with 10 waves over 19 weeks. Students reported weekly participation in 17 learning activities (both online and offline), plus effort and happiness; Wave 1 also captured stable engagement style and motivations. The analysis combined correlations, trend analyses, and comparisons of assessment vs non-assessment weeks and high/low wellbeing groups.

The main conclusion is that engagement appears largely holistic: students who are engaged in one learning activity tend to be engaged across many others. Engagement generally declines over the term, but increases when assessments are due, and higher effort/happiness are associated with greater participation. However, the paper also reports an unexpected negative relationship between some engagement measures and grades, especially for behavioural engagement and some activity-specific participation. Because the design is observational and based on self-report, the authors emphasize that these are correlational findings rather than causal effects.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that engagement and wellbeing were positively related overall: cognitive engagement correlated with happiness (rho=0.30), academic motivation correlated with both effort (rho=0.28) and happiness (rho=0.29), and many learning activities were more frequent among students reporting higher effort or happiness. At the same time, engagement declined over the term while happiness increased (Kendall tau=0.36), so the temporal pattern was not uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Self-reported engagement style, effort scale, happiness/wellbeing scale, and weekly participation in learning activities

finding.finding_summary: Academic performance, measured as credit-weighted average module grade across the term, was positively correlated with behavioural engagement (rho=0.24) but not with cognitive engagement (rho=0.02). Several activity-specific relationships with grades were negative, including retail facilities (rho=-0.22), catering facilities (rho=-0.32), and attending a teaching session (rho=-0.17), which the authors describe as unexpected.
finding.measure: Credit-weighted average module grades and correlations with engagement/activity measures

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that assessment periods are associated with broad increases in student engagement across most learning activities, while engagement generally falls over the term and varies across online/offline and social/academic contexts. These results are framed as useful for institutional monitoring and student support, but the evidence is descriptive rather than intervention-based.
finding.measure: Comparisons of assessment-week vs non-assessment-week participation; term-long trends in engagement and wellbeing

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how formative assessment can be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard, in a university setting. The authors argue that frequent low-stakes assessment with immediate feedback can strengthen learning, reduce the distance between instruction and feedback, and potentially improve students’ performance on later summative examinations.

The study proposes weekly or fortnightly Blackboard-based quizzes with detailed feedback and reports survey data from students at Swinburne University of Technology’s Sarawak Campus. The sample spans Business, Engineering, and IT students and uses a questionnaire with closed and open-ended items to gauge perceptions of continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and online testing. Reliability statistics are reported for the survey instrument, along with a small set of statistical comparisons between student streams.

Overall, students were generally supportive of the Blackboard formative assessment approach, especially because it broke content into smaller topics, provided immediate feedback, and offered flexibility. The paper concludes that formative assessment may support ongoing engagement and could improve summative grades, but it does not present direct achievement data or a counterfactual comparison of learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent online formative assessments were helpful because they promoted steady learning, provided immediate feedback, and helped them stay in touch with the subject throughout the semester. The paper does not report outcome scores for motivation or engagement, but the survey responses indicate broadly favorable attitudes toward the assessment approach.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment, feedback, and online test implementation (questionnaire responses)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly discusses feedback helping students understand strengths and weaknesses and check whether they are on track, which relates to metacognition and self-monitoring. Students also said the approach would help them learn topics progressively and improve preparation for summative exams, but no direct skill test or performance effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions related to self-monitoring, reflection, and progressive learning

finding.finding_summary: Students generally favored splitting course work into 10 or 12 weekly Blackboard assessments and preferred the online test option over classroom testing because it supported learning in small steps and offered immediate feedback. The evidence is survey-based rather than an objective achievement comparison, so the paper supports perceived benefits for subject learning but not measured gains in grades or completion.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness of formative assessment for course learning and preparation for semester examinations

paper_profiles.title: A review of problem- and team-based methods for teaching statistics in Higher Education
paper_profiles.venue: Teaching Mathematics and its Applications: An International Journal of the IMA
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews problem-based learning (PBL) and team-based learning (TBL) as collaborative, active-learning approaches for teaching statistics in higher education, with an emphasis on introductory undergraduate statistics but also relevance to more advanced courses and postgraduate service courses. The authors ask whether these approaches can improve statistics learning compared with traditional lecture-based instruction, and what practical considerations matter when implementing them in higher-education classrooms.

The paper synthesizes prior literature rather than reporting a new primary empirical study. It contrasts the structure of PBL and TBL, including group formation, readiness assurance, facilitation, assessment, and classroom logistics, and then reviews evidence for effects on end-of-module performance, longer-term retention, student engagement, and staff experience. Across the literature, the strongest and most consistent evidence is for improved short-term academic performance and positive student perceptions, especially for TBL and some cooperative learning approaches, while evidence for long-term retention is limited and mixed.

The review concludes that group-based learning is a plausible and often beneficial alternative to lecture-only statistics teaching, particularly for applied or practical statistics courses. However, the authors caution that effectiveness depends on implementation details, student preparation, group dynamics, and available staff/resources; they also note that evidence is weaker for more theoretical mathematics-heavy statistics modules and for long-term retention outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that small-group or collaborative learning can improve end-of-module statistics achievement, especially for cooperative/collaborative approaches such as TBL, but not consistently for inquiry-based/PBL approaches. The cited meta-analysis by Kalaian and Kasim (2014) found cooperative or collaborative learning effective versus lecture, while no evidence of improved academic achievement was found for inquiry-based methods; the paper also notes examples of better statistics assessment performance after PBL-type courses and improved grades on module tests with TBL.
finding.measure: End-of-module statistics assessments, module grades, academic achievement

finding.finding_summary: The review finds broadly positive student responses to PBL/TBL, including greater enjoyment, engagement, and perceived accessibility of material, though not all students enjoy group learning. It cites studies showing increased attendance in PBL sessions and positive perceptions of TBL, with some concerns that weaker students may find teams intimidating or that some students may coast on others' work.
finding.measure: Student enjoyment, engagement, attendance, perceptions of the course

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the review is that PBL and TBL support development of soft skills such as collaboration, communication, teamwork, problem solving, and deeper conceptual explanation. The paper frames these as important outcomes of group-based learning, citing literature on group dynamics and communication in mathematics/statistics, but it does not report a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Collaboration, communication, teamwork, problem solving, group dynamics

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses implementation efficiency and staffing tradeoffs rather than learner outcomes, noting that TBL is more practical than traditional PBL because it does not require a facilitator for each group and can work in lecture theatres. It also describes successful modified PBL models that use fewer staff and online tools, suggesting that group-based methods can be implemented with manageable resources.
finding.measure: Staff resources, feasibility of running sessions, classroom logistics

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review and practical guide on how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback. The paper is organized around an established formative assessment framework and asks how LLMs can help educators clarify learning goals, diagnose where learners currently are, and provide actionable guidance to move learning forward.

Rather than reporting a primary empirical study, the authors synthesize prior research and give examples of prompting strategies and classroom uses of LLMs. They discuss generic LLMs, domain-specialized LLMs, and LLM-integrated educational platforms, with examples ranging from rewriting student-friendly learning objectives to generating prompts for co-constructing success criteria and producing sample work of varying quality. The paper also highlights limitations of current evaluation methods for LLM-generated feedback, especially that many metrics do not capture task-, process-, and self-regulatory feedback distinctions.

The intended context is broad educational practice, but many of the examples are framed for classroom teaching and include higher-education scenarios, especially an undergraduate fMRI course. The authors conclude that LLMs can meaningfully augment formative assessment when used with expert pedagogy, careful prompting, and attention to the risk of overreliance. They call for future work on robust pedagogically grounded metrics, prompt repositories, and AI-aware assessment strategies that promote transferable skills.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can save educators time by automating or accelerating formative-assessment tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating discussion prompts, creating exemplars, and drafting feedback. However, this is presented as a conceptual/practical claim rather than a measured effect, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Not a direct empirical measure; proposed efficiency gains in teacher workflow and time savings

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that LLM-supported formative assessment can foster transferable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, and self-regulation by using prompts that encourage reflection, critique of exemplars, and process-level feedback. These benefits are discussed as design goals and illustrative use cases, not as outcomes from a controlled study.
finding.measure: Proposed development of critical thinking, metacognition, self-regulation, and transferable skills

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents LLMs as useful for improving educational task materials outside a single core subject area, especially by generating student-friendly learning objectives and sample work in higher-education science contexts such as an undergraduate fMRI course. The examples suggest improved clarity and alignment with course goals, but the paper does not report quantified student learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Quality and clarity of AI-generated learning objectives, exemplars, and feedback prompts

paper_profiles.title: Are Educational Escape Rooms More Effective Than Traditional Lectures for Teaching Software Engineering? A Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a virtual educational escape room is more effective than a traditional lecture for teaching software modeling in an undergraduate software engineering course. The authors motivate the study by noting that prior work on educational escape rooms has often lacked control groups, pre/post testing, or sufficiently strong causal evidence, especially in higher education and computing education.

The intervention was a face-to-face, fully virtual escape room delivered through the Escapp web platform and compared against a conventional lecture covering the same UML modeling topics. The study used a cluster randomized controlled trial with pretest/post-test measures and included 326 second-year software engineering students enrolled in a course at Universidad Politécnica de Madrid (164 experimental, 162 control). Students in both groups improved significantly from pretest to post-test, but the escape-room group improved more and achieved higher post-test scores after controlling for pretest performance (ANCOVA, r=0.25, p<0.001).

Beyond achievement, the paper also reports strongly positive student perceptions of the escape room, including high enjoyment, immersion, acceptance of the digital platform, and preference for the escape room over a traditional lecture. The authors conclude that, for this topic and context, educational escape rooms can outperform traditional teaching in short-term knowledge acquisition and are well received by students, while also noting that the study does not address long-term retention or transfer.

finding.finding_summary: Students who learned software modeling through the educational escape room outperformed those who learned through a traditional lecture on the post-test, after controlling for pretest scores. The between-group difference was statistically significant (p<0.001) with a small-to-medium effect size (r=0.25) in favor of the escape room; the study included 326 undergraduate software engineering students (164 experimental, 162 control).
finding.measure: Software modeling knowledge test (10 multiple-choice items; pretest/post-test; ANCOVA on post-test with pretest as covariate)

finding.finding_summary: Students reported very positive perceptions of the educational escape room, describing it as fun, immersive, well organized, and preferable to a traditional lecture. The perceptions questionnaire was completed by the experimental group only (n=164), and the authors report high acceptance of the activity and of the Escapp platform; the questionnaire internal consistency was Cronbach’s α=0.80.
finding.measure: Perceptions questionnaire (Likert items plus closed-ended items on enjoyment, acceptance, and preference)

finding.finding_summary: The escape room was designed around team-based play and the authors argue that it may support collaboration and related soft skills, but these were not directly measured as outcomes. The paper’s empirical evidence in this category is limited to students’ positive perceptions of the team-based activity and its organization, rather than a direct assessment of collaboration or metacognition.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: AI Literacy and LLM Engagement in Higher Education: A Cross-National Quantitative Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This cross-national study examines how university students in the United States and Bangladesh perceive and use large language models (LLMs) in higher education. The paper asks how AI literacy, motivational beliefs, and educational context shape LLM engagement, and what academic and ethical outcomes students perceive from that engagement.

Using an online survey of 318 students (171 U.S., 147 Bangladesh), the authors measured AI literacy, AI familiarity, frequency of LLM use, perceived literacy benefits, optimism, ethical concern, and self-reported grade impact. The study is non-experimental and correlational: it analyzes correlations, t-tests, and ANOVAs rather than any intervention or counterfactual design.

The main findings suggest moderate LLM use, high optimism about academic potential, but low formal AI literacy. Greater LLM use was associated with higher perceived literacy benefits (r = .59, p < .001), higher optimism (r = .41, p < .001), and higher AI familiarity (r = .40, p < .001). Cross-national and disciplinary differences were also found: U.S. students and STEM majors reported more frequent LLM use, while Bangladeshi students perceived greater literacy benefits and U.S. students expressed more optimism. The paper concludes that higher education institutions should strengthen AI literacy instruction, address ethical concerns, and tailor policies and pedagogy to local and disciplinary contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that LLM use was associated with perceived improvements in literacy-related academic work, especially writing and broader literacy practices. Perceived literacy impact was moderately correlated with LLM use frequency (r = .59, p < .001), and Bangladeshi students reported higher perceived literacy benefits than U.S. students (M = 3.12 vs. 2.78; t(316) = -4.59, p < .001, d = 0.56).
finding.measure: Self-reported perceived literacy impact / literacy benefits from LLM use
finding.std_deviation: SD = 0.65 for perceived literacy impact; SD = 0.56 and 0.68 for country comparison

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined motivational beliefs and optimism toward LLM use as central predictors of engagement. LLM use frequency correlated positively with optimism (r = .41, p < .001), and descriptive results showed relatively high optimism about academic potential (M = 3.68, SD = 0.47) alongside moderate ethical concern (M = 3.17, SD = 0.89).
finding.measure: Optimism, motivational beliefs, ethical concern, and LLM use frequency
finding.std_deviation: SD = 0.47 (optimism); SD = 0.89 (ethical concern); SD = 1.00 (LLM use frequency)

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses durable-skill-related concerns, especially critical thinking, as part of its conceptual framing and self-reported ethical concerns, but it does not measure critical thinking directly with a performance task. Ethical concern was weakly negatively correlated with AI literacy (r = - .18, p < .05), suggesting that greater literacy slightly reduced apprehension about responsible use, while the discussion warns about overreliance and possible erosion of critical thinking.
finding.measure: Ethical concern and self-reported concerns about critical thinking/overreliance

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes self-reported grade impact as an academic outcome, but group differences by country were not significant. Descriptively, grade impact was relatively high (M = 4.08, SD = 0.49), yet the comparison between U.S. and Bangladeshi students showed no difference (t = -0.88, p = .379).
finding.measure: Self-reported grade impact from LLM use

paper_profiles.title: ‘Getting out of the closet’: Scientific authorship of literary fiction and knowledge transfer
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether scientists who write literary fiction use those books as mechanisms of knowledge transfer, and whether this varies by whether the author is academic or non-academic and by scientific field. The authors position literary fiction as a form of ‘non-formal knowledge transfer’ because it is created in spare time, involves copyrights, and sits outside standard university technology-transfer channels.

The study combines conceptual analysis, a quantitative analysis of 541 fiction books published in 2015 by publishers in Catalonia and the Valencian Community (Spain), and qualitative interviews with 15 scientific writers. The quantitative component identifies whether fiction books were authored by scientists and whether the plot/themes matched the author’s research lines; the qualitative interviews probe direct, indirect, and reverse knowledge transfer. Scientific authors made up 11% of the fiction sample, and direct knowledge transfer was detected in 32% of scientific-authored books. The interviews suggest that non-academic scientists were more likely than academic scientists to embed direct knowledge transfer in their fiction, while academic scientists more often experienced indirect and reverse transfer through engagement with cultural audiences. The paper also finds that knowledge transfer is more common in Other Humanities than in other fields, and that Linguistics and Literature may be underestimated by external coding because the fiction form and research object overlap.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that literary fiction can function as a non-formal knowledge transfer mechanism and provides evidence that this mechanism is shaped by institutional logic and field. In the Spanish sample (541 fiction books; 61 scientific authors), scientific authorship was 11% of fiction output, and direct knowledge transfer was more common for non-academic scientists than academic scientists, suggesting institutional context matters for how knowledge reaches the public.
finding.measure: Scientific authorship of fiction; direct knowledge transfer in fiction; interviews on transfer mechanisms
finding.study_size: n=541 books; n=61 scientific authors; n=15 interviews

paper_profiles.title: Measuring Axiomatic Soundness of Counterfactual Image Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to evaluate counterfactual image generation models when true counterfactuals are not observable. The authors argue that existing deep generative models for counterfactual inference are difficult to assess because counterfactual identifiability is generally impossible from observational data alone, especially in high-dimensional settings such as images.

To address this, they derive evaluation criteria from Pearl’s axiomatic definition of counterfactuals—composition, reversibility, and effectiveness—and turn these into quantitative soundness metrics that can be applied to black-box counterfactual generators. The paper then studies conditional VAEs and conditional GANs as approximate counterfactual functions, including regularizers for composition and optional reversibility constraints.

Empirically, the paper evaluates these metrics on three computer-vision benchmarks: colour MNIST, 3D Shapes, and CelebA-HQ. It shows that confounding can substantially degrade counterfactual quality, that simulated interventions can partially recover performance when the joint distribution has full support, and that there is often a trade-off between faithfulness to the input and adherence to counterfactual conditions. The main conclusion is methodological: the proposed framework can compare counterfactual models without access to ground-truth counterfactuals, and it highlights how confounding and model design affect counterfactual soundness.

paper_profiles.title: An Exploration of Higher Education Course Evaluation by Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can be used to automate higher-education course evaluation, a process that is traditionally subjective, labor-intensive, and difficult to scale. The authors frame the problem as one of quality assurance and institutional decision-making: universities need more timely, consistent, and interpretable evaluations of courses than can be provided by end-of-semester surveys, classroom observations, or expert reviews alone.

The paper studies two uses of LLMs. First, at the micro level, it uses GPT-4o to analyze a sample classroom discussion from a flipped classroom and generate feedback on discussion organization, instructor questioning, and individual student participation using Bloom's taxonomy as an interpretive lens. Second, at the macro level, it evaluates 100 university courses from a major institution in China, comparing Kimi, Llama, and a fine-tuned version of Llama (Llama-UKP) on a structured rubric covering course design, instructional team, teaching resources, assessment, and teaching effectiveness. Human expert scores are used as the reference for validating model outputs.

The main conclusion is that LLMs can produce structured and interpretable course evaluations, and that fine-tuning substantially improves alignment with human judgments. Llama-UKP showed better score distribution properties, stronger correlation with the expert rater (Pearson 0.754; Spearman 0.843), and more human-like calibration than the base Llama model or Kimi. The paper argues that LLMs are promising tools for reducing evaluator workload and supporting institutional quality assurance in higher education, though it also notes limitations related to ambiguity, domain specificity, and cross-context generalizability.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that LLMs can automate both micro-level classroom discussion analysis and macro-level course review, reducing the workload associated with manual observation and evaluation. In the 100-course study, Llama-UKP produced structured scores and comments that were more discriminative and closer to expert judgments, indicating practical efficiency gains for institutional course review processes.
finding.measure: Course evaluation workflow efficiency; ability to generate structured evaluation outputs from classroom transcripts and course packages
finding.study_size: n=100 courses (macro-level); one illustrative classroom discussion transcript (micro-level)

finding.finding_summary: The study concludes that LLM-based evaluation can support university quality assurance and educational decision-making at scale. Across the 100-course case study, the fine-tuned Llama-UKP aligned more closely with human expert ratings than Kimi, with Pearson correlation 0.754 and Spearman correlation 0.843, suggesting institutional usefulness for standardized course review.
finding.measure: Course evaluation scores, score distributions, and correlation with human expert ratings

finding.finding_summary: In the micro-level discussion analysis, the LLM interprets instructor questioning as promoting higher-order thinking aligned with Bloom's taxonomy, including analyzing, evaluating, and creating. The generated feedback suggests that structured questioning supported students' critical thinking and reasoning during the environmental protection discussion, though this is based on a single illustrative transcript rather than a controlled comparison.
finding.measure: Bloom's taxonomy–based qualitative analysis of classroom discussion dynamics and student participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that classroom discussion feedback generated by the LLM can help students reflect on their participation and identify strengths and areas for improvement. In the example discussion, the model rated student contributions and described differences in engagement and communication quality, implying support for reflective learning and participation-related motivation, but no direct outcome data were collected.
finding.measure: LLM-generated feedback on student discussion participation and performance

paper_profiles.title: The Effects of Higher Education on Midlife Depression: Quasi-Experimental Evidence from South Korea
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether completing higher education causally improves women’s mental health in midlife, focusing on depression outcomes in South Korea. The authors are motivated by the broader debate on whether education has measurable health benefits beyond correlational associations, and by the limited causal evidence on mental health effects of college education, especially for women and in non-Western settings.

To identify causal effects, the study uses South Korea’s 1993 higher-education reform as a quasi-experimental source of variation in college completion. The authors combine two nationally representative datasets: KNHANES (2007–2021) for physician-diagnosed depression and KLoWF (2007–2022) for self-reported depressive symptoms and daily affect/stress. They estimate two-stage least squares models using birth-cohort exposure to the reform as an instrument, and also test possible mediating pathways through income, employment, health behaviors, and physical health.

Across both datasets, the findings consistently indicate that college completion is associated with better mental health. In KNHANES, college completion reduces physician-diagnosed depression by 2.4 percentage points in the baseline model and 1.6 percentage points after adjusting for mediators. In KLoWF, college completion reduces weekly depressive symptoms by about 16.4 percentage points, with similar improvements in daily affect/stress; broader cohort windows produce larger but less precise estimates. The authors conclude that expanded access to higher education can yield meaningful mental-health benefits for midlife women, partly through improved economic conditions and physical health, though substantial unexplained effects remain.

finding.finding_summary: Using the 1993 South Korean higher-education reform as an instrument, the paper finds that expanded college access increased college completion and had downstream benefits for women’s mental health. The main causal estimates suggest that higher education can function as a structural lever for reducing midlife depression among women in a non-Western context, with null placebo tests supporting the identification strategy.
finding.measure: College completion induced by the 1993 higher-education reform; downstream mental-health outcomes
finding.study_size: KNHANES n=2,912; KLoWF n=751 individuals / 4,396 person-wave observations

paper_profiles.title: Course-Skill Atlas: A National Longitudinal Dataset of Skills Taught in U.S. Higher Education Curricula
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a measurement gap in higher education research: while labor-market skill taxonomies are well developed, there has been far less systematic, granular documentation of which skills are taught in college curricula. The authors argue that degree counts and credit totals are too coarse to represent the skills students actually encounter, especially given variation across institutions, majors, and time.

To address this, the paper introduces Course-Skill Atlas, a public longitudinal dataset built from over 3 million syllabi at 2,761 U.S. colleges and universities. The authors develop Syllabus2O*NET, an NLP pipeline that segments syllabi, removes logistics-related text, embeds learning-content sentences and O*NET work activities with SBERT, and computes semantic similarity to infer coverage of detailed work activities, tasks, and derived abilities. These inferred skill scores are aggregated at the institution-year-field-of-study level, producing a national dataset with 281,153 records.

The population studied is U.S. higher education syllabi, spanning mostly postsecondary institutions and fields of study from 2000–2017. The paper does not test an instructional intervention or student outcomes; instead, it validates the measurement approach descriptively, reports duplicate-syllabus rates, and analyzes representativeness and coverage relative to institutional and CIP distributions. The main conclusion is that syllabi can be transformed into a scalable, public, longitudinal proxy for curricular skill content, enabling future research on workforce preparation, curricular change, and education–labor market alignment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper develops an automated NLP pipeline (Syllabus2O*NET) to convert syllabi into skill vectors and produce institution-year-field-of-study aggregates, reducing the need for manual coding of curricular content. The authors report that the framework processes 3,162,747 syllabi and creates a public dataset with 281,153 aggregated records, suggesting substantial gains in scalability and data production efficiency.
finding.measure: Automated extraction and aggregation of skill content from course syllabi

finding.finding_summary: The core contribution is a national dataset of curricular skill profiles across 2,761 U.S. higher education institutions, fields of study, and years. The authors argue that the dataset can support research on curriculum design, institutional differences, labor-market alignment, and workforce development, with representativeness analyses showing broad coverage across states and sectors.
finding.measure: National coverage/representativeness of higher-education curricular skill profiles

paper_profiles.title: Automated Prompt Generation for Creative and Counterfactual Text-to-Image Synthesis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of counterfactual controllability in text-to-image generation, specifically the challenge of generating images that deliberately violate common-sense size relations (for example, a tiny walrus beside a giant button). The authors argue that while text-to-image models have become strong at realism and prompt adherence, they remain weak at reliably producing counterfactual outputs, which matters for creative and exploratory applications.

To tackle this, the paper proposes AutoContra, an automatic prompt engineering framework with three parts: an image evaluator, a supervised prompt rewriter, and a DPO-trained prompt ranker. Because no public dataset existed for counterfactual-size prompt–image pairs, the authors create a new dataset from 91 objects and 2,070 base prompts, then build 7,304 positive/negative rewritten triplets for training. The system is evaluated on the open-source CoMat text-to-image model, with ChatGPT-4o and Promptist as baselines.

The experiments show that the full framework outperforms the baselines on the task of producing faithful counterfactual-size images, though absolute accuracy remains low overall. The prompt ranker provides a small but consistent gain over the rewriter alone, and the custom image evaluator aligns well with human judgments in an ablation study. Overall, the paper concludes that evaluator-guided prompt rewriting can improve counterfactual image synthesis and provides a dataset and method intended to support future research in controllable generation.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed automatic prompt engineering pipeline improves the efficiency and effectiveness of generating counterfactual text-to-image outputs compared with baseline prompt-rewriting methods. On a test set of 1,004 object pairs, AutoContra achieved 30.3% accuracy versus 29.1% for the same system without the ranker, 27.5% for ChatGPT-4o, 10.2% for base prompts, and 8.2% for Promptist, indicating that the ranker and evaluator-guided workflow help automate a difficult prompt-optimization task.
finding.measure: Accuracy of generated images meeting the evaluator threshold for counterfactual size faithfulness

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly targets counterfactual controllability, a form of creative and exploratory reasoning in prompt design, and shows that the framework better captures non-trivial semantic constraints than baseline approaches. However, the evidence is task-specific to image generation rather than a broader educational durable-skill context, so this assignment is limited to the paper's emphasis on counterfactual reasoning and prompt refinement as a capability.
finding.measure: Counterfactual-size faithfulness / success rate in generated images

paper_profiles.title: What if...?: Thinking Counterfactual Keywords Helps to Mitigate Hallucination in Large Multi-modal Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of hallucination in large multi-modal models (LMMs), where the model produces responses that are inconsistent with the visual input. The authors ask whether prompting models with self-generated counterfactual keywords can induce "counterfactual thinking" and reduce hallucinated outputs without any additional fine-tuning.

The proposed method, Counterfactual Inception, asks an LMM to generate plausible but intentionally misleading keywords at the object, attribute, and relation levels for a given image. These keywords are then passed back into the model through a counterfactual prompt that instructs it to avoid those keywords while answering the user’s question. To improve keyword quality, the paper also introduces a Plausibility Verification Process (PVP) that filters keywords using CLIP similarity thresholds, keeping only those that are neither too factual nor too irrelevant.

The study evaluates several open-source and proprietary LMMs, including LLaVA-1.5, InternLM-XComposer2, LLaVA-NeXT, InternVL 1.5, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and GPT-4V, on hallucination-oriented benchmarks such as POPE, MMVP, CHAIR, and MMHal-Bench. Across these benchmarks, the method generally improves object-level discrimination and reduces hallucinated content in generated descriptions, with stronger models benefiting more consistently. The paper concludes that counterfactual prompting is a training-free way to improve visual grounding and reduce hallucination in LMMs.

finding.finding_summary: The method improves the reliability of model outputs without additional training, reducing hallucination and making responses more usable in downstream multimodal tasks. Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report better accuracy/F1 on POPE and higher average accuracy on MMVP after adding Counterfactual Inception, indicating more efficient and reliable inference-time behavior.
finding.measure: Hallucination-related benchmark performance (POPE accuracy/precision/recall/F1; MMVP average accuracy; CHAIR hallucination metrics; MMHal-Bench overall score and hallucination rate)

paper_profiles.title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (theoretical paper drawing on K-12 classroom examples, not a single empirical study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a theoretical framework for formative assessment and argues for a more coherent account of how formative interactions work in classrooms. Black and Wiliam revisit earlier formative-assessment work and propose that formative assessment can be understood through five strategies: clarifying learning intentions and criteria, engineering classroom discussions and tasks to elicit evidence, providing feedback that moves learners forward, activating peers as instructional resources, and activating students as owners of their own learning.

A major focus of the paper is the micro-process of teacher-learner interaction: how teachers interpret student responses, how they decide what feedback to give, and how feedback should be aligned with broader pedagogical aims. To develop this account, the authors connect formative assessment with self-regulated learning, cognitive acceleration, dynamic assessment, and classroom discourse research. They argue that formative assessment is fundamentally about creating and capitalizing on moments of contingency in instruction, where evidence of learning can be used to make better-founded decisions about next steps.

The paper is not an intervention study and does not report a new sample, treatment effect, or counterfactual comparison. Instead, it synthesizes prior literature and uses classroom examples to illustrate why teachers need theories of learners’ cognition, motivation, and task interpretation in order to provide effective feedback. The main conclusion is that formative assessment is best understood as a structured, theory-informed pedagogy rather than a mere list of classroom techniques, and that its effectiveness depends on teachers’ ability to diagnose learner thinking and respond strategically within subject-specific contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively theorizes metacognition, self-regulation, and learner autonomy as central purposes of formative assessment, but it does not report a new empirical effect estimate. It argues that practices such as self-assessment, peer assessment, and feedback can strengthen learners’ capacity to monitor and regulate their own learning, drawing on prior literature and illustrative classroom cases rather than original data.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses motivation, engagement, persistence, and well-being as important mediators of formative assessment, especially in the self-regulated learning literature it reviews. It does not provide new quantitative evidence, but it argues that feedback can either support growth-oriented engagement or trigger avoidance and well-being-protective responses depending on how students interpret tasks and teacher responses.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment is most effective when aligned to subject-specific aims and disciplinary understanding, and it uses examples from mathematics, science, and classroom discourse to illustrate this claim. However, it provides no original empirical estimate; the conclusion is theoretical, based on synthesis of earlier work and classroom examples.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Blended learning: the new normal and emerging technologies
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines blended learning (BL) in higher education as an increasingly common instructional modality and asks what outcomes it appears to support. The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it synthesizes prior research and reports institution-level data from the University of Central Florida (UCF) on course success, withdrawal, and student perceptions of instruction across blended, online, and face-to-face modalities.

The authors frame blended learning as a broader structural shift in higher education and argue that its effects should be interpreted cautiously because “blend” configurations are not equivalent across studies. They compare large-scale UCF enrollment and outcome data from fall 2014 through fall 2015, including minority/non-minority subgroup analyses, and analyze student evaluation data using CART decision trees. The institution-level results show slightly higher success and sometimes lower withdrawal in blended courses than in online or face-to-face courses, with similar patterns for minority and non-minority students. The student evaluation analysis suggests that perceptions of instructional excellence are driven primarily by three items: helping students achieve course objectives, creating an environment that helps students learn, and communicating ideas and information.

Overall, the paper concludes that blended learning at UCF maintained or improved access and success, while student judgments of course quality were largely independent of modality, expected grade, or desire to take the course. The authors also emphasize that end-of-course ratings contain formative elements and may be useful for faculty development, though they are not direct measures of learning. The article is primarily descriptive and interpretive, with no randomized counterfactual design.

finding.finding_summary: Across fall 2014 through fall 2015, blended courses showed slightly higher student success rates than online and face-to-face courses at UCF. Success was defined as earning A, B, C, or S grades, and blended sections reached 91-95% success across terms (e.g., n=17,954 in fall 2014; n=19,368 in fall 2015), compared with 87-91% for face-to-face sections and 89-92% for online sections.
finding.measure: Course success rate (A/B/C/S grades)
finding.study_size: multiple semesters; term-level n ranged from 6,492 to 19,368 for blended sections

finding.finding_summary: Blended learning was associated with slightly lower withdrawal rates, which the authors interpret as supporting persistence and retention. Withdrawal rates in blended sections were typically 2-3% across terms, compared with 3-4% in online and face-to-face sections, suggesting a modest advantage for student continuation.
finding.measure: Course withdrawal rate (W, WF, WP grades; exclusions noted)
finding.study_size: multiple semesters; term-level n ranged from 6,710 to 21,482 for blended sections

finding.finding_summary: At the institutional level, the paper concludes that blended learning maintained or increased access while producing improved success rates for both minority and non-minority students. The study also reports that the institution’s blended modality outperformed or matched other modalities on access-related indicators and that faculty development was required to support blended course redesign.
finding.measure: Institution-level access, success, and withdrawal patterns by modality and minority status
finding.study_size: fall 2014-fall 2015 enrollment data across multiple courses; blended n by term ranged from 6,492 to 19,368

finding.finding_summary: The decision-tree analysis of course evaluations found that students judged instructor excellence mainly on three pedagogically oriented factors: helping them achieve course objectives, creating a learning environment, and communicating ideas clearly. When students rated these three items as excellent, the probability of an overall excellent instructor rating was .99; conversely, poor ratings on all three yielded a 99% chance of an overall poor rating.
finding.measure: Student perception of instruction / overall instructor rating predicted by CART decision tree

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that blended learning reduces on-ground seat time and can address practical burdens such as parking and commuting time, while also supporting faculty development for course redesign. These benefits are presented as institutional efficiencies rather than direct experimental outcomes.
finding.measure: Reduced on-ground time; faculty development and course redesign implications

paper_profiles.title: Creating Experience Value to Build Student Satisfaction in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how student satisfaction in higher education can be improved through the creation of experience value, with a particular focus on co-creation. The authors argue that students do not simply purchase instructional services, but rather accumulate experience across the full university journey, from entry through alumni status, and that this experience can be shaped by students’ active participation in campus activities.

Using a survey of 357 students drawn from 32 universities in South Sumatra Province, Indonesia, the study applies structural equation modeling to test relationships among co-creation, experience value, and student satisfaction. The model treats co-creation as an antecedent to experience value and student satisfaction, and experience value as a mediator. The study finds that co-creation strongly and significantly predicts experience value (estimate = 0.90, t = 11.43), and experience value strongly and significantly predicts student satisfaction (estimate = 0.85, t = 8.29). Co-creation does not have a statistically significant direct effect on student satisfaction (estimate = 0.05, t = 0.58), suggesting an indirect pathway through experience value.

Overall, the paper concludes that universities should focus on building stronger student engagement and participation in institutional activities, including curriculum-related collaboration, to raise experience value and thereby improve satisfaction. The findings are presented as evidence that experience value is a key intervening mechanism linking co-creation to student satisfaction in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: Co-creation was strongly associated with higher experience value, which the authors interpret as reflecting greater student engagement and attachment to the institution. In the SEM model, co-creation predicted experience value with an estimate of 0.90 (t=11.43, R²=0.82) in a sample of 357 students.
finding.measure: Experience value / student experience scale

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that institutional co-creation practices are associated with higher student satisfaction indirectly through experience value. Experience value significantly predicted student satisfaction (estimate = 0.85, t=8.29, R²=0.80), while the direct path from co-creation to satisfaction was not significant (estimate = 0.05, t=0.58).
finding.measure: Student satisfaction scale; SEM path estimates

paper_profiles.title: Are Educational Escape Rooms More Effective Than Traditional Lectures for Teaching Software Engineering? A Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a virtual educational escape room is more effective than a traditional lecture for teaching software modeling in an undergraduate software engineering course. The authors respond to a broader gap in the escape-room literature, which they argue has often lacked control groups, pre/post testing, and robust counterfactual comparisons.

The study used a cluster randomized controlled trial with pretest and post-test measures in a second-year course, "Software engineering fundamentals," at Universidad Politécnica de Madrid. A total of 326 students participated: 164 in the experimental group learned software modeling through a face-to-face virtual escape room, and 162 in the control group received a traditional lecture covering the same UML topics for the same duration. Learning was measured with a 10-item multiple-choice test on UML diagrams, and the escape room group also completed a perceptions questionnaire.

Results showed significant learning gains in both groups, but the escape room group outperformed the lecture group on post-test performance after controlling for pretest scores. The between-group difference favored the escape room with a small-to-medium effect (r = 0.25, p < 0.001). Students in the escape room condition also reported highly positive perceptions, including strong enjoyment, acceptance, and preference for the activity over traditional lecture. The authors conclude that educational escape rooms can improve knowledge acquisition in software engineering and may be more effective than traditional teaching, while noting that long-term retention and generalization to other topics were not tested.

finding.finding_summary: Students taught software modeling through the educational escape room performed significantly better than those taught by traditional lecture on the post-test, controlling for pretest scores. The post-test between-group difference was statistically significant (p < 0.001) with a small-to-medium effect size (r = 0.25), based on 326 undergraduate software engineering students.
finding.measure: Knowledge test on software modeling / UML diagrams (10 multiple-choice items scored 0-10); ANCOVA on post-test with pretest as covariate

finding.finding_summary: Students in the experimental group reported very positive perceptions of the escape room, describing it as fun, immersive, well organized, and worth recommending. The questionnaire also indicated high acceptance of the activity and a strong preference for escape rooms over traditional lecture, suggesting increased engagement and motivation, although no standardized engagement effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions questionnaire, including overall opinion, acceptance, enjoyment/immersion, and preference items

finding.finding_summary: The intervention required team-based collaboration in 4-6 person groups and was designed to support communication, teamwork, and problem solving while completing puzzles under time constraints. However, the paper did not directly measure durable skills with a dedicated instrument, so evidence here is indirect and based mainly on the structure of the activity and student perceptions.
