finding.measure: Team-based participation and perceptions of the activity; no direct durable-skills outcome measure reported

paper_profiles.title: Research on College Students' Innovation and Entrepreneurship Education from The Perspective of Artificial Intelligence Knowledge-Based Crowdsourcing
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Vocational and Technical Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence–enabled knowledge-based crowdsourcing can support college students’ innovation and entrepreneurship education. The author argues that knowledge-based crowdsourcing fits the needs of university students because it relies on human intelligence for tasks such as image annotation, language recognition, and knowledge collection, and because students can participate flexibly while also developing practical entrepreneurship experience.

The study combines literature review, a questionnaire survey of 835 university students, and a small practice-based implementation in which some students participated in crowdsourcing projects such as map marking and image recognition through a third-party organization. The paper reports that most students had little prior knowledge of knowledge-based crowdsourcing, although many expressed interest in learning about it and participating in related tasks. Based on the survey and the author’s practice observations, the paper concludes that universities should better recognize the value of knowledge-based crowdsourcing, that students need more realistic expectations about participation, and that online platforms are needed to aggregate and distribute crowdsourcing opportunities.

Overall, the paper is primarily descriptive and conceptual rather than evaluative: it does not compare against a counterfactual condition or measure delayed outcomes such as retention, transfer, or course completion. Its main contribution is to propose knowledge-based crowdsourcing as a practical pathway for innovation and entrepreneurship education in the AI era and to document student awareness and interest in such activities.

finding.finding_summary: In a survey of 835 university students, 660 (79.04%) said they were willing to learn more about knowledge-based crowdsourcing, suggesting substantial curiosity and openness toward participation. The paper interprets this as evidence of student interest and readiness to engage with this type of innovation and entrepreneurship activity, though no validated engagement or motivation scale was used.
finding.measure: Survey item on willingness to learn about knowledge-based crowdsourcing

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that knowledge-based crowdsourcing can provide a practical and efficient channel for student participation in innovation and entrepreneurship education by aggregating tasks through online platforms and third-party matching. This is a conceptual conclusion supported by the author’s small-scale practice observations, but no productivity, time-on-task, or efficiency metrics are reported.
finding.measure: Practice observations and author interpretation of platform-based task matching

finding.finding_summary: The study concludes that universities should more fully recognize knowledge-based crowdsourcing as a mechanism for innovation and entrepreneurship education and better connect it with institutional teaching and practice. This conclusion is based on a survey of 835 students and the author’s implementation experience, but it does not report institutional outcome measures or a controlled evaluation.
finding.measure: Survey of student awareness plus practice-based implementation commentary

paper_profiles.title: Experiential Learning Approach for Software Engineering Courses at Higher Education Level
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a common challenge in higher-education software engineering courses: students often struggle to connect theory, project planning, and real development practice, especially when design-implement tasks become too technical and distract them from process learning. The authors propose an integrated experiential learning approach intended to better align teaching activities with intended learning outcomes and to help students experience software project management in a controlled setting.

The intervention combines traditional lectures with two serious-game simulations of software project planning—one plan-driven and one agile—followed by a small-scale design-implement task using LEGO Mindstorms systems. The game activities expose student teams to requirements, planning, estimation, risk, uncertainty, and changing project conditions, while the subsequent development task asks them to apply and reflect on those experiences in a real implementation context. The course took place at Blekinge Institute of Technology in 2018 and 2019 with master’s students in engineering, mostly in their second year, organized into teams.

The evaluation used multiple data sources: assessment rubrics for successive project-plan submissions, an open-ended student survey, and end-of-course reflective reports. The findings suggest that the integrated approach supported knowledge acquisition, reinforced theoretical concepts, and helped students recognize challenges resembling real software projects. The project-plan scores generally improved across submissions, and student reflections indicated that the games and task were perceived as meaningful and aligned with course objectives. Because the study is qualitative/mixed-methods and lacks a counterfactual comparison group, the evidence is best interpreted as supportive process evidence rather than causal proof of learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The integrated approach appears to strengthen students' planning, reflection, and collaboration in software project work. Project-plan rubric scores improved between successive submissions across both the plan-driven and agile game instances, and student reflections reported that the activities helped them understand and respond to project challenges, estimate work, and negotiate changing requirements.
finding.measure: Project plan rubric scores; open-ended survey responses; reflective reports
finding.study_size: n=58 (2018) and n=24 (2019); 14 teams in 2018 and 7 teams in 2019

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that the game and development activities were motivating and engaging, and the authors note that the gamified exercise had a clear motivational effect even though game outcomes did not affect grades. The survey and reflection data suggest the approach supported persistence and student engagement with the course activities.
finding.measure: Student survey responses and reflective reports
finding.study_size: n=45 survey respondents in 2018; n=15 survey respondents in 2019

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies software engineering learning outcomes, especially understanding of development processes, project planning, requirements work, testing, and agile/plan-driven practices. Across the qualitative data and rubric-based project-plan assessments, the authors conclude that the integrated approach promoted knowledge acquisition and reinforced theoretical concepts aligned with the course objectives.
finding.measure: Project plan rubric scores; survey responses; reflective reports

finding.finding_summary: The approach was designed to help instructors monitor student progress and provide feedback on planning and development practices, and the paper reports that rubric-based assessment and workshops allowed teaching staff to identify missing or weak project-planning practices. The study does not quantify workload reduction, but it suggests the method can support process monitoring and formative feedback during the course.
finding.measure: Instructor assessment of project plans; workshop feedback process
finding.study_size: n=14 teams in 2018; n=7 teams in 2019

paper_profiles.title: The Quantitative Reasoning for College Science (QuaRCS) Assessment, 1: Development and Validation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for a valid, non-proprietary assessment of quantitative reasoning for college students, especially those in general education science courses. The authors argue that such courses are a promising but underused venue for supporting numeracy, and they develop the Quantitative Reasoning for College Science (QuaRCS) instrument to measure students' quantitative skills and attitudes.

The QuaRCS was developed and refined over eight semesters (2010-2015) through educator surveys, pilot testing in free-response and multiple-choice formats, item analysis, and validation across multiple course contexts. The final instrument includes 25 quantitative items and 25 demographic/attitudinal items, with expert-reviewed skill alignment across graph reading, table reading, arithmetic, proportional reasoning, estimation, percentages, statistics/probability, area/volume, error, and unit conversions/dimensional analysis.

The primary validation sample was spring 2015 general-education science students at a large research university in the southwestern U.S. (n=1480), with additional validation data from STEM majors (n=261) and other earlier administrations. The paper concludes that the QuaRCS can distinguish varying levels of quantitative literacy and appears valid for both general-education science students and at least one STEM-major population. The authors also report that students' confidence does not reliably track correctness, that low-stakes online administration and self-reported effort matter for data quality, and that the assessment is sensitive to calculator use and item ordering effects among low-effort respondents.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the final QuaRCS instrument validly distinguishes varying levels of quantitative literacy among undergraduates in general education science and STEM courses. In the largest validation sample (n=1480 general-education science students), the assessment showed a wide score distribution (mean=13.8/25, SD=5.3), and item statistics indicated acceptable difficulty/discrimination for most items; the instrument also remained valid in a STEM-major differential equations course (n=261).
finding.measure: QuaRCS quantitative reasoning assessment scores; item difficulty (pD) and discrimination statistics
finding.study_size: n=1480 (general education science); n=261 (STEM validation course)
finding.std_deviation: SD=5.3 on Spring 2015 pre-semester score distribution

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes evidence that many students misjudge their own performance: among incorrect responses, 44% of respondents still reported being confident or very confident, suggesting weak calibration of metacognitive awareness. The authors also report that self-reported effort varies substantially and is associated with completion behavior and score patterns, indicating that motivation/persistence influences test performance.
finding.measure: Self-reported confidence after each item; self-reported effort on the assessment; completion-time patterns

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper is primarily an assessment-development study, it explicitly grounds the instrument in science-literacy contexts and validates that the selected skills are those educators deem most important for science literacy. The QuaRCS was designed for general-education science courses, and the authors conclude that it validly measures quantitative skills relevant to interpreting scientific information in introductory college science settings.
finding.measure: Expert survey on skills important for science literacy; alignment of QuaRCS items to science-literacy-relevant quantitative skills
finding.study_size: 48 educator survey respondents; 15 expert item-sorters; student validation samples n=1480 and n=261

paper_profiles.title: Motivations of Educators for Participating in NITARP, an Authentic Astronomy Research Experience Professional Development Program
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how educators describe their motivations for participating in NITARP, a year-long authentic astronomy research professional development program. The authors are interested in understanding why teachers commit substantial unpaid time to a sustained research experience and how their motivations relate to their needs for support during the program.

The study analyzes open-ended survey responses collected from 74 educators across up to four waypoints during the 13-month NITARP cycle, spanning the 2010–2017 cohorts. Using iterative qualitative coding and a constructivist/narrative analysis lens, the authors map motivations onto a continuum from inward-focused goals (personal learning, networking, gaining new skills) to outward-focused goals (benefits for students, sharing with other teachers). A key finding is that participants are distributed across this continuum and often shift over time toward more outward-focused responses as the year progresses.

The population is primarily high school teachers, but it also includes middle school teachers, community college faculty, and informal educators. The paper concludes that both inward- and outward-focused motivations are legitimate reasons for participation and that understanding where educators fall on this continuum can help program staff better support participants through challenging parts of the research experience. The study is descriptive and does not test a counterfactual intervention, but it provides evidence about participant motivation, team dynamics, and the kinds of support needed in sustained professional development.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that educators’ motivations for joining NITARP span a continuum from inward-focused personal learning goals to outward-focused goals centered on student benefit and sharing with colleagues. Across the 74 educators and up to four survey waypoints per educator, participants often shifted over time toward more outward-focused responses, suggesting evolving motivation and engagement during the 13-month program.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of open-ended survey responses for motivation-related themes and location on an inward/outward focus continuum

finding.finding_summary: The program appears to foster collaboration, reflection, and persistence as educators work in teams over a year-long research project. The analysis shows that teachers frequently reference team interaction, colleagues, and the challenges of sustained collaborative research, and the authors argue that participants move toward greater outward focus and teamwork-related language over time.
finding.measure: Qualitative survey coding of references to team, colleagues, self, students, and teachers; longitudinal thematic change across waypoints

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that NITARP functions as a model for scalable, high-quality teacher professional development and informs how such programs should support participants. The authors conclude that understanding educator motivations has implications for program design, participant support, and selection of candidates who will gain most from the experience and share it broadly.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of educator survey responses and program participation patterns
finding.study_size: n=74 educators (surveyed subset); program history includes 103 educators

paper_profiles.title: Rising Stargirls: Benefits of a Creative Arts-Based Approach to Astronomy Education for Middle-School Girls from Underrepresented Groups
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a creative arts-based astronomy outreach program, Rising Stargirls, is associated with changes in girls’ engagement with science and their science identity. The authors focus on a longstanding problem in STEM education: girls from historically underrepresented groups often lose interest in science before college, and middle school is presented as a critical transition point for nurturing persistence and identity.

The intervention is not a controlled experiment but a retrospective analysis of anonymous pre/post workshop surveys from six Rising Stargirls workshops conducted between 2015 and 2023. The program combined astronomy content with arts-based activities such as freewriting, visual art, theater, storytelling, and exoplanet-design tasks, delivered in both in-person and virtual formats. Participants were middle-school girls, many from underrepresented minority groups, in after-school or summer workshop settings across the United States.

The authors report consistent positive pre-to-post shifts in two engagement items and two science-identity items. Across workshops, participants more often talked to family and friends about science, reported greater enjoyment or excitement about science classes, more strongly believed they could do well in science, and more strongly saw themselves as science people. The strongest and most consistent gains were in science engagement and self-identification, with effect sizes often in the moderate-to-large range in the virtual workshops (e.g., dAw up to 1.07). The paper concludes that integrating creative arts into astronomy education can strengthen girls’ engagement and science identity, while noting important limitations including lack of a control group, retrospective survey bias, and short duration.

finding.finding_summary: The workshop included astronomy and astrobiology activities designed to encourage curiosity and scientific thinking, but the paper does not directly report a standardized scientific-reasoning test. Evidence is indirect: participants’ engagement with science increased and authors infer improved scientific thinking from activities like exoplanet design, but no direct outcome metric or effect size for reasoning was reported.
finding.measure: Indirect participation in astronomy/astrobiology learning activities and self-reported science engagement/identity surveys
finding.study_size: n=126 total workshop participants across six workshops; survey Ns varied by item

finding.finding_summary: Participants showed consistent pre-to-post gains in science engagement and science identity. In the combined in-person workshops, talking to family/friends about science increased with a small gain (g=0.2344, dAw=0.4268; NB/NA=26/24), and in virtual workshops the same item showed a moderate gain (g=0.4906, cave=0.4958, dAw=1.0700; NB/NA=66/66). Belief in doing well in science and seeing oneself as a science person also improved, especially in the virtual workshops (e.g., dAw=0.8201 and 0.6235, respectively).
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey items on talking about science, liking science classes, believing one can do well in science, and seeing oneself as a science person
finding.study_size: n=126 total participants across six workshops; analytical Ns varied by item and workshop
finding.effect_size: dAw=1.0700 (largest reported combined virtual effect; other reported effects ranged from dAw=0.4268 to 0.8201 for key outcomes)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests gains in active participation and communication—such as discussing science with family and friends and sharing ideas during workshop activities—which are framed as engagement-related behaviors. However, these are not directly measured as durable skills, so the assignment is based on the communication/collaboration aspect of the survey items and workshop design rather than a dedicated durable-skills instrument.
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of talking to family and friends about science; participation in collaborative arts-based workshop activities
finding.study_size: n=126 total participants across six workshops; combined in-person and virtual Ns reported above
finding.effect_size: dAw=1.0700 for the communication-related item in virtual workshops; dAw=0.4268 in combined in-person workshops

paper_profiles.title: Learning and Motivational Impact of Game-Based Learning: Comparing Face-to-Face and Online Formats on Computer Science Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teacher-authored educational video games are effective for learning and motivation in computer science education, and whether their effectiveness differs when used face-to-face versus online. The authors frame the study around a practical problem in engineering education: high dropout rates, especially in online settings, and the need for motivating learning activities that are easy for teachers to create and deploy.

The intervention is a teacher-authored game-based learning activity built with the SGAME authoring tool and delivered as a Flappy Bird-style educational video game. The game embedded short self-assessment learning objects about basic principles of software design (abstraction, modularity, information hiding, coupling, cohesion). Students completed a pre-test, played the game for about 50 minutes, then took a post-test and a questionnaire. The study used a quasi-experimental comparison between 104 students who completed the activity online during the 2019-20 academic year and 217 students who completed it face-to-face during 2020-21.

Results showed significant learning gains in both groups from pre-test to post-test, with medium-to-large within-group effects (online d=0.79; face-to-face d=0.71), and no significant difference in learning gains between formats (d=0.05). Questionnaire responses were highly positive in both conditions, indicating that the game was engaging, motivating, easy to use, and well integrated. Some perceptions were more favorable in the face-to-face condition, including overall opinion, perceived learning, fun, future use, and preference over traditional materials, but motivation and usability were similar across formats. The authors conclude that teacher-authored educational video games can support knowledge acquisition and motivation in undergraduate computer science, and that they are usable in both face-to-face and online settings, though face-to-face delivery may enhance some experiential aspects such as fun.

finding.finding_summary: Students showed significant gains in knowledge of basic principles of software design after the game-based learning activity in both conditions. In the face-to-face group (n=217), pre-test scores increased from M=6.03 (SD=1.77) to M=7.76 (SD=1.66), with paired-samples t-test p<0.001 and Cohen’s d=0.71. In the online group (n=104), scores increased from M=5.69 (SD=1.57) to M=7.51 (SD=1.68), with p<0.001 and d=0.79; the between-group difference in learning gains was not significant (d=0.05).
finding.measure: Pre-test and post-test scores on 10 multiple-choice questions about basic principles of software design
finding.effect_size: d=0.71 (face-to-face within-group); d=0.79 (online within-group); d=0.05 (between-group learning gains)

finding.finding_summary: Students reported very high motivation and positive experience ratings in both formats, indicating that the game-based activity was engaging and enjoyable. Questionnaire results showed high means for engagement/motivation (item 5: face-to-face M=4.37, SD=0.82; online M=4.23, SD=0.98) and fun (item 6: face-to-face M=4.38, SD=0.85; online M=4.20, SD=0.99), with the fun item showing a small but statistically significant advantage for face-to-face delivery (d=0.20, p=0.05).
finding.measure: Likert-scale questionnaire items on engagement, motivation, fun, overall opinion, future use, and preference over traditional materials
finding.effect_size: d=0.36 (overall opinion), d=0.20 (fun), d=0.25 (self-reported learning effectiveness), d=0.29 (future use), d=0.39 (preference over traditional materials)
finding.std_deviation: SD values reported per item in questionnaire table

finding.finding_summary: The study includes self-reported learning effectiveness and preference-related measures that reflect students’ perceptions of learning agency and metacognitive judgment, but these were not the central outcomes and were not measured as durable skills in a direct way. The paper reports that students believed the game helped them learn (item 2: face-to-face M=4.59, SD=0.66; online M=4.41, SD=0.84; p=0.01; d=0.25) and strongly preferred game-based learning over traditional materials (item 9: face-to-face M=4.30, SD=0.96; online M=3.98, SD=1.01; p<0.01; d=0.39).
finding.measure: Self-reported learning effectiveness and preference items on the questionnaire
finding.effect_size: d=0.25 (helped me learn), d=0.39 (prefer educational games over traditional materials)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that teacher-authored games created with SGAME and ViSH Editor are easy for teachers to build and for students to use, but the empirical evidence is primarily student usability and integration ratings rather than teacher workload metrics. Students rated the game as easy to use (item 3: face-to-face M=4.76, SD=0.55; online M=4.69, SD=0.73) and well integrated with the virtual platform (item 7: face-to-face M=4.66, SD=0.63; online M=4.62, SD=0.77), with no significant differences between formats.
finding.measure: Questionnaire items on ease of use and platform integration

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that teacher-authored educational video games can be deployed in both face-to-face and online university contexts without loss of learning effectiveness, which has implications for course delivery during disruptions such as the COVID-19 pandemic. However, the paper does not measure institutional outcomes directly; its evidence is limited to comparative performance and perceptions across two delivery formats in one course.
finding.measure: Comparison of learning gains and student perceptions across face-to-face and online course delivery formats
finding.effect_size: d=0.05 (between-format learning gains); d=0.36 to 0.39 on some perceptions favoring face-to-face

paper_profiles.title: Educational Perspectives on Quaternions: Insights and Applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a pedagogical and expository treatment of quaternions aimed at helping higher-education students understand their history, algebraic structure, and applications. The authors frame quaternions as an important extension of complex numbers and argue that teaching them through historical context, concrete examples, and connections to rotations can improve comprehension and interest among students in advanced mathematics and related fields.

The paper does not test an instructional intervention with a counterfactual design; instead, it surveys prior educational work and develops explanatory material on quaternion algebra, matrix representations, and rotations in two and three dimensions. It includes detailed worked examples showing how quaternions represent rotations, how they connect to matrix groups such as SO(2), and how they relate to the quaternion group, the Klein group, and physical concepts like spin and Pauli matrices.

The target audience is students in the final semesters of undergraduate programs and graduate programs. The main conclusion is that quaternions are an important and accessible topic when taught with historical grounding and applied geometric examples, and that this approach may support deeper conceptual understanding in higher education. The paper is primarily theoretical and instructional, rather than empirical, and it does not report student outcome data or a formal evaluation of learning effects.

paper_profiles.title: Opportunities for Adaptive Experiments to Enable Continuous Improvement in Computer Science Education
paper_profiles.venue: WCCCE ’24 (Western Canadian Conference on Computing Education)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that adaptive experimentation can help computer science instructors continuously improve online instruction by using real-time data to allocate students toward better learning conditions as evidence accumulates. The authors frame the work as a bridge between research and practice, contrasting traditional randomized A/B tests with adaptive multi-armed bandit experiments that can update assignment probabilities during the course of an intervention.

The paper uses a case study from an undergraduate CS1 course at a public North American research university. In the intervention, students completed online homework problems in which the experimental condition was whether a self-explanation prompt appeared after an initial multiple-choice answer; a second multiple-choice question served as the proximal outcome reward. The adaptive version used Thompson Sampling with a burn-in period of 100 and batch updates of 10 interactions, and it was compared side-by-side with uniform random assignment.

Results showed that the self-explanation prompt improved immediate answer accuracy in both the traditional and adaptive analyses, with the traditional experiment reporting means of 0.608 versus 0.512 and a Wald Z statistic of 2.122. The adaptive policy allocated far more students to the better condition (82.6% to the prompt condition, versus 50% in the traditional assignment), illustrating the main benefit of adaptive experimentation: more students can receive the better-performing condition while data are still being collected. The paper is primarily methodological and forward-looking, emphasizing opportunities, limitations, and the need for further work on long-term outcomes such as retention.

finding.finding_summary: Adding a self-explanation prompt to an online CS1 homework item improved immediate performance on a follow-up multiple-choice question. In the traditional experiment, the prompt condition had higher accuracy than no prompt (M=0.608 vs. 0.512; Wald Z=2.122), and the adaptive experiment estimated a similar advantage (M=0.599 vs. 0.539).
finding.measure: Correctness/accuracy on a follow-up multiple-choice homework question
finding.study_size: n=921 total across both assignment policies (483 traditional, 438 adaptive)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention specifically targeted self-explanation, a metacognitive prompt intended to encourage students to articulate reasoning. The paper reports a positive effect on immediate answer correctness, but it does not provide a direct measure of metacognitive skill; the evidence is indirect through the learning task outcome.
finding.measure: Self-explanation prompt use; immediate response accuracy as a proxy outcome
finding.study_size: n=921 total across both assignment policies

paper_profiles.title: The Rise of Artificial Intelligence in Educational Measurement: Opportunities and Ethical Challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This white paper examines the expanding use of artificial intelligence in educational measurement and the ethical challenges that accompany it. It focuses on how AI is being used for automated item generation, automated scoring, multimodal stimulus generation, and score reporting/feedback, while also discussing broader concerns such as bias, fairness, transparency, privacy, automation bias, and environmental impact.

The paper is not an empirical evaluation of a single intervention; instead, it synthesizes existing research, standards, and illustrative examples to propose ethical and methodological guidance for researchers, developers, and assessment organizations. Examples include automated essay scoring and automated writing evaluation, as well as brief case illustrations using AP Chinese writing and NAEP open-ended response scoring to highlight issues of agreement, subgroup bias, and fairness. The authors conclude that AI can improve efficiency and feedback quality in assessment, but only if it is deployed with strong human oversight, representative data, transparency, and rigorous validity/fairness evidence.

Because the paper is primarily a conceptual and policy-oriented review, it does not study a specific student population in a counterfactual design. Its intended audience is educators, psychometricians, assessment developers, policymakers, and other stakeholders in educational measurement.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools can substantially reduce scoring and feedback workload by enabling automated scoring, rapid item generation, and personalized feedback. It cites prior research showing that automated writing evaluation and automated scoring can speed up feedback delivery and streamline assessment processes, but the paper itself does not report a new effect estimate.
finding.measure: Assessment scoring and feedback efficiency; educator workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is guidance on governance, ethics, and institutional standards for AI in educational measurement. It argues that AI can improve assessment systems, but only if institutions address validity, fairness, transparency, privacy, and accountability; the paper provides no new quantitative institutional outcome estimate.
finding.measure: Ethical governance, validity/fairness standards, institutional policy guidance

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses literacy-related applications primarily through automated writing evaluation and automated scoring of essays and short responses. It cites prior studies reporting writing-quality improvements in tertiary and L2 settings with effect sizes ranging from 0.38 to 0.98, while also noting mixed effects on motivation and concerns about generic feedback and subgroup fairness.
finding.measure: Writing quality, automated essay scoring, automated writing evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that AI-supported writing tools can affect motivation and self-efficacy, but the direction is not uniformly positive. It cites prior work showing some motivational benefits while also describing cases in which high-achieving students became demotivated when automated feedback was less favorable than teacher feedback.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-efficacy, attitudes toward writing feedback

paper_profiles.title: Creativity Training for Future Engineers: Preliminary Results from an Educative Experience
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 7th International Conference on Education and New Learning Technologies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports a preliminary evaluation of a new elective university course designed to develop creativity-related cognitive abilities in future engineers. The authors argue that engineering curricula should better prepare students for innovation by teaching the cognitive processes underlying creativity, not just creativity techniques. They therefore built a 45-hour course, "Creativity in applied sciences and engineering," grounded in a cognitive-science framework and including warm-up exercises, lectures/discussions, a design project, an observation log, forums, and readings.

The study was conducted at École Polytechnique de Montréal across two semesters (Fall 2014 and Winter 2015) with a total of 31 students (9 in Fall, 22 in Winter) from undergraduate and graduate engineering programs. The evaluation used a pre-post design with the CEDA (Creative Engineering Design Assessment) administered at the start and end of the course, plus anonymous qualitative feedback collected through a web forum and survey questions. The authors report significant gains on some CEDA dimensions (fluidity, flexibility, and usefulness), but not a strong increase in originality, and they note possible practice/fixation effects from using the same test twice.

Qualitative responses were broadly positive: students valued the relevance of the course, reported better understanding of the creative process, greater awareness of their own cognition, and increased confidence that they could apply creativity tools in later coursework and professional practice. Overall, the paper concludes that creativity can be improved through a course focused on cognitive processes, while also emphasizing that longer exposure and more validated assessment tools are needed.

finding.finding_summary: The course was associated with improved creative-process performance and students reported greater awareness of their own creative cognition. On the CEDA pre-post assessment (n=31), the authors report significant gains in fluidity, flexibility, and usefulness, but not in originality; qualitative feedback also indicated students learned to "pay attention" to their creative process and better understand how creativity works.
finding.measure: CEDA (Creative Engineering Design Assessment) pre-post scores; anonymous student survey/forum responses about metacognition and creative process understanding

finding.finding_summary: Students reported positive attitudes toward the course and increased confidence in their ability to participate in creative work. In the anonymous survey, students said they felt more confident about being open-minded to creativity and more willing to participate in creative sessions, suggesting improved motivation and self-efficacy around creative tasks.
finding.measure: Anonymous end-of-course survey/forum responses on perceived relevance, confidence, and willingness to use creativity approaches

finding.finding_summary: The course was designed to improve creativity in an engineering education context, and the authors conclude that such training can increase students' creative performance. Quantitatively, they report significant pre-post improvements on three of four scored CEDA criteria (fluidity, flexibility, usefulness) among engineering students, though originality did not improve substantially.
finding.measure: CEDA creative engineering design performance

paper_profiles.title: The Study of Peer Assessment Impact on Group Learning Activities
paper_profiles.venue: FECS'21 (The 17th International Conference on Frontiers in Education: Computer Science and Computer Engineering)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how peer assessment affects group learning activities in higher education, with a focus on student perceptions of fairness, conflict, contribution, and the role of feedback. The authors frame peer assessment as a formative process that can improve learning in group work, but note common concerns such as freeloading, biased marking, and discomfort giving negative feedback.

The study uses multiple exploratory methods: a preliminary survey of 582 students across several computer science modules (276 responses), focus group interviews with 12 participants (10 undergraduates and 2 PhD students), and a case study of an HCI coursework group project using Facebook for collaboration and evidence of contribution. The case study collected 27 questionnaires; the paper reports descriptive percentages rather than inferential tests or counterfactual comparisons.

Findings suggest that many students see peer assessment as fairer when online tools like Facebook make contributions visible, and most participants report enjoying group work in the case study. At the same time, the survey and discussions show persistent problems: 37% preferred individual work, students cited conflict and unequal contribution as major issues, and participants wanted clearer rules, transparency, and more structured procedures to reduce bias and freeloading. The paper concludes that peer assessment can support formative assessment and group learning when it is made transparent, constructive, and well managed, but it does not present strong causal evidence of delayed outcomes such as retention or course completion.

finding.finding_summary: Across the survey, focus groups, and case study, peer assessment was associated with both positive and negative student experiences. In the case study, 82.1% of 28 students said they enjoyed working in a group with Facebook as a communication tool, but survey data also showed that 37% would choose individual work over group work and many students reported discomfort with negative feedback and fairness concerns.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of enjoyment, fairness, comfort with feedback, and willingness to work in groups (survey, focus group, exit questionnaire)
finding.study_size: n=582 surveyed (276 responses); n=12 focus group participants; n=28 case study respondents

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily examines collaboration and peer-feedback processes in group work, which are central durable skills. Descriptively, 89.3% of the 28 case-study students said they could demonstrate their skills through group work, while survey responses identified unequal contribution, conflict, and disruptive behavior as major barriers to effective collaboration.
finding.measure: Self-reported collaboration, contribution, and peer-feedback experiences in group work
finding.study_size: n=582 surveyed (276 responses); n=28 case study respondents

gaps: Only one clearly relevant source snippet is present, and it is from a single computer science education article; this does not yet cover K-12 and postsecondary uses of formative assessment broadly.

The sweep has not yet surfaced foundational definitions or reviews that distinguish formative assessment from summative, feedback, and diagnostic assessment in a general educational measurement sense.
No evidence yet on the core components of formative assessment (e.g., eliciting evidence of learning, interpreting evidence, feedback/action, student self-regulation).
No studies or reviews yet summarizing the learning outcomes typically used to evaluate effects (e.g., achievement, retention, self-efficacy, engagement, metacognition, self-regulation).

No coverage yet of major educational contexts and populations beyond a narrow postsecondary/non-CS-major context; missing K-12 classrooms, higher education across disciplines, teacher education, and potentially online/blended settings.

The sweep has only one clearly relevant definition/source snippet and it is limited to a programming-course context; it does not yet cover a general K-12/postsecondary definition of formative assessment across education.

Core distinctions are incomplete: summative assessment is partially covered, but feedback versus formative assessment and diagnostic assessment versus formative assessment are not yet directly sourced.

There is no evidence yet of sources synthesizing the core components of formative assessment (e.g., eliciting evidence, interpreting evidence, feedback, adjustment of teaching/learning, student self-regulation).

The learning outcomes used in formative-assessment effect studies are not yet identified (e.g., achievement, conceptual understanding, retention, motivation, self-regulation, engagement), nor are representative study designs or reviews/meta-analyses on effects.

Educational contexts and populations are undercovered: there is little to no evidence from K-12 classrooms, higher education beyond a single introductory programming course, or from specific populations such as STEM, teacher education, low-achieving students, or diverse age groups.
The sweep found a few potentially relevant formative-assessment intervention papers, but it does not yet establish the standard counterfactuals/comparator practices in the literature.

Comparator types are not characterized: no clear evidence yet on whether studies typically compare formative assessment to business-as-usual instruction, alternative feedback-only interventions, test-only conditions, mastery learning, dynamic assessment, or other assessment-based approaches.
The sweep is missing synthesis/review and methodology papers that explicitly discuss what the expected counterfactual is in formative assessment studies.
